author: claude-sonnet-5
title: A Cross-Crop Data Synthesis of Circadian-Gated Vesicle Trafficking Nodes That Constrain Cytokinesis Under Heat Stress
abstract: Plant cytokinesis depends on the coordinated delivery of Golgi- and trans-Golgi network (TGN)-derived vesicles to the phragmoplast midzone, where they fuse to build the new cell plate. Heat stress destabilizes this process, but it remains unclear whether thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis is a fixed molecular property or is instead modulated by the time of day at which heat occurs—an interaction long documented for other stress-responsive pathways but never examined at the level of membrane trafficking machinery that builds the mesoscale structures underlying cell division. This project will synthesize publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic datasets across a phylogenetically diverse panel of species (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, and perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach for which chromosome-scale genomes already exist) to test whether circadian gating of heat-responsive gene expression converges on a conserved, tractable set of endomembrane trafficking regulators required for cell plate biogenesis. We will assemble a curated compendium of RNA-seq experiments that vary time-of-day and temperature treatment, reprocess them through standardized, reproducible pipelines (e.g., GEMmaker/Nextflow) to generate harmonized gene expression matrices, and construct context-specific gene co-expression networks that explicitly model and remove confounding technical and biological variables. Network modules enriched for known cytokinesis- and TGN/UPS-associated genes (e.g., phragmoplast-associated kinesins, cell plate SNAREs, exocyst components, autophagy machinery implicated in membrane remodeling) will be cross-referenced against circadian clock output genes and heat-shock regulons to identify candidate 'bottleneck' nodes whose expression is simultaneously time-of-day gated and heat-responsive. Comparative analysis across annual (short-cycle, heat-exposed field crops) and perennial (long-lived, chronically stressed orchard) species will test whether these regulatory nodes are evolutionarily conserved or lineage-specific, leveraging existing genome assemblies and orthology maps already generated by consortium members. Publicly deposited live-cell imaging datasets and organelle proteomics repositories will be mined to validate whether predicted trafficking bottleneck genes correspond to known markers of phragmoplast/cell plate maturation, connecting network-level predictions back to organelle-scale phenotypes. This synthesis requires the combined expertise of the team: mechanistic knowledge of phragmoplast dynamics and cell plate trafficking, circadian and thermal stress physiology, endomembrane/UPS biology, and large-scale computational network construction—expertise that individually exists in separate labs but has never been integrated across this many species and data modalities. The project directly targets a mesoscale emergent property (how sub-organellar trafficking coordination scales up to determine whether a cell successfully divides under stress) and cannot be addressed by any single dataset or lab alone. All harmonized expression matrices, network models, and analysis workflows will be released as an open, versioned resource, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible multi-species network biology, cross-institution data integration, and comparative genomics, building a template for future mesoscale synthesis efforts linking gene regulatory dynamics to subcellular structural outcomes.
background_and_significance: Cytokinesis in land plants is executed not by an actomyosin contractile ring but by the phragmoplast, a bipolar microtubule-based scaffold that guides Golgi- and TGN-derived vesicles to a defined equatorial plane, where they fuse to construct a new cell wall in the form of a cell plate. This process is exquisitely sensitive to membrane trafficking fidelity: kinesin motors direct vesicle transport along phragmoplast microtubules, SNARE complexes and exocyst subunits mediate vesicle tethering and fusion, and unconventional/autophagy-related trafficking routes contribute additional membrane material during cell plate maturation and expansion. Disruption at any of these mesoscale nodes—structures intermediate in scale between single biomolecules and whole organelles—can stall or misdirect cytokinesis, with cascading consequences for tissue patterning, organ growth, and, ultimately, agricultural yield. Heat stress is a well-established disruptor of this system, destabilizing microtubule arrays, delaying phragmoplast expansion, and impairing cell plate formation, but nearly all such studies have treated thermal sensitivity as a static, temperature-dependent property. A large and independent body of work on circadian regulation demonstrates that many abiotic stress responses—including transcriptional heat-shock responses—are gated by the time of day, such that identical thermal insults produce markedly different molecular outcomes depending on when they occur relative to the internal clock. This gating phenomenon has never been examined for the endomembrane trafficking machinery that physically builds the cell plate, leaving a fundamental gap: does the circadian clock modulate whether cytokinesis succeeds or fails under heat stress by gating the expression of trafficking regulators themselves? Addressing this question requires reconciling three literatures that have developed largely in isolation—phragmoplast/cell plate cell biology, circadian and thermal stress physiology, and endomembrane trafficking—and doing so across multiple species to distinguish conserved regulatory logic from lineage-specific adaptation. No single dataset captures all the necessary dimensions (time-of-day, temperature, species, and trafficking gene annotation), and no single laboratory possesses the full complement of expertise or infrastructure to integrate them. However, the public data landscape has matured to the point where this integration is feasible: large RNA-seq compendia with time-course and stress designs exist for Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, and wheat; chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies now exist for perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach; and organelle proteomics and live-cell imaging repositories provide independent, orthogonal evidence for trafficking protein localization and dynamics. Synthesizing these resources offers a tractable route to identifying conserved 'bottleneck' genes governing the intersection of circadian timing, thermal stress, and cell-plate trafficking—an emergent mesoscale property with direct relevance to crop resilience under a warming climate, and a question that is significant precisely because it sits at the unexplored interface of three mature but historically disconnected fields.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project addresses three interlocking questions. First, is the transcriptional sensitivity of cytokinesis-associated trafficking genes to heat stress gated by time of day, analogous to previously documented circadian gating of other stress regulons? We hypothesize that a discrete subset of trafficking genes—particularly those encoding phragmoplast-associated kinesins, cell-plate SNAREs, exocyst components, and autophagy-linked membrane remodeling factors—will show heat-responsiveness that is strongly time-of-day dependent rather than uniform across the diel cycle, mirroring gating patterns previously reported for canonical heat-shock regulons. Second, do these gated trafficking nodes form a conserved regulatory module across phylogenetically distant crop species, or are they lineage-specific outcomes of independent adaptation to distinct thermal regimes? We hypothesize that a core set of trafficking bottleneck genes will be conserved across both annual, short-cycle field crops (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat) and perennial, chronically stressed orchard species (apple, pear, peach), reflecting deep conservation of cell-plate biogenesis machinery, while a secondary, lineage-specific layer of gating will reflect differences in life history, exposure duration, and thermal ecology between annual and perennial growth habits. Third, do network-predicted bottleneck genes correspond to independently observed organelle-scale phenotypes—specifically, delayed or aberrant phragmoplast/cell plate maturation—captured in existing live-cell imaging and organelle proteomics datasets? We hypothesize that genes occupying central, highly connected positions in context-specific co-expression modules enriched for trafficking and cytokinesis annotations will disproportionately correspond to proteins already documented, through imaging or proteomic evidence, as spatially or temporally associated with cell plate maturation stages, providing convergent, multi-modal support for their functional importance. Collectively, these hypotheses reframe thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis not as a fixed biochemical property but as an emergent outcome of the interaction between circadian regulatory architecture and trafficking network topology—a property that can only be detected by integrating time-resolved transcriptomic data, cross-species genomic annotation, and orthogonal organelle-scale evidence at a scale no single laboratory's dataset can support. A critical secondary question concerns methodology: can existing network inference approaches, when adapted to explicitly model diel and thermal covariates, reliably distinguish genuine circadian-heat interaction signals from confounding batch, developmental, or tissue-specific variation across heterogeneous public datasets originating from dozens of independent laboratories? We hypothesize that context-specific network construction, incorporating explicit covariate modeling, will substantially reduce spurious co-expression relationships relative to naive aggregation, yielding higher-confidence candidate gene lists suitable for downstream cross-species and cross-modality validation. Together these questions and hypotheses define a tractable, falsifiable synthesis project whose resolution requires exactly the kind of multi-species, multi-omic, cross-disciplinary integration that individual investigators, working within a single species or data type, cannot achieve.
methods_and_approach: The project proceeds in four integrated phases. Phase 1 (Data Curation): We will systematically identify and catalog publicly available RNA-seq datasets from NCBI SRA/GEO and species-specific repositories that include explicit time-of-day and/or temperature-treatment metadata for Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, apple, pear, and peach, prioritizing studies with paired control and heat-stress conditions sampled across multiple circadian time points. Metadata harmonization will standardize treatment, genotype, tissue, and sampling-time annotations into a unified schema. Phase 2 (Reprocessing and Harmonization): All selected raw sequence data will be reprocessed through a standardized, containerized GEMmaker/Nextflow pipeline to generate reproducible, comparably normalized gene expression matrices for each species, eliminating batch effects introduced by heterogeneous original processing pipelines. Existing chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies and annotation sets for the perennial crops will anchor expression quantification, while established orthology resources will be used to map trafficking, cytokinesis, and circadian clock gene orthologs across all seven species. Phase 3 (Network Construction and Bottleneck Identification): Using the Knowledge Independent Network Construction framework, we will build context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs) for each species that explicitly incorporate time-of-day and temperature as covariates, statistically testing and removing edges attributable to confounding technical or developmental variables. Within each network, modules will be tested for enrichment of curated gene sets representing phragmoplast microtubule motors, cell-plate SNAREs, exocyst subunits, autophagy-related membrane remodeling factors, circadian clock output genes, and canonical heat-shock regulon members. Candidate bottleneck nodes—genes exhibiting both strong circadian-gated expression and heat-responsiveness within trafficking-enriched modules—will be ranked by network centrality and cross-species conservation of orthologous module membership. Phase 4 (Cross-Modal Validation): Candidate genes will be cross-referenced against publicly deposited organelle proteomics datasets and live-cell imaging repositories documenting phragmoplast and cell-plate marker localization, testing whether network-predicted bottlenecks correspond to proteins with documented spatial or temporal association with cell-plate maturation. Comparative statistical analyses (e.g., module preservation statistics, orthogroup enrichment tests) will formally assess conservation versus divergence between annual and perennial lineages. Throughout, all code, containers, and intermediate data products will be version-controlled and benchmarked against held-out datasets to assess pipeline robustness. This approach requires no new experimental data generation; it depends entirely on the reprocessing, harmonization, and multi-modal integration of existing public resources, executed through workflows whose scale and cross-species scope exceed the capacity of any single contributing laboratory.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis will deliver a ranked, cross-species catalog of candidate trafficking bottleneck genes linking circadian timing to heat-sensitive cytokinesis, accompanied by harmonized expression matrices and context-specific co-expression networks spanning seven crop species. Scientifically, the project will establish whether circadian gating of thermal stress responses extends to the mesoscale trafficking machinery governing cell division, resolving a previously unexamined intersection between two mature but disconnected research areas and reframing cytokinetic thermal sensitivity as an emergent, time-dependent property rather than a fixed biochemical threshold. Agriculturally, identification of conserved versus lineage-specific bottleneck nodes will inform breeding and management strategies aimed at mitigating heat-induced yield loss in both annual field crops and long-lived perennial orchard systems, an increasingly urgent concern under climate change. Methodologically, the project will produce a validated, reusable framework for detecting circadian-environment interaction signals in heterogeneous public transcriptomic data, generalizable to other stress-response systems beyond cytokinesis. The resulting network models and validated gene lists will directly inform testable hypotheses for future hypothesis-driven experiments, effectively de-risking future mechanistic work by prioritizing candidates with convergent transcriptomic, orthological, and organelle-imaging support. Broader impacts include establishing a template for integrating gene regulatory network synthesis with organelle-scale phenotypic data, applicable across NCEMS's mesoscale research priorities. The project will also generate durable community resources—harmonized expression compendia and annotated network models—that lower the barrier for future researchers studying circadian-stress interactions in crop species lacking dedicated experimental infrastructure, thereby expanding participation from researchers at institutions without access to large-scale sequencing or growth chamber facilities.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS policy. Raw data sources will be exclusively drawn from public repositories (SRA, GEO, and species-specific genome databases), with full provenance tracking from original accession to final processed output. All reprocessing will be executed through containerized, version-controlled Nextflow workflows (building on established GEMmaker infrastructure), ensuring that any researcher can reproduce harmonized expression matrices from raw reads using identical software environments. Network construction code, covariate models, and statistical testing scripts will be deposited in public version-controlled repositories (e.g., GitHub, archived via Zenodo for permanent citation) with comprehensive documentation and example datasets. Harmonized expression matrices, context-specific co-expression networks, and ranked candidate gene lists will be released as versioned, citable data products through appropriate community repositories, accompanied by metadata conforming to FAIR data standards. Analysis notebooks documenting the full workflow from data curation through cross-modal validation will be made publicly available to enable independent verification and reuse. The project will maintain a public project website and preregistration of core analytical hypotheses prior to full-scale network analysis, distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory findings. Regular team meetings will document decision points and analytical choices in shared, publicly accessible logs. All resulting manuscripts will be deposited as preprints prior to journal submission, and final publications will pursue open-access routes wherever possible. This comprehensive commitment to transparent, reproducible workflows ensures that the synthesized resources remain usable and extensible by the broader community long after project completion, fulfilling the collaborative, team-science mandate central to NCEMS-supported research.
budget_and_resources: This project requires resources appropriate to a data synthesis effort rather than new experimental data generation. Primary budget needs include: (1) Personnel—support for a postdoctoral researcher with computational genomics expertise to lead pipeline development and network construction, and graduate student trainees at partner institutions contributing to species-specific data curation, orthology mapping, and cross-modal validation, distributed across the collaborating labs to ensure integrated training; (2) Computational infrastructure—cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient to reprocess large-scale RNA-seq compendia across seven species through containerized Nextflow workflows, plus storage for harmonized expression matrices and network models; (3) Software and workflow development—support for extending existing Knowledge Independent Network Construction and GEMmaker infrastructure to accommodate explicit circadian and thermal covariate modeling across multiple species; (4) Travel and coordination—funding for in-person working group meetings to integrate cross-disciplinary expertise in phragmoplast biology, circadian physiology, endomembrane trafficking, and network science, alongside virtual coordination tools for ongoing collaboration among geographically distributed team members; (5) Publication and data deposition costs—open-access publication fees and repository deposition costs to ensure all data products remain freely available. This project explicitly requires NCEMS support because it demands sustained computational infrastructure, cross-institutional personnel coordination, and integration of expertise distributed across five independent laboratories—resources and coordination mechanisms that exceed what any single grant-funded lab could assemble. NCEMS's existing data science and computational support infrastructure will be leveraged for pipeline scaling and network analysis, while the collaborating institutions will contribute existing genome assemblies, annotation pipelines, and domain expertise already developed through prior independently funded work, ensuring efficient use of requested resources and avoiding duplication of existing capabilities.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Nucleosome Mechanics to Cell-Type Identity: A Multiscale Synthesis of Chromatin Polymer Physics, Condensate Biochemistry, and Single-Cell 3D Genomes to Explain Disease-Relevant Genome Folding in the Human Brain
abstract: A central unsolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how nanometer-scale nucleosome-nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensate formation give rise to megabase-scale chromatin compartments and loop domains that differ systematically across human cell types—and how these emergent architectures channel genetic risk into cell-type-specific disease phenotypes. This gap sits squarely at the mesoscale NCEMS prioritizes: it cannot be resolved by structural biology, polymer physics, or population genetics alone, but requires their synthesis. This Working Group proposes to integrate four classes of existing public data that have never been jointly modeled: (1) single-cell diploid 3D genome structures (Dip-C/scHi-C) spanning dozens of human and mouse brain cell types; (2) nucleosome- and chromatin-fiber-resolution structural and simulation data (cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, mesoscale oligonucleosome models, cohesin-loop Hi-C perturbation datasets); (3) biochemical and structural characterizations of chromatin-associated condensate components (corepressor oligomers, histone-modifying enzyme complexes, RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation); and (4) population-scale functional genomics linking genetic variation to cell-type-specific gene expression and disease risk (brain-wide eQTL atlases, GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease). Our central hypothesis is that cell-type-specific genome folding emerges from a hierarchy of physical rules—entropic and electrostatic steric pressures generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators at the nucleosome scale, cooperative condensate formation by transcriptional corepressor/coactivator complexes at the sub-domain scale, and loop-extrusion/compartmentalization dynamics at the topologically associating domain scale—and that this hierarchy is a mechanistic intermediate between GWAS variants and their cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. We will build coarse-grained, mechanistically grounded polymer models of chromatin fibers parameterized from structural and biophysical data, validate emergent compartment and loop predictions against single-cell Dip-C structures across neuronal and glial subtypes, and test whether condensate-forming regulatory complexes (e.g., corepressor tetramers, methyltransferase-associated assemblies, RNA-binding phase-separating proteins) quantitatively explain observed heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences between cell types. We will then map disease-associated eQTL and GWAS loci onto these physically resolved chromatin states to ask whether variants disrupting predicted condensate-nucleation or loop-anchor regions preferentially explain the cell-type specificity of psychiatric versus neuroimmune disease associations already reported in public datasets. This effort requires collaboration across structural biophysics, polymer theory, single-cell genomics, and population-scale systems immunology/genetics—expertise that no single lab possesses, but that our team collectively spans. Deliverables include an open, versioned multiscale chromatin simulation framework linked to public single-cell 3D genome and eQTL/GWAS resources, reproducible pipelines for condensate-informed loop-domain prediction, and training modules pairing biophysical modeling with population genomics for graduate students and postdocs across participating institutions. By unifying nucleosome-scale biophysics with population-scale genetics through existing data alone, this project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: resolving how physical emergence at the mesoscale of chromatin organization constrains and explains cellular identity and disease susceptibility in the human brain.
background_and_significance: The three-dimensional folding of the human genome is a canonical example of biological emergence: compartments, topologically associating domains, and loop anchors arise from local physical and biochemical rules operating far below the megabase scale at which these structures are conventionally observed. Decades of structural biology have characterized how nucleosomes, linker histones, pioneer transcription factors, and chromatin-modifying enzyme complexes interact at atomic-to-nanometer resolution. In parallel, polymer physics has produced mesoscale models describing how oligonucleosome fibers fold under the influence of steric, electrostatic, and entropic forces, including those generated by intrinsically disordered regions of chromatin-associated proteins. Independently, single-cell 3D genome methods have revealed that compartment and loop architecture differs systematically across human and mouse brain cell types, and population-scale functional genomics has mapped disease-associated genetic variants onto cell-type-specific expression programs implicated in schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease. Despite the maturity of each of these literatures, they remain almost entirely disconnected: nucleosome-scale structural and biophysical data have not been used to mechanistically explain cell-type-specific compartment structures observed in single-cell Hi-C-type data, and neither has been connected to the eQTL and GWAS variants whose cell-type-restricted effects they may explain. This disconnect is not a matter of insufficient data; it is a synthesis problem. The relevant datasets already exist in public repositories, but integrating them requires reconciling incompatible resolutions, formats, and theoretical frameworks spanning structural biology, statistical polymer physics, single-cell genomics, and population genetics—a task beyond the scope, tools, or expertise of any single laboratory. This gap is precisely the kind of mesoscale emergence phenomenon that motivates NCEMS: understanding how molecular-scale interactions among nucleosomes and their regulatory partners give rise to nuclear-scale architecture, and how that architecture in turn shapes cell-type-specific phenotypic and disease outcomes. Resolving it has substantial biomedical significance. Psychiatric and neuroimmune diseases show strikingly cell-type-restricted genetic associations—for example, neuronal enrichment for schizophrenia risk contrasted with immune cell enrichment for multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease—yet the mechanistic basis for why the same variant class produces cell-type-restricted effects remains largely unexplained. A physically grounded model connecting nucleosome-scale interactions, condensate formation, and genome folding to these expression and disease patterns would provide a mechanistic bridge currently missing from the field, transforming correlative eQTL/GWAS cell-type enrichment findings into testable structural hypotheses. This proposal directly targets that bridge using only existing, publicly available data, fulfilling the community-scale synthesis mission of integrating disparate large-scale resources that have never been jointly modeled to answer a fundamental question about how molecular-scale physical rules generate cellular-scale identity and disease vulnerability.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This Working Group is organized around three linked research questions that move systematically from nucleosome-scale biophysics to population-scale disease genetics. Research Question 1: Can nucleosome- and fiber-scale structural and biophysical parameters, drawn from cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, linker histone perturbation datasets, and biophysical measurements of steric pressure generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators, be used to parameterize coarse-grained polymer models that quantitatively reproduce compartment and loop-domain features observed in single-cell diploid genome structures? We hypothesize that a substantial fraction of the compartment-level heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences observed across brain cell types can be explained by measurable differences in nucleosome-fiber mechanical properties and linker histone occupancy inferred from existing structural and epigenomic datasets, without invoking cell-type-specific novel physical parameters. Research Question 2: Do biomolecular condensates formed by chromatin-associated regulatory complexes—including transcriptional corepressor oligomers, histone methyltransferase-associated assemblies, and RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation—provide a quantitatively necessary intermediate scale between nucleosome-level fiber mechanics and megabase-scale compartmentalization? We hypothesize that condensate-forming regulatory complexes act as nucleation centers whose oligomerization state and local concentration, as characterized in existing structural and biochemical datasets, predict the boundaries and strength of compartment domains observed in single-cell 3D genome data better than fiber mechanics alone, particularly in cell types where these complexes are differentially expressed. Research Question 3: Do disease-associated eQTL and GWAS variants preferentially localize to genomic regions predicted by our integrated model to function as condensate-nucleation sites or loop anchors, and does this localization pattern differ systematically between neuronal cell types implicated in psychiatric disease and immune/glial cell types implicated in neuroimmune and neurodegenerative disease? We hypothesize that psychiatric disease risk variants are disproportionately located within predicted condensate-nucleation regions specific to neuronal chromatin states, whereas multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease risk variants are disproportionately located within loop-anchor or compartment-boundary regions specific to immune and glial chromatin states, reflecting distinct physical mechanisms by which genetic variation is channeled into cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. Collectively, these hypotheses predict a testable, falsifiable causal chain: nucleosome-scale mechanical and condensate properties determine sub-domain architecture; sub-domain architecture determines compartment and loop structure; and that structure determines which disease-associated variants exert cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Because each hypothesis makes quantitative, data-derivable predictions using structures, simulations, and functional genomics datasets that already exist publicly, none require new experimental data collection. The value of this Working Group lies precisely in its capacity to test these cross-scale hypotheses jointly, which is not achievable using any single existing dataset or disciplinary framework in isolation.
methods_and_approach: The project proceeds in three integrated phases, each combining datasets and expertise that no single participating laboratory holds independently. Phase 1 (Nucleosome-to-fiber parameterization): We will compile and harmonize existing cryo-EM structures of nucleosome–pioneer-factor complexes, biophysical measurements of steric pressure generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators, and linker histone perturbation datasets (including chromatin architectural profiling from H1-loss models) to parameterize coarse-grained oligonucleosome polymer models. These models will be implemented within an existing mesoscale chromatin simulation framework, extended to incorporate condensate-forming regulatory complexes as explicit interaction terms rather than as implicit chromatin marks. Phase 2 (Validation against single-cell 3D genomes): Using publicly available Dip-C and related single-cell diploid genome structure datasets spanning multiple human and mouse brain cell types, we will benchmark simulated compartment and loop-domain outputs against empirically observed structures, stratified by neuronal and glial subtype. Validation metrics will include compartment strength, loop-anchor positioning, and radial genome organization, compared using established structural similarity statistics. We will systematically test whether adding condensate-nucleation terms—parameterized from biochemical and structural data on corepressor oligomerization, methyltransferase-associated complex assembly, and RNA-binding protein phase separation—improves model fit relative to fiber-mechanics-only models, using nested model comparison and cross-validation across independent cell-type datasets. Cohesin-loop perturbation Hi-C datasets will serve as an orthogonal validation set, testing whether our model correctly predicts the observed elimination of loop domains with preserved compartment structure under cohesin loss. Phase 3 (Mapping to population genetics): We will overlay our physically resolved chromatin state annotations—condensate-nucleation regions, loop anchors, compartment boundaries—onto existing brain-wide eQTL atlases and GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease. Using stratified functional enrichment methods and colocalization analyses standard in statistical genetics, we will test whether disease- and cell-type-specific variant enrichment patterns align with predicted physical chromatin states, following established frameworks for linking cell-type transcriptomic and epigenomic annotations to genetic risk. All datasets will be accessed through public repositories including but not limited to 4D Nucleome, GEO, the Sequence Read Archive, PDB/EMDB, and publicly deposited GWAS/eQTL summary statistics. The Working Group will meet through structured in-person workshops and virtual sprints, with subteams organized around each phase and cross-cutting integration sessions to reconcile resolution mismatches, coordinate coordinate-system harmonization across datasets from different genome assemblies, and jointly interpret discrepancies between model predictions and empirical structures. Computational pipelines will be developed collaboratively and tested against held-out cell types not used in initial parameterization to assess generalizability.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This Working Group will produce a mechanistic, physically grounded framework connecting nucleosome-scale interactions, condensate formation, and genome-scale architecture to cell-type-specific disease risk—an integrative advance not achievable from any single existing dataset or discipline. Primary outcomes include a validated multiscale chromatin polymer model parameterized entirely from public structural, biophysical, and single-cell genomic data; quantitative evidence for or against condensate-mediated mechanisms of compartment formation across brain cell types; and a map of disease-associated genetic variants stratified by their predicted physical role in chromatin organization. These outcomes will directly address a long-standing puzzle regarding why genetic risk for psychiatric versus neuroimmune diseases localizes to distinct cell types, offering a structural and biophysical explanation to complement existing statistical genetic associations. Scientifically, the project will demonstrate whether mesoscale physical emergence—rather than cell-type-specific novel biochemistry alone—can account for major features of genome architecture, informing broader questions about emergent organization in other chromatin contexts and cell types beyond brain tissue. Methodologically, the resulting simulation framework and variant-mapping pipelines will be reusable by the broader community for other tissues and diseases, extending the impact well beyond the initial brain-focused application. The project will also generate training materials that bridge biophysical modeling and population genomics, disciplines rarely taught together, equipping trainees with cross-disciplinary computational skills increasingly needed in data-intensive molecular and cellular bioscience. By demonstrating that a mechanistic, cross-scale question of this complexity can be resolved entirely through synthesis of existing public data, this project will serve as a template for future NCEMS-supported efforts addressing other mesoscale emergence phenomena, reinforcing the broader case for community-scale data synthesis as a distinct and necessary mode of scientific discovery.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All work in this Working Group will rely exclusively on publicly available datasets, and all derived resources will be released under open licenses consistent with NCEMS and community open-science standards. Harmonized and reprocessed versions of single-cell 3D genome structures, structural and biophysical parameter sets, and chromatin-state annotations will be deposited in public repositories with full provenance tracking linking back to original data sources. The multiscale chromatin simulation framework will be developed as versioned, openly licensed software with containerized environments to ensure computational reproducibility across institutions and hardware. All analysis code, including model parameterization scripts, validation pipelines, and variant-mapping workflows, will be maintained in public version-controlled repositories with continuous documentation, example datasets, and tutorials enabling independent replication. Intermediate outputs, including simulated chromatin structures and predicted condensate-nucleation and loop-anchor annotations, will be released as queryable public resources rather than static supplementary files, allowing other researchers to build upon them directly. The Working Group will adopt pre-registration of key validation analyses, including model comparison criteria established prior to full dataset integration, to guard against post hoc interpretation. Regular internal reproducibility checks will require that any result be independently regenerated by a second team member using only the public code and data repository before inclusion in outputs. Findings will be disseminated through preprints posted prior to journal submission, with data and code availability statements meeting or exceeding FAIR principles. Training materials developed for graduate students and postdocs will likewise be made publicly available as open educational resources, including annotated notebooks demonstrating the full analytical pipeline from structural data to disease variant mapping, explicitly designed to lower barriers for future researchers entering this cross-disciplinary synthesis space.
budget_and_resources: This project requires NCEMS support primarily for personnel, computational infrastructure, and coordination costs rather than data generation, consistent with its synthesis-only design. Budget priorities include partial salary support for a postdoctoral researcher and a graduate student trainee to serve as integration leads across the structural, polymer physics, and population genomics subteams, ensuring continuity of technical work between in-person meetings. Computational resources are needed for large-scale coarse-grained polymer simulations parameterized across dozens of cell types and for genome-wide colocalization analyses linking chromatin-state predictions to eQTL and GWAS summary statistics; cloud or high-performance computing allocation is requested accordingly. Funds are requested for two in-person Working Group workshops per year, bringing together investigators with structural biophysics, chromatin polymer modeling, single-cell genomics, and population genetics expertise, plus supplementary virtual working sessions to maintain momentum between meetings. Modest travel support will enable trainee participation in workshops, ensuring direct training benefit rather than restricting collaborative sessions to senior investigators. Data management costs cover curation, harmonization, and public deposition of integrated datasets and derived resources, including repository maintenance beyond the funding period. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the community-scale synthesis mandate. The distributed nature of required expertise—spanning structural biology, biophysical modeling, single-cell genomics, and functional/population genetics located across multiple institutions—necessitates NCEMS-level coordination and infrastructure support that exceeds what any individual laboratory's existing grants could provide, particularly for sustaining the cross-disciplinary integration meetings essential to reconciling disparate data types and theoretical frameworks into a single coherent multiscale model.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Functional Redundancy as a Mesoscale Buffer: Synthesizing Ancient and Modern Metagenomes with Host Proteo-Genomic Atlases to Test the Stability of Microbiome-Host Molecular Modules
abstract:
A central puzzle in microbial ecology is why host phenotypes associated with the microbiome often remain stable despite enormous taxonomic turnover in microbial communities across individuals, populations, and evolutionary time. One resolution is that functional modules—conserved sets of microbial genes encoding metabolic pathways such as short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—represent an emergent, mesoscale level of biological organization that buffers taxonomic variability and directly couples to host molecular physiology. This project will synthesize publicly available shotgun metagenomic data spanning contemporary human cohorts (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and ancient microbiomes (dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived shotgun datasets from Paleolithic through historical periods) with large-scale human proteogenomic and metabolomic resources (UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, plasma cis-pQTL maps, NMR metabolomic panels) to test whether specific microbial functional modules show consistent, genetically anchored associations with host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of which taxa or strains carry them, and whether this coupling is stable across evolutionary timescales.

We will reprocess all metagenomes using a standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based taxonomic and functional binning pipeline to build a harmonized cross-cohort, cross-era atlas of functional module abundance, explicitly accounting for degradation and contamination artifacts characteristic of low-biomass ancient samples using established authentication and decontamination frameworks. Strain- and gene-family-level phylogenetic network methods (NeighborNet and related split-decomposition approaches) will be used to quantify the degree of taxonomic substitutability underlying each functional module, generating a quantitative 'redundancy index' per pathway. In parallel, we will mine existing microbiome-host GWAS summary statistics and cis-pQTL/metabolite-QTL resources to identify host genetic variants associated with both circulating protein/metabolite levels and microbiome functional module abundance, applying Mendelian randomization and genetic colocalization to test causal or bidirectional relationships between microbial functional capacity and host proteomic/metabolomic states. Modules showing robust host-molecular coupling in modern cohorts will then be evaluated in ancient samples paired with available ancient human genomic data, providing a natural, deep-time test of whether these host-microbiome molecular relationships are evolutionarily conserved or population/era-specific artifacts of recent lifestyle change.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise unavailable within any single laboratory: metagenomic algorithm development and phylogenetic network theory, ancient DNA authentication and low-biomass contamination control, and human proteogenomic/statistical genetics analysis at biobank scale. The resulting open-access resource—a versioned, reproducible workflow and 'Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas' spanning contemporary and ancient timescales—will provide the field with a principled, falsifiable framework for identifying which microbiome-associated molecular phenotypes represent robust emergent mesoscale properties versus incidental, taxon-specific correlations, directly informing biomarker and therapeutic target prioritization in microbiome-related disease research. All code, intermediate outputs, and harmonized datasets will be deposited under FAIR principles, with structured training modules for graduate students and postdocs spanning computational metagenomics, paleogenomics, and human genetics.
background_and_significance:
Microbiome science has repeatedly documented a striking paradox: while the taxonomic composition of gut, oral, and skin microbial communities varies enormously between individuals, across populations, and over evolutionary time, many host phenotypes linked to the microbiome—metabolic homeostasis, immune tone, circulating metabolite profiles—remain comparatively stable. This has motivated the hypothesis that functional capacity, rather than taxonomic identity, is the biologically meaningful unit of microbiome-host interaction. Pathways such as short-chain fatty acid production, secondary bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism are frequently encoded by phylogenetically unrelated organisms, suggesting that functional modules constitute an emergent, mesoscale organizational layer sitting between individual microbial genomes and whole-community, whole-host physiology. If true, this reframes microbiome-host coupling as a property of gene-function ecology rather than species ecology, with direct implications for how researchers interpret microbiome-disease associations and prioritize therapeutic targets.

Despite the conceptual appeal of functional redundancy, it has never been rigorously tested at scale against host molecular phenotypes, nor examined across deep evolutionary time. Three barriers have historically prevented this test. First, contemporary metagenomic cohorts (HMP, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) have been processed with heterogeneous bioinformatic pipelines, precluding harmonized functional comparison across studies. Second, ancient metagenomic datasets from dental calculus and paleofeces—spanning Paleolithic through historical periods—carry well-documented risks of DNA damage, low biomass, and exogenous contamination that require specialized authentication frameworks before functional inference is credible. Third, linking microbial function to host molecular physiology at genetic resolution requires integration with large human proteogenomic resources such as the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project and plasma cis-pQTL/metabolite-QTL maps, a scale of statistical genetics infrastructure rarely available to microbiome research groups.

No single laboratory possesses the full combination of expertise needed to resolve this problem: high-throughput metagenomic alignment and functional binning algorithm development, ancient DNA decontamination and authentication methodology, phylogenetic network theory for quantifying taxonomic substitutability, and biobank-scale human genetic and proteomic analysis. This is precisely the kind of problem for which community-scale data synthesis is uniquely suited. By reprocessing existing public datasets under a single harmonized framework and linking them for the first time to existing human proteogenomic atlases, this project can test whether functional modules are genuinely emergent, evolutionarily conserved buffers of host physiology, or whether apparent redundancy is an artifact of coarse functional annotation. Resolving this question addresses a fundamental problem in mesoscale biology: how molecular-level compositional variability is filtered and stabilized into consistent higher-order phenotypes, directly aligned with NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties bridging molecular and cellular scales of organization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project is organized around four interlocking research questions, each addressed exclusively through synthesis of existing public data.

RQ1: Do microbial functional modules show greater cross-individual and cross-cohort stability than the taxa that encode them? We hypothesize that functional module abundance profiles, once harmonized across cohorts, will exhibit substantially lower variance and higher cross-cohort correlation than species- or strain-level abundance profiles for the same biological samples, consistent with functional redundancy acting as a buffering mechanism.

RQ2: Are specific functional modules genetically and causally coupled to host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of the taxa carrying them? We hypothesize that a subset of modules—particularly those governing short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—will show reproducible associations with host cis-pQTL and metabolite-QTL profiles, and that Mendelian randomization and colocalization analyses will support directional or bidirectional causal relationships between microbial functional capacity and host protein/metabolite levels, rather than these associations being explained by confounding taxonomic composition alone.

RQ3: Can taxonomic substitutability underlying each functional module be quantified, and does this 'redundancy index' predict the strength of host-molecular coupling? We hypothesize that modules with higher redundancy indices (i.e., encoded by a broader, more phylogenetically diverse set of taxa, as revealed through gene-family-level split-decomposition network analysis) will show more stable and reproducible host-molecular associations across cohorts, because taxonomic turnover does not erode the functional signal available for host coupling.

RQ4: Are host-microbiome functional-molecular relationships evolutionarily conserved, or are they recent artifacts of industrialized lifestyles? Using ancient dental calculus and paleofeces metagenomes paired with available ancient human genomic data, we hypothesize that functional modules identified as robustly coupled to host physiology in modern cohorts will also be detectable, at comparable relative abundance and with congruent directionality of association where ancient host genetic data permit, in pre-industrial and pre-agricultural populations—supporting deep evolutionary conservation of these molecular relationships rather than recent lifestyle-driven artifacts.

Collectively, these questions test a specific, falsifiable model: that functional modules constitute a genuine emergent mesoscale layer of biological organization, mechanistically decoupled from taxonomic identity, that mediates a substantial fraction of microbiome-host molecular interaction and has been conserved across major transitions in human diet, sanitation, and lifestyle. An alternative, equally informative outcome—that apparent functional stability is largely an artifact of coarse pathway annotation, or that host-molecular coupling is dominated by strain-specific rather than pathway-level effects—would itself represent a significant advance, refining how the field interprets functional metagenomic signatures in disease biomarker studies. Because this hypothesis can only be tested by integrating heterogeneous, large-scale public datasets spanning modern biobanks, historical and prehistoric metagenomes, and existing GWAS/QTL summary statistics, it exemplifies the type of question requiring coordinated, cross-institutional synthesis rather than single-lab experimentation.
methods_and_approach:
The working group will execute a four-stage synthesis pipeline built entirely on existing public data.

Stage 1 – Harmonized reprocessing of metagenomes: All contemporary shotgun metagenomic samples (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and available ancient shotgun datasets (published dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived samples spanning Paleolithic to historical periods) will be reprocessed through a single standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based pipeline for taxonomic and functional binning against curated protein reference databases. Ancient samples will additionally be passed through established aDNA authentication workflows, including damage-pattern verification, fragment length distribution analysis, and application of consensus contamination-screening criteria for low-biomass samples, ensuring that functional signal is not confounded by exogenous or modern DNA contamination.

Stage 2 – Redundancy index construction: For each functional module of interest, gene-family sequences across all taxa carrying the pathway will be extracted and subjected to phylogenetic network analysis using NeighborNet and related split-decomposition methods to quantify the breadth and structure of taxonomic diversity underlying the function. This yields a per-module, per-cohort redundancy index that captures the degree of taxonomic substitutability, allowing formal comparison of functional versus taxonomic stability (RQ1, RQ3).

Stage 3 – Host genetic and molecular integration: Harmonized functional module abundances will be tested for association with existing microbiome-host GWAS summary statistics, plasma cis-pQTL maps, and NMR-based metabolomic QTL resources drawn from large biobank proteogenomic studies. Mendelian randomization and genetic colocalization analyses will be applied to distinguish causal, reverse-causal, and confounded relationships between microbial functional capacity and host circulating protein/metabolite levels (RQ2). Sparse modeling approaches will be used to prioritize modules with the most robust and reproducible signals across independent cohorts.

Stage 4 – Deep-time validation: Functional modules identified as robustly host-coupled in Stage 3 will be evaluated in the harmonized ancient metagenome atlas from Stage 1, cross-referenced where possible with available ancient human genomic data, to test whether module abundance patterns and inferred host associations are detectable and directionally consistent across major dietary and lifestyle transitions (RQ4).

Throughout, quality control will include sensitivity analyses excluding low-coverage or high-contamination-risk ancient samples, cross-validation across independent modern cohorts, and explicit reporting of statistical power limitations for ancient samples given smaller effective sample sizes. Team responsibilities map directly onto complementary expertise: metagenomic algorithm development and functional binning infrastructure; ancient DNA authentication, contamination control, and archaeological sample interpretation; and proteogenomic statistical genetics, GWAS/QTL integration, and causal inference modeling. Regular working group meetings will coordinate pipeline validation, cross-check redundancy index calculations against independent taxonomic profiling, and ensure consistent interpretation of colocalization results across data modalities.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will produce a versioned, reproducible 'Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas' integrating harmonized functional module abundances across contemporary and ancient metagenomic datasets alongside host proteogenomic and metabolomic associations. This resource will provide the first systematic, falsifiable test of functional redundancy as a mesoscale buffering mechanism, distinguishing modules with genuine emergent, genetically anchored host coupling from those whose apparent stability reflects annotation artifacts or taxon-specific effects. A quantitative redundancy index framework, generalizable beyond this project, will offer the broader field a reusable metric for evaluating functional versus taxonomic stability in any metagenomic dataset.

Scientifically, results will clarify which microbiome-associated molecular phenotypes represent robust, evolutionarily conserved emergent properties suitable for biomarker or therapeutic target prioritization, versus those likely to be population- or era-specific. This directly informs translational microbiome research, where taxonomic biomarkers have often shown poor replicability across cohorts. Methodologically, the harmonized pipeline and deep-time validation approach establish a template for integrating ancient and modern 'omics data with host genetics—an underused synthesis strategy with broad applicability beyond the microbiome field.

Broader impacts include establishing open, reusable computational infrastructure for cross-era metagenomic harmonization, advancing NCEMS's mesoscale emergence research agenda by providing a concrete, testable case study of how molecular-level compositional variability filters into stable higher-order phenotypes, and training a cohort of graduate students and postdocs in transdisciplinary skills spanning computational metagenomics, ancient DNA methodology, and statistical genetics—skills increasingly essential for the future data-intensive molecular and cellular sciences workforce.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
All aspects of this synthesis project will adhere to FAIR and open science principles. Source metagenomic and proteogenomic datasets used are already publicly available through established repositories (SRA, ENA, curatedMetagenomicData, UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, GWAS Catalog); no new experimental data will be generated. All reprocessing pipelines, including the standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN functional binning workflow, ancient DNA authentication scripts, redundancy index calculation code, and Mendelian randomization/colocalization analysis scripts, will be deposited in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub/Zenodo) with persistent DOIs, containerized for computational reproducibility, and accompanied by detailed documentation enabling independent replication.

Harmonized intermediate outputs—including functional module abundance matrices, redundancy indices per pathway and cohort, and summary statistics from genetic association analyses—will be released as structured, versioned datasets under open licenses, with clear provenance tracking linking each output back to original public accessions. Analysis workflows will be implemented in reproducible pipeline frameworks (e.g., Snakemake or Nextflow) to ensure computational transparency and portability across computing environments.

The working group will follow community-endorsed standards for reporting low-biomass and ancient DNA analyses, including explicit contamination and authentication metrics, to ensure that ancient metagenomic findings meet current field-wide reproducibility expectations. Pre-registration of primary hypotheses and analysis plans will be posted prior to Stage 3 genetic integration analyses to guard against analytic flexibility. All data products, code, and documentation will be made available prior to or concurrent with publication, and results will be disseminated through open-access publications, preprints, and public presentation of the Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas as a standing community resource, explicitly designed for reuse and extension by independent research groups.
budget_and_resources:
This proposal requests NCEMS support for personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination costs that exceed the capacity of any individual laboratory. Personnel support includes partial salary for two postdoctoral researchers—one focused on metagenomic pipeline harmonization and phylogenetic network analysis, one focused on statistical genetics integration (GWAS/QTL, Mendelian randomization, colocalization)—and one graduate student contributing to ancient DNA authentication and functional annotation quality control, providing direct cross-disciplinary training embedded in the working group's core research activities.

Computational resources are substantial given the scale of reprocessing required: high-performance computing allocation for DIAMOND-based alignment of thousands of contemporary and ancient shotgun metagenomic samples against large protein reference databases, storage for harmonized intermediate outputs and the versioned atlas, and cloud or institutional cluster access for genome-wide Mendelian randomization and colocalization analyses across biobank-scale summary statistics.

Coordination funds will support two in-person working group meetings per year to integrate results across the three core expertise areas, plus regular virtual meetings for pipeline validation and cross-checking of redundancy index and genetic association findings. Modest travel funds will enable postdoc and graduate student participation in relevant scientific conferences to present synthesis outputs and receive community feedback.

No funds are requested for new data generation, laboratory reagents, or sample collection, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this project. Existing institutional computing infrastructure at team member institutions will be leveraged where possible to minimize costs, with NCEMS support specifically targeted at the incremental computational scale, cross-disciplinary personnel time, and coordination overhead required to integrate ancient metagenomics, modern metagenomics, and human proteogenomics into a single reproducible analytical framework—an integration that no participating laboratory could accomplish independently.
