author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Mapping the Coupling Between Regulatory Cell-State Transitions and Mesoscale Condensate Architecture Across the Bacterial Kingdom
abstract:
Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles, yet an increasing number of proteinaceous mesoscale assemblies—BR-bodies, PopZ microdomains, ParB/parS partition complexes, cold-shock and stress granules—are now recognized as functionally important, phase-separated or phase-separation-like structures. What remains unknown is whether the assembly and disassembly of these structures is systematically encoded in the transcriptional and regulatory logic of the cell, such that physiological transitions (growth phase, stress, quorum-sensing state, biofilm commitment) predictably reorganize the mesoscale proteome. This project will synthesize three classes of public data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) large bacterial gene-expression compendia spanning thousands of conditions and dozens of species (e.g., PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, proteomic abundance databases such as PaxDb), (2) sequence-based biophysical predictors of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder (catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop) applied proteome-wide, and (3) curated experimental catalogs of known bacterial condensate components together with comparative genomic and evolution-experiment data (ALEdb, clinical isolate genome collections, long-term evolution lineages) documenting mutations in regulatory circuits such as quorum-sensing systems and efflux pumps.

The working group will first build a cross-species atlas linking condition-specific transcriptional/proteomic states to the predicted phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome, testing whether physiological transitions (e.g., entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress) are consistently accompanied by co-regulated shifts in the abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich proteins relative to their low-propensity partners. This addresses a mesoscale question central to NCEMS's mission: does gene-regulatory network architecture function, in part, as a control layer for mesoscale self-organization, translating discrete transcriptional states into emergent, spatially organized biomolecular assemblies? Second, using biophysical/polymer-based condensate models—of the associative-polymer type used to explain multiphase architecture and viscosity tuning in reconstituted systems—the team will translate measured or inferred stoichiometric shifts in expression atlases into predictions of condensate composition, phase boundaries, and internal architecture, generating testable hypotheses about which regulons are poised to nucleate or dissolve specific mesoscale structures under specific conditions. Third, the team will exploit existing evolution-experiment and clinical-isolate genomic datasets to ask whether naturally occurring or experimentally evolved loss-of-function mutations in regulatory genes (quorum-sensing regulators, efflux pumps, two-component systems) shift the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins, thereby altering emergent mesoscale organization as a byproduct of adaptive evolution—paralleling known cases where regulatory mutations have unexpected downstream physiological consequences.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in bacterial evolutionary genomics and regulatory network biology with quantitative condensate biophysics and polymer theory, a combination not resident in any single laboratory. It leverages exclusively existing public datasets, produces an open, versioned, and queryable atlas linking transcriptomic state to predicted mesoscale organization across bacterial diversity, and provides trainees hands-on experience integrating heterogeneous omics, evolutionary, and biophysical modeling data—directly building the data-science workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously unaddressed question about the origins of mesoscale order in cells lacking organelles.
background_and_significance:
Eukaryotic cells achieve compartmentalization through membrane-bound organelles, but a growing body of work demonstrates that bacteria accomplish analogous functional organization through membraneless, often phase-separated or phase-separation-like mesoscale assemblies. BR-bodies concentrate RNA-degradation machinery, PopZ microdomains scaffold polar signaling complexes, ParB/parS partition complexes organize chromosome segregation, and stress- and cold-shock granules sequester translation machinery under adverse conditions. These structures are increasingly understood through the lens of biomolecular condensate biophysics, in which multivalent, often intrinsically disordered proteins self-assemble via associative interactions that can be tuned by concentration, post-translational modification, and interaction valence. Parallel advances in bacterial systems biology have produced extraordinarily rich, standardized gene-expression compendia (PRECISE for E. coli regulatory states, COLOMBOS and SRA-derived RNA-seq atlases spanning many species, PaxDb proteomic abundance data) that capture how transcriptional and regulatory networks reorganize gene products across thousands of physiological conditions, including growth-phase transitions, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress, and biofilm commitment. Independently, sequence-based biophysical predictors—catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop—now permit proteome-scale estimation of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder without requiring new experimental measurement.

Despite the maturity of each of these resources individually, no existing study has integrated them to ask whether bacterial regulatory logic systematically encodes instructions for mesoscale reorganization. That is, when a cell shifts regulatory state—entering stationary phase, activating quorum sensing, mounting an envelope-stress response—does the expressed proteome shift in a coordinated way toward or away from condensate-forming character, and is this shift conserved across bacterial diversity or lineage-specific? This is a foundational question about emergence at the mesoscale: it asks whether higher-order spatial organization within cells lacking organelles is a predictable, encoded output of lower-level regulatory network architecture, rather than an incidental byproduct of protein biophysics alone.

Answering this question additionally requires evolutionary and comparative genomic context. Extensive experimental evolution datasets (e.g., ALEdb) and clinical/environmental isolate genome collections document recurrent loss-of-function mutations in regulatory circuits, including quorum-sensing regulators and efflux systems, that produce unexpected downstream physiological consequences, including altered virulence and stress phenotypes. Whether such mutations also perturb the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins—and thereby alter mesoscale organization as an unselected consequence of adaptation—has never been examined. Addressing this synthesis-scale question requires simultaneous fluency in regulatory genomics, comparative evolutionary biology, and quantitative polymer/condensate biophysics, a combination that does not exist within any single laboratory and that is precisely the kind of cross-disciplinary, data-intensive integration NCEMS is positioned to enable. The proposed working group will produce the first cross-species, condition-resolved atlas connecting regulatory state to predicted mesoscale organization, establishing a new synthesis framework for understanding organelle-free cellular compartmentalization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project addresses three linked research questions, each testable using exclusively existing public data.

Question 1: Is bacterial regulatory network architecture systematically coupled to shifts in the phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome? We hypothesize that physiological transitions with well-characterized regulatory signatures—entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope and cold-shock stress, biofilm commitment—are accompanied by conserved, co-regulated shifts in the relative abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich condensate-forming proteins versus their low-propensity structural or metabolic partners. We further hypothesize that this coupling is strongest for regulons directly controlling known condensate components (e.g., RNase E/BR-body machinery, ParB, PopZ, cold-shock proteins) but extends more broadly to co-regulated operons whose products have not yet been experimentally implicated in phase separation, generating testable predictions for previously unrecognized condensate constituents.

Question 2: Can polymer-physics models of associative condensate assembly translate observed or inferred stoichiometric shifts in expression atlases into quantitative predictions of condensate phase behavior? Building on associative-polymer frameworks that explain multivalent-network stoichiometry, client recruitment, and multiphase architecture in reconstituted systems, we hypothesize that regulatory-state-dependent changes in the relative abundance of scaffold and client proteins predict shifts in condensate phase boundaries, internal demixing, and material properties (e.g., viscosity, multiphase coexistence) in a manner consistent with known behavior of characterized bacterial condensates and generalizable to under-studied species and structures.

Question 3: Do naturally occurring or experimentally evolved regulatory mutations alter the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins as an emergent consequence of adaptation? Motivated by documented cases in which loss-of-function mutations in regulatory circuits—including quorum-sensing regulators and antibiotic efflux systems—produce unanticipated downstream physiological effects, we hypothesize that such mutations, captured in long-term evolution-experiment lineages and clinical/environmental isolate genome collections, systematically shift the balance of high- versus low-propensity proteins in ways that predict altered mesoscale organization, even when condensate phenotypes were not directly selected upon.

Collectively, these questions probe whether mesoscale self-organization in bacteria is an actively encoded, evolvable output of regulatory network architecture rather than a passive byproduct of protein biophysics. Confirmation of systematic coupling (Question 1) combined with quantitative, physics-based translation into condensate predictions (Question 2) would establish a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale reorganization directly from transcriptomic or proteomic state, applicable across the bacterial kingdom. Evidence for evolutionary modulation of this coupling (Question 3) would reveal mesoscale organization as a previously unrecognized axis along which regulatory mutations exert pleiotropic effects, with implications for understanding stress adaptation, antibiotic resistance evolution, and virulence.
methods_and_approach:
The project is structured as a three-phase synthesis workflow, entirely reliant on public data integration and computational/statistical analysis, requiring no new experimental generation.

Phase 1 – Cross-species expression-to-propensity atlas. We will assemble condition-annotated transcriptomic datasets from PRECISE, COLOMBOS, and curated SRA RNA-seq collections spanning model and non-model bacterial species, harmonizing metadata for physiological state (growth phase, stress type, quorum-sensing activity, biofilm status) using controlled-vocabulary ontologies. Proteomic abundance data from PaxDb will be integrated where available to cross-validate transcript-level inferences against measured protein abundance. Every annotated proteome will be scored genome-wide for phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder using catGRANULE, PScore, and FuzDrop, producing a per-condition, per-species distribution of expressed propensity scores. Statistical models (mixed-effects regression, controlling for species phylogeny and technical batch) will test whether propensity-score distributions shift systematically and reproducibly across defined physiological transitions, both within and across species.

Phase 2 – Biophysical translation via polymer-based condensate modeling. Using associative-polymer modeling frameworks previously applied to explain multivalent network stoichiometry and multiphase architecture in reconstituted systems, we will map condition-specific shifts in scaffold-to-client protein abundance ratios (derived from Phase 1) onto predicted phase diagrams for characterized bacterial condensates (BR-bodies, PopZ, ParB/parS, cold-shock granules). This generates quantitative, falsifiable predictions of condensate assembly propensity, internal demixing, and material properties as functions of regulatory state, benchmarked against existing experimental characterizations of these structures in the literature.

Phase 3 – Evolutionary and comparative genomic integration. Using ALEdb long-term evolution-experiment data and curated clinical/environmental bacterial isolate genome collections, we will identify recurrent mutations in regulatory genes (quorum-sensing regulators, efflux pump components, two-component systems) and determine, via matched or inferred expression data, whether these mutations are associated with predicted shifts in condensate-forming protein balance, using the atlas and models from Phases 1–2 as an interpretive framework.

All data integration, propensity scoring, statistical modeling, and polymer-model simulations will be implemented in reproducible, version-controlled computational pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized environments). Cross-disciplinary working sessions will pair regulatory-genomics expertise with condensate-biophysics expertise at each phase transition to ensure biologically grounded and physically consistent modeling decisions, with trainees embedded across all three phases to gain integrated computational and conceptual training.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The primary deliverable is an open, versioned, queryable cross-species atlas linking bacterial regulatory/physiological states to predicted mesoscale condensate organization, accompanied by reproducible pipelines for propensity scoring, polymer-based phase prediction, and evolutionary mutation-expression integration. Scientifically, the project will establish whether mesoscale self-organization in bacteria is systematically encoded by regulatory network architecture, resolving a fundamental gap in understanding organelle-free cellular compartmentalization and providing a generalizable predictive framework applicable to newly sequenced or poorly characterized species. The atlas will generate a catalog of previously unrecognized candidate condensate-forming proteins and regulons for experimental follow-up by the broader community, effectively seeding future hypothesis-driven studies beyond this working group. The evolutionary component will reveal whether mesoscale organization constitutes an overlooked pleiotropic consequence of regulatory adaptation, with direct relevance to interpreting resistance and virulence evolution in clinically important pathogens. Methodologically, the project establishes a reusable template for integrating transcriptomic/proteomic compendia, sequence-based biophysical predictors, and evolutionary genomic datasets—a synthesis strategy applicable to future mesoscale questions beyond bacterial condensates. Broader impacts include cross-training of trainees in regulatory genomics, evolutionary biology, and quantitative biophysics, cultivating exactly the data-fluent, interdisciplinary scientific workforce NCEMS seeks to develop, and demonstrating a scalable model for team-based synthesis science addressing emergence phenomena at the molecular-to-cellular interface.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All source datasets used in this project—PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, PaxDb, ALEdb, and public clinical/environmental isolate genome repositories—are already publicly available, and no new experimental data will be generated. All harmonized metadata, propensity-scoring outputs, polymer-model parameters and code, and evolutionary-mutation annotation tables will be deposited in a public repository (Zenodo/GitHub with permanent DOI) under an open license, structured for programmatic reuse. Computational workflows will be implemented using workflow-management systems (Snakemake or Nextflow) within containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to ensure exact computational reproducibility across computing environments and by external users. Version control will track all pipeline code, parameter choices, and intermediate data products, with releases tied to each major analytical milestone. Documentation will follow FAIR data principles, including standardized metadata schemas for physiological/condition annotation to maximize interoperability with future datasets. The working group will adhere to community-endorsed open and team science practices, including pre-registration of key hypotheses prior to full-scale statistical testing, transparent reporting of negative or null results (e.g., species or transitions where propensity coupling is not observed), and open working-group meeting notes where appropriate. All analysis code and derived atlas products will be released prior to or concurrent with publication, and the working group will actively solicit community feedback through public preprints and open working-group presentations to ensure the atlas is broadly usable by the bacterial systems biology and condensate biophysics communities.
budget_and_resources: This project requires computational and personnel resources appropriate to a data-synthesis working group rather than experimental infrastructure. Primary budget needs include: (1) salary support for one postdoctoral researcher with computational and comparative genomics skills to lead data harmonization and evolutionary-genomic integration, and one graduate student trainee to support propensity scoring, statistical modeling, and pipeline development; (2) cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation for proteome-wide biophysical propensity scoring and polymer-model simulations across dozens of species and thousands of conditions; (3) travel support for in-person working-group meetings to enable direct collaboration between regulatory-genomics and condensate-biophysics expertise, particularly at phase-transition milestones requiring joint interpretation; (4) modest funds for data storage and repository maintenance (Zenodo/GitHub, containerized environment hosting) to support open-science deliverables. No funds are requested for wet-lab experimentation, reagents, or new data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained, structured collaboration between investigators with non-overlapping expertise (bacterial evolutionary/regulatory genomics and quantitative condensate biophysics) who would not otherwise have a mechanism or shared resource base to undertake joint, large-scale computational synthesis. NCEMS-provided computational infrastructure, working-group coordination support, and trainee-training frameworks directly enable the cross-disciplinary integration and reproducible pipeline development that neither laboratory could achieve independently, while NCEMS's emphasis on open science ensures the resulting atlas and tools are positioned for maximal community reuse.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Nonlinear Collapse of Protein Interaction Networks at Stability Thresholds: A Cross-Kingdom Synthesis of Deep Mutational Scanning and Interactome Data
abstract:
A central puzzle in molecular systems biology is why some mutations that destabilize a protein produce negligible phenotypic consequences while others trigger abrupt, disproportionate loss of cellular function. We propose that this threshold-like behavior is an emergent property of the coupling between a protein's biophysical stability and its position within interaction networks, rather than an intrinsic property of the mutation itself. This working group will synthesize three classes of publicly available data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) proteome-wide thermodynamic stability measurements from deep mutational scanning and mega-scale stability assays (e.g., MaveDB, ProteinGym, Tsuboyama et al. stability atlas, deep receptor scanning datasets for GPCRs), (2) protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction network data from curated interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, the Arabidopsis interactome AtPIN, and plant immune signaling networks), and (3) evolutionary and population-genetic datasets capturing selection on protein variants (gnomAD, ClinVar, dN/dS estimates, experimental evolution fitness landscapes).

Our central hypothesis, motivated by prior observations of threshold-like fitness relationships in antibiotic resistance enzymes and by the differential trafficking behavior of destabilized membrane proteins such as CFTR and GPCRs, is that network connectivity buffers the phenotypic consequences of destabilizing mutations up to a critical free-energy threshold, beyond which interaction networks undergo sharp, nonlinear rewiring or collapse. We predict that highly connected hub proteins exhibit wider stability buffering zones due to redundant or cooperative binding interfaces, while peripheral proteins collapse at smaller perturbations, and that this relationship generalizes across kingdoms despite divergent protein architectures (human membrane-embedded receptors and channels versus plant cytoplasmic immune regulators).

To test this, we will build a unified computational pipeline that maps ΔΔG values from deep mutational scanning onto network centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) and models how progressive destabilization propagates through interactome topology using percolation and network robustness frameworks. We will compare human disease-relevant systems (CFTR, GPCRs, KCNQ1-type ion channels) with plant immune signaling hubs (e.g., NPR1-centered networks) to ask whether energetic-topological coupling constitutes a conserved organizing principle of cellular systems or is contingent on compartment-specific biophysics (membrane insertion energetics versus cytosolic folding). Single-cell transcriptomic data will be incorporated to test whether cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners modulates the effective stability threshold in situ.

This project requires integration of expertise that no single lab possesses: membrane protein folding thermodynamics and pharmacological chaperone biophysics, network-based systems biology and plant immune signaling, and evolutionary protein biophysics and fitness landscape modeling. The resulting open-source framework, datasets, and reproducible workflows will be released publicly, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary skills spanning biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics, directly addressing NCEMS's mission to reveal mesoscale emergent principles connecting molecular energetics to cellular network behavior.
background_and_significance: A long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology concerns the disconnect between a mutation's biophysical effect on protein stability and its ultimate phenotypic consequence. Many destabilizing substitutions are tolerated with little functional cost, while others of similar or even smaller thermodynamic magnitude precipitate catastrophic loss of function. This nonlinearity has been documented repeatedly in disparate contexts: gain- and loss-of-function ion channel variants whose surface expression depends on subtle shifts in folding efficiency, membrane receptors whose biosynthetic fidelity is exquisitely sensitive to sequence context, antibiotic-resistance enzymes exhibiting threshold-like fitness landscapes under selection, and plant immune regulators whose signaling capacity collapses abruptly when destabilized by pathogen effectors. These observations, generated independently across biomedical, plant biology, and evolutionary biophysics communities, point toward a shared but unarticulated principle: that phenotypic robustness to destabilization is not an intrinsic property of a protein's fold alone but emerges from its embedding within larger interaction networks. A protein's tolerance for destabilizing perturbation may depend fundamentally on whether it occupies a highly buffered, redundantly connected hub or a sparsely connected periphery of the interactome. Despite the intuitive appeal of this idea, it has never been rigorously tested at proteome scale because the datasets required to do so have been generated in isolation by different research communities. Deep mutational scanning and mega-scale stability assays now provide ΔΔG measurements for thousands of variants across hundreds of proteins, spanning cytosolic domains, membrane-embedded receptors, and channels. Simultaneously, curated interactome databases document the topology of protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction networks across humans, plants, and other model systems. Population-genetic and evolutionary datasets independently capture the selective consequences of variation at these same positions. No existing study has integrated these three data classes to ask whether network position quantitatively predicts the stability threshold at which phenotypic collapse occurs, nor whether this relationship is conserved across kingdoms with fundamentally different proteomic architectures. This gap represents precisely the kind of emergent, mesoscale question NCEMS is positioned to address: a phenomenon that arises from the coupling of molecular energetics with network-scale organization, requiring synthesis of biophysical, systems-biology, and evolutionary datasets that individually exist in public repositories but have never been jointly mined. Resolving this question would provide a mechanistic, quantitative foundation for predicting when destabilizing mutations become pathogenic or adaptive, with direct implications for interpreting variant effects in human disease (e.g., cystic fibrosis, channelopathies) and for understanding robustness and evolvability in plant immune signaling networks. The proposed synthesis is significant not only because it addresses a fundamental unresolved question but because it establishes a generalizable analytical framework linking thermodynamic and topological data that can be extended to other biological systems and future datasets as they emerge.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group is organized around three interlocking research questions. First, does a protein's position within an interaction network quantitatively determine its tolerance to destabilizing mutation, such that highly connected hub proteins exhibit wider ranges of ΔΔG before functional collapse compared to peripheral proteins? Second, is the transition from buffered to collapsed network states nonlinear and threshold-like, consistent with percolation-type behavior in network science, rather than a gradual, proportional decline in function? Third, is this energetic-topological coupling a conserved organizing principle across kingdoms, or is it contingent on compartment-specific biophysical constraints such as membrane insertion energetics in animal systems versus cytosolic folding and effector-driven destabilization in plant immune networks? Our central hypothesis is that network connectivity acts as a buffering mechanism against destabilizing mutation, with redundant or cooperative binding interfaces at hub proteins absorbing folding defects up to a critical free-energy threshold, beyond which interaction networks undergo abrupt, disproportionate rewiring or collapse. We derive three testable sub-hypotheses. First, we predict a positive correlation between network centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) and the magnitude of ΔΔG tolerated before measurable loss of interaction capacity or trafficking efficiency, drawing on precedent from destabilized ion channels and receptors that nonetheless reach the cell surface at functional levels due to compensatory interactions. Second, we predict that the relationship between stability and network collapse is nonlinear and better described by percolation or robustness models with defined critical thresholds than by linear dose-response models, mirroring threshold-like fitness relationships previously observed in antibiotic-resistance enzymes under selection. Third, we predict that while the qualitative form of this relationship (buffering followed by threshold collapse) will generalize across human and plant systems, the quantitative parameters of the threshold will differ systematically according to compartment-specific biophysics, with membrane-embedded proteins showing distinct threshold behavior from cytosolic immune regulators due to differences in folding energetics, quality-control stringency, and interaction geometry. A fourth, more exploratory question addresses whether cell-type-specific expression patterns of interaction partners, captured in single-cell transcriptomic atlases, modulate the effective stability threshold observed in bulk biochemical or population-genetic data, potentially explaining tissue-specific penetrance of destabilizing variants in human disease. Testing these hypotheses requires simultaneous access to and integration of stability, interactome, evolutionary, and expression datasets at a scale and diversity no single laboratory currently possesses, and requires reconciling heterogeneous data structures, normalization conventions, and network annotation standards across human and plant systems. The working group's combined expertise in membrane protein biophysics, plant systems network biology, and evolutionary protein energetics is specifically suited to resolving these methodological and conceptual challenges collaboratively.
methods_and_approach: The project is structured around three synthesis phases executed collaboratively across the working group's expertise. Phase one focuses on data harmonization. We will assemble ΔΔG stability measurements from deep mutational scanning repositories (MaveDB, ProteinGym, the Tsuboyama et al. mega-scale stability atlas) and receptor-specific biosynthesis datasets, standardizing thermodynamic units and mutation coordinate systems across proteins with divergent domain architectures, including membrane-embedded receptors and channels and cytosolic plant immune regulators. In parallel, we will curate interaction network data from BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, and the Arabidopsis interactome resource, constructing unified graph representations with consistent confidence-weighting schemes and computing centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient, k-core) for all proteins with corresponding stability data. Evolutionary and population-genetic annotations from gnomAD, ClinVar, and dN/dS estimates will be mapped onto the same variant coordinates to provide independent readouts of selective consequence. Phase two involves statistical and computational modeling of the coupling between stability and topology. We will fit variant-level models relating ΔΔG to network centrality and to functional or clinical outcome annotations, testing for threshold effects using changepoint detection and percolation-based network robustness simulations that model progressive node or edge removal as a function of destabilization. These models will be applied comparatively to matched sets of human disease-relevant proteins (CFTR, GPCRs, KCNQ1-family channels) and plant immune signaling hubs (NPR1-centered networks and interacting partners), enabling direct cross-kingdom comparison of threshold parameters and buffering capacity. Percolation simulations will be validated against known functional outcomes, such as surface trafficking efficiency for membrane proteins and immune signaling output for plant regulators, to ensure that predicted collapse points align with independently measured phenotypic transitions. Phase three integrates single-cell transcriptomic data to test whether cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners shifts the effective network topology and therefore the predicted stability threshold, using coexpression and regulatory network inference approaches applied to existing single-cell atlases. Throughout, the team will develop a modular, open-source computational pipeline implemented in Python, leveraging established network analysis and machine learning libraries, designed for extensibility to additional proteins, species, and future datasets. Regular working group meetings will coordinate cross-disciplinary quality control, ensuring that biophysical interpretation of ΔΔG values, network-theoretic modeling choices, and evolutionary genetic annotations are jointly validated rather than siloed within individual disciplinary perspectives. Sensitivity analyses will assess robustness of conclusions to interactome curation biases and dataset incompleteness, an essential consideration given known ascertainment differences between human and plant interactome resources.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis will produce a quantitative, generalizable framework describing how protein network position modulates tolerance to destabilizing mutation, directly addressing a long-standing gap between biophysical and systems-level understanding of genotype-phenotype relationships. Primary deliverables include a validated computational pipeline linking thermodynamic stability data to network robustness models, a cross-kingdom comparative dataset annotating centrality-buffering relationships for hundreds of proteins, and empirically derived threshold parameters distinguishing membrane-embedded from cytosolic systems. These outputs will advance interpretation of variant pathogenicity in human disease contexts such as cystic fibrosis and channelopathies by providing network-informed priors for variant effect prediction, complementing existing clinical variant classification pipelines. In plant biology, the framework will offer new mechanistic insight into robustness and fragility of immune signaling networks under pathogen-driven destabilization, informing future breeding and engineering strategies for disease resistance. More broadly, the project establishes network-position-dependent buffering as a candidate general principle of mesoscale emergence connecting molecular energetics to cellular-scale network behavior, a central conceptual target of NCEMS's mission. The comparative cross-kingdom design will clarify which aspects of this principle are universal versus contingent on compartment-specific biophysics, informing future synthesis efforts extending to additional organisms and protein classes. Methodologically, the project will yield reusable analytical tools applicable beyond the specific systems studied here, lowering the barrier for future researchers to integrate stability and network data. The collaborative structure, spanning membrane protein biophysics, plant systems biology, and evolutionary protein science, will also serve as a template for future interdisciplinary synthesis efforts, while directly training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in transferable skills bridging biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All data used in this project derive from existing public repositories, including MaveDB, ProteinGym, the Tsuboyama et al. stability atlas, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, the Arabidopsis interactome resource, gnomAD, ClinVar, and public single-cell transcriptomic atlases; no new experimental data will be generated. The working group commits to full adherence to FAIR data principles throughout the project. All harmonized datasets, including standardized stability measurements, network centrality annotations, and merged variant-level tables, will be deposited in appropriate public repositories with persistent identifiers and clear provenance documentation linking back to original source datasets. All computational pipelines, including data harmonization scripts, network construction and centrality calculation code, percolation and robustness simulation frameworks, and statistical modeling notebooks, will be developed under version control in a public repository, documented with clear installation and usage instructions, and structured to support reproducibility by external users applying the framework to new proteins or species. We will use containerized computational environments to ensure long-term reproducibility independent of software version drift. Intermediate and final analysis outputs, including derived threshold parameters and comparative cross-kingdom results, will be released alongside publications as structured supplementary datasets rather than static figures alone, enabling reuse and reanalysis by the broader community. The working group will follow community-endorsed open and team science practices, including preregistration of key analytical hypotheses where appropriate, transparent reporting of negative or null results arising from threshold model testing, and regular public sharing of intermediate progress through preprints. All trainees involved will be instructed in reproducible research practices, including literate programming, version control workflows, and open data deposition standards, as a core component of their training experience within the working group.
budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project requires resources primarily supporting personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, consistent with its exclusive reliance on existing public data. Requested funds will support partial salary or effort for one postdoctoral researcher with expertise in network science and computational biology, and partial support for graduate student trainees at each of the three participating institutions, enabling direct hands-on training in cross-disciplinary synthesis methods. Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient for large-scale network robustness simulations and machine learning model training across proteome-wide datasets, alongside data storage for harmonized public datasets and derived analytical products. Modest travel funds are requested to support in-person working group meetings at least twice during the project period, essential for integrating biophysical, network-theoretic, and evolutionary perspectives and for coordinating cross-institutional trainee mentorship. Additional funds will support publication costs, including open-access fees, ensuring findings and datasets are freely available. NCEMS support is essential because this project's scope, spanning proteome-wide stability data, multi-species interactome integration, and evolutionary genetic annotation, exceeds the analytical and personnel capacity of any single participating laboratory, and no existing collaboration among the three research groups currently possesses the shared computational infrastructure or cross-disciplinary training pipeline required. NCEMS's role in convening working group meetings, providing data science training resources, and supporting reproducible workflow infrastructure will substantially accelerate the pace and rigor of this synthesis relative to what could be achieved through informal collaboration alone. The requested budget is deliberately modest and synthesis-focused, reflecting the project's foundation entirely on existing public data and its emphasis on computational integration, model development, and cross-disciplinary training rather than new data generation.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Sequence-to-Structure-to-Condensate: A Multi-Scale Synthesis Framework Linking RNA Secondary Structure Ensembles to Protein-RNA Condensate Composition and Emergent Material Properties
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates that concentrate RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) — stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles — display emergent material properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase architecture) that cannot be predicted from single-molecule biophysics alone. A major unresolved question is how the structural ensemble of RNA itself (not just its sequence composition or RBP motif content) shapes which proteins are recruited into a condensate and what physical state results. Despite an explosion of public data relevant to this question — large-scale RBP-RNA interactome datasets (CLIP-seq, eCLIP across ENCODE), condensate proteomic/transcriptomic atlases, high-throughput condensate-forming sequence screens, and computational RNA secondary/tertiary structure prediction tools — no existing resource integrates RNA structural information with condensate composition and biophysical outcome data at scale. This gap exists precisely because closing it requires expertise spanning RNA structural modeling, condensate biology/proteomics, and large-scale data integration — capabilities distributed across our two labs and beyond, and unattainable within a single lab's toolkit.

We propose a Working Group that assembles a harmonized, multi-database resource linking three previously siloed data types: (1) genome-wide RBP-RNA binding data (eCLIP/PAR-CLIP repositories, RNAct, POSTAR3), (2) predicted and experimentally-derived RNA structural ensembles (using established structure prediction and SHAPE/DMS chemical probing datasets deposited in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO), and (3) condensate composition and material property datasets, including proteomic/RNA-seq atlases of stress granules, nucleoli, and paraspeckles, plus recently published high-throughput pooled condensate-propensity screens covering thousands of protein sequences. By computationally reconstructing structural context around RBP binding sites transcriptome-wide, we will test whether RNAs with particular secondary structure signatures (e.g., extended single-stranded regions, specific stem-loop densities, or multivalent structured motifs) preferentially nucleate condensates, recruit particular RBP repertoires, or correlate with reported condensate viscoelastic properties. We will further apply Rosetta-based structural energy modeling to characterize how RNA structural stability and flexibility relate to the multivalency principles known to govern phase separation, generating a predictive framework that goes beyond current sequence-only phase-separation predictors.

This synthesis requires reconciling incompatible experimental formats, resolving differing genome builds/annotations, and building shared computational pipelines across RNA structural biology and condensate proteomics — work far beyond any single lab's scope, and ideal for a distributed working group including trainees who will gain cross-disciplinary data science skills. Deliverables include an open-access integrated database and analysis pipeline (RNAstruct-Condensome), a set of testable structural determinants of RNA-driven condensate assembly, and machine-learning models predicting condensate partner recruitment from RNA structure. All workflows, code, and harmonized datasets will be released under open science standards, providing the community a reusable resource and establishing RNA structural context as a previously underappreciated axis of emergent mesoscale organization in the cell.
background_and_significance:
Membraneless organelles such as stress granules, nucleoli, and paraspeckles are archetypal examples of mesoscale emergence: bulk material properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase layering, aging kinetics) arise from thousands of weak, multivalent interactions among proteins and RNAs, and these properties are not straightforwardly predictable from the biophysics of any single interacting pair. Over the past decade, the field has made substantial progress explaining condensate formation through the lens of RBP intrinsic disorder, multivalent domain architecture, and motif-level RNA recognition. However, a critical variable has remained comparatively underexplored at scale: the structural ensemble of the RNA itself. RNAs are not passive strings of sequence motifs: they fold into secondary and tertiary structures that can occlude or expose binding sites, create multivalent scaffolding through repeated stem-loops, and alter local flexibility in ways that plausibly shape both which proteins are recruited into a condensate and the emergent material state of the resulting assembly. This structural axis is mechanistically distinct from sequence-composition or motif-density explanations currently dominant in phase-separation prediction, yet it has never been systematically tested at the transcriptome or condensate-atlas scale.

The reason this question remains unanswered is not a lack of data but a lack of integration. Genome-wide RBP-RNA interaction maps (eCLIP across ENCODE, PAR-CLIP repositories, aggregated resources such as POSTAR3 and RNAct) exist independently from RNA structural probing data (SHAPE/DMS reactivity profiles archived in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO) and independently again from condensate-level proteomic, transcriptomic, and biophysical characterization datasets (stress granule and nucleolar proteomic atlases, paraspeckle composition studies, and emerging high-throughput condensate-propensity screens covering thousands of protein and RNA sequences). Each of these data classes was generated by different communities, using incompatible genome builds, annotation standards, and file formats, and each requires distinct domain expertise to interpret correctly: RNA structural modeling and energetics, condensate biology and quantitative proteomics, and large-scale computational data harmonization. No individual laboratory possesses the full complement of expertise and bandwidth to responsibly integrate all three layers, which is precisely why this question has persisted as an open problem despite the availability of relevant public data.

This proposal is directly responsive to NCEMS's mission to catalyze synthesis of publicly available molecular and cellular data to resolve fundamental questions about emergent mesoscale phenomena. By combining RNA structural modeling expertise with condensate biology, proteomics, and phase-separation biophysics, our Working Group is positioned to establish RNA structural ensembles as a new, quantitatively tractable axis of condensate emergence — reframing a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale cell biology and producing a resource of lasting value to the broader community of RNA biologists, condensate biophysicists, and computational structural biologists.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group is organized around one overarching synthesis question and three tractable sub-questions, each addressable only through integration of existing public datasets spanning RNA structural biology and condensate proteomics.

Overarching question: Does the structural ensemble of an RNA molecule — independent of its sequence-level motif content — systematically influence which RBPs it recruits into biomolecular condensates and what emergent material properties result?

Sub-question 1 (structure and recruitment specificity): Do RNAs enriched within specific condensates (stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles) exhibit distinctive secondary structural signatures — such as elevated stem-loop density, characteristic single-stranded region length distributions, or recurring multivalent structured motifs — relative to transcriptome-wide background and relative to one another? We hypothesize that condensate identity correlates with distinguishable structural fingerprints beyond what is explained by RBP motif content alone, reflecting a structure-mediated layer of specificity in RNA partitioning.

Sub-question 2 (structural context at RBP binding sites): Does the local structural context surrounding experimentally mapped RBP binding sites (from eCLIP/PAR-CLIP) differ systematically between RBPs that are core, stable condensate residents versus those that are transient or peripheral components, as defined by existing condensate proteomic atlases? We hypothesize that stable condensate-resident RBPs preferentially bind RNA regions with specific structural accessibility profiles (e.g., moderately structured, dynamically breathing regions rather than either fully rigid duplexes or fully unstructured stretches), consistent with a structural “sweet spot” that supports multivalent, exchangeable interactions.

Sub-question 3 (structure and material properties): Do RNA structural features aggregated at the transcript or condensate-transcriptome level correlate with reported condensate biophysical properties — viscosity, interfacial tension, propensity for multiphase architecture, or aging/hardening kinetics — as documented across the condensate literature and high-throughput condensate-propensity screens? We hypothesize that RNAs with higher densities of stable, multivalent structural elements contribute to increased network connectivity and thus correlate with more viscous or gel-like condensate states, while RNAs dominated by flexible, unstructured regions correlate with more liquid-like states.

These hypotheses are motivated by established biophysical principles of multivalency-driven phase separation, in which network connectivity and interaction valency govern material state, combined with the recognition that RNA secondary structure itself constitutes a source of multivalent, cooperative interaction surfaces (via stem-loops, junctions, and higher-order motifs) that has been comparatively neglected relative to protein-side multivalency. Rosetta-derived energetic modeling of RNA structural stability and flexibility, applied at scale across condensate-associated transcripts, offers a principled way to quantify these structural properties beyond simple secondary-structure diagrams.

Critically, none of these questions can be answered using any single existing dataset. Each requires cross-referencing RBP binding maps, RNA structural probing data, and condensate composition/biophysical annotations that were collected by separate consortia for separate purposes. Answering them constitutes genuine community-scale synthesis: the Working Group will produce, for the first time, a jointly harmonized dataset and analytical framework capable of testing whether RNA structure is a previously underappreciated determinant of condensate emergence, generating hypotheses that can subsequently be tested experimentally by the broader community.
methods_and_approach:
The project proceeds in four integrated phases, each assigned to the team members whose expertise most directly applies, with shared computational infrastructure ensuring reproducibility across phases.

Phase 1 — Data harmonization: We will assemble and standardize three public data layers onto a common genome build and transcript annotation (GENCODE-based). RBP-RNA interaction data will be drawn from ENCODE eCLIP, additional PAR-CLIP datasets, and pre-aggregated resources (POSTAR3, RNAct), retaining peak coordinates, RBP identity, and binding confidence metrics. RNA structural data will be compiled from SHAPE/DMS chemical probing experiments deposited in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO, supplemented by transcriptome-wide computational structure predictions where experimental probing is unavailable, using established secondary-structure prediction algorithms. Condensate composition and biophysical data will be compiled from published stress granule, nucleolar, and paraspeckle proteomic/transcriptomic atlases, and from recently released high-throughput condensate-propensity screening datasets covering thousands of protein sequences. All datasets will be ingested into a unified relational schema with transcript-level and nucleotide-level resolution.

Phase 2 — Structural feature extraction: For every transcript represented across the harmonized dataset, we will compute a standardized set of structural descriptors: base-pairing probability profiles, stem-loop density and length distributions, single-stranded region statistics, and structural ensemble diversity (Shannon entropy of base-pairing). For a curated subset of condensate-relevant transcripts with especially strong evidence of biological importance, we will apply Rosetta-based energetic modeling to estimate structural stability and conformational flexibility, providing a physically grounded complement to purely statistical secondary-structure descriptors.

Phase 3 — Integrative statistical and machine-learning analysis: Using the harmonized dataset, we will test Sub-questions 1–3 through complementary approaches: (a) enrichment analyses comparing structural feature distributions across condensate-associated versus background transcripts; (b) binding-site-centered analyses comparing local structural context between stably condensate-resident and transient/peripheral RBPs, using existing proteomic stability/enrichment metrics as ground truth; and (c) supervised machine-learning models (gradient-boosted trees and neural architectures suited to structured biological data) trained to predict condensate material-property classifications from RNA structural feature vectors, benchmarked against sequence/motif-only baseline models to isolate the structural contribution.

Phase 4 — Validation and synthesis: Findings will be cross-validated against independent, held-out condensate datasets not used in model training, and against orthogonal structural probing datasets, to assess robustness. Trainees will lead specific sub-analyses (e.g., condensate-specific structural fingerprinting, RBP-binding-site context modeling) under joint mentorship, gaining hands-on experience in cross-domain data integration.

Throughout, working group meetings will reconcile methodological choices (e.g., structure prediction thresholds, RBP confidence cutoffs) via documented, version-controlled decisions, ensuring that all integration steps are transparent, auditable, and reproducible by external users of the resulting RNAstruct-Condensome resource.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The Working Group will deliver: (1) RNAstruct-Condensome, an open, harmonized database linking RNA structural features, RBP binding data, and condensate composition/biophysical annotations at transcript and nucleotide resolution; (2) a reproducible computational pipeline for extracting structural descriptors and Rosetta-based energetic metrics transcriptome-wide; (3) a set of statistically validated structural signatures associated with condensate identity, RBP recruitment stability, and reported material properties; and (4) machine-learning models predicting condensate partner recruitment and material-state tendencies from RNA structural input, benchmarked against existing sequence-only predictors.

Scientifically, this work will establish whether RNA structural ensembles constitute an independent, quantifiable axis of mesoscale emergence in condensate biology — a conceptual advance relevant to stress granule dysfunction in neurodegeneration, nucleolar stress responses, and paraspeckle-mediated gene regulation. By demonstrating (or rigorously constraining) the role of RNA structure, the project will refine mechanistic models of phase separation currently dominated by protein-centric multivalency frameworks.

Methodologically, the harmonization pipeline itself is a reusable community resource: it resolves long-standing incompatibilities between RNA structural probing data, CLIP-based interactome data, and condensate proteomic atlases, lowering the barrier for future synthesis projects in RNA biology and condensate research. Trainees engaged in the project will acquire transferable skills in cross-domain data integration, structural bioinformatics, and machine learning applied to heterogeneous molecular datasets, contributing to NCEMS's workforce-development goals. Broader impact extends to experimentalists who can use predicted structural determinants to design targeted follow-up perturbation experiments, accelerating hypothesis-driven research into RNA-directed condensate assembly and material control.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
All components of this project will be developed and released under open science principles consistent with NCEMS and community standards for reproducible synthesis research. Source data are exclusively drawn from publicly accessible repositories (ENCODE, GEO, RNA Mapping Database, POSTAR3, RNAct, and published condensate atlases), and all harmonization scripts, annotation-mapping tables, and structural feature extraction pipelines will be deposited in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub, with archival snapshots on Zenodo) under permissive open-source licenses.

The integrated RNAstruct-Condensome database will be released with full provenance tracking, documenting the original source, access date, and processing steps applied to every data point, enabling exact reconstruction of derived features. Machine-learning models, including trained weights, hyperparameters, and evaluation code, will be shared alongside standardized benchmark datasets so that external groups can reproduce reported performance metrics or apply the models to new transcripts. Analysis workflows will be containerized to ensure computational environment consistency across collaborating institutions and for future community reuse.

We will adopt FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable outputs, and will register the project's data dictionary and schema early in the project to solicit community feedback before finalizing the resource architecture. Intermediate analysis decisions (e.g., structure-prediction confidence thresholds, RBP peak-calling criteria) will be documented in a public methods log to support transparency and enable alternative reanalysis. Consistent with NCEMS's emphasis on team science, we will hold regular open working-group meetings with notes archived publicly, and will prioritize preprinting all findings to accelerate community access ahead of formal publication, ensuring the resource and its insights are available to the broadest possible audience of RNA biologists, condensate researchers, and computational scientists.
budget_and_resources:
This proposal requests NCEMS support structured around personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative training activities rather than experimental costs, consistent with the project's purely synthesis-based scope. Primary budget allocation will support a postdoctoral researcher or senior graduate trainee with combined computational structural biology and data engineering skills to lead data harmonization and pipeline development, alongside partial support for a second trainee focused on condensate proteomic data integration and machine-learning model development, providing direct cross-disciplinary training experience central to NCEMS's workforce goals.

Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient for transcriptome-wide structure prediction, Rosetta-based energetic modeling of selected transcript sets, and training/validation of machine-learning models across large condensate-associated datasets; storage costs for the harmonized multi-terabyte integrated database and its versioned releases are also requested.

Travel funds are requested to support two in-person working-group meetings per year, bringing together the two co-PI labs and invited domain experts (e.g., proteomics data curators, RNA structural probing specialists) to resolve harmonization decisions, validate emerging findings, and coordinate trainee mentorship — activities that benefit substantially from concentrated in-person collaboration beyond routine virtual meetings.

Modest publication and data-repository fees are requested to support open-access publication and permanent archival deposition (Zenodo/GitHub releases) of code, data, and models. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the project's exclusive reliance on existing public datasets. This budget structure reflects the project's core need: dedicated personnel time and computational capacity to accomplish an integration task that exceeds the bandwidth of either contributing lab operating independently, precisely the gap NCEMS support is intended to fill.
