author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding Environmental Selection Pressures on Condensate-Forming Sequence Grammars: A Multiscale Data Synthesis Across the Prokaryotic-to-Eukaryotic Thermal and Salinity Continuum
abstract:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) drive biomolecular condensation through sequence-encoded 'sticker-and-spacer' grammars, yet whether these grammars are themselves products of environmental selection remains unknown. Organisms spanning psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, and halophiles have evolved proteomes under vastly different physicochemical constraints (temperature, ionic strength, crowding), but no systematic effort has linked these environmental gradients to the biophysical 'rules' governing mesoscale self-assembly. This project will synthesize four classes of publicly available data that, to date, have never been integrated at scale: (1) curated proteome and IDR annotation databases (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt) spanning thousands of species with documented optimal growth temperatures and salinities; (2) condensate-associated protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DrLLPS) identifying known or predicted phase-separating proteins and their partners; (3) parameterized coarse-grained simulation frameworks (e.g., Mpipi-class models) that translate sequence composition and patterning into predicted phase diagrams, saturation concentrations, and critical solution temperatures; and (4) structural/ultrastructural datasets from cryo-electron tomography, cryo-EM, and SAXS repositories (EMDB, PDB, EMPIAR) that reveal in vivo or in vitro condensate architecture for a subset of these proteins, particularly in bacterial systems where mesoscale organization has been directly visualized.

We will computationally extract sequence-grammar features (aromatic/cationic sticker density, charge patterning, spacer composition and length, net charge per residue) from IDRs across organisms occupying extreme versus moderate environmental niches, then apply existing coarse-grained simulation engines to predict each sequence's phase behavior (critical temperature, droplet viscoelasticity, salt/temperature sensitivity) without generating new experimental data. These predictions will be statistically correlated with organismal growth conditions to test whether specific grammatical features (e.g., increased spacer flexibility or altered stickers valence) systematically track thermal or osmotic adaptation, analogous to known compensatory strategies in folded-protein stability. Where cryo-ET or structural data exist for homologous condensate-scaffolding proteins (e.g., bacterial polar organizing proteins, RNA-binding stress granule components), we will cross-validate simulation-derived phase behavior against observed ultrastructural features (filament versus droplet morphology, interfacial properties) to determine whether sequence-encoded adaptations manifest as predictable changes in mesoscale architecture.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in structural/mesoscale bacterial biology, physics-based coarse-grained modeling of condensates, and sequence-to-function mapping of disordered regions—capabilities distributed across our three groups and not achievable within any single lab. The project will produce an open-access, queryable atlas linking environmental parameters, IDR sequence grammar, predicted phase behavior, and (where available) structural ground truth, providing a resource for the community to test hypotheses about evolutionary constraints on emergent mesoscale organization. Findings will illuminate whether phase separation itself is an evolvable, selectable trait shaped by environmental pressure, offering a new framework for understanding how molecular-scale sequence features generate cell-scale adaptive phenotypes. All code, curated datasets, and simulation outputs will be released under FAIR principles, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary integration of genomics, biophysical simulation, and structural data analysis.
background_and_significance: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation represent a fundamental mechanism by which cells organize biochemistry in space and time without membrane boundaries. A growing body of work has established that condensate formation is governed by sequence-encoded 'sticker-and-spacer' grammars within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), wherein aromatic and charged residues act as adhesive stickers embedded within flexible spacer sequences that modulate valence, density, and interaction strength. Coarse-grained simulation frameworks now allow near-quantitative prediction of phase behavior directly from sequence, and structural techniques including cryo-electron tomography have begun to reveal how these sequence-encoded interactions manifest as higher-order mesoscale architectures inside cells, including filamentous and droplet-like assemblies in bacteria. Despite these advances, a critical dimension remains unexplored: whether the biophysical rules governing condensation are themselves shaped by environmental selection pressure. Organisms have diversified across an extraordinary range of thermal and osmotic environments, from psychrophiles surviving near-freezing temperatures to halophiles thriving in saturated brines, and it is well established that folded protein stability, membrane composition, and metabolic strategies have co-evolved with these environmental constraints. Whether disordered regions and their condensation-prone sequence grammars have undergone analogous adaptive tuning is unknown, despite condensates being centrally implicated in stress response, RNA metabolism, and cellular organization across all domains of life. This gap persists not for lack of relevant data, but because the data required to address it are scattered across disconnected resources: proteome and disorder annotation databases, condensate-protein catalogs, biophysical simulation parameterizations, and structural repositories have each matured independently without cross-integration. No existing effort has systematically linked organismal growth-condition metadata to predicted or observed condensate biophysics at proteome scale. Addressing this question requires simultaneous fluency in comparative genomics and disorder prediction, physics-based simulation of sequence-to-phase-behavior relationships, and structural interpretation of mesoscale organization—an interdisciplinary combination rarely present within a single laboratory. By synthesizing these four data classes into a unified analytical framework, this project will determine whether phase separation should be understood as an evolvable, selectable cellular trait, analogous to known compensatory mechanisms in folded-protein thermostability. This reframing carries significant implications for understanding how molecular-scale sequence features generate cell-scale adaptive phenotypes, and for interpreting condensate biology within an evolutionary and ecological context rather than solely as a cell-biological curiosity. The resulting synthesis directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent mesoscale properties and their influence on higher-order cellular outcomes, using purely existing public data integrated at a scale beyond individual-lab capacity.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project is organized around three interconnected research questions. First, do sequence-encoded condensation grammars—sticker density, sticker valence, spacer length and flexibility, and net charge patterning—differ systematically between IDR-containing proteins from organisms adapted to divergent thermal and osmotic environments? We hypothesize that psychrophilic and halophilic proteomes will exhibit distinct compensatory signatures relative to mesophiles: specifically, that thermal adaptation will manifest as shifts in aromatic sticker density and spacer composition analogous to known compensatory strategies for maintaining marginal stability in folded proteins, while osmotic adaptation will manifest primarily through altered charge patterning and net charge per residue, reflecting the need to maintain condensation competence under high ionic strength. Second, do these sequence-level differences translate into predictable differences in simulated phase behavior—critical solution temperature, saturation concentration, and salt sensitivity—when processed through validated coarse-grained simulation engines? We hypothesize that organisms from extreme environments will show simulated phase diagrams shifted in a direction that preserves condensation competence under native physiological conditions, effectively demonstrating that phase separation propensity is buffered against environmental perturbation through sequence adaptation rather than being an incidental byproduct of proteome composition. Third, where structural or ultrastructural data exist for condensate-scaffolding proteins or their homologs, particularly bacterial polar organizing proteins and stress-granule-associated RNA-binding proteins, do observed in vivo or in vitro architectural features (filament versus droplet morphology, interfacial properties, multiphase organization) correspond to the phase behavior predicted from sequence-grammar analysis? We hypothesize that structurally characterized condensate systems from organisms occupying extreme niches will exhibit architectural signatures consistent with environmentally tuned biophysical parameters, providing an empirical bridge between sequence-level prediction and observed mesoscale organization. Collectively, these hypotheses test whether condensate-forming sequence grammars constitute an adaptive trait under selection, rather than a conserved, environment-independent property of disordered regions. A null hypothesis of no systematic relationship between environmental parameters and sequence grammar or predicted phase behavior is equally informative, as it would suggest that condensation-relevant sequence features are constrained by requirements largely independent of the thermal or osmotic niche, pointing toward alternative regulatory mechanisms (e.g., post-translational modification, partner protein co-evolution, or cellular-scale buffering) that compensate for environmental variation. Testing these questions requires assembling proteome-scale disorder annotations, condensate-protein catalogs, simulation-derived biophysical predictions, and structural datasets into a single comparative framework—an undertaking that exceeds the scope of any individual dataset or laboratory and necessitates the collaborative, cross-disciplinary synthesis approach outlined here.
methods_and_approach: The working group will execute a four-stage synthesis pipeline built entirely on publicly available resources. Stage one involves data acquisition and harmonization: we will compile proteome-wide IDR annotations from MobiDB and DisProt, cross-referenced with UniProt taxonomic and physiological metadata to assign documented optimal growth temperature and salinity to each source organism, drawing on curated microbial trait databases where organismal metadata is incomplete. In parallel, we will extract known and predicted phase-separating proteins from PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, and DrLLPS to identify condensate-associated IDRs meriting focused analysis alongside genome-wide background comparisons. Stage two involves computational feature extraction: for each IDR sequence, we will calculate established sequence-grammar descriptors, including aromatic and cationic sticker density, sticker spacing and clustering statistics, spacer length and compositional bias, net charge per residue, and charge patterning metrics, using existing open-source sequence analysis tools. Stage three applies validated coarse-grained simulation frameworks, including Mpipi-class models, to predict phase behavior for representative sequences spanning the environmental gradient, generating estimates of critical solution temperature, saturation concentration, and salt/temperature sensitivity without performing any new wet-lab experiments; simulations will be run at a scale sufficient to capture statistical trends across environmental categories rather than exhaustively simulating every sequence, using stratified sampling informed by phylogenetic and environmental diversity. Stage four performs structural cross-validation: for the subset of proteins with available cryo-electron tomography, cryo-EM, or SAXS data in EMDB, PDB, or EMPIAR, we will extract quantitative architectural descriptors (filament versus droplet morphology, interfacial curvature, packing density) and statistically compare these against simulation-derived predictions for matched or homologous sequences. Statistical analysis across all stages will employ mixed-effects models to account for phylogenetic non-independence among species, alongside permutation-based significance testing to guard against spurious correlations arising from database sampling biases. Given the observational, cross-species nature of this synthesis, particular attention will be paid to controlling for confounding variables such as genome GC content, proteome size, and phylogenetic clustering of sequenced extremophiles. The three collaborating groups will contribute distinct, complementary expertise: bacterial mesoscale structural biology and condensate ultrastructure interpretation; physics-based coarse-grained simulation development and parameterization; and sequence-to-function mapping of disordered regions and molecular grammar analysis. Regular cross-group working sessions will ensure methodological consistency, with shared computational infrastructure supporting reproducible pipeline execution across all analytical stages. Trainees will be embedded across each stage to gain hands-on experience spanning comparative genomics, biophysical simulation, and structural data analysis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis will produce a publicly accessible, queryable atlas integrating environmental parameters, IDR sequence-grammar features, simulation-derived phase behavior predictions, and available structural ground truth across thousands of species. This resource will enable the broader community to test additional hypotheses about condensate evolution without needing to independently assemble and harmonize the underlying disparate datasets. Scientifically, the project will establish whether condensate-forming sequence grammars constitute an adaptive, selectable trait, providing a new conceptual framework linking molecular-scale sequence variation to organismal-scale environmental adaptation. This reframes phase separation biology within an evolutionary context, complementing existing mechanistic and structural understanding with a population-level, comparative perspective. Findings will directly inform ongoing efforts to engineer condensate-forming proteins for biotechnological applications requiring stability across temperature or ionic strength ranges, and will generate testable predictions for future experimental validation by the broader research community. The interdisciplinary methodology developed here, combining comparative genomics, physics-based simulation, and structural cross-validation, will serve as a template for future synthesis efforts addressing other emergent mesoscale phenomena. By demonstrating that large-scale public data integration can resolve previously inaccessible evolutionary questions in condensate biology, this project exemplifies the transformative potential of community-scale synthesis research, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand emergent mesoscale properties and their influence on higher-order cellular outcomes. Trainees engaged in this project will develop transferable, high-demand skills spanning genomics, biophysical modeling, and structural bioinformatics, contributing to the development of a data-fluent next-generation research workforce.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles consistent with community standards for reproducible, team-based research. Source data will be drawn exclusively from established public repositories (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt, PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DrLLPS, EMDB, PDB, EMPIAR), and all curated, harmonized datasets generated during integration will be deposited in an open, version-controlled repository with persistent identifiers. Analysis code, including sequence-feature extraction scripts, simulation configuration files, and statistical analysis pipelines, will be maintained in publicly accessible version-controlled repositories with comprehensive documentation enabling independent replication. Coarse-grained simulation parameters and output trajectories will be archived in accordance with community standards for computational reproducibility, allowing other researchers to rerun or extend analyses without requiring proprietary software or restricted-access data. Intermediate data products, including the harmonized environmental-metadata-to-IDR mapping and the resulting sequence-grammar feature atlas, will be released incrementally rather than only upon publication, enabling community feedback throughout the project lifecycle. The working group will adopt standardized metadata conventions to ensure interoperability with existing disorder and condensate databases, facilitating future integration efforts by other research teams. All manuscripts arising from this work will be posted as preprints prior to peer review, and final publications will be made available through open-access channels. Regular working group meetings will document decision points and analytical choices in shared, publicly logged records to support transparency and reproducibility. This commitment to open, team-based science ensures that the resulting atlas functions not merely as a static output but as a living, extensible community resource, directly fulfilling NCEMS's expectation that synthesis projects generate durable, reusable infrastructure for the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.
budget_and_resources: This project requires resources primarily supporting computational infrastructure, personnel time, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, consistent with its synthesis-only design. Funding will support salary contributions for one postdoctoral researcher and two graduate students distributed across the three collaborating groups, each contributing complementary expertise in structural data interpretation, coarse-grained simulation, and sequence-based disorder analysis. Computational resources will include allocation on high-performance computing clusters sufficient to run coarse-grained simulations across a stratified sample of IDR sequences spanning the environmental gradient, alongside cloud-based storage for hosting the integrated database and associated code repositories. Modest funds are requested for data engineering support to build and maintain the harmonized, queryable atlas interface, ensuring long-term accessibility beyond the project period. Travel support will enable in-person working group meetings at least twice yearly to facilitate cross-disciplinary integration, methodological alignment, and trainee mentorship, alongside virtual meeting infrastructure for ongoing coordination between institutions. Additional funds will support trainee participation in relevant scientific conferences to disseminate emerging findings and receive community feedback. NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination across three geographically distributed laboratories with distinct disciplinary expertise, computational infrastructure exceeding what any single lab typically maintains for this scale of cross-database integration, and dedicated personnel time to perform the labor-intensive harmonization of disparate, non-standardized public datasets. No individual lab possesses the combined structural biology, simulation, and sequence-analysis expertise necessary to execute this synthesis independently, and existing informal collaborations lack the sustained resourcing required to complete a project of this scope. The requested budget reflects a lean, synthesis-appropriate allocation focused on personnel, computation, and coordination rather than experimental costs, maximizing scientific return relative to investment.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Copy-Number Amplicons to Proteostatic Stress: A Multiscale Synthesis of 3D Genome Reorganization, Protein Complex Stoichiometry, and Cellular Fitness in Cancer Cell Lines
abstract: A central unresolved question in cancer cell biology is how genomic amplification events—particularly extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) and focal copy-number gains—propagate through intermediate, mesoscale layers of cellular organization to produce emergent phenotypes such as drug resistance or engineered fitness dependencies. Existing studies typically examine single layers in isolation: genomic amplicon structure, 3D chromatin architecture, protein complex stoichiometry, or CRISPR-based fitness screens. No public synthesis has yet connected these layers into a coherent multiscale model linking DNA-level amplification to chromatin domain reorganization, to protein-level stoichiometric imbalance and misfolding stress, to cell-level dependency and drug response. This project will integrate five classes of publicly available data across matched or overlapping cancer cell lines: (1) CCLE/DepMap genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, CRISPR dependency, and drug-response datasets; (2) Hi-C and related 3D genome architecture data from the 4D Nucleome and ENCODE consortia; (3) ecDNA amplicon structural catalogs (e.g., ecDNA Atlas, AmpliconArchitect outputs); (4) structural proteomics resources including limited-proteolysis and cross-linking mass spectrometry datasets, PDB and AlphaFold structural models, and CORUM protein complex annotations; and (5) public single-cell CRISPR/Perturb-seq datasets probing regulatory and proteostatic responses to genetic perturbation. Our central hypothesis is that copy-number amplification—especially via ecDNA, which decouples genomic loci from native chromosomal 3D context—triggers characteristic reorganizations of chromatin domains and looping architecture that produce transcriptional dosage imbalance among interacting protein complex subunits. This imbalance generates measurable proteostatic stress, detectable as elevated misfolding-prone or entangled conformational states in structural proteomics data, which in turn constrains cellular fitness landscapes captured by DepMap dependency scores and drug sensitivity profiles. We will build a statistical and machine-learning integration framework—combining probabilistic graphical models for cross-layer dependency structure, positive-unlabeled learning to handle sparsely annotated misfolding/entanglement states, and network-based approaches adapted from epidemiological exposure modeling—to quantify how amplicon-driven 3D genome perturbations transmit through the proteome to shape emergent cellular vulnerabilities. This effort requires collaboration well beyond any single laboratory: expertise in cancer multi-omics and ecDNA biology, 3D genome organization and single-cell regulatory genomics, protein folding/misfolding biophysics and statistical fitness-landscape modeling, and machine-learning frameworks for heterogeneous multi-omic and network data. No new experimental data will be generated; the project synthesizes and harmonizes existing public repositories into a unified analytical pipeline and predictive model, released as open-source workflows and annotated multiscale integration datasets. Deliverables include a public database linking amplicon architecture to chromatin domain shifts, protein stoichiometric imbalance scores, and dependency/drug-response outcomes across hundreds of characterized cell lines, alongside trainee-led modules teaching multi-omic data harmonization, structural bioinformatics, and cross-scale statistical modeling. By formally connecting genomic, chromatin, and proteomic mesoscale phenomena to whole-cell phenotypic emergence, this work will resolve a long-standing gap in understanding how structural genomic instability manifests as exploitable cellular vulnerability, offering a generalizable template for multiscale synthesis in molecular and cellular biosciences.
background_and_significance: Focal copy-number amplification, and extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) in particular, is now recognized as a pervasive driver of oncogene overexpression, intratumor heterogeneity, and rapid adaptive drug response across many cancer types. ecDNA elements exist outside the constraints of native chromosomal packaging, freely segregating during mitosis and clustering into transcriptionally hyperactive hubs. While the genomic architecture of these amplicons has been mapped with increasing precision through tools such as AmpliconArchitect and large-scale ecDNA atlases, and while separate consortia have generated extensive chromatin conformation data (Hi-C, ChIA-PET) and cell-state resources (CCLE, DepMap, TCGA), these data streams have been analyzed largely in isolation. The consequence is a fragmented understanding of how a genomic-scale event—amplicon formation—cascades through intermediate, mesoscale layers of cellular organization to generate the phenotypic outcomes that matter clinically: drug resistance, oncogene dependency, and selective cellular vulnerability. Three mechanistic gaps remain unresolved. First, it is unclear how ecDNA-driven decoupling of loci from native chromosomal context reshapes local and long-range chromatin domains, topologically associating domains, and enhancer-promoter looping relative to matched non-amplified contexts. Second, even where transcriptional dosage effects of amplification are documented, their propagation to the protein level—specifically, whether amplified genes produce subunits of multiprotein complexes in stoichiometric excess relative to non-amplified partners—has not been systematically examined at scale. Excess, unincorporated subunits are a well-established source of proteostatic burden, promoting misfolding, entanglement, and aggregation-prone states; yet this connection has not been tested using existing structural proteomics resources such as limited-proteolysis and cross-linking mass spectrometry datasets alongside computational structural models. Third, whether such proteostatic stress signatures predict or explain observed CRISPR dependency profiles and drug sensitivity patterns in DepMap remains an open and testable question, one that requires joint analysis of genomic, structural, and functional-genomic layers that currently reside in disconnected repositories. Addressing this gap is significant for two reasons. Scientifically, it would establish a mechanistic, cross-scale explanation for why amplicon-bearing cells exhibit specific, exploitable dependencies—reframing genomic instability not merely as a marker of malignancy but as a source of quantifiable, targetable cellular stress. Practically, a validated multiscale model linking amplicon structure to proteostatic vulnerability could nominate new biomarkers of drug sensitivity and new dependency classes for therapeutic targeting, informed entirely by synthesis of existing public data. This problem is intrinsically an emergence question central to the mesoscale mission of this funding initiative: it asks how molecular-scale genomic events give rise to higher-order chromatin and proteomic organization, and how that organization in turn constrains whole-cell phenotype. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in ecDNA structural genomics, 3D genome architecture, structural proteomics of misfolding, and cross-omic statistical modeling needed to test this hypothesis, making it an ideal candidate for community-scale data synthesis.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project is organized around three linked research questions, each addressing a distinct transition across mesoscale layers, and a unifying hypothesis connecting genomic amplification to emergent cellular vulnerability. RQ1 (Genome-to-Chromatin): Does ecDNA-based amplification produce characteristic, reproducible reorganizations of 3D chromatin architecture—altered topologically associating domain boundaries, novel long-range loops, or loss of native insulation—distinguishable from architecture at matched focal amplicons that remain chromosomally integrated? We hypothesize that ecDNA amplicons, freed from native positional constraints, will show systematically altered domain boundary strength and an enrichment of inter-amplicon or amplicon-hub contacts relative to intrachromosomal amplifications of comparable copy number, detectable through comparative analysis of Hi-C data from cell lines with characterized ecDNA status. RQ2 (Chromatin/Genome-to-Proteome): Does amplification-driven transcriptional dosage imbalance among genes encoding interacting protein complex subunits produce detectable proteostatic stress signatures? We hypothesize that genes amplified via ecDNA disproportionately encode subunits whose obligate complex partners are not co-amplified, generating stoichiometric excess that is measurable as increased proteolytic susceptibility, altered cross-linking contact patterns, or elevated structural entanglement propensity in existing structural proteomics datasets, relative to subunits from balanced, non-amplified complexes annotated in CORUM and modeled via AlphaFold and PDB structures. RQ3 (Proteome-to-Phenotype): Does this proteostatic stress signature explain or predict cell-level functional outcomes captured in CRISPR dependency and drug-response data? We hypothesize that cell lines exhibiting predicted stoichiometric imbalance and proteostatic burden will show increased dependency on proteostasis-associated machinery (e.g., chaperones, proteasomal components, autophagy regulators) in DepMap CRISPR screens, and altered sensitivity to proteostasis-perturbing compounds, compared to cell lines with matched copy-number burden but balanced stoichiometry. The overarching hypothesis linking these three questions is that ecDNA-mediated decoupling of amplicons from native chromosomal context is a mechanistic driver—not merely a correlate—of a cascading vulnerability pathway: altered 3D genome organization produces transcriptional dosage imbalance, dosage imbalance produces proteostatic stress, and proteostatic stress constrains the cellular fitness landscape in ways that are quantifiable and predictive. A secondary, methodological question asks whether cross-layer dependency structure can be modeled using techniques originally developed in adjacent domains—probabilistic graphical models for latent structure inference, positive-unlabeled learning for sparsely annotated misfolding states, and network-based exposure models adapted from spatial epidemiology—to formally quantify propagation strength across scales rather than rely on layer-by-layer correlation. Successful validation of these hypotheses would resolve a persistent puzzle in cancer cell biology: why structurally similar amplification events produce divergent phenotypic consequences across cell lines, an outcome plausibly explained by differences in downstream chromatin and proteomic context rather than amplicon genomic content alone.
methods_and_approach: The working group will assemble a harmonized cell-line-matched dataset spanning five public data classes. Genomic and functional layers will be drawn from CCLE and DepMap, including copy-number segmentation, RNA-seq, proteomic (reverse-phase protein array and mass spectrometry-based), CRISPR dependency scores, and drug-response profiles; ecDNA status and amplicon structure will be assigned using existing AmpliconArchitect-derived calls and ecDNA Atlas annotations, stratifying cell lines into ecDNA-positive, chromosomally-amplified, and non-amplified groups matched on tissue lineage and copy-number magnitude. Chromatin architecture will be sourced from Hi-C and related contact datasets in the 4D Nucleome and ENCODE repositories for cell lines with available profiles, with domain boundary calling, loop detection, and compartment analysis performed using established, validated pipelines to enable direct architectural comparison across amplicon classes. Structural proteomics evidence for misfolding and entanglement will be integrated from public limited-proteolysis and cross-linking mass spectrometry datasets, cross-referenced against CORUM complex membership and AlphaFold/PDB structural models to identify subunits exhibiting non-native proteolytic or cross-linking signatures consistent with proteostatic stress. Perturb-seq and single-cell CRISPR datasets will provide an independent, orthogonal readout of regulatory and proteostatic response to genetic perturbation, used to validate inferred dosage-imbalance-to-stress relationships at single-cell resolution. Analytically, the project proceeds in three integrated phases. Phase 1 establishes cross-dataset harmonization: cell line identity reconciliation across repositories, gene and protein identifier mapping, and construction of a matched-cohort table linking amplicon status, chromatin profiles, and proteomic/functional readouts. Phase 2 develops the statistical integration framework, comprising (a) probabilistic graphical models to infer conditional dependency structure across genomic, chromatin, and proteomic layers while controlling for tissue lineage and overall amplification burden; (b) positive-unlabeled learning classifiers trained on limited confirmed misfolding/entanglement examples to score subunit-level proteostatic risk across the full CORUM complex catalog, addressing the sparsity of labeled structural stress states; and (c) network-based propagation models, adapting exposure-diffusion approaches from spatial epidemiology, to quantify how chromatin-level perturbation signals transmit through protein interaction networks to functional outcome nodes (dependency scores, drug sensitivity). Phase 3 performs validation and benchmarking through held-out cell-line cross-validation, comparison against null models preserving copy-number burden but permuting chromatin/proteomic layers, and consistency checks against Perturb-seq perturbation responses. Reproducibility will be embedded through containerized, version-controlled pipelines with explicit provenance tracking for every public dataset used. Monthly working-group meetings and quarterly in-person or virtual workshops will coordinate cross-institutional analysis, with trainees leading specific pipeline modules under joint mentorship from computational and structural biology team members.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The primary outcome is a validated, quantitative multiscale model linking ecDNA-driven genomic amplification to chromatin reorganization, protein stoichiometric imbalance, and cellular fitness constraints, tested across hundreds of characterized cancer cell lines. This model will be released as an open, queryable database annotating each cell line with amplicon architecture, chromatin domain shift scores, protein-complex stoichiometric imbalance and proteostatic risk scores, and corresponding dependency/drug-response profiles, enabling the broader research community to generate and test new hypotheses without independent data collection. A second outcome is a generalizable computational framework—combining probabilistic graphical modeling, positive-unlabeled learning, and network propagation methods—applicable beyond ecDNA biology to any multiscale synthesis problem involving sparse structural annotation and heterogeneous omic layers. Scientifically, confirmation of the central hypothesis would resolve a long-standing puzzle regarding phenotypic heterogeneity among amplicon-bearing tumors, reframing proteostatic stress as a mechanistic intermediate and a candidate therapeutic vulnerability rather than an incidental byproduct of amplification. Clinically, the identification of proteostasis-associated dependencies specific to ecDNA-positive contexts could nominate new combination therapy strategies pairing amplicon-targeting or chaperone-targeting agents with existing oncogene-directed treatments. Beyond the immediate scientific contribution, this project will demonstrate a template for synthesis-driven discovery in molecular and cellular biosciences, showing how existing genomic, structural, and functional-genomic repositories—collected independently and for disparate original purposes—can be reanalyzed jointly to reveal emergent, cross-scale biological principles inaccessible to any single dataset or laboratory.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All analyses will rely exclusively on publicly available data, and all derived resources will be released under permissive open licenses consistent with community standards for reproducible science. Data harmonization scripts, statistical integration models, and validation pipelines will be developed under version control in publicly accessible repositories, with containerized computational environments to ensure exact reproducibility of results across institutions and future users. Each analytical step will carry explicit data provenance documentation, tracing every derived quantity back to its original public source (CCLE, DepMap, 4D Nucleome, ENCODE, ecDNA Atlas, PDB, AlphaFold Database, CORUM, and public Perturb-seq repositories), enabling independent verification and reuse. The integrated multiscale database—linking amplicon architecture, chromatin domain metrics, protein stoichiometric imbalance scores, and functional dependency outcomes—will be deposited in a stable, community-accessible repository with a persistent identifier, accompanied by structured metadata following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles. Analytical workflows will be documented as modular, well-annotated notebooks and pipeline definitions suitable for direct reuse or extension by other research groups, explicitly designed to lower the barrier for labs lacking dedicated computational infrastructure to engage with multiscale cancer genomics questions. The working group commits to preregistering core hypotheses and analysis plans prior to full-scale integration to guard against post hoc overfitting, and to releasing negative or null results alongside positive findings. Regular working-group calls will include reproducibility checkpoints in which independent team members re-execute pipeline components on shared computing infrastructure to confirm consistency before results are incorporated into shared deliverables. All trainee-authored code modules will undergo peer code review within the group prior to public release, ensuring both scientific rigor and pedagogical value as teaching resources for future data-intensive researchers in molecular and cellular biosciences.
budget_and_resources: The project requires resources primarily for personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, consistent with its purely synthesis-based design. Budget priorities include partial salary support for a postdoctoral scientist and two graduate trainees who will lead cross-layer data harmonization, statistical model development, and structural proteomics integration, working jointly across the participating laboratories. Cloud and high-performance computing allocation is requested to support large-scale processing of Hi-C contact matrices, single-cell Perturb-seq datasets, and structural model repositories, alongside storage costs for the integrated multiscale database and its associated metadata. Funding is also requested to support in-person working-group workshops at least twice yearly, bringing together team members from cancer genomics, 3D genome biology, structural proteomics, and computational modeling backgrounds to coordinate cross-disciplinary integration and resolve methodological disagreements that cannot be efficiently addressed remotely. Modest travel support will enable trainee participation in relevant scientific conferences to present integrated findings and receive community feedback. Software development effort is budgeted for building and maintaining the public-facing database interface and reproducible pipeline repository, including documentation suitable for external reuse. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the project's exclusive reliance on existing public repositories. The requested support directly addresses needs beyond the capacity of any individual laboratory: sustained cross-institutional coordination, dedicated trainee time for large-scale data harmonization across five distinct data modalities, and computational infrastructure capable of handling genome-scale chromatin, proteomic, and single-cell datasets simultaneously. This investment is justified by the scale of integration required and by the training value embedded throughout the pipeline development process, which will equip participating trainees with transferable skills in multi-omic data synthesis, structural bioinformatics, and cross-scale statistical modeling applicable well beyond the immediate scientific questions addressed here.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Cross-Scale Morphodynamic Grammar of Membrane-Bound Organelle Shape Change: Integrating Whole-Cell Volumetric Imaging with Cytoskeletal Agent-Based Simulations to Learn Generalizable Rules of Mesoscale Shape Transitions
abstract:
Organelles such as cilia, mitochondria, and the nuclear envelope undergo characteristic, reproducible shape transitions—elongation, curvature inversion, budding, shedding—that emerge from the interplay of cytoskeletal forces, membrane mechanics, and motor activity. Despite decades of organelle-specific study, it remains unknown whether a common, quantitative 'morphodynamic grammar' governs how mesoscale cytoskeletal organization is translated into organelle shape across otherwise unrelated systems. Testing this requires reconciling two data types that are rarely combined: high-resolution static and time-resolved whole-cell volumetric imaging (soft X-ray tomography, cryo-electron tomography, lattice light-sheet, and correlative EM datasets now populating public repositories such as CIL, EMPIAR, and the Cell Image Library) and biophysical simulation outputs from agent-based and continuum models of cytoskeletal self-organization (actomyosin cortices, microtubule bundles, septin scaffolds) deposited in supplementary archives and modeling repositories. No single lab possesses both the breadth of curated whole-cell image datasets across organelle types and the diversity of validated cytoskeletal simulation frameworks needed to ask whether shape-change trajectories are governed by shared low-dimensional physical rules.

This working group will assemble and harmonize (1) publicly available 3D/4D organelle imaging datasets spanning cilia, mitochondria, nuclear envelope, and cortical actin systems, extracting standardized morphometric descriptors (curvature spectra, surface-area-to-volume trajectories, topological transition events) using automated segmentation and shape-quantification pipelines; and (2) simulation-derived shape and force trajectories from published agent-based and continuum cytoskeletal models, re-parameterized where necessary from reported model specifications to generate comparable synthetic morphodynamic time series. A central methodological innovation is the use of optimal-transport-based time series comparison (building on Gromov-Wasserstein type distances) to align organelle shape trajectories from disparate imaging modalities, temporal resolutions, and organelle identities into a shared morphodynamic space, and to compare these empirical trajectories against simulated trajectories from mechanistically distinct cytoskeletal models. We will then apply transfer learning: representations learned from the better-sampled, mechanistically well-characterized systems (e.g., ciliary shedding, actomyosin ring constriction) will be used to predict and interpret shape transitions in less-characterized organelle systems, testing whether cytoskeletal-force signatures inferred from simulation generalize across biological contexts.

The expected outcome is a data-derived taxonomy of mesoscale shape-transition classes and their associated cytoskeletal force signatures, clarifying whether phenomena such as whole-organelle shedding, curvature inversion, or symmetry-breaking site selection reflect convergent physical solutions to shared mechanical constraints rather than organelle-specific evolutionary innovations. This directly addresses the Center's mesoscale emergence mandate by linking molecular-scale cytoskeletal mechanics to cell-scale organelle phenotypes purely through synthesis of existing image and simulation data. The project requires collaboration between imaging-data curation expertise, biophysical modeling expertise, and time-series/optimal-transport methodology—capacities distributed across our team and beyond what either lab could assemble alone. All harmonized datasets, segmentation pipelines, distance metrics, and trained transfer-learning models will be released as open, versioned, reproducible workflows, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative imaging analysis and biophysical simulation, building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.
background_and_significance:
Membrane-bound organelles routinely undergo dramatic, stereotyped shape transitions that are essential to their function: cilia elongate, resorb, or are shed wholesale; mitochondria fission and fuse into networks with characteristic curvature profiles; the nuclear envelope buds and remodels during division and stress; cortical actin assemblies constrict, flow, and reorganize during cytokinesis and migration. Decades of organelle-specific research have identified the molecular players responsible for individual transitions—motor proteins, severing enzymes, membrane-shaping coat complexes, and cytoskeletal polymers—yet these findings remain siloed within organelle-specific literatures. It is unknown whether these seemingly distinct phenomena reflect a small set of shared physical solutions to common mechanical constraints (bending energy minimization, force-driven symmetry breaking, motor-generated stress redistribution) or whether each organelle system has evolved an independent, non-generalizable mechanism.

Answering this question has become newly tractable due to two independent, rapidly growing bodies of publicly available data. First, whole-cell volumetric imaging modalities—soft X-ray tomography, cryo-electron tomography, lattice light-sheet microscopy, and correlative light-electron microscopy—now populate public repositories (e.g., EMPIAR, the Cell Image Library, and related community resources) with three- and four-dimensional reconstructions of organelle geometry at sub-micron resolution across many cell types and genetic backgrounds. Second, decades of cytoskeletal biophysical modeling—agent-based simulations of actomyosin cortices, microtubule bundle self-organization, and septin scaffold assembly, alongside continuum mechanics treatments of contractile rings—have generated simulation outputs and parameterizations documented in publications and supplementary archives, but rarely compared systematically to empirical shape trajectories or to one another.

The central barrier is not a shortage of data but the absence of a shared analytical framework capable of aligning heterogeneous organelle shape trajectories—collected at different temporal resolutions, spatial scales, and imaging modalities—with heterogeneous simulation outputs generated under different modeling assumptions. This is precisely the kind of problem for which synthesis at scale, rather than additional primary data generation, is required: it demands curation and harmonization of dispersed imaging datasets, reinterpretation and re-parameterization of published simulation frameworks, and development of novel comparative methodology capable of bridging modalities. No single laboratory possesses simultaneously the breadth of organelle-imaging curation expertise and the diversity of validated cytoskeletal modeling frameworks necessary to test whether shape-change trajectories obey shared low-dimensional physical rules. This proposal directly addresses the Center's mandate to understand emergent mesoscale properties—the translation of molecular-scale cytoskeletal mechanics into cell-scale organelle phenotypes—through rigorous synthesis of existing public data, offering a rare opportunity to resolve a long-standing, cross-cutting puzzle in cell biology using resources that already exist but have never been integrated.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group is organized around one overarching question: Does a common, quantitative morphodynamic grammar govern the translation of mesoscale cytoskeletal organization into organelle shape change across otherwise unrelated biological systems? We decompose this into three specific research questions.

Question 1: Can organelle shape trajectories from structurally and temporally disparate imaging datasets (cilia, mitochondria, nuclear envelope, cortical actin) be projected into a shared, quantitatively comparable morphodynamic space? We hypothesize that curvature spectra, surface-area-to-volume trajectories, and topological transition events (e.g., budding, fission, whole-structure loss) extracted from heterogeneous volumetric datasets can be aligned using optimal-transport-based distances despite differences in imaging modality, resolution, and acquisition frequency, revealing recurring trajectory motifs shared across organelle identities.

Question 2: Do published cytoskeletal simulation frameworks—agent-based models of actomyosin and microtubule self-organization, continuum models of contractile ring dynamics, and septin scaffold models—generate force and shape trajectories that map onto the same low-dimensional morphodynamic space as empirical organelle data? We hypothesize that specific classes of cytoskeletal force regimes (e.g., depolymerization-coupled severing, motor-driven constriction, autocatalytic symmetry breaking) correspond to distinguishable, reproducible trajectory signatures in this shared space, and that mechanistically distinct simulations converge on similar signatures when the underlying force balance is analogous, supporting a convergent-solutions interpretation of organelle shape change.

Question 3: Can representations learned from well-characterized, densely sampled systems (e.g., ciliary shedding kinetics, actomyosin ring constriction) be transferred to predict or interpret shape transitions in less-characterized organelle systems (e.g., mitochondrial curvature inversion, nuclear envelope budding)? We hypothesize that transfer learning from data-rich systems will improve classification and interpretation of shape transitions in data-sparse systems beyond what can be achieved using each organelle dataset in isolation, and that transfer performance will be strongest for organelle pairs whose simulated force signatures are closest in the shared morphodynamic space—providing a testable, quantitative link between molecular mechanism and phenotypic outcome.

A unifying null hypothesis is that organelle shape trajectories are organelle-specific and do not cluster according to shared cytoskeletal force signatures; rejecting this null in favor of convergent, mechanism-linked clustering would constitute direct evidence for a generalizable mesoscale morphodynamic grammar. These questions cannot be answered by any single organelle-focused study; they require simultaneous access to curated imaging data across organelle types and a representative sampling of validated cytoskeletal simulation frameworks, motivating a working-group structure rather than a single-investigator effort.
methods_and_approach:
The project proceeds in three integrated phases, each relying exclusively on publicly available data and previously published models.

Phase 1 – Imaging data harmonization: We will systematically identify and curate 3D and 4D organelle imaging datasets spanning cilia, mitochondria, nuclear envelope, and cortical actin systems from public repositories including EMPIAR, the Cell Image Library, and associated supplementary data from soft X-ray tomography, cryo-electron tomography, and lattice light-sheet studies. Building on established deep-learning segmentation pipelines for volumetric data, we will apply and extend automated segmentation workflows to extract organelle surface meshes, from which standardized morphometric descriptors—curvature spectra, surface-area-to-volume ratios, and discrete topological transition events (fission, budding, whole-structure shedding)—will be computed. Datasets will be cataloged with metadata on modality, temporal resolution, and biological context to support downstream cross-modality comparison, following practices established in prior systematic curation of the whole-cell imaging literature.

Phase 2 – Simulation data reconstruction and re-parameterization: We will compile shape and force trajectories from published agent-based and continuum models of cytoskeletal self-organization, including actomyosin cortex reorganization, microtubule bundle dynamics, septin scaffold assembly, and contractile ring constriction. Where original simulation outputs are unavailable but model specifications are reported, we will reimplement models using documented parameter ranges and, where parameter constraints are underdetermined, apply Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to generate parameter sets consistent with reported qualitative behaviors, producing synthetic morphodynamic time series comparable in structure to the empirical dataset.

Phase 3 – Cross-modality alignment and transfer learning: To compare trajectories across organelle identities, imaging modalities, and simulation frameworks with differing dimensionality and temporal sampling, we will employ optimal-transport-based time series comparison methods, building on Gromov-Wasserstein-type distances and Fused Gromov-Wasserstein barycenters previously validated for oscillatory biological time series. This will yield a shared morphodynamic embedding space in which empirical and simulated trajectories can be directly compared and clustered. Transfer learning models will then be trained on data-rich, mechanistically well-characterized systems and evaluated on their ability to predict or classify shape transitions in less-characterized systems, with performance assessed via held-out validation and cross-organelle generalization tests.

Throughout, the working group will hold structured joint analysis sessions to reconcile domain-specific interpretation of morphometric features with modeling assumptions, ensuring biological plausibility is preserved at each computational step. All pipelines will be modular and version-controlled to support iterative refinement as additional public datasets are identified.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will produce a curated, harmonized repository of organelle shape trajectories and matched cytoskeletal simulation outputs; a validated optimal-transport-based framework for cross-modality, cross-organelle time series comparison; and a data-derived taxonomy of mesoscale shape-transition classes linked to specific cytoskeletal force signatures. A key scientific outcome will be a rigorous, quantitative test of whether phenomena such as whole-organelle shedding, curvature inversion, and symmetry-breaking site selection represent convergent physical solutions to shared mechanical constraints, resolving a question that has remained implicit but untested across separate organelle literatures. Methodologically, the transfer-learning framework developed here will offer a reusable strategy for interpreting shape dynamics in emerging or poorly characterized organelle systems using mechanistic insight borrowed from better-studied systems, with applicability extending beyond the organelles considered here to any membrane-bound compartment amenable to volumetric imaging. Scientifically, this directly advances the Center's mesoscale emergence mission by establishing whether higher-order cellular phenotypes can be explained by shared, low-dimensional physical rules linking molecular-scale cytoskeletal mechanics to organelle-scale outcomes. Practically, the harmonized datasets and pipelines will lower the barrier for future synthesis studies in cell morphology, providing a template for integrating static imaging, time-resolved imaging, and simulation data across biological systems. The project also demonstrates a generalizable model for community-scale synthesis: reconciling data types and modeling traditions that have historically remained disconnected due to disciplinary boundaries rather than technical infeasibility.
open_science_and_reproducibility: This project is built entirely on publicly available imaging datasets and previously published simulation frameworks, and will generate no new experimental data, consistent with NCEMS's synthesis mandate. All curated dataset catalogs, segmentation outputs, extracted morphometric descriptors, reconstructed simulation parameter sets, and shared morphodynamic embeddings will be deposited in open, version-controlled repositories with persistent identifiers, accompanied by structured metadata describing provenance, modality, and processing steps. All analysis code—including segmentation pipelines, optimal-transport distance computations, MCMC-based parameter reconstruction routines, and transfer-learning models—will be released under permissive open-source licenses with containerized environments to ensure computational reproducibility across platforms. We will adopt community standards for reporting volumetric imaging analyses, informed by prior systematic assessments of reporting practices in the whole-cell imaging literature, to ensure that curated datasets and derived descriptors are usable by the broader community. Intermediate outputs, including the harmonized morphodynamic embedding space, will be made available prior to final publication to enable community feedback and reuse. Analysis workflows will be documented as modular, well-annotated pipelines rather than monolithic scripts, explicitly designed to allow other research groups to incorporate additional organelle systems or simulation frameworks as new public data become available. All findings will be disseminated through open-access publications, with preprints posted at submission, and through public presentation of workflows at relevant computational biology and cell biology venues to maximize transparency and reuse.
budget_and_resources: Requested support will focus on personnel time, computational resources, and collaborative infrastructure rather than data generation. Primary costs include partial salary support for a postdoctoral researcher with expertise in image-based morphometrics and segmentation pipeline development, and a graduate student trainee focused on optimal-transport methodology and transfer-learning model development, both jointly mentored across the two participating labs to ensure integration of imaging and modeling perspectives. Computational resources include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation for large-scale volumetric segmentation, simulation reconstruction via MCMC sampling, and training of transfer-learning models on high-dimensional trajectory data. Modest funds are requested for data storage and repository hosting to support open deposition of harmonized datasets and derived products. Travel funds will support in-person working group meetings to coordinate cross-disciplinary integration between imaging-focused and modeling-focused personnel, as well as participation in relevant scientific meetings to disseminate methodology and recruit additional collaborators as the project identifies further relevant public datasets. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this project. The requested resources directly reflect the project's dependence on capabilities distributed across the two labs—whole-cell imaging curation and quantitative shape analysis on one hand, and cytoskeletal simulation and time-series methodology on the other—and the additional computational and personnel support needed to integrate them at the scale required to test a genuinely cross-organelle hypothesis, which exceeds what either lab could resource independently.
