author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Emergent Mesoscale Regulation of Torpor: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensates and Mitochondrial Reorganization in Independently Evolved Hibernators
abstract: Mammalian hibernation has evolved independently across at least eight lineages—including ursids, sciurid rodents, bats, and even a primate (the fat-tailed dwarf lemur)—yet all hibernators achieve strikingly similar phenotypes: reversible suppression of metabolic rate, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative activity at low body temperature, followed by rapid, damage-free rewarming. While comparative genomic scans have identified candidate genes under selection in hibernators, and tissue-level transcriptomic studies (including our own multi-tissue brown bear resource) have characterized pathway-level shifts in gene expression, little is known about whether convergent evolution acts at the mesoscale—the level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that sits between individual gene products and organismal physiology. Emerging evidence in non-hibernator systems shows that temperature- and stress-sensitive phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules, and reorganization of mitochondrial supercomplexes, can rapidly and reversibly reprogram translation and respiration without new transcription. We hypothesize that hibernators have convergently co-opted or tuned these mesoscale mechanisms as a shared molecular strategy for entering and exiting torpor, and that signatures of this convergence are detectable in existing genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets. This project will synthesize publicly available whole-genome assemblies and orthology databases (NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia), multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating relatives (SRA, GEO), and proteome-wide intrinsic disorder and phase-separation propensity predictions (e.g., catGRANULE, PScore, MobiDB) to build a cross-species map of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting proteins. We will test for convergent molecular signatures—accelerated evolution, shared amino acid substitutions, or parallel shifts in expression timing—in genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors across independently evolved hibernating lineages, using phylogenetic comparative methods that explicitly correct for shared ancestry versus convergence. Where available, we will integrate low-temperature in vitro transcriptomic and metabolic data (e.g., cultured fibroblast time-series data) to link predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization events to measured shifts in metabolic and circadian gene expression across torpor-arousal cycles. This effort requires expertise spanning comparative and population genomics, hibernation physiology and multi-tissue transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical modeling of protein phase behavior and mitochondrial dynamics—capacities that exceed any single lab and necessitate a working group uniting evolutionary genomicists, hibernation biologists, and biophysicists studying condensates and organelle-scale emergence. The synthesis directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale mandate by asking how molecular-scale, temperature-sensitive assembly processes give rise to an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) and whether this emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules. All genomic pipelines, orthology assignments, condensate-propensity scores, and comparative statistical frameworks will be released as open, reusable resources, providing a template for future mesoscale evolutionary synthesis studies and training opportunities for postdocs and graduate students at the interface of genomics, physiology, and biophysics.
background_and_significance: Hibernation is one of the most dramatic reversible phenotypic transitions in mammalian biology, involving coordinated suppression of metabolic rate, body temperature, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, followed by rapid, damage-free arousal. This capacity has arisen independently in at least eight mammalian lineages—ursids, several rodent clades, multiple bat lineages, and the fat-tailed dwarf lemur—representing a striking case of convergent evolution on a complex physiological state. Decades of comparative genomic and transcriptomic work have identified candidate genes and pathways associated with hibernation, including shifts in lipid metabolism, circadian regulation, and stress-response signaling. Multi-tissue and time-series transcriptomic resources, including publicly deposited brown bear datasets spanning active, hibernating, and fed states, have further revealed pathway-level reprogramming during torpor-arousal cycles. However, these studies operate primarily at the level of gene expression and sequence divergence, leaving a critical gap: whether convergent evolution also acts at the mesoscale, the organizational level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that mediates rapid, reversible cellular reprogramming without requiring new transcription or translation. Emerging biophysical literature demonstrates that many organisms use temperature- and stress-sensitive liquid-liquid phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules and related condensates to rapidly halt translation, and that mitochondrial supercomplex reorganization can rapidly modulate respiratory efficiency, both without new gene expression. These mechanisms are mechanistically well-suited to the rapid, reversible, and energy-conservative demands of torpor entry and arousal, yet they remain almost entirely unexplored in the context of hibernation evolution. This represents a significant conceptual gap: existing genomic and transcriptomic datasets, though extensive, have not been synthesized through a mesoscale lens capable of detecting convergent tuning of condensate-forming proteins or mitochondrial assembly factors across independently evolved hibernators. Addressing this gap requires integrating disparate public data types—whole-genome assemblies, orthology databases, multi-tissue and single-cell/time-series transcriptomes, and proteome-wide biophysical predictions—across taxonomically distant lineages, a task that exceeds the scope of any single laboratory's data, tools, or disciplinary expertise. This proposal directly addresses NCEMS's core scientific mandate by asking whether an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) arises from predictable, convergent tuning of molecular-scale assembly processes at the mesoscale. Successfully mapping such convergence would resolve a long-standing puzzle in hibernation biology—why phenotypically similar torpor states arise from divergent genomic backgrounds—while also providing a generalizable framework for detecting mesoscale convergence in other emergent cellular phenotypes, with translational relevance for metabolic disease, organ preservation, and induced hypometabolic states in non-hibernating species, including humans.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project is organized around three interconnected research questions targeting mesoscale convergence in hibernation biology. First, do genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins with high phase-separation propensity, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors show signatures of convergent molecular evolution—accelerated substitution rates, shared amino acid changes, or parallel shifts in selective constraint—across independently evolved hibernating lineages, relative to their non-hibernating sister taxa? We hypothesize that such convergence will be concentrated in intrinsically disordered regions governing condensate assembly and in mitochondrial contact-site proteins, reflecting repeated evolutionary tuning of mesoscale assembly properties rather than convergence at conserved catalytic residues. Second, do publicly available multi-tissue and time-series transcriptomic datasets from hibernators reveal coordinated expression dynamics of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-reorganization genes across the torpor-arousal cycle that are consistent with predicted phase-separation and supercomplex-remodeling behavior? We hypothesize that transcripts encoding high-propensity condensate proteins will show rapid, non-monotonic expression or translation-associated signatures timed to temperature transitions, distinguishing them from genes undergoing purely transcriptional reprogramming, and that this pattern will recur across taxonomically independent hibernators despite differences in tissue sampling and experimental design. Third, where in vitro time-series data are available (e.g., temperature-manipulated cultured fibroblasts), can we link predicted mesoscale reorganization events—condensate formation, mitochondrial supercomplex shifts—to measured changes in metabolic output and circadian gene expression, thereby establishing a mechanistic bridge between molecular-scale assembly and cellular-scale metabolic suppression? We hypothesize that temperature-dependent shifts in condensate-propensity scores will correlate with measured reductions in ATP production and altered circadian transcript timing, supporting a causal role for mesoscale reorganization in hypometabolic phenotypes. Underlying all three questions is an overarching hypothesis: hibernation represents a case in which natural selection has repeatedly and independently converged not on identical genetic solutions, but on shared mesoscale physical strategies—tunable, reversible, temperature-sensitive assembly and disassembly of protein and organelle structures—that provide a more evolutionarily accessible route to the shared phenotype than convergent point mutations in catalytic genes alone. Testing this hypothesis requires explicit phylogenetic comparative methods capable of distinguishing convergence from shared ancestry, applied jointly to sequence, expression, and biophysical prediction data, a synthesis task that no existing single dataset or single-lab analysis has undertaken. Confirming or refuting these hypotheses will directly inform whether mesoscale emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules, a question of central importance to NCEMS's broader effort to understand how molecular-scale organization gives rise to higher-order biological phenotypes across systems beyond hibernation.
methods_and_approach: This synthesis project will proceed in four integrated phases, drawing exclusively on publicly available data and analytical tools. Phase 1 will assemble a curated cross-species genomic resource by retrieving whole-genome assemblies and orthology calls for hibernating and non-hibernating sister taxa from NCBI, Ensembl, and the Zoonomia comparative genomics database, spanning ursids, sciurids, bats, and the fat-tailed dwarf lemur alongside closely related non-hibernating outgroups. Orthologous gene sets will be curated for stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors based on established annotation databases and literature curation. Phase 2 will apply proteome-wide biophysical prediction tools, including catGRANULE, PScore, and MobiDB, to score phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder for all curated orthologs across species, generating a comparative condensate-propensity matrix. Phase 3 will implement phylogenetic comparative methods, including branch-site models of molecular evolution (e.g., HyPhy, PAML) and convergence-detection frameworks that explicitly model shared ancestry, to test for accelerated evolution, parallel substitutions, or shifts in selective constraint at condensate- and mitochondria-associated loci across independently hibernating branches relative to non-hibernating lineages. Phase 4 will integrate existing multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets deposited in SRA and GEO, including multi-tissue brown bear expression atlases and time-series in vitro fibroblast datasets under temperature manipulation, to test whether expression dynamics of condensate- and mitochondria-associated transcripts show patterns consistent with mesoscale reorganization across the torpor-arousal cycle. Differential expression, co-expression network, and time-series trajectory analyses will be harmonized across datasets using batch-correction and meta-analytic frameworks suited to heterogeneous public data. Where in vitro metabolic measurements (e.g., ATP production time-series) are available, we will statistically test associations between predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization signatures and measured metabolic shifts using mixed-effects and time-series correlation models. Throughout, uncertainty from heterogeneous sequencing depth, assembly quality, and experimental design across public datasets will be explicitly modeled and reported. The working group will meet through structured virtual and in-person synthesis workshops to iteratively refine gene curation lists, computational pipelines, and statistical models, ensuring that evolutionary genomics, transcriptomics, and biophysical modeling expertise are jointly applied at each analytic stage rather than sequentially siloed. This tightly integrated, multi-domain workflow—requiring simultaneous fluency in comparative genomics, hibernation transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical prediction—is precisely the kind of cross-disciplinary synthesis that exceeds single-lab capacity and motivates the proposed NCEMS-supported working group structure, including regular consultation with NCEMS computational and data science staff to ensure scalable, reproducible implementation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will produce the first cross-species, mesoscale-focused synthesis of hibernation biology, generating a curated comparative dataset of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting orthologs across independently evolved hibernating lineages, together with associated phase-separation propensity scores, molecular evolution statistics, and expression trajectory annotations. A primary scientific outcome will be a rigorous test of whether convergent evolution in hibernators acts preferentially at the mesoscale rather than solely through canonical coding or regulatory changes, directly addressing a long-standing puzzle regarding the mechanistic basis of phenotypic convergence in torpor. If supported, this hypothesis will reframe hibernation as a model system for mesoscale evolutionary innovation, with implications extending to other reversible hypometabolic and stress-adaptive phenotypes across taxa. The resulting resources—curated ortholog sets, condensate-propensity matrices, and comparative evolutionary statistics—will provide a reusable foundation for future studies of induced hypometabolism relevant to therapeutic hypothermia, organ preservation, and metabolic disease research. Methodologically, the project will establish a generalizable analytical template for detecting mesoscale convergence by jointly leveraging genomic, transcriptomic, and biophysical prediction data, offering a model applicable to other emergent cellular phenotypes beyond hibernation. The working group structure will also generate durable interdisciplinary collaborations bridging evolutionary genomics, physiology, and biophysics, fields that rarely intersect methodologically. Trainees involved in the project will gain hands-on experience with comparative genomics pipelines, large-scale transcriptomic meta-analysis, and biophysical prediction tools, developing cross-disciplinary data science skills directly aligned with NCEMS's workforce training goals. Broader impacts include advancing conceptual understanding of how molecular-scale physical processes give rise to emergent organismal phenotypes, a question central to NCEMS's mesoscale research mandate, while providing openly available tools and datasets that will accelerate future synthesis research across the molecular and cellular sciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All aspects of this synthesis project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. Raw and processed public datasets used in this project—including genome assemblies, orthology tables, and transcriptomic datasets from NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia, SRA, and GEO—will be explicitly cited with persistent accession identifiers, and all derived data products, including curated ortholog lists, condensate-propensity matrices, and molecular evolution statistics, will be deposited in appropriate public repositories (e.g., Dryad, Zenodo) under permissive licenses. All computational pipelines, including genome annotation curation scripts, phylogenetic comparative analysis code, and transcriptomic meta-analysis workflows, will be developed using version-controlled, containerized environments (Git, Docker/Singularity) to ensure exact reproducibility across computing environments. Analysis workflows will be structured using literate programming frameworks (e.g., Jupyter, R Markdown) with full parameterization documented to enable independent replication and extension by outside researchers. Intermediate and final results, including statistical models and visualization code, will be made available through public code repositories with clear documentation and tutorials designed for reuse by future synthesis teams studying convergence or mesoscale phenomena in other systems. The working group will follow FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of all synthesized resources. Regular internal data and code audits will be conducted to verify pipeline reproducibility before public release. Findings will be disseminated through preprints and open-access publications, with preregistration of key comparative hypotheses where appropriate to enhance transparency. Training materials developed for trainees participating in the working group, including workshop materials on comparative genomics and biophysical prediction tools, will also be made publicly available to extend training impact beyond the immediate project team, consistent with NCEMS's mission to cultivate a broader, data-savvy scientific workforce equipped for reproducible, collaborative synthesis research.
budget_and_resources: This project requests NCEMS support primarily for personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative working group activities, reflecting its status as a data synthesis effort rather than a data generation project. Budget priorities include partial salary support for a postdoctoral researcher with expertise in comparative genomics and phylogenetic comparative methods, who will lead pipeline development and cross-species evolutionary analyses, and a graduate student trainee focused on transcriptomic meta-analysis and biophysical prediction integration, providing direct training opportunities central to NCEMS's workforce development goals. Modest computational resources are requested for cloud or high-performance computing access to support genome-scale orthology analyses, phylogenetic model fitting, and large-scale transcriptomic meta-analyses across multiple species and datasets. Funds are also requested to support two in-person working group synthesis workshops bringing together the evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, and biophysical modeling collaborators to jointly refine analytical frameworks, interpret emerging results, and coordinate manuscript and resource development; virtual meeting support will sustain collaboration between workshops. Additional funds will support open-access publication costs and data repository deposition fees to ensure full compliance with open science requirements. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with NCEMS's synthesis-only scope. The project will also benefit from NCEMS-provided computational consultation and data science training resources, which will enhance pipeline scalability and reproducibility. Existing institutional resources at each collaborating institution, including established computing clusters and prior genomic and transcriptomic datasets generated by team members, will be leveraged in-kind to minimize costs. This lean budget structure reflects the project's core identity as a cross-disciplinary synthesis effort whose primary needs are collaborative coordination, computational integration, and trainee support rather than new data collection, aligning directly with NCEMS's funding priorities for community-scale synthesis research.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Residue Couplings to Circuit Memory: A Cross-Scale Synthesis Linking Coevolutionary Statistics, Allosteric Dynamics, and Phase-Separation Propensity to Regulatory Network Hysteresis
abstract: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how local, residue-level physical couplings within individual proteins propagate upward to produce circuit-level emergent behaviors such as bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in gene regulatory networks. Existing work has separately characterized (i) coevolutionary statistical couplings among residues using Potts models and statistical coupling analysis across protein families, (ii) dynamic allosteric pathways and temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact networks extracted from molecular dynamics trajectories, (iii) sequence-encoded propensities for intrinsically disordered regions and biomolecular condensate formation, and (iv) network-level dynamical properties of transcriptional regulatory systems, including memory and irreversibility following perturbation. No study has yet asked whether these layers are mechanistically linked: does the architecture of coevolutionary coupling and conformational dynamics within individual regulatory proteins predict which nodes of a transcriptional network will exhibit hysteretic, switch-like, or irreversible behavior? This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to test that hypothesis by integrating four classes of publicly available data that no single lab currently combines: (1) multiple sequence alignments and derived direct-coupling/statistical-coupling matrices for transcription factors and signaling proteins (Pfam, UniProt); (2) publicly deposited molecular dynamics trajectories and contact-network datasets for homologous or orthologous regulatory and allosteric proteins (e.g., MDDB, GPCRmd, Dynameomics-type repositories); (3) curated intrinsically disordered region and condensate-propensity annotations (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB) for the same protein families; and (4) reconstructed bacterial regulatory network topologies and previously published perturbation-response datasets characterizing irreversibility and hysteresis in transcriptional circuits (e.g., RegulonDB/EcoCyc-derived networks). Using information-theoretic measures of coupling entropy and coevolutionary sector structure alongside graph-theoretic and machine-learning analyses of MD-derived allosteric pathways (including random-forest classifiers previously validated for predicting channel-gating states), we will quantify whether proteins with strong long-range coevolutionary coupling and multistable dynamic ensembles are disproportionately embedded in network motifs associated with hysteresis and irreversibility, and whether disorder/condensate propensity modulates this relationship by providing an additional slow, cooperative mode of regulatory memory. The synthesis will produce an open, versioned, FAIR-compliant multi-scale dataset and analysis pipeline—a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas'—linking residue-level statistical physics, protein dynamics, mesoscale assembly propensity, and network dynamics for a curated set of well-characterized regulatory systems. This effort requires collaboration across evolutionary systems biology, coevolutionary sequence statistics, computational biophysics/MD, and data infrastructure expertise, exceeding what any single lab's data or toolset can address, and will generate testable, falsifiable predictions about which molecular architectures give rise to emergent network-level memory. Training modules will teach graduate students and postdocs to integrate sequence-based statistical models, trajectory-based dynamics, and network reconstruction within reproducible open-science workflows, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand how mesoscale molecular organization gives rise to cellular-scale emergent properties.
background_and_significance: Emergent behaviors in gene regulatory networks—bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching—are among the most consequential mesoscale phenomena in cell biology, underlying processes from bacterial adaptation to developmental commitment. Prior network analyses have established that certain transcriptional circuits, particularly those built around positive-feedback motifs, exhibit memory: once perturbed, they fail to return to their original state even after the perturbing signal is removed. Reconstructed regulatory networks in model organisms such as Escherichia coli have been used to predict which genes, upon transient perturbation, will show such irreversibility, implicating proximity to positive circuits as a key structural determinant. However, this network-level description treats each regulatory protein as a node with fixed logical function, abstracting away the residue-level biophysics that actually implements switching behavior. In parallel, an entirely separate research tradition has used coevolutionary statistical models—Potts-model direct coupling analysis and statistical coupling analysis—to identify collectively evolving residue networks (sectors) within protein families, linking these sectors to allosteric communication, functional constraint, and evolvability. A third tradition, rooted in molecular dynamics simulation, has characterized how temperature-, ligand-, and mutation-sensitive contact networks reconfigure dynamically to produce multistable conformational ensembles, with graph-theoretic and machine-learning approaches now able to classify gating or activation states directly from simulated contact patterns. A fourth body of work has shown that intrinsically disordered regions and condensate-forming sequences confer additional slow, cooperative modes of assembly and disassembly, potentially serving as an independent memory mechanism operating on timescales relevant to cellular decision-making. Despite deep individual maturity, these four literatures remain unconnected. No existing study asks whether the coevolutionary architecture and dynamic multistability of a regulatory protein itself predicts whether the network node it occupies will behave hysteretically. This is a fundamental gap in understanding emergence: circuit-level memory is currently explained structurally (network topology) without reference to the molecular biophysics of the proteins that implement it, while molecular-level multistability is characterized without reference to its systems-level consequences. Bridging these scales requires simultaneous access to curated sequence alignments and coupling matrices, deposited MD trajectories for homologous regulatory proteins, disorder/condensate annotations, and previously published network perturbation-response datasets—resources that are individually public but have never been integrated within a single analytical framework. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in coevolutionary statistics, biomolecular simulation analysis, disorder/condensate bioinformatics, and regulatory network reconstruction necessary to perform this synthesis, nor the computational infrastructure to harmonize these heterogeneous, large-scale public datasets. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by testing whether mesoscale molecular organization—residue coupling architecture, conformational multistability, and condensate propensity—systematically gives rise to a higher-order cellular property, regulatory network memory, using exclusively existing public data through cross-disciplinary, collaborative synthesis.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project is organized around one overarching question and three linked sub-questions, each addressed through synthesis of existing public datasets rather than new experimentation. Overarching question: Does the residue-level physical and evolutionary architecture of a regulatory protein predict whether the network node it occupies exhibits hysteretic or irreversible behavior following perturbation? Sub-question 1 (Coevolutionary architecture and network position): Are transcription factors and signaling proteins with strong, long-range coevolutionary coupling—indexed by sector size, coupling entropy, and direct-coupling network connectivity derived from Potts models and statistical coupling analysis—preferentially found at nodes embedded in positive-feedback motifs previously associated with irreversibility in reconstructed bacterial regulatory networks? We hypothesize that long-range coevolutionary coupling reflects an evolved capacity for concerted, cooperative conformational transitions, and that this capacity is enriched among proteins occupying hysteretic network positions, because such positions place a premium on robust, switch-like molecular responses. Sub-question 2 (Dynamic multistability and switching behavior): Do molecular dynamics-derived contact-network signatures of multistability—quantified via graph-theoretic descriptors of alternative contact states and validated by machine-learning classifiers previously shown to predict gating states in ion channels—correlate with the degree of hysteresis observed at the corresponding network node? We hypothesize that proteins whose simulated ensembles show clearly separable, temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact states will map onto network nodes with sharper, more bistable perturbation-response curves, because discrete conformational states provide a molecular implementation of discrete regulatory logic states. Sub-question 3 (Disorder/condensate propensity as an additional memory channel): Does the presence of condensate-forming intrinsically disordered regions in a regulatory protein modulate the relationship between coevolutionary/dynamic architecture and network hysteresis, either by amplifying switch-like behavior through cooperative assembly or by providing an independent, structure-decoupled memory mechanism? We hypothesize that disorder/condensate propensity acts as a secondary, slower memory channel, most influential at nodes where folded-domain coupling and dynamics alone predict weak hysteresis, thereby explaining outlier cases in the network dataset. These questions are deliberately falsifiable: a null result—no statistical association between coevolutionary/dynamic signatures and network hysteresis—would itself be highly informative, indicating that circuit-level memory arises predominantly from topological rather than molecular constraints, and redirecting the field's causal model of emergence. Because each sub-question requires integrating data types that are curated and maintained by different scientific communities (sequence databases, simulation repositories, disorder/condensate databases, and regulatory network reconstructions), no single laboratory's existing data holdings are sufficient to test them. The working group is explicitly structured to bring together complementary expertise in molecular evolution and coevolutionary statistics, computational biophysics and MD-based machine learning, phase-separation and condensate biology, and regulatory network dynamics, ensuring that each sub-question is addressed with methodological rigor appropriate to its data type while remaining integrated within a single cross-scale analytical framework.
methods_and_approach: The project proceeds in four coordinated phases, each built entirely on curation and reanalysis of existing public resources. Phase 1 – Protein family and dataset curation: We will assemble a curated set of regulatory and allosteric proteins with (a) available multiple sequence alignments in Pfam/UniProt suitable for direct-coupling analysis, (b) at least one publicly deposited MD trajectory or trajectory ensemble for a homologous or orthologous structure, (c) disorder/condensate annotations in DisProt, MobiDB, or PhaSepDB, and (d) a mapped node in a reconstructed bacterial regulatory network (RegulonDB/EcoCyc) with previously published perturbation-response data. Cross-referencing these databases via UniProt identifiers and structural homology mapping will define the tractable intersection dataset, prioritizing transcription factors and sensor/signaling proteins with the richest cross-database coverage. Phase 2 – Coevolutionary and dynamic feature extraction: For each protein family, we will compute Potts-model direct coupling matrices and statistical coupling analysis sectors from existing alignments, deriving quantitative descriptors of coupling range, sector size, and coupling entropy. In parallel, for proteins with deposited MD trajectories, we will apply established multi-ensemble contact-network analysis, graph-theoretic descriptors of alternative contact states, and previously validated random-forest classifiers to quantify conformational multistability and identify allosteric pathways connecting coupled residues to functional sites. Disorder and condensate propensity scores will be extracted directly from curated database annotations without additional computation. Phase 3 – Network hysteresis quantification: Using previously published perturbation-response datasets and reconstructed network topologies, we will quantify, for each mapped node, the degree of irreversibility following transient perturbation, replicating and extending existing network-analysis pipelines that link circuit position (e.g., proximity to positive-feedback loops) to memory behavior. Phase 4 – Cross-scale statistical integration: We will use multivariate regression, information-theoretic association measures, and machine-learning models (trained and validated with cross-validation across protein families to avoid phylogenetic confounds) to test whether coevolutionary coupling descriptors and MD-derived multistability metrics predict network hysteresis scores, and whether disorder/condensate propensity provides additional predictive power or interacts with the other two feature classes. Robustness will be assessed via family-holdout validation, permutation testing against random network rewiring, and sensitivity analyses across alternative coupling-matrix inference methods. All code, intermediate feature matrices, and integrated datasets will be version-controlled and containerized to support exact reproducibility. Data harmonization challenges—differing residue numbering schemes, structural coverage gaps in MD datasets, and inconsistent disorder-annotation granularity—will be addressed through a shared mapping ontology maintained collaboratively by the working group, itself a key deliverable of the synthesis effort.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis will produce the first cross-scale, empirically grounded dataset and analytical pipeline linking residue-level coevolutionary architecture, protein conformational dynamics, disorder/condensate propensity, and regulatory network memory. The primary scientific deliverable, a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas,' will provide quantitative, falsifiable evidence for or against the hypothesis that molecular-level coupling architecture predicts circuit-level hysteresis, reframing how emergent network behaviors are explained mechanistically. Regardless of directionality, results will refine causal models of regulatory network dynamics: a positive association would establish molecular biophysical signatures as predictive features for identifying hysteretic nodes in uncharacterized networks, with implications for synthetic biology circuit design and antimicrobial target prioritization; a null or partial association would clarify the relative contribution of topology versus molecular implementation in producing network memory, redirecting future mechanistic studies. The integrated pipeline itself constitutes a durable community resource, enabling other researchers to extend the analysis to additional protein families, organisms, or perturbation datasets without re-deriving the harmonization infrastructure. By explicitly linking statistical genetics, biophysical simulation, and systems biology methodologies, the project advances NCEMS's mesoscale emergence agenda, demonstrating a generalizable template for cross-scale synthesis applicable to other emergent cellular phenomena. The collaborative structure—requiring coordinated expertise unavailable in any single lab—exemplifies the transdisciplinary, data-synthesis model NCEMS seeks to catalyze, while trainee involvement in each analytical layer builds a workforce fluent in integrating sequence, structure, dynamics, and network data.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All aspects of this synthesis will adhere to FAIR data principles and community-endorsed open, team, and reproducible science practices. Because the project uses exclusively public data, full provenance tracking from original source (Pfam, UniProt, MD trajectory repositories, DisProt/MobiDB/PhaSepDB, RegulonDB/EcoCyc) through each transformation step will be maintained using version-controlled workflows and containerized computational environments to guarantee exact reproducibility across computing platforms. Coevolutionary coupling matrices, extracted MD-derived contact-network features, disorder/condensate annotations, and network hysteresis scores will be deposited as harmonized, versioned datasets in an open repository with persistent identifiers, accompanied by comprehensive metadata describing residue-numbering mappings and structural homology assignments. All analysis code—including coupling-matrix inference scripts, graph-theoretic and machine-learning pipelines, and statistical integration models—will be released under permissive open-source licenses with executable notebooks enabling independent replication of every reported result. Consistent with emerging community standards for biomolecular simulation data management, MD-derived features will be documented following FAIR-compliant simulation metadata conventions to maximize reuse by the broader biophysics community. The working group will hold regular open lab meetings and pre-register key analytical decisions (feature definitions, validation splits, statistical thresholds) prior to full-scale analysis to guard against post hoc bias. Intermediate and final datasets, along with the coupling-to-circuit atlas, will be made publicly available on submission of manuscripts, with preprints posted concurrently. Documentation will be written for reuse by non-specialists, including tutorials suitable for trainees new to any one of the four constituent data modalities, ensuring the resource serves both as a scientific product and as an educational platform.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget supports a distributed working group requiring computational, personnel, and coordination resources beyond individual lab capacity. Personnel costs will fund two postdoctoral researchers (bridging coevolutionary statistics/network biology and computational biophysics/MD analysis, respectively) and two graduate student trainees embedded across partner labs, ensuring cross-training in all four data modalities. Computational resources include allocation on high-performance computing clusters for reprocessing publicly deposited MD trajectories and running graph-theoretic/machine-learning pipelines at scale, plus cloud storage for hosting harmonized intermediate datasets and the final coupling-to-circuit atlas with redundant backup. Modest funds are requested for data engineering support to build and maintain the cross-database identifier mapping and metadata harmonization infrastructure central to this synthesis, a task requiring dedicated effort distinct from domain-specific scientific analysis. Travel funds will support twice-yearly in-person working group meetings to coordinate analytical decisions, resolve cross-database harmonization challenges, and conduct joint trainee workshops, alongside conference travel to disseminate results to evolutionary biology, biophysics, and systems biology communities. A small allocation is dedicated to open-access publication fees and repository deposition costs to ensure all deliverables remain freely available. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal. The requested resources are proportionate to a multi-institutional, multi-year collaborative effort and reflect genuine infrastructure and personnel needs that exceed what any single participating laboratory currently supports, justifying NCEMS's distinctive role in enabling this cross-disciplinary, data-integrative research program.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Flux, Function, and Fitness: A Cross-Species Synthesis Linking Genome-Scale Metabolic Network Architecture to Signatures of Natural Selection
abstract: A central puzzle in molecular evolution is why some metabolic genes are under strong purifying selection while others tolerate substantial standing variation, and why certain pathways repeatedly become targets of adaptive selection across independent lineages. We propose that this puzzle can be resolved by treating metabolism as a mesoscale emergent system: the topological and flux-based organization of genome-scale metabolic networks (GSMs)—modularity, flux coupling, redundancy, and control-coefficient distributions—should predict the strength and mode of selection acting on the underlying genes, and conversely, recurrent environmental pressures (diet, temperature, nutrient stress, immune activation) should preferentially reshape specific network modules. This hypothesis has never been tested systematically because it requires integrating two data ecosystems that rarely intersect: curated genome-scale metabolic reconstructions (BiGG, AGORA2, ModelSEED, KBase) and population-genomic diversity/selection datasets (1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD, SNP-chip panels from adaptation studies, and model-organism diversity panels for yeast, Arabidopsis, and maize). Synthesizing these resources demands expertise that no single lab possesses: constraint-based metabolic modeling and flux-variability/flux-coupling analysis, population genetic inference of selection (site-frequency-spectrum statistics, iHS, dN/dS, and simulation-trained deep learning classifiers such as GAN/CNN discriminators), and machine-learning interpretability methods to link network-derived features to genomic signal. Our working group will assemble a cross-species compendium pairing existing GSMs with publicly available selection-scan outputs for the same organisms and genes, computing per-reaction/per-gene topological metrics (centrality, flux control coefficients, module membership, redundancy/backup pathway counts) from steady-state and context-specific models (including previously published macrophage and maize nitrogen-stress GSMs) and aligning them with locus-specific selection statistics. We will use interpretable convolutional and tree-based classifiers, building on existing GAN/CNN selection-inference pipelines, to test whether network position predicts selection strength independent of gene expression breadth or essentiality, and to identify whether known adaptive sweeps (e.g., FADS1/FADS2 fatty-acid desaturase selection in Arctic populations, TBX15/WARS2 archaic introgression affecting adipose metabolism) preferentially localize to specific mesoscale structures such as flux-bottleneck reactions or lipid-metabolism modules with limited redundancy. A second aim will extend this framework comparatively across humans, crops, and microbes to ask whether 'evolvability hotspots' in metabolic architecture are conserved across kingdoms or are lineage-specific consequences of network rewiring. This project uses exclusively existing public data, requires collaborative integration of metabolic modeling and population-genomic inference pipelines that individually exist in different communities, and will produce an open, reproducible workflow and annotated cross-species dataset linking network architecture to evolutionary constraint. Beyond resolving a long-standing question about the evolutionary logic of metabolic robustness, the framework offers a predictive tool for metabolic engineering—flagging which reactions are evolutionarily malleable versus constrained—and provides rich training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs to gain dual fluency in systems biology and population genomics, directly building the interdisciplinary, data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.
background_and_significance: Metabolic networks constitute a paradigmatic mesoscale system: thousands of individual enzymatic reactions, encoded by distinct genes, are wired into pathways and modules whose emergent flux behavior determines organismal fitness in ways that cannot be predicted from any single gene in isolation. Decades of population genetics have documented striking heterogeneity in selective constraint across metabolic genes—some enzymes are nearly invariant across billions of years of divergence, while paralogous or pathway-adjacent genes accumulate substantial standing variation and repeatedly serve as substrates for local adaptation (e.g., lactase persistence, FADS1/FADS2 desaturase variation in Arctic and other populations, alcohol dehydrogenase variation across human and Drosophila lineages). Parallel advances in systems biology have produced genome-scale metabolic (GSM) reconstructions for hundreds of organisms, enabling precise, mechanistic characterization of network topology, flux coupling, redundancy, and control-coefficient distributions. Despite the obvious complementarity of these two literatures, they have developed almost entirely in isolation: population geneticists rarely incorporate flux-based network architecture into models of selection, and metabolic modelers rarely test whether their computed topological metrics carry evolutionary signal. This disconnect represents both a scientific and an infrastructural gap. Scientifically, we lack a mechanistic account of why metabolic robustness (redundancy, alternate flux routes, low control coefficients) should buffer certain genes from selection while flux-bottleneck reactions—by analogy to network theory in other biological contexts—might be disproportionately exposed to both purifying and positive selection. Infrastructurally, testing this hypothesis requires simultaneously fluent handling of constraint-based modeling formats (SBML, COBRA-compatible reconstructions), population-scale variant call data, and machine learning frameworks trained on coalescent or forward-simulation output—a combination of skills that is essentially never resident in a single laboratory. Our working group is uniquely positioned to close this gap: it combines expertise in genome-scale metabolic reconstruction and constraint-based flux analysis with population genetic inference of selection using both classical statistics and modern simulation-trained deep learning classifiers. This synthesis is explicitly a mesoscale emergence problem in the sense central to NCEMS's mission: the network-level organization of metabolism, an emergent property of thousands of molecular interactions, shapes higher-order evolutionary outcomes at the level of the gene, the pathway, and ultimately the organism's adaptive trajectory. Resolving why certain network positions are evolutionary hotspots while others are frozen would settle a long-debated puzzle in molecular evolution and, simultaneously, generate a predictive framework of direct value to metabolic engineering, agricultural genomics, and precision medicine, where knowing which reactions are evolutionarily malleable versus constrained informs the design of robust synthetic pathways and the interpretation of disease-associated metabolic variants.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will address three interlocking research questions using exclusively existing, publicly available data. RQ1: Does the topological and flux-based position of a gene within a genome-scale metabolic network predict the strength and mode of natural selection acting on that gene, independent of confounders such as expression breadth, essentiality, and gene age? We hypothesize that genes encoding reactions with high flux control coefficients, low structural redundancy, and central positions within tightly coupled modules experience stronger purifying selection, reflected in reduced nucleotide diversity, lower dN/dS, and depleted rare-variant load in population-scale sequencing panels (1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD). Conversely, we hypothesize that genes in peripheral, redundant, or weakly coupled network positions show relaxed constraint and are disproportionately represented among loci bearing signatures of recent positive selection (elevated iHS, extended haplotype homozygosity, or population-differentiation statistics), because such positions permit adaptive exploration without destabilizing core network flux. RQ2: Do recurrent environmental pressures—dietary shifts, thermal stress, nutrient limitation, and immune activation—preferentially target specific, identifiable mesoscale modules (e.g., lipid metabolism, nitrogen assimilation, redox balance) rather than being randomly distributed across the metabolic network? We hypothesize that well-documented adaptive sweeps such as FADS1/FADS2 variation associated with dietary polyunsaturated fatty acid intake in Arctic populations, and the TBX15/WARS2 archaic-introgressed haplotype affecting adipose differentiation, occupy flux-bottleneck reactions or modules with constrained redundancy, and that this pattern generalizes to independently evolved selection signals in maize under nitrogen stress and in microbial genomes under nutrient or host-immune pressure. RQ3: Are 'evolvability hotspots'—network positions disproportionately enriched for adaptive selection—conserved across kingdoms as an intrinsic property of metabolic network architecture, or are they lineage-specific outcomes of differential network rewiring during evolutionary history? We hypothesize a partial conservation model: core, highly connected reactions central to universal pathways (e.g., glycolysis, TCA cycle) will show consistently strong purifying selection across humans, plants, and microbes, whereas peripheral biosynthetic modules subject to lineage-specific environmental pressures (fatty acid desaturation in humans, nitrogen assimilation in maize, biodegradative pathways in bacteria such as Rhodopseudomonas palustris) will show kingdom-specific evolvability signatures shaped by each lineage's ecological history. Each hypothesis is directly testable through synthesis of existing reconstructions and selection-scan datasets, and each requires the combined constraint-based modeling and population-genomic inference expertise assembled in this proposal, satisfying the requirement that the work exceed what any individual laboratory or existing collaboration could accomplish alone.
methods_and_approach: The working group will execute a three-phase synthesis pipeline built entirely on existing public resources. Phase 1 (Data Compendium Construction): We will assemble a cross-species compendium pairing curated GSM reconstructions from BiGG, AGORA2, ModelSEED, and KBase (including previously published context-specific human macrophage and maize nitrogen-stress models) with gene-level identifiers harmonized against population-genomic resources including 1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD, adaptation-focused SNP-chip panels (e.g., Greenlandic Inuit cohorts), and diversity panels for yeast, Arabidopsis, and maize. Careful ortholog and gene-identifier mapping (via Ensembl Compara, KEGG orthology, and UniProt cross-references) will ensure that network-derived and population-genomic features refer to the same loci across organisms. Phase 2 (Feature Computation): For each reconstruction, we will compute standardized topological and flux-based metrics using constraint-based modeling tools (COBRApy, flux variability analysis, flux coupling analysis) including reaction centrality, flux control coefficients, module membership (via community detection on flux-coupled reaction graphs), and redundancy/backup pathway counts. In parallel, we will compute or extract population genetic summary statistics (nucleotide diversity, Tajima's D, dN/dS, iHS, cross-population differentiation) from public variant call datasets, and where simulation-trained classifiers are advantageous, we will adapt existing GAN/CNN selection-inference pipelines, retrained on coalescent simulations appropriate to each species' demographic history, to generate probabilistic selection calls at each locus. Phase 3 (Integration and Modeling): We will merge network-derived and evolutionary features into unified per-gene tables and apply interpretable machine learning—gradient-boosted trees and shallow CNNs with SHAP-based feature attribution—to test whether network position predicts selection signal after controlling for known confounders (expression breadth from public transcriptomic atlases, essentiality from knockout/fitness screens, evolutionary rate baselines). We will specifically test enrichment of known adaptive loci (FADS1/FADS2, TBX15/WARS2) within predicted evolvability hotspots, and extend cross-kingdom comparison using matched analyses in maize and microbial systems. All statistical models will include permutation-based null distributions generated from randomized network topologies to guard against structural confounds. Milestones include: compendium release (months 1–6), feature computation and validation (months 6–14), integrative modeling and hypothesis testing (months 14–22), and cross-kingdom comparative synthesis and manuscript preparation (months 22–30). Regular working group meetings (biweekly video, twice-yearly in-person) will ensure iterative cross-disciplinary quality control between metabolic modelers and population geneticists at each phase.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis will produce four concrete outputs. First, an open, versioned cross-species compendium linking genome-scale metabolic network features to population-genomic selection statistics, structured for reuse by both the systems biology and population genetics communities. Second, a validated, interpretable machine learning framework quantifying the relationship between network architecture and evolutionary constraint, generalizable to newly released reconstructions or selection scans without requiring new experimental data. Third, a set of empirically grounded 'evolvability maps' for human, plant, and microbial metabolism identifying specific modules and reactions as constrained versus malleable, directly informing metabolic engineering strain-design efforts by flagging targets more likely to tolerate genetic intervention without unpredictable fitness costs. Fourth, a resolution—or substantial refinement—of a decades-old puzzle regarding heterogeneous selective pressure across metabolic genes, reframed through the lens of network-level emergent constraint rather than gene-by-gene analysis alone. Scientifically, this reframes metabolic evolution as a mesoscale phenomenon, directly advancing NCEMS's core mission of understanding emergent properties bridging molecular and cellular scales. Practically, the predictive evolvability framework has direct translational relevance to synthetic biology, crop improvement under environmental stress, and interpretation of human disease-associated metabolic variants. The project's cross-disciplinary design—uniting constraint-based modeling and population genomic inference—will also produce a template methodology other synthesis teams can adapt to different molecular subsystems, and will generate publicly documented training materials that lower the barrier for future researchers to work across these traditionally separate fields, fulfilling NCEMS's mandate to cultivate an interdisciplinary, data-fluent research workforce.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All data used in this project are already public; no new experimental data will be generated. We commit to depositing the full harmonized cross-species compendium, including gene-identifier mapping tables, computed network metrics, and extracted population genetic statistics, in a public, version-controlled repository (Zenodo/GitHub with DOI-minted releases) under permissive open licenses compatible with source data terms. All analysis code—COBRA-based flux analysis scripts, population genetic statistic pipelines, and machine learning training/evaluation code—will be developed in containerized, dependency-pinned environments (Docker/Conda) and released alongside detailed computational notebooks documenting each analytical step, following FAIR and community-endorsed reproducible-science standards. We will adopt a pre-registration approach for the primary hypothesis tests in RQ1–RQ3, specifying confound-control variables and null-model construction prior to full-scale analysis, with any post hoc analyses clearly flagged as exploratory. Intermediate outputs (per-gene feature tables, trained classifier weights, permutation null distributions) will be archived at each project milestone to support independent verification and reanalysis. We will hold data and workflows to community standards emerging from the genomics (GA4GH) and metabolic modeling (COMBINE/SBML) communities, ensuring interoperability with existing public infrastructure such as BiGG, KBase, and public variant repositories. Documentation will be written with training use in mind, including annotated tutorials suitable for graduate coursework, explicitly supporting NCEMS's goal of building a data-savvy workforce capable of working across systems biology and population genetics. A public project website will track compendium releases, code versions, and links to all downstream publications, and we will submit software tools to appropriate community registries (e.g., Bioconda, PyPI) to maximize long-term accessibility and reuse well beyond the funding period.
budget_and_resources: This proposal requests support calibrated to a data-synthesis working group rather than a data-generation project, reflecting NCEMS's emphasis on computational and personnel resources over experimental costs. Primary budget categories include: (1) Personnel—partial salary support for one postdoctoral researcher with dual training in constraint-based modeling and population genetics to serve as the integrative lead, and graduate student support at each partner institution to enable direct mentorship and cross-training in both domains; (2) Computational Infrastructure—cloud computing credits or institutional high-performance computing allocations for flux variability/coupling analyses across hundreds of GSM reconstructions and for training/retraining CNN and GAN-based selection classifiers on large population genomic datasets; (3) Working Group Coordination—travel support for two in-person working group meetings per year to enable intensive collaborative integration sessions, plus videoconferencing infrastructure for biweekly virtual meetings; (4) Data and Software Management—modest costs for repository hosting, DOI minting, and long-term archival storage of the compendium and derived datasets beyond standard institutional allocations; (5) Dissemination—support for open-access publication fees and presentation of results at relevant systems biology and population genetics conferences to maximize cross-community visibility. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this project. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained, structured collaboration across historically separate research communities—constraint-based metabolic modeling and population genomic inference—along with computational resources and coordination infrastructure exceeding what any single laboratory's existing grants provide. The requested resources are scaled to enable full execution of the three-phase pipeline (compendium construction, feature computation, integrative modeling) within a 30-month period, with built-in flexibility to extend cross-kingdom comparative analyses should early results reveal additional promising directions warranting deeper investigation.
