author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Mesoscale Coordination of Proteome Turnover: Synthesizing Public Degradation Kinetics with Complex, Condensate, and Disorder Architecture to Discover Emergent Proteostasis Modules
abstract: Protein turnover—the balance of synthesis and degradation—has been measured in hundreds of public datasets using SILAC, dynamic SILAC, 15N/heavy-water metabolic labeling, and pulse-chase mass spectrometry across yeast, mouse tissues, human cell lines, and iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. These datasets, generated by dozens of independent labs under different physiological conditions (oxidative stress, hypoxia/hyperoxia, aging, cardiovascular disease models), are rarely integrated with structural and interaction data that describe how proteins are organized at the mesoscale—as stable complexes, transient assemblies, or biomolecular condensates. We propose to build a unified, harmonized turnover atlas that cross-references public half-life datasets with complex membership (CORUM, hu.MAP, BioGRID), intrinsic disorder annotations (MobiDB, IUPred-derived scores), liquid-liquid phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB), and tissue/single-cell expression atlases (Human Protein Atlas, GTEx). Our central question is whether mesoscale organization is a primary determinant of emergent proteostatic behavior: do subunits within stable complexes exhibit coordinated (concerted) degradation kinetics that buffer stoichiometric imbalance, while orphan or condensate-resident proteins show discordant, individually regulated turnover? We hypothesize that loss of this coordination—rather than changes in individual protein half-lives—constitutes an emergent signature of proteostatic collapse in aging and disease, distinguishable only when turnover data are analyzed jointly with structural context rather than protein-by-protein. To test this, we will (1) computationally harmonize turnover rate constants across >30 public datasets spanning organisms, tissues, and physiological perturbations (oxygen tension, replicative and organismal aging, ER/oxidative stress, cardiomyopathy models) using batch-correction and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to place disparate experimental designs on a common kinetic scale; (2) quantify turnover concordance within known complexes and condensates versus size-matched control sets of unrelated proteins, testing whether concordance scales with disorder content, complex stoichiometry, and evolutionary conservation; (3) map how concordance is perturbed under stress and aging conditions already profiled in existing datasets, identifying mesoscale modules whose turnover synchrony breaks down first; and (4) validate cross-tissue generalizability using existing in vivo turnover measurements from heart, lung, and brain under varying oxygen tension and cardiovascular disease models. This effort requires expertise spanning classical proteomic turnover measurement and kinetic modeling, translation and stress-response systems biology, structural/disorder bioinformatics, and cardiovascular tissue-specific proteomics—none of which resides in a single lab, and none of which has previously been assembled at this scale. The project will produce an open, versioned turnover-mesoscale database and reproducible analytical pipeline (containerized, deposited on GitHub/Zenodo), enabling the community to query turnover coordination for any complex, condensate, or disease gene set. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-lab data harmonization, hierarchical Bayesian kinetic modeling, and structural bioinformatics integration, directly building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously inaccessible question about how molecular-scale turnover gives rise to emergent, mesoscale proteostatic robustness and its breakdown in aging and disease.
background_and_significance: Cellular proteostasis depends not merely on the absolute rate at which individual proteins are synthesized and degraded, but on how these rates are coordinated across functionally related sets of proteins. Over the past fifteen years, metabolic labeling approaches—including SILAC, dynamic SILAC, stable isotope (15N) and heavy-water labeling, and pulse-chase mass spectrometry—have generated proteome-wide half-life measurements spanning budding yeast, primary mouse tissues, human cell lines, and increasingly complex model systems such as iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. These datasets have accumulated across dozens of independent studies covering diverse physiological states, including oxidative and hypoxic stress, organismal and replicative aging, and disease models relevant to cardiovascular and neurodegenerative pathology. Individually, each dataset has advanced understanding of protein-specific turnover regulation. Collectively, however, they remain an underexploited resource: turnover measurements are rarely placed in a common kinetic framework across studies, and even more rarely cross-referenced with independent structural and organizational annotations describing how proteins physically associate at the mesoscale—as members of stable multiprotein complexes, as transient interaction partners, or as constituents of biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation. This gap is significant because a growing body of evidence suggests that proteostatic control operates not simply at the level of single polypeptides but at the level of higher-order assemblies, where imbalanced production or degradation of one subunit can destabilize an entire complex, and where intrinsically disordered regions and condensate participation may confer distinct degradation vulnerabilities compared to well-folded, complex-embedded proteins. Whether such organization-dependent turnover coordination is a general, quantifiable property of the proteome—and whether its breakdown constitutes an early, mechanistic signature of proteostatic collapse in aging, oxidative stress, and cardiovascular disease—cannot be answered from any single existing dataset or organism-specific model system. It requires joint reanalysis of turnover kinetics across many independent experimental designs, coupled to structural, disorder, and condensate annotation resources that themselves are distributed across separate community databases (CORUM, hu.MAP, BioGRID, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, Human Protein Atlas, GTEx). This is precisely the type of previously inaccessible, emergence-oriented question that community-scale data synthesis is positioned to resolve. By harmonizing public turnover measurements with independently curated mesoscale organizational data, this project will test whether coordinated degradation is a fundamental design principle of proteome organization and whether its disruption offers a generalizable, cross-tissue biomarker of proteostatic dysfunction. The resulting synthesis addresses a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how molecular-scale kinetic behavior gives rise to emergent, higher-order cellular robustness—using only data that already exists but has never been assembled or analyzed at this scale or with this structural lens.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project is organized around one overarching question and three testable sub-hypotheses concerning the relationship between proteome turnover kinetics and mesoscale structural organization. Overarching question: Is coordinated degradation kinetics among physically or functionally associated proteins an emergent property of mesoscale organization, and does its disruption constitute a generalizable signature of proteostatic dysfunction across cell types, tissues, and physiological perturbations? Hypothesis 1 (Complex-level concordance): Subunits of stable, stoichiometric protein complexes exhibit significantly more concordant turnover rates than size-matched sets of functionally unrelated proteins, reflecting co-regulatory mechanisms—such as coupled translation, co-translational assembly, or degradation of unassembled subunits—that buffer against stoichiometric imbalance. We predict that concordance will scale positively with the degree of obligate stoichiometry and evolutionary conservation of the complex, and negatively with the proportion of intrinsically disordered regions among its members, since disordered segments are associated with more autonomous, context-dependent degradation signals. Hypothesis 2 (Condensate discordance): Proteins that participate in biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation, in contrast to stable complex members, will show weaker turnover concordance with their interaction partners, consistent with the more dynamic, concentration- and context-dependent exchange kinetics that characterize condensate residency. We further predict that condensate scaffold proteins and client proteins will display distinguishable turnover signatures, reflecting their different roles in maintaining phase-separated assemblies. Hypothesis 3 (Concordance breakdown as an emergent stress/aging signature): Physiological perturbations already profiled in existing public datasets—oxidative stress, altered oxygen tension, replicative and organismal aging, and cardiomyopathy-associated genetic backgrounds—will preferentially disrupt turnover concordance within specific mesoscale modules (e.g., mitochondrial respiratory complexes, nuclear lamina-associated assemblies, cytoskeletal complexes) before changes are detectable in the average half-life of any single constituent protein. This hypothesis directly tests whether emergent, module-level dyscoordination—rather than protein-by-protein half-life shifts—is the more sensitive and mechanistically informative readout of proteostatic decline. A secondary but integral question concerns generalizability: does the complex-versus-condensate concordance pattern observed in yeast and cultured human cells reproduce in vivo, across mouse heart, lung, and brain tissue under varying oxygen tension and in cardiovascular disease models, and in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte and endothelial systems? Confirming cross-species and cross-tissue reproducibility is essential to establishing that mesoscale turnover coordination reflects a conserved organizational principle rather than a cell-type-specific artifact. Collectively, these questions cannot be resolved using any single existing dataset, model organism, or structural annotation resource in isolation; they require the systematic cross-referencing and re-analysis of dozens of independently generated turnover datasets against multiple, non-overlapping structural and interaction databases—precisely the scale and diversity of data integration that motivates this proposal.
methods_and_approach: The project proceeds in four integrated aims, each relying exclusively on existing, publicly available datasets. Aim 1 – Data harmonization: We will systematically curate turnover datasets from public repositories (PRIDE, MassIVE, GEO, and supplementary data from published metabolic labeling studies) spanning SILAC, dynamic SILAC, 15N/heavy-water labeling, and pulse-chase designs across yeast, mouse tissue, human cell lines, and iPSC-derived cardiovascular cell types. Because these datasets differ in labeling duration, sampling density, and kinetic modeling assumptions, we will re-derive turnover rate constants where raw or intermediate quantification data are available, and apply Bayesian hierarchical models that treat dataset-of-origin as a random effect, allowing borrowing of statistical strength across studies while explicitly modeling batch-specific technical variance. This produces harmonized, uncertainty-quantified half-life estimates on a common kinetic scale for proteins across conditions and species-matched orthology mappings (using established ortholog databases) to enable cross-species comparison. Aim 2 – Mesoscale annotation integration: Harmonized turnover data will be cross-referenced with complex membership from CORUM and hu.MAP, protein-protein interaction data from BioGRID, intrinsic disorder scores from MobiDB and IUPred-based predictions, and condensate participation from PhaSepDB and LLPSDB. Tissue- and cell-type-specific expression context will be layered in using the Human Protein Atlas and GTEx to restrict analyses to biologically plausible co-expression contexts. Aim 3 – Concordance quantification: For each annotated complex, condensate, and interaction module, we will compute a turnover concordance statistic (e.g., coefficient of variation or intraclass correlation of half-lives among members) and compare this against null distributions generated from size- and abundance-matched random protein sets, using permutation-based significance testing. Regression and mixed-effects models will test whether concordance scales with disorder content, stoichiometric constraint, and evolutionary conservation, per Hypotheses 1 and 2. Aim 4 – Perturbation and cross-tissue mapping: Using existing datasets profiling oxidative stress, hypoxia/hyperoxia, aging, and cardiomyopathy models, we will compute condition-specific concordance shifts for each mesoscale module, identifying which modules show early or disproportionate loss of coordination (Hypothesis 3). In vivo heart, lung, and brain turnover data under varying oxygen tension will serve as an independent validation cohort to assess whether concordance patterns and their perturbation-induced breakdown generalize beyond cultured cell systems. All analytical code will be developed collaboratively across sites using version-controlled, containerized workflows to ensure reproducibility and to support iterative refinement as new public datasets become available during the project period.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will deliver a versioned, publicly queryable turnover-mesoscale atlas linking harmonized protein half-life estimates to complex, condensate, and disorder annotations across species and physiological states, along with a documented, containerized analytical pipeline for computing turnover concordance for any user-specified gene set. Scientifically, the work will resolve whether coordinated degradation is a general organizing principle of the proteome and establish concordance breakdown as a candidate mechanistic biomarker of proteostatic dysfunction in aging and cardiovascular disease—insights inaccessible from any single dataset or model system. This reframes existing turnover data, much of it originally collected for narrower, condition-specific purposes, as a resource for addressing a fundamental emergence question in cellular organization. The atlas will enable downstream hypothesis generation across the community: researchers studying specific complexes, disease genes, or condensates will be able to query whether turnover coordination is altered in their systems of interest without generating new data. By connecting kinetic, structural, and disease-relevant datasets that have previously remained siloed within separate subfields (classical proteomics, structural bioinformatics, condensate biology, cardiovascular tissue biology), the project models the kind of cross-disciplinary synthesis NCEMS is designed to catalyze, and produces reusable infrastructure with lasting value beyond the funding period.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All work will adhere to open, reproducible science principles consistent with NCEMS community policies. Harmonized turnover estimates, mesoscale annotation mappings, and concordance statistics will be deposited as versioned releases in a public repository (Zenodo, with DOI minting) alongside raw provenance metadata linking every derived value back to its original public dataset and accession number, ensuring full traceability. Analytical code—including data harmonization scripts, Bayesian hierarchical modeling pipelines, and concordance statistics—will be developed under version control (GitHub) and packaged in containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to guarantee computational reproducibility across computing environments and institutions. We will adopt standardized data schemas and controlled vocabularies where available (e.g., UniProt identifiers, PSI-MI interaction formats) to maximize interoperability with existing proteomics and interactomics resources. Intermediate and final analysis outputs will be accompanied by detailed documentation and vignettes enabling other researchers to query the atlas for their own protein or complex of interest. Working group meetings, analytical decisions, and pipeline development milestones will be logged in a shared, publicly accessible project wiki to support transparency and enable community contributions during and after the funding period. Trainees will be given explicit responsibility for maintaining documentation standards, reinforcing reproducible practices as a core professional skill. Where underlying datasets carry usage restrictions, we will comply fully with original data-sharing licenses while maximizing openness of all derived, harmonized products consistent with permitted redistribution.
budget_and_resources: Given the project's reliance exclusively on publicly available data, the budget centers on personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs. Requested support includes salary for one postdoctoral researcher with expertise in Bayesian kinetic modeling and one graduate student trainee focused on structural bioinformatics integration, both jointly supervised across participating labs to ensure cross-disciplinary training. Computational resources include cloud or institutional high-performance computing allocation sufficient for hierarchical modeling across >30 large-scale datasets and for hosting containerized pipelines and the versioned atlas database. Funds are requested for data storage and repository deposition fees (Zenodo/GitHub sustained hosting), as well as software licensing where necessary for structural or disorder prediction tools not otherwise freely available. Travel funds will support in-person working group meetings at least twice annually to coordinate cross-lab analytical decisions, resolve harmonization discrepancies, and conduct hands-on training workshops in Bayesian modeling and structural data integration for trainees across sites. Modest funds are allocated for dissemination, including open-access publication fees and presentation of results at relevant scientific meetings spanning proteomics, systems biology, and cardiovascular research communities. This project explicitly requires NCEMS-level support because it demands sustained coordination among investigators with non-overlapping expertise in proteomic kinetic modeling, translation/stress-response systems biology, structural and condensate bioinformatics, and cardiovascular tissue proteomics, together with computational infrastructure and collaborative time investment exceeding what any single laboratory's existing grant support could provide. The requested resources are scoped to be sufficient but modest, prioritizing personnel and computation over any new data generation, consistent with the synthesis-focused mission of this proposal.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Transcript Counts to Molecular Choreography: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework Linking Spatial Expression Atlases to Single-Molecule Biophysical States of Trafficking Machinery
abstract: A central unsolved question in cell biology is whether the mesoscale biophysical behavior of a protein complex—its oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficient, membrane residence time, or reaction kinetics—can be predicted from the transcriptomic and proteomic context of the cell in which it resides. Decades of single-molecule biophysics have produced quantitative measurements of protein oligomerization, diffusion, and binding kinetics for specific molecular machines (e.g., copper transporters, membrane trafficking complexes, transcription factor–DNA interactions) in isolated cell types and controlled conditions, while single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases now provide expression and localization maps of these same machineries across hundreds of cell types, tissues, and disease states. These two data universes—molecular-scale kinetic/stoichiometric measurements and cellular-scale expression/spatial context—have never been formally integrated, despite an implicit hypothesis in the field that mesoscale organization (clustering, oligomerization, complex assembly) emerges from, and feeds back onto, the local molecular composition of the cell. We propose to build a public, reusable synthesis framework that curates quantitative single-molecule biophysical parameters (stoichiometry, diffusion, kon/koff, residence times) reported in the literature and repositories for a defined set of trafficking-related and metal-homeostasis machineries (Ctr1, ATP7A/B, Atox1, CCS, and associated chaperones/trafficking regulators), and formally links them, via Bayesian hierarchical latent-variable models, to matched single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic profiles from public atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, HuBMAP, and existing brain snRNA-seq/spatial MERFISH datasets) spanning the same or comparable cell types, brain regions, and disease states (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Wilson's/Menkes-related neurodegeneration). The model will treat measured single-molecule parameters as noisy, condition-specific observations governed by latent biophysical state variables, and will estimate how these latent states depend on local expression levels, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular context, explicitly propagating measurement uncertainty and cross-study heterogeneity using probabilistic inference methods drawn from single-molecule photon-counting statistics. The framework will be validated by predicting biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions where single-molecule measurements do not yet exist but transcriptomic/spatial data do, generating falsifiable, quantitative predictions (e.g., expected oligomeric state of ATP7A in a specific reactive astrocyte subtype) that can guide future targeted experiments. This effort requires collaboration beyond any single lab: computational expertise in spatial transcriptomic integration and cell-state annotation, deep domain knowledge of copper homeostasis and membrane trafficking biophysics, and Bayesian modeling expertise for heterogeneous, noisy single-molecule data. The resulting open-source pipeline, curated biophysical parameter database, and trained hierarchical models will be released under FAIR data principles, providing a template applicable to other molecular machines beyond copper transport, and offering hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative single-molecule biophysics and computational spatial genomics—directly addressing NCEMS's mission to explain how mesoscale molecular organization emerges from and shapes higher-order cellular states.
background_and_significance:
The mesoscale—the regime between individual biomolecules and organelles—is where emergent cellular behaviors first become manifest: proteins oligomerize into functional complexes, diffuse through crowded and compartmentalized environments, and engage in transient, kinetically defined interactions that ultimately determine cellular phenotype. Single-molecule biophysics has, over three decades, generated a rich but fragmented body of quantitative knowledge describing these behaviors for specific molecular machines. Copper-handling and membrane trafficking systems—including the importer Ctr1, the P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B, and the cytosolic chaperones Atox1 and CCS—have been characterized in exquisite biophysical detail using single-molecule tracking, fluorescence resonance energy transfer, magnetic tweezers, and photon-counting statistics, yielding parameters such as oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficients, membrane residence times, and on/off kinetics. However, these measurements are almost always obtained in a small number of engineered cell lines or reconstituted systems under tightly controlled conditions, disconnected from the broader cellular and tissue contexts in which these same machines actually operate.

Simultaneously, single-cell and spatial transcriptomic and proteomic technologies have produced expression and localization atlases spanning hundreds of cell types, developmental stages, and disease states, including brain-wide single-nucleus RNA-seq datasets, spatial transcriptomic maps generated by imaging-based multiplexing, and antibody-based tissue atlases. These resources capture the expression context—transcript abundance, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular niches—for the very genes encoding the molecular machines studied at the single-molecule level, yet they contain no information about the biophysical behavior of the encoded proteins. The result is two rich, mature, and independently valuable data universes that have never been formally reconciled.

This gap is scientifically consequential because a foundational but untested hypothesis pervades molecular cell biology: that mesoscale biophysical organization—oligomeric state, complex assembly, residence time—is not fixed but instead emerges from, and dynamically reflects, the local molecular composition of the cell. If true, this hypothesis implies that biophysical parameters measured in one cellular context should be predictable, within quantifiable uncertainty, in other cell types and disease states purely from their expression and spatial profiles. Testing this hypothesis requires exactly the kind of large-scale, cross-study data synthesis that individual laboratories are not positioned to perform, since it demands simultaneous fluency in single-molecule kinetic modeling, hierarchical Bayesian statistics for heterogeneous noisy measurements, and computational integration of spatial and single-cell atlases. By formally linking these domains for a well-characterized model system—metal homeostasis and trafficking machinery, with direct relevance to neurodegenerative diseases such as Wilson's, Menkes, and Parkinson's disease—this project will establish whether mesoscale biophysical states are quantitatively predictable from transcriptomic and spatial context, providing a rigorous, generalizable test of a long-standing but implicit assumption in the field, and directly advancing NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project is organized around one overarching synthesis question and three testable sub-questions, each addressing a distinct layer of the proposed integration between molecular-scale biophysics and cellular-scale expression context.

Overarching question: Can quantitative single-molecule biophysical parameters of trafficking and metal-homeostasis machinery be predicted, with well-calibrated uncertainty, from the transcriptomic and spatial expression context of the cell in which the machinery operates?

Sub-question 1 (Compositional dependence): Does the oligomeric stoichiometry and diffusion behavior of a given trafficking complex (e.g., ATP7A, Ctr1, Atox1-CCS interactions) vary systematically with the expression levels of its direct binding partners and co-regulated chaperones across cell types, rather than remaining an invariant molecular property? We hypothesize that latent biophysical states are structured by local stoichiometric ratios among interacting partners, such that cell types with elevated chaperone-to-transporter expression ratios exhibit measurably shorter membrane residence times or altered oligomeric distributions, reflecting more efficient hand-off kinetics.

Sub-question 2 (Spatial and disease-state modulation): Do spatial transcriptomic neighborhoods—capturing tissue microenvironment and cell-cell contact context—explain additional variance in biophysical parameters beyond what is captured by cell-intrinsic expression alone, particularly in reactive or disease-associated cell states? We hypothesize that disease-associated cell states (e.g., reactive astrocytes in Parkinson's disease models, hepatocytes in Wilson's disease contexts) exhibit shifted latent biophysical states relative to their homeostatic counterparts, detectable as systematic deviations in the hierarchical model's cell-state-specific parameters, consistent with copper dyshomeostasis contributing mechanistically to pathological trafficking behavior.

Sub-question 3 (Cross-study generalizability and prediction): Can a hierarchical Bayesian model trained on existing single-molecule measurements, appropriately accounting for cross-study heterogeneity in imaging modality and experimental condition, generate falsifiable quantitative predictions of biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions that have never been directly measured but for which transcriptomic or spatial proteomic data exist? We hypothesize that such predictions will be quantitatively accurate within experimentally meaningful tolerance for cell types transcriptomically similar to measured reference types, while explicitly flagging low-confidence predictions for transcriptomically divergent or rare cell states, thereby providing a principled uncertainty-aware extrapolation tool rather than an overconfident black-box predictor.

Collectively, these questions test whether mesoscale biophysical organization is a generalizable, context-dependent property of cellular composition rather than a fixed molecular constant, and whether this relationship can be formally modeled using existing public data alone. Confirmation of these hypotheses would establish a new class of testable, quantitative links between gene expression atlases and biophysical function; refutation or partial confirmation would itself be scientifically informative, revealing where mesoscale behavior is decoupled from bulk expression context and motivating new single-molecule experiments targeted at specific discrepant cell states. Either outcome directly advances mechanistic understanding of how molecular-scale composition shapes mesoscale cellular organization, the central scientific focus of this synthesis effort.
methods_and_approach:
The project proceeds in three integrated phases, each relying exclusively on publicly available data and requiring the combined expertise of the assembled team.

Phase 1 – Curation of single-molecule biophysical parameters: We will systematically extract quantitative biophysical parameters (oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficients, kon/koff rates, membrane residence times) for Ctr1, ATP7A, ATP7B, Atox1, CCS, and associated trafficking regulators from published single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, FRET, magnetic-tweezer, and photon-counting studies, alongside metadata on cell type, experimental condition, imaging modality, and measurement uncertainty. Parameters will be harmonized into a structured, versioned database with explicit provenance tracking, enabling downstream propagation of study-specific measurement noise and technical heterogeneity.

Phase 2 – Integration of transcriptomic and spatial atlases: For each cell type or condition represented in the curated database, we will extract matched or closely analogous expression profiles from public resources including the Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, HuBMAP, and existing single-nucleus RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomic (e.g., MERFISH-based) datasets covering relevant brain regions and copper-homeostasis-related tissues. Cell-type harmonization across studies and platforms will employ established single-cell integration approaches to project heterogeneous datasets into a shared embedding space, from which local expression levels, co-expression neighborhood statistics, and spatial niche descriptors will be computed for each gene of interest.

Phase 3 – Hierarchical Bayesian latent-variable modeling: We will construct a hierarchical Bayesian model in which observed single-molecule parameters are treated as noisy realizations of latent, cell-type- and condition-specific biophysical states. These latent states will be modeled as functions of local transcriptomic/proteomic covariates (expression levels, co-expression ratios, spatial neighborhood composition), with hierarchical priors pooling information across related cell types and studies to stabilize inference given sparse single-molecule data. Measurement-level uncertainty will be explicitly modeled using likelihood structures informed by photon-counting and localization-based error models established in the single-molecule biophysics literature, allowing heterogeneous experimental precision to be properly weighted. Posterior inference will be performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational approximations as appropriate for model complexity, with rigorous posterior predictive checks against held-out measurements.

Validation will proceed via leave-one-cell-type-out cross-validation: for cell types with existing single-molecule measurements, the model will be retrained excluding that cell type's biophysical data (while retaining its transcriptomic data) and used to predict its biophysical parameters, quantifying predictive accuracy and calibration. The validated model will then generate prospective predictions for cell types and disease states with transcriptomic or spatial data but no existing single-molecule measurements, explicitly reporting posterior uncertainty to distinguish confident extrapolations from those requiring new experimental validation. All curation scripts, integration pipelines, and model code will be version-controlled and containerized to ensure full computational reproducibility across collaborating institutions.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will produce four concrete deliverables. First, a curated, versioned, publicly hosted database of single-molecule biophysical parameters for copper-homeostasis and trafficking machinery, annotated with cell type, condition, and measurement uncertainty metadata, serving as a durable community resource beyond this project's scope. Second, an open-source computational pipeline for harmonizing single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases with heterogeneous biophysical measurements, generalizable to other molecular machines and complex families. Third, validated hierarchical Bayesian models quantifying the relationship between local expression context and mesoscale biophysical state, including calibrated, falsifiable predictions for previously unmeasured cell types and disease-associated states, such as specific reactive glial populations or hepatocyte subtypes in metal-overload conditions. Fourth, a set of concrete, experimentally testable hypotheses linking transcriptomic cell-state signatures to expected biophysical behavior, directly informing future single-molecule and structural studies.

Scientifically, this work will provide the first rigorous, quantitative test of whether mesoscale biophysical organization is predictable from cellular composition, addressing a foundational and previously untestable assumption in molecular cell biology. Confirmed predictive relationships would establish a new paradigm for using expression atlases to infer biophysical function at scale, dramatically reducing the experimental burden of characterizing rare or difficult-to-access cell types. Identified discrepancies between predicted and expected behavior would highlight cell states where mesoscale organization is decoupled from bulk expression, motivating targeted follow-up experiments and refining mechanistic models of neurodegenerative disease pathogenesis linked to copper dyshomeostasis. Beyond the specific biological system studied, the modeling framework and integration pipeline will serve as a reusable template applicable to other molecular machines, advancing NCEMS's broader mission of understanding emergence at the mesoscale through data synthesis.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. The curated single-molecule biophysical parameter database will be deposited in a public, version-controlled repository with a permissive open license, accompanied by structured metadata describing provenance, experimental condition, and measurement uncertainty to enable independent reuse and extension by the broader research community. All data integration, harmonization, and modeling code will be developed openly on a public code repository from project inception, organized as modular, documented, and containerized workflows to ensure computational reproducibility across computing environments and institutions.

Model specifications, prior choices, inference diagnostics, and posterior predictive checks will be fully documented and released alongside trained model objects, allowing independent verification of all reported predictions and uncertainty estimates. Intermediate outputs, including harmonized cell-type embeddings and covariate matrices linking expression context to biophysical parameters, will be archived as reusable data products rather than treated as disposable intermediate files, maximizing downstream value to the community.

The project will follow FAIR data principles throughout: all deliverables will be findable through persistent identifiers, accessible through standard public repositories, interoperable through use of community-standard file formats and metadata schemas for single-cell and spatial data, and reusable through comprehensive documentation and permissive licensing. Analysis workflows will be captured using literate programming practices, enabling transparent, step-by-step reconstruction of all reported results. Regular public releases of intermediate milestones, rather than a single end-of-project release, will allow the community to engage with and critique the framework as it matures, consistent with team and reproducible science practices emphasized by NCEMS.
budget_and_resources:
This project requests support for a coordinated working group spanning computational biology, single-molecule biophysics, and Bayesian statistical modeling, reflecting the interdisciplinary expertise required and unavailable within any single laboratory. Primary budget needs include salary support for one postdoctoral researcher with expertise in spatial transcriptomic data integration and one graduate student trainee focused on hierarchical Bayesian modeling of heterogeneous single-molecule data, both jointly mentored across participating labs to ensure cross-disciplinary training. Modest computational resources are requested for cloud-based or institutional high-performance computing access to support Markov chain Monte Carlo inference and integration of large-scale spatial transcriptomic datasets, along with data storage costs for hosting the curated biophysical parameter database and derived data products.

Funds are also requested to support in-person and virtual working group meetings bringing together team members from distinct institutions and geographic locations to coordinate database curation standards, model specification decisions, and validation strategy, along with travel support for trainees to present integrated findings at relevant scientific conferences spanning biophysics and computational biology communities. Modest publication and data deposition costs are included to support open-access dissemination and repository hosting fees consistent with FAIR data commitments.

No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal; all biophysical parameters and expression/spatial data will be drawn from existing published studies and public repositories. NCEMS support is specifically required to enable sustained, coordinated collaboration among team members with complementary but non-overlapping expertise, to provide dedicated personnel time for the labor-intensive curation and harmonization steps that individual labs lack capacity to undertake alone, and to support trainees in acquiring interdisciplinary skills bridging single-molecule biophysics and computational spatial genomics that are not readily available through any single existing training pathway.

title: From Chemical Marks to Mesoscale Machines: A Multi-Omics and Molecular Dynamics Synthesis of How tRNA Modification Loss Drives Ribosome Collision Condensates and Translational Stress Phenotypes
abstract: A fundamental unsolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how discrete chemical modifications on individual RNA molecules propagate upward to generate emergent, mesoscale ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies that reshape cellular physiology. tRNA modifications (e.g., wobble-position thiolation, dihydrouridine, queuosine) are known to tune translation speed and codon decoding fidelity at the molecular scale, and prior work has shown that loss of these modifications increases ribosome pausing genome-wide. Separately, stalled and collided ribosomes are increasingly recognized as nucleation sites for mesoscale quality-control condensates involving factors such as ZNF598, Pelota/Hbs1, and stress-granule components. Yet no systematic framework connects the biophysics of individual modification-deficient tRNA-ribosome complexes to the assembly thermodynamics of these collision-triggered condensates, nor to their downstream consequences for cellular stress phenotypes, proteostasis, and disease. This project will synthesize four classes of existing public data—(1) curated tRNA modification enzyme and modification-site databases (MODOMICS, bacterial and eukaryotic epitranscriptomic maps) together with comparative genomics of modification enzyme conservation and redundancy; (2) ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) datasets across bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines under modification-enzyme-deficient versus wild-type conditions; (3) cryo-EM structures of collided/stalled ribosome complexes and quality-control factor assemblies deposited in the PDB and EMDB; and (4) proteomic, single-cell transcriptomic/epigenomic, and condensate-composition datasets (e.g., DrLLPS, PhaSepDB, TCGA/ICGC proteomic subtyping cohorts, and postmortem brain single-cell epigenomic atlases) that report stress-granule/RNP condensate signatures in disease contexts such as leukemia and neurodegeneration. We will use residue-resolution coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics to model how loss of specific tRNA modifications alters codon-anticodon geometry, decoding kinetics, and interface energetics at collided ribosome junctions, generating physically grounded predictions of collision propensity and condensate nucleation likelihood. These structural predictions will be integrated with cross-organism Ribo-seq pausing signatures and condensate proteomic composition using graph-based imputation and similarity-network-fusion clustering to identify conserved “modification–pausing–condensation” axes, and validated against phenotypic outcomes captured in existing multi-omic disease cohorts. This work directly targets NCEMS’ mesoscale mandate: it treats ribosome collision complexes and stress condensates as an intermediate organizational layer between single biomolecule chemistry and cellular/organismal phenotype, an integration no single lab can achieve alone, requiring RNA modification biology, biomolecular simulation, AI-driven multi-omic integration, and clinical proteomic/epigenomic expertise simultaneously. All modeling pipelines, curated datasets, and integrative code will be released as open, reproducible workflows, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs across wet-lab microbial genetics, computational biophysics, and biomedical data science, producing a new generation of researchers fluent in bridging atomistic simulation with population-scale omics synthesis.
background_and_significance: Transfer RNA modifications constitute one of the most ancient and conserved layers of gene expression regulation, decorating anticodon loops and stems with chemical marks—thiolated uridines, dihydrouridine, queuosine, and dozens of others—that fine-tune codon-anticodon pairing geometry, wobble decoding, and translocation kinetics. Decades of biochemical and structural work, spanning bacteria to humans, have established that loss of individual modification enzymes perturbs local translation speed and can produce ribosome pausing at specific codons. More recently, transcriptome-wide ribosome profiling has revealed that these local kinetic perturbations are not isolated events: modification loss can produce genome-wide shifts in pausing landscapes, implicating a broader, systems-level consequence to what was once considered a codon-specific phenomenon. In parallel, an independent research trajectory has established that ribosome collisions—events in which a trailing ribosome physically contacts a stalled leading ribosome—serve as sensing platforms for quality-control machinery, including the E3 ubiquitin ligase ZNF598, the Pelota/Hbs1 rescue complex, and integrated stress response components. Under conditions of persistent stalling, these collision complexes can nucleate larger mesoscale RNP condensates that resemble stress granules, structures whose composition, material properties, and disease relevance have been extensively catalogued in curated condensate databases and multi-omic disease cohorts. Despite the depth of knowledge accumulated independently in tRNA modification biochemistry, ribosome structural biology, and condensate biophysics, these three literatures remain largely disconnected. No existing study has systematically asked whether the biophysical signature of a modification-deficient decoding event—altered anticodon loop geometry, altered dwell time, altered A-site sampling—is quantitatively predictive of collision frequency, and whether collision frequency in turn predicts condensate nucleation propensity and its associated cellular stress phenotypes. This gap represents precisely the kind of mesoscale emergence problem that motivates NCEMS: a molecular-scale chemical perturbation (loss of a single modified nucleoside) propagating through an intermediate structural complex (the collided ribosome) to produce an emergent, higher-order assembly (the RNP condensate) with organismal and disease consequences (proteostasis collapse, neurodegeneration, leukemic proteome remodeling). Addressing this gap requires simultaneous fluency in molecular dynamics of nucleic acid-protein complexes, comparative genomics of modification enzyme conservation, ribosome profiling analytics across three domains of life, structural interpretation of cryo-EM collision complexes, and multi-omic disease cohort analysis—an assembly of expertise that essentially never resides in one laboratory. The public data ecosystem, however, is now sufficiently mature to permit this synthesis without new experiments: MODOMICS and epitranscriptomic atlases catalogue modification sites across organisms; the Sequence Read Archive and GEO host dozens of Ribo-seq datasets under modification-enzyme-deficient conditions; the PDB and EMDB contain a growing set of collided-ribosome and quality-control complex structures; and condensate and cancer/neurodegeneration proteomic databases document downstream phenotypic consequences. This proposal is designed to knit these resources into the first mechanistic, cross-scale framework linking chemical modification loss to mesoscale condensate emergence and disease phenotype.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group is organized around three tightly linked research questions, each addressed exclusively through synthesis of existing public data. Research Question 1 asks: does the biophysical signature of a modification-deficient tRNA at the ribosomal A-site—altered codon-anticodon geometry, altered dwell time, altered interface free energy—quantitatively predict the probability of ribosome collision at the corresponding codon? We hypothesize that specific modification losses (e.g., loss of wobble-uridine thiolation or queuosine) generate distinctive, computable signatures of decoding delay whose magnitude, when mapped onto codon usage and mRNA sequence context, will predict collision hotspots identified independently in public Ribo-seq disome/collision datasets across bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines. Research Question 2 asks: do the structural and energetic properties of collided ribosome junctions determine which complexes proceed to recruit quality-control and condensate-nucleating factors, and can this determination be predicted from existing cryo-EM structures of stalled/collided ribosome-factor complexes deposited in the PDB and EMDB? We hypothesize that specific interface geometries at the collided ribosome junction—particularly those altered by non-canonical decoding events—create preferential binding surfaces for ZNF598 and Pelota/Hbs1 recruitment, such that collision complexes arising from modification loss are structurally biased toward productive condensate nucleation rather than resolution. Research Question 3 asks: does the resulting modification-loss-to-condensation axis manifest as detectable, conserved molecular signatures in disease-relevant multi-omic cohorts, and do these signatures correlate with clinically documented proteostasis and stress phenotypes? We hypothesize that tissues and cell states exhibiting reduced tRNA modification enzyme expression or activity (inferred from transcriptomic/proteomic profiling in existing cohorts) will show elevated condensate-associated proteomic signatures and stress-granule marker enrichment, correlating with adverse phenotypic outcomes in datasets spanning acute myeloid leukemia proteomic subtypes and postmortem neurodegenerative brain atlases. Collectively, these hypotheses predict a conserved, cross-organism, cross-scale causal chain: modification loss → altered decoding biophysics → increased collision propensity → structurally favored condensate nucleation → detectable proteomic/transcriptomic stress signature → phenotypic consequence. Testing this chain requires no new experiments; rather, it requires the coordinated reanalysis, harmonization, and structural-computational modeling of data already deposited across at least six distinct public repositories spanning structural biology, functional genomics, and clinical multi-omics. A secondary, methodological question threads through the biological hypotheses: can graph-based imputation and similarity-network-fusion approaches, developed originally for single-cell and multi-omic cancer subtyping, be adapted to integrate structural-simulation-derived features with sequencing-derived pausing scores and proteomic condensate signatures into a single, cross-organism analytical framework? Establishing this methodological bridge is itself a significant contribution, as it would provide a reusable template for connecting atomistic biophysical prediction to population-scale omics synthesis in other mesoscale emergence problems beyond translation.
methods_and_approach: The project is organized into four integrated work packages, each built entirely on existing public resources. Work Package 1 (Modification and Enzyme Curation) will assemble a harmonized cross-organism catalogue of tRNA modification sites and their cognate enzymes using MODOMICS, bacterial and eukaryotic epitranscriptomic mapping datasets, and comparative genomic analyses of enzyme conservation and functional redundancy across bacteria, yeast, and human systems, producing a unified reference table linking modification identity, enzyme, organism, and known phenotypic consequences of loss. Work Package 2 (Structural and Biophysical Modeling) will use residue-resolution coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics, parameterized against existing cryo-EM structures of ribosome-tRNA and collided-ribosome-factor complexes from the PDB and EMDB, to simulate decoding at modified versus unmodified anticodon positions, quantifying differences in dwell time, interface free energy, and A-site sampling geometry; separately, structural ensembles of collided ribosome junctions bound to ZNF598 and Pelota/Hbs1 will be analyzed for interface features correlated with productive complex formation versus resolution. Work Package 3 (Cross-Organism Ribo-seq Integration) will reprocess publicly deposited Ribo-seq and disome-profiling datasets from modification-enzyme-deficient and wild-type bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines using standardized pausing-score and collision-detection pipelines, enabling direct comparison of empirically observed pausing/collision hotspots against the biophysical predictions generated in Work Package 2. Work Package 4 (Multi-Omic Disease Phenotype Integration) will mine condensate composition databases (DrLLPS, PhaSepDB) alongside proteomic, single-cell transcriptomic, and single-cell epigenomic datasets from disease cohorts—including proteomic acute myeloid leukemia subtyping data and postmortem brain single-cell epigenomic atlases—to quantify condensate-associated and stress-granule marker signatures, correlating them with inferred modification-enzyme expression/activity levels and clinical/phenotypic annotations. Integration across work packages will employ graph-based feature propagation methods to impute and denoise sparse single-cell and proteomic measurements, followed by similarity-network-fusion clustering to identify conserved modification–pausing–condensation axes across organisms and disease contexts. Structural predictions from Work Package 2 will be encoded as quantitative features (interface energies, geometric descriptors) and fused with sequencing-derived pausing scores and proteomic condensate scores within this unified network, allowing statistical testing of the proposed causal chain via cross-organism concordance analysis and phenotype correlation. All computational workflows will be version-controlled, containerized, and benchmarked against held-out organism/dataset combinations to assess generalizability. Monthly working group meetings will rotate leadership across the structural biophysics, RNA modification genomics, single-cell/proteomic bioinformatics, and clinical data domains to ensure balanced integration and to surface cross-disciplinary methodological conflicts early, with quarterly synthesis retreats devoted to consolidating cross-work-package findings into unified manuscripts and public data products.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis will produce the first quantitative, cross-scale model linking specific tRNA modification losses to ribosome collision propensity, condensate nucleation likelihood, and disease-relevant proteostasis phenotypes. Primary deliverables include a harmonized public database of modification-enzyme conservation and phenotypic consequence annotations; a structurally validated biophysical scoring function for collision propensity at modification-deficient codons; a cross-organism atlas of Ribo-seq collision hotspots reanalyzed under standardized pipelines; and an integrative similarity-network-fusion framework linking structural, sequencing, and proteomic condensate features to clinical outcomes in leukemia and neurodegeneration cohorts. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing disconnect between RNA modification biochemistry and ribosome quality-control biophysics, establishing whether collision-triggered condensation is a generalizable, conserved consequence of translational fidelity loss rather than an organism- or context-specific curiosity. Methodologically, the project will demonstrate a reusable template for fusing atomistic simulation output with population-scale multi-omic data, a capability broadly transferable to other mesoscale emergence problems in molecular and cellular biology, directly advancing NCEMS's core analytical mission. Translational impact includes identifying candidate biomarkers of modification-loss-driven proteostatic stress in leukemia proteomic subtypes and neurodegenerative epigenomic atlases, potentially informing future biomarker or therapeutic strategies targeting condensate-associated stress pathways. Broader impacts include establishing an open, extensible computational pipeline that other groups can apply to additional modification systems, organisms, or disease cohorts, and generating cross-training experiences that equip early-career scientists with integrated skills spanning wet-lab RNA biology, molecular simulation, and biomedical data science—directly addressing the workforce development goals central to this funding mechanism.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All data used in this project are drawn exclusively from public repositories, including MODOMICS, NCBI GEO and Sequence Read Archive Ribo-seq datasets, the Protein Data Bank and Electron Microscopy Data Bank, DrLLPS, PhaSepDB, TCGA, ICGC, and publicly deposited single-cell epigenomic brain atlases; no new experimental data will be generated. Consistent with NCEMS open science policy, every curated dataset, harmonized annotation table, simulation input/output file, and analysis script will be deposited in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub for code, Zenodo or OSF for data and simulation trajectories) under permissive open-source licenses, with persistent identifiers assigned to enable citation and reuse. Molecular dynamics simulation protocols, force field parameters, and analysis pipelines will be packaged as containerized, executable workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow) accompanied by comprehensive documentation to ensure independent reproducibility by external groups lacking specialized simulation expertise. Ribo-seq reprocessing and similarity-network-fusion integration code will be structured as modular, well-documented packages with unit tests and example datasets, enabling adaptation to additional organisms or modification systems beyond those studied here. The working group will adopt pre-registration of key hypotheses and analysis plans for the cross-organism concordance tests, and will release intermediate data products (e.g., harmonized pausing scores, structural feature tables) prior to final manuscript submission to maximize community utility. All findings, including negative or null results regarding proposed causal linkages, will be reported transparently in preprints deposited on bioRxiv prior to journal submission. Regular working group calls will include explicit review of data provenance and licensing compliance to ensure all synthesized resources are used and redistributed according to their original terms. This commitment to transparent, modular, and reusable infrastructure ensures that the project's primary scientific product is not only its findings but also a durable, community-usable synthesis platform.
budget_and_resources: Requested resources focus on personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination rather than experimental costs, reflecting the project's pure synthesis design. Personnel support includes partial salary for a postdoctoral researcher with expertise in molecular dynamics and structural bioinformatics, a graduate student trainee focused on Ribo-seq reprocessing and comparative genomics, and a data scientist trainee specializing in multi-omic integration and similarity-network-fusion methods, providing direct cross-disciplinary training opportunities central to the RFP's workforce development goals. Computational resources include allocation on high-performance computing clusters for coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of ribosome-tRNA complexes, along with cloud storage and compute credits for large-scale reprocessing of public Ribo-seq and single-cell proteomic/epigenomic datasets. Modest funds are requested for working group coordination, including quarterly in-person or hybrid synthesis retreats to integrate findings across the four work packages, and travel support enabling trainees to present integrative findings at relevant scientific conferences. Software licensing costs are minimized through reliance on open-source simulation (e.g., GROMACS, OpenMM) and analysis (Python/R-based) tools. A small budget line supports data curation efforts, including manual harmonization of modification-enzyme annotations across organisms and quality control of reprocessed sequencing datasets. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, reagents, or human/animal subject costs, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal. The requested budget explicitly leverages NCEMS-provided computational infrastructure and collaborative support mechanisms, as the scale of cross-organism, cross-data-type integration proposed here exceeds what any single participating laboratory currently possesses, justifying the requirement for centralized synthesis center support to enable this multidisciplinary, multi-institutional collaboration.
