author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the 'Organelle Signature' Landscape: A Genomic Deconvolution Framework for Discovering Novel Protein- and Lipid-Bounded Compartments Across Bacteria and Archaea
abstract: Bacterial and archaeal organelles—carboxysomes, encapsulins, magnetosomes, ferrosomes, and their atypical relatives—represent striking cases of mesoscale emergence, where discrete sets of genes assemble into compartments with properties (selective permeability, biomineralization, redox control) absent from their individual protein components. Despite decades of discovery, our catalog of prokaryotic organelles remains almost certainly incomplete: current identification relies on manual inspection of gene neighborhoods and homology to a handful of known shell or membrane systems, an approach poorly suited to the scale of modern genomic and metagenomic databases. This project proposes to reframe organelle discovery as a signature-deconvolution problem, adapting mutational-signature-style matrix factorization methods (as used in large-scale cancer genomics) to genomic co-occurrence data. Instead of decomposing mutation spectra into additive processes, we will decompose gene-cluster architectures—shell/membrane protein paralogs, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulatory genes—across hundreds of thousands of public bacterial and archaeal genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes (IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, NCBI) into a small number of recurring 'organelle signatures.' Known systems (carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical 'JEEP' loci) will serve as ground-truth anchors to validate the factorization, while residual, previously uncharacterized signatures will be flagged as candidate novel compartments. For each candidate signature, we will integrate structural predictions from AlphaFold/ESMFold databases to assess whether component proteins form shell-like oligomers or membrane-remodeling folds, and will cross-reference public proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics datasets to infer physiological context (e.g., iron/heme handling, cofactor regeneration, anaerobic metabolism) and predict conditions under which candidate organelles are expressed. This directly extends existing team expertise: comparative genomic characterization of magnetosome and encapsulin diversity, mechanistic understanding of iron-storing ferrosomes and heme homeostasis, structural and functional dissection of microcompartment shell proteins and their 'just-enough-parts' atypical loci, and quantitative signature-extraction methodology drawn from large-scale cancer genomic synthesis. No single lab in this consortium possesses the full combination of large-scale comparative genomics infrastructure, organelle biogenesis expertise across iron- and carbon-based systems, and quantitative signature-deconvolution methodology needed to execute this synthesis; the project inherently requires pooling of distinct public data streams (genomic, structural, proteomic) and distinct disciplinary lenses. Deliverables include an open, versioned organelle-signature database and reproducible computational pipeline, a ranked list of candidate novel bacterial/archaeal organelles with predicted structural and functional annotations for community follow-up, and training materials introducing trainees to matrix-factorization approaches for genomic architecture discovery—bridging molecular structural biology, microbial genomics, and quantitative signature analysis. By treating organelle emergence as a generalizable, learnable pattern in genomic architecture rather than a case-by-case discovery, this work aims to substantially expand the known diversity of subcellular compartmentalization in prokaryotes and provide a template method transferable to other classes of mesoscale molecular machines.
background_and_significance: Prokaryotic organelles occupy a privileged position in the study of mesoscale emergence: they demonstrate how a bounded set of genes—encoding shell or membrane proteins, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulators—self-assembles into compartments whose functional properties (selective permeability, biomineralization, redox buffering) cannot be predicted from any single component in isolation. Carboxysomes concentrate CO2 for carbon fixation; encapsulins sequester reactive enzymatic chemistry; magnetosomes template magnetite biomineralization; ferrosomes store iron to counter host nutritional immunity. Each of these systems was discovered through decades of painstaking, largely manual investigation of individual gene clusters, guided by homology to a small number of already-known shell or membrane architectures. This case-by-case discovery paradigm has been productive but is now a bottleneck: public sequence repositories such as IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, and NCBI contain hundreds of thousands of bacterial and archaeal genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes, vastly exceeding what manual curation can survey. Recent comparative-genomic work has already revealed 'atypical' organelle-like loci (e.g., JEEP systems) that retain only a minimal subset of canonical structural genes, suggesting that a much broader, largely uncatalogued space of compartmentalization strategies exists in nature, hidden in plain sight within public sequence data. The core significance of this problem is that prokaryotic organelles are a natural laboratory for studying how emergent subcellular structure arises from combinatorial gene-cluster architecture—a question directly aligned with NCEMS's mesoscale mission. Yet no systematic, quantitative, genome-scale framework currently exists to detect recurring architectural 'signatures' of organelle-forming loci the way mutational-signature analysis has revealed recurring, biologically interpretable patterns within noisy, high-dimensional cancer genomic data. This proposal imports that logic: gene-cluster composition across genomes can be treated as a high-dimensional co-occurrence matrix amenable to non-negative matrix factorization, extracting a small number of additive 'signatures' that represent recurring organelle-genesis programs, including combinations never previously described. This reframing is significant because it converts organelle discovery from an artisanal, homology-dependent search into a scalable, statistically grounded synthesis task built entirely on existing public data. It also creates a template applicable well beyond iron- and carbon-handling organelles, to any mesoscale molecular machine defined by a recurring, non-random gene-cluster grammar. Because the requisite genomic architecture expertise, iron/heme organelle biogenesis knowledge, microcompartment structural biology, and quantitative signature-extraction methodology are each concentrated in different labs, this problem cannot be solved through incremental single-lab effort; it requires the exact kind of cross-disciplinary data synthesis NCEMS is designed to catalyze.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project addresses three interlocking research questions. First: can recurring, biologically meaningful 'organelle signatures'—additive combinations of shell/membrane paralogs, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulatory genes—be extracted directly from public genomic co-occurrence data using matrix factorization, without prior assumption of which combinations constitute a functional organelle? We hypothesize that known organelle systems (carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical JEEP loci) will resolve as distinct, high-loading signatures when the factorization is applied to a sufficiently large and taxonomically diverse genome set, validating the approach against established ground truth. Second: does the residual signature space—components of the factorization not explained by known systems—contain coherent, reproducible architectural patterns consistent with undescribed compartmentalization systems, rather than statistical noise or lineage-specific artifacts? We hypothesize that a subset of residual signatures will show the hallmarks of genuine organelle-forming loci: phylogenetically dispersed but architecturally conserved gene-cluster co-occurrence, enrichment for protein folds associated with oligomeric shell formation or membrane curvature, and physiological gene neighbors (transporters, redox enzymes, biomineralization-associated genes) analogous to those flanking known organelle loci. Third: can structural and functional context inferred purely from public data—AlphaFold/ESMFold structural predictions, proteomic and transcriptomic expression patterns, and metabolomic association—be used to prioritize candidate novel organelle signatures for likely biological function and expression conditions, without new experimentation? We hypothesize that integrating structural fold predictions (shell-like oligomerization propensity, membrane-remodeling curvature motifs) with condition-specific expression data (e.g., iron limitation, anaerobiosis, oxidative stress, cofactor imbalance) will allow us to rank candidate signatures by functional plausibility and predict the physiological niches in which they are deployed, mirroring the way ferrosome and encapsulin functions were originally inferred from genomic context before mechanistic follow-up. A unifying hypothesis underlies all three questions: organelle-forming capacity in prokaryotes is not idiosyncratic to a handful of well-studied systems but is a generalizable, statistically learnable pattern of gene-cluster architecture, such that the same combinatorial logic that produces carboxysomes and magnetosomes recurs, with variation, across a much larger and largely undiscovered space of microbial compartments. Confirming this hypothesis would fundamentally reframe organelle emergence as a predictable outcome of genomic architecture rather than a rare evolutionary accident, with direct implications for understanding how mesoscale structure arises from molecular parts lists more broadly. Disconfirming evidence—for instance, if residual signatures fail to show structural or contextual coherence—would itself be informative, suggesting that known organelle systems occupy a narrower, more constrained region of architectural space than currently assumed, refining the search strategy for future synthesis efforts.
methods_and_approach: The project unfolds in four coordinated phases, each built entirely on public data and requiring the combined expertise of the team. Phase 1, Data Assembly and Locus Extraction: we will compile a comprehensive gene-cluster dataset by mining IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, and NCBI genome and metagenome-assembled genome collections, using existing annotation pipelines and profile-HMM searches to identify candidate organelle-associated loci based on presence of shell/membrane protein paralogs, cargo enzyme families, transporters, and regulators. Loci will be represented as feature vectors encoding gene family composition, order, and co-occurrence frequency, generating a large sparse matrix analogous to the mutation-context matrices used in cancer signature analysis. Phase 2, Signature Extraction and Validation: non-negative matrix factorization (and complementary approaches such as Bayesian NMF and topic models) will be applied to decompose this matrix into a minimal set of additive signatures. Known systems—carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical JEEP loci—already characterized through comparative genomic and structural work by team members, will serve as labeled anchors to tune factorization rank, assess signature stability via bootstrapping, and establish quantitative benchmarks (reconstruction accuracy, signature reproducibility across resampled genome subsets) for distinguishing genuine biological signal from technical artifact. Phase 3, Candidate Prioritization via Structural and Functional Integration: residual signatures not explained by known systems will be extracted as candidate novel organelle architectures. For each candidate, constituent proteins will be cross-referenced against AlphaFold and ESMFold structural databases to assess propensity for shell-like oligomerization or membrane-remodeling folds, using established structural criteria from prior microcompartment shell characterization. Public proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics datasets (e.g., expression atlases, stress-condition transcriptomes) will be mined to infer likely physiological contexts—iron/heme handling, cofactor regeneration, anaerobic or oxidative stress metabolism—by testing for condition-specific co-expression of candidate loci, paralleling the contextual inference previously used to characterize ferrosome and encapsulin function. Phase 4, Synthesis and Ranking: candidates will be scored on a composite index integrating factorization confidence, structural plausibility, phylogenetic breadth, and functional context coherence, producing a ranked, annotated catalog for community follow-up. Throughout, computational workflows will be modularized and version-controlled, with quantitative benchmarking methodology (analogous to composite-index validation approaches used in clinical data synthesis) applied to ensure the ranking metric is interpretable and reproducible. Regular cross-team working sessions will pair genomic/computational analysis with structural and physiological interpretation, ensuring candidates are evaluated against the mechanistic criteria established for known organelle systems.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis project will produce three primary deliverables. First, an open, versioned organelle-signature database cataloging both validated known-system signatures and newly discovered candidate architectures, annotated with taxonomic distribution, structural predictions, and inferred physiological context. Second, a reproducible, modular computational pipeline for genomic signature extraction, structural cross-referencing, and functional context integration, designed for extension by the broader community to additional organelle classes or genomic feature sets. Third, a ranked, publicly available list of candidate novel bacterial and archaeal organelles, prioritized for experimental follow-up by the wider research community, effectively seeding future hypothesis-driven work well beyond this consortium's own capacity. Scientifically, this project will substantially expand the known diversity of prokaryotic compartmentalization strategies and provide the first quantitative, generalizable framework for treating organelle emergence as a learnable pattern in genomic architecture rather than a series of isolated discoveries. This reframing has direct relevance to NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mission, illustrating how discrete molecular parts combine combinatorially to generate system-level properties absent from individual components. Methodologically, the adaptation of signature-deconvolution approaches from cancer genomics to microbial genomic architecture establishes a transferable template applicable to other classes of mesoscale molecular machines defined by recurring, non-random gene-cluster grammars—condensates, secretion systems, or multi-enzyme metabolic assemblies. Training materials generated from this pipeline will introduce trainees to matrix-factorization methodology in a genomics context, cultivating a workforce fluent in both structural microbiology and quantitative data science, directly advancing NCEMS's talent-development goals while generating durable, reusable community resources.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All aspects of this project will adhere to open science principles from inception. Source data are drawn exclusively from public repositories (IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, NCBI, AlphaFold/ESMFold databases, and public proteomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic archives), with no new experimental data generated. All locus-extraction scripts, feature matrices, factorization code, and candidate-scoring pipelines will be developed in version-controlled public repositories (e.g., GitHub, archived via Zenodo for citable, immutable releases), accompanied by containerized environments to ensure computational reproducibility across platforms. The organelle-signature database itself will be released under an open license, structured for programmatic access (API and bulk download), and designed for community extension as new genomes and structural predictions become available. Analytical decisions—factorization rank selection, validation benchmarks, structural and functional scoring thresholds—will be documented in preregistered analysis plans and detailed methods notebooks, allowing independent reproduction of every candidate ranking. Intermediate outputs, including rejected or low-confidence signatures, will be released alongside final candidates to support transparent community evaluation and avoid selective reporting. The project will follow FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of all generated resources. Working group members will coordinate through shared electronic lab notebooks and regular public progress updates, consistent with community-endorsed team-science practices. Preprints will be posted prior to formal publication, and all resulting manuscripts will target open-access venues. By committing to full pipeline transparency and data availability from the outset, this project ensures that its central contribution—the organelle-signature framework—can be independently validated, critiqued, extended, or repurposed by other research groups, maximizing its value as a durable community resource rather than a one-time analysis.
budget_and_resources: This project requires computational and personnel resources appropriate to a data-synthesis working group rather than laboratory experimentation. Primary costs include support for a postdoctoral researcher or senior computational trainee with expertise in matrix factorization and genomic data pipelines, who will lead locus extraction, factorization implementation, and pipeline integration under joint mentorship from all four investigators. A graduate student trainee will focus on structural cross-referencing and functional context integration, gaining direct training in both structural bioinformatics and microbial physiology. Computational costs include high-performance computing allocation for processing hundreds of thousands of genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes, storage for intermediate feature matrices and structural prediction datasets, and cloud or institutional cluster access for iterative factorization runs and bootstrapped validation. Modest travel funds will support two in-person working group meetings annually to synchronize genomic, structural, and physiological interpretation across sites, alongside regular virtual coordination. Because the four investigators are distributed across institutions with complementary but non-overlapping infrastructure—large-scale comparative genomics resources, organelle structural biology facilities, and iron/heme physiology expertise—NCEMS support is essential to fund the shared computational infrastructure, data integration personnel, and coordination mechanisms that no single lab's existing grants are structured to provide. NCEMS resources will also support publication costs for open-access dissemination and Zenodo/database hosting fees to guarantee long-term public availability of the organelle-signature database beyond the funding period. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this proposal; all resources are directed toward personnel, computation, and coordination needed to integrate and reanalyze existing public genomic, structural, and omics datasets at a scale and cross-disciplinary depth unattainable by any individual participating laboratory.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Decoding Cytokinetic Resilience: Synthesizing Context-Specific Multi-Omic Networks to Understand Mesoscale Emergence Under Thermal Stress
abstract: Plant cytokinesis represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence. During this transient developmental window, molecular components—including cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, trans-Golgi network-derived vesicles, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a novel, higher-order structure: the cell plate. This highly dynamic process acts as a severe architectural bottleneck that is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly extreme temperature fluctuations and heat waves. While isolated studies have mapped individual components of the cytokinetic machinery or global plant stress responses, a massive knowledge gap remains: how do diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress? Addressing this complex phenomenon requires a scale of inquiry beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. We propose a community-scale data synthesis project, utilizing strictly publicly available data, to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience. Leveraging vast public repositories—such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), PRIDE, and various open-access bioimage databases—we will integrate spatiotemporal transcriptomes, vesicle proteomics, and cellular imaging across diverse plant systems ranging from key models like Arabidopsis to vital crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, to manage the immense scale and heterogeneity of these multi-omic data, we will deploy massively scalable, containerized computational workflows to process tens of thousands of raw RNA-seq samples uniformly. By applying advanced, noise-aware network construction toolkits, we will generate context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out confounding cross-dataset variables to isolate distinct regulatory modules that are activated exclusively at the intersection of specific times-of-day and high-temperature stress. We will bridge these transcriptomic network predictions to mesoscale cellular phenotypes by synthesizing public proteomic and image data, applying shape-based computational modeling to evaluate how environmental stress alters division-plane orientation, phragmoplast navigation, and unconventional protein secretion pathways. This transdisciplinary approach uniquely fuses chronobiology, endomembrane cell biology, and computational genomics. We aim to identify how the circadian clock temporally gates the trafficking of essential cell wall components during heat stress, and whether redundant genetic mechanisms reorganize the 4D temporal organellome to prevent catastrophic cell division failure. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative Working Group will not only answer fundamental questions about subcellular emergence but also serve as a premier training ground. Trainees will gain cutting-edge expertise at the intersection of biological synthesis, AI-driven network analysis, and scalable cloud computing. In strict adherence to open science principles, all resulting multi-omic matrices, context-specific networks, and reproducible computational pipelines will be made fully accessible to the global scientific community.
background_and_significance:
Mesoscale emergence in biological systems bridges the gap between individual macromolecules and macroscopic cellular behaviors. One of the most striking examples of this phenomenon in the molecular and cellular biosciences is plant cytokinesis. During this highly coordinated developmental window, distinct molecular components—including trans-Golgi network (TGN) derived vesicles, cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a higher-order structure: the cell plate. Driven by the phragmoplast, this mesoscale assembly process requires rigorous navigation and membrane remodeling to ensure accurate division-plane orientation. Because cell division is an architectural bottleneck, cytokinesis is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly thermal stress. With global temperatures rising and heat waves becoming more frequent, catastrophic failures in cytokinesis represent a major threat to plant development and ecosystem stability.

Despite decades of research, our understanding of cytokinetic resilience remains fragmented. Isolated studies have extensively mapped the canonical pathways of cell plate biogenesis, the circadian gating of global abiotic stress responses, and the fundamental dynamics of the plant endomembrane system. However, a significant knowledge gap persists at the intersection of these fields: we lack a systems-level understanding of how diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress. Addressing this compelling scientific question requires synthesizing heterogeneous layers of biological information—ranging from transcriptomics and vesicle proteomics to shape-based morphometrics and chronobiology—at a scale that far exceeds the capacity of any individual research laboratory.

The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) is uniquely positioned to catalyze this transdisciplinary investigation. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience using strictly publicly available data. By integrating multi-omic datasets across diverse plant taxa, including key model organisms like Arabidopsis and critical agricultural crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species, this project will unearth the fundamental principles governing mesoscale adaptability. 

This synthesis will reveal how the circadian clock synchronizes endomembrane trafficking to protect the phragmoplast during peak temperature loads. Furthermore, it will illuminate the role of unconventional protein secretion pathways and redundant genetic mechanisms in maintaining division plane fidelity when canonical cellular machineries are thermally compromised. The significance of this project is two-fold. First, it addresses a long-standing puzzle regarding how complex subcellular structures maintain functional emergence under thermodynamic duress. Second, it develops innovative, noise-aware analytical strategies to mine vast public data repositories, extracting context-specific regulatory modules that govern mesoscale resilience. Ultimately, the insights generated by this NCEMS Working Group will redefine our understanding of the temporal organellome while providing the foundational knowledge necessary to engineer heat-tolerant biological systems in an era of unprecedented climate change.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This community-scale synthesis project will address three fundamental, interconnected research questions aimed at decoding mesoscale emergence and resilience during plant cytokinesis under thermal stress. By synthesizing massive public datasets, we will test the following hypotheses:

Research Question 1: How does the circadian clock temporally gate the transcriptomic and proteomic networks governing cell plate assembly to prevent catastrophic failure during heat stress?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the circadian clock acts as a temporal master regulator, restricting the transcription and translation of critical cytokinetic network modules—specifically those controlling phragmoplast navigation and microtubule dynamics—to specific times of day. By gating these processes, the clock ensures that the most vulnerable mesoscale assembly phases do not coincide with peak daily thermal loads. Utilizing context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs) derived from publicly available time-course and temperature-stress transcriptomes, we will identify rhythmic regulatory modules that buffer the division machinery against diurnal heat extremes.

Research Question 2: In what ways do temporal organellome dynamics and endomembrane trafficking reorganize at the mesoscale to sustain cell wall deposition during severe temperature fluctuations?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that extreme thermal stress triggers an emergent reorganization of the plant endomembrane system, shifting cargo routing from canonical trans-Golgi network (TGN) pathways to unconventional protein secretion (UPS) and autophagy-related pathways. This spatial and temporal rerouting serves as an adaptive mechanism to sustain the delivery of essential polysaccharides and membrane material to the expanding cell plate. By integrating publicly available vesicle proteomics and spatiotemporal transcriptomic data, we will track the shifting gradients of organelle abundance and cargo trafficking, mapping how these unconventional pathways emerge as dominant survival mechanisms when canonical secretion is thermally compromised.

Research Question 3: What redundant spatial and genetic mechanisms preserve division-plane orientation and phragmoplast navigation under heat stress?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that plant cells rely on redundant, shape-based constraints and alternative cytoskeletal navigational cues to rescue division-plane fidelity when primary structural networks are disrupted by heat. Utilizing public cellular imaging datasets and shape-based computational models, we will quantify heat-induced division-plane defects across diverse plant species. We will correlate these morphometric changes with genetic redundancies identified through our massive RNA-seq synthesis, revealing a complex fail-safe network that protects the architecture of the dividing cell.

Together, these questions form a cohesive transdisciplinary framework. We aim to understand how temporal pacing (Question 1), molecular supply chains (Question 2), and spatial architecture (Question 3) integrate to yield emergent cytokinetic resilience. Answering these questions requires precisely the type of community-scale, multi-omic data synthesis that NCEMS is designed to support, transforming isolated datasets into a unified understanding of mesoscale biological robustness.
methods_and_approach:
To decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience, we will conduct a massive community-scale data synthesis using entirely publicly available datasets, generating zero new experimental data. Our methodology relies on advanced computational genomics, multi-omic integration, and shape-based modeling, executed through highly reproducible workflows.

Data Acquisition and Curation: We will harvest public datasets from repositories such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), PRIDE (for proteomics), and the BioImage Archive. The synthesis will span key model organisms (Arabidopsis thaliana) and economically critical crops with diverse genomic architectures (Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, and Rosaceae species). Data will be strictly filtered for high-quality spatiotemporal, circadian, and heat-stress experimental designs, yielding tens of thousands of individual omics samples.

Massively Scalable Transcriptomic Processing: Analyzing tens of thousands of heterogeneous RNA-seq samples requires robust, reproducible infrastructure. We will deploy highly scalable, containerized computational workflows (e.g., Nextflow-based GEMmaker pipelines) to process massive datasets across heterogeneous cloud and HPC environments. This approach ensures uniform read alignment, transcript quantification, and quality control without exceeding available data storage capacities, generating massive, standardized gene expression matrices.

Noise-Aware, Context-Specific Network Construction: Traditional gene co-expression networks (GCNs) built from massive, heterogeneous datasets suffer from high false-positive rates due to confounding variables. To isolate modules specifically related to heat stress, cytokinesis, and time-of-day, we will utilize advanced, knowledge-independent network construction toolkits. By applying rigorous statistical testing, we will construct context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out up to 97% of misleading network edges caused by diverse experimental backgrounds, isolating precise transcriptional modules that activate exclusively at the intersection of circadian gating and thermal stress.

Multi-Omic Integration and Proteomic Synthesis: Transcriptomic predictions will be grounded in mesoscale reality by synthesizing public vesicle proteomics and organellomic data. We will map identified csGCN modules onto proteomic profiles of the trans-Golgi network, phragmoplast, and unconventional protein secretion (UPS) pathways. By tracking temporal organellomic gradients and protein abundance shifts in public thermal-stress studies, we will empirically validate the network-predicted rerouting of cell wall machinery.

Shape-Based Morphometric Modeling: To bridge molecular networks to cellular phenotypes, we will synthesize public microscopic imaging datasets of dividing plant cells under stress. We will apply shape-based computational models to these images to quantify altered division-plane orientations and phragmoplast geometries. By correlating morphometric deviations with transcriptomic network states across different species, we will uncover how redundant geometric and genetic mechanisms rescue cellular architecture during heat waves.

Through this transdisciplinary approach—combining highly scalable data processing, advanced noise-aware AI network analytics, and multi-scale modeling—we will synthesize isolated molecular parts into a coherent understanding of mesoscale emergence. The workflows will remain highly modular, allowing the global scientific community to easily update the synthesis as new public data becomes available.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This proposed community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly align with the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence. By mathematically formalizing the emergent resilience of plant cytokinesis under thermal stress, we will solve a long-standing puzzle regarding how the circadian clock, temporal organellome, and redundant spatial mechanisms collaborate to protect architectural bottlenecks in cell division. We expect to discover entirely novel, context-specific regulatory modules that govern unconventional protein secretion and phragmoplast navigation exclusively under heat wave conditions.

The scientific impact of this work will span multiple disciplines. For cell biology and chronobiology, we will provide a unified, multi-omic model of how time-of-day dictates cellular susceptibility to stress. For agricultural sciences, translating these fundamental mesoscale principles from Arabidopsis to vital crops like Sorghum, maize, and pear will identify distinct genetic targets for breeding climate-resilient plants capable of surviving increasingly severe temperature fluctuations.

Beyond biological discovery, this project will drive significant methodological impact. We will establish and validate highly scalable, noise-aware computational frameworks capable of filtering massive confounding variables from heterogeneous public datasets to construct highly accurate, context-specific networks. 

Crucially, this NCEMS Working Group will serve as an elite training incubator for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will be cross-trained in biological synthesis, cloud computing, advanced multi-omics integration, and open science practices. Trainees will not only engage in cutting-edge transdisciplinary research but also learn to manage complex, multi-institutional collaborations. By empowering diverse new talent to answer complex biological questions using existing data, this project will cultivate the next generation of leaders in computational biosciences and systems biology.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest gold-standard practices in open, team, and reproducible science. Recognizing that the value of community-scale synthesis lies in its accessibility, every aspect of our methodology and output will adhere strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles.

All computational workflows, including the scalable Nextflow pipelines and noise-aware network construction toolkits, will be developed using containerized software (e.g., Docker and Singularity) to ensure complete computational reproducibility across any local, HPC, or cloud infrastructure. All scripts, algorithms, and shape-based computational models will be maintained in version-controlled, public GitHub repositories under open-source licenses, accompanied by comprehensive, user-friendly documentation and tutorial vignettes.

While no new experimental data will be generated, the massive, highly curated expression matrices, vesicle proteomics mappings, and context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs) represent highly valuable secondary resources. Furthermore, we will create an interactive, web-based public portal that allows researchers globally to query our context-specific networks and visualize temporal organellome dynamics without requiring advanced computational expertise. Through this rigorous adherence to open science principles, our synthesis project will not only answer fundamental questions about mesoscale emergence but also provide the broader cellular and molecular biosciences community with robust, reusable tools and integrated data resources.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence in the 3D Genome: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Polymer Physics Data to Uncover IDP-Driven Chromatin Reorganization in Neuro-Immune Phenotypes
abstract:
The three-dimensional organization of the eukaryotic genome represents a profound emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale. Through the local coordination of epigenetic modifications, structural proteins, and transcription factors, linear DNA spontaneously folds into dynamic 3D architectures, such as loop domains and phase-separated hubs. These mesoscale structures ultimately dictate macroscopic cellular responses. Recent experimental advances have generated vast amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell chromatin conformation maps (e.g., Dip-C, Hi-C), single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). However, a critical synthesis gap remains: we lack a unified theoretical and computational framework that bridges the physical forces governing mesoscale chromatin architecture—specifically, the entropic and steric pressures exerted by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and pioneer factors—with systemic, genome-wide transcriptional outcomes. 

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the biophysical rules of emergent 3D genome architectures and their cascading effects on neuro-immune cellular plasticity. This working group will entirely leverage existing, publicly available data from the 4D Nucleome Project, the Human Cell Atlas, and GTEx. By integrating single-cell genomics, structural bioinformatics, and deep clinical transcriptomic profiling, our project aims to answer a longstanding mystery: how do local biophysical interactions, such as IDP-driven liquid-liquid phase separation and loop extrusion, generate the highly specific, emergent chromatin topologies required for coordinated cellular responses?

Our transdisciplinary approach is structured around three primary synthesis aims. First, we will utilize machine learning and AI-driven data science to fuse diverse multi-omic datasets (scRNA-seq, ATAC-seq, structural proteomics, and 3D genomics) across diverse human brain and immune cell types. This will create a unified, multi-layered atlas of cell-type-specific 3D genome configurations. Second, we will apply coarse-grained polymer physics modeling and biophysical simulations to these integrated datasets to infer the mechanical transmission and steric pressures exerted by IDPs and pioneer factors at domain boundaries. We hypothesize that biophysical parameters extracted from massive genomic datasets can reliably predict the physical thresholds required for chromatin opening and decompaction. Third, we will map these structural biophysical rules onto complex biological phenotypes, specifically analyzing how systemic perturbations—such as severe infection or neurological stress—remodel the genome's mesoscale architecture to drive maladaptive neuro-inflammatory and psychiatric phenotypes.

This synthesis project fundamentally demands the support of NCEMS, as it surpasses the capacity of any single laboratory by requiring the convergence of systems immunology, single-cell genomics, chromatin biophysics, and polymer physics. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, machine learning models, and polymer simulation pipelines will be made freely available as an open-source "Biophysical 3D-Omics" analytical suite. Furthermore, this working group will deeply integrate trainees, providing postdocs and graduate students with a unique, cross-disciplinary environment to master the synthesis of clinical multi-omics and theoretical biophysics, thereby training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore emergent biological complexity.
background_and_significance:
The three-dimensional organization of the eukaryotic genome stands as a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. At the microscale, individual biomolecules—such as intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), epigenetic modifiers, pioneer transcription factors, and linker histones—interact with linear DNA. Through fundamental physical principles, including steric pressure generation and liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), these localized molecular events spontaneously give rise to complex, mesoscale 3D structures like topologically associating domains (TADs), chromatin loops, and phase-separated transcriptional hubs. These emergent architectures serve as the mechanical and topological foundations for macroscopic cellular behaviors, dictating gene expression plasticity in response to developmental cues and systemic stressors.

Over the past decade, consortium efforts such as the 4D Nucleome (4DN) Project, the Human Cell Atlas (HCA), and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project have generated an unprecedented wealth of publicly available data. These datasets include high-resolution single-cell chromatin conformation capture (e.g., Dip-C, Hi-C), single-cell multi-omics (scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq), high-throughput mass spectrometry proteomics, and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). However, these massive data reservoirs remain largely siloed by discipline. Genomicists map the structural correlations; systems immunologists and neurobiologists characterize phenotypic transcriptional states; and biophysicists simulate the polymer dynamics of isolated chromatin segments. A critical synthesis gap exists: there is currently no unified framework capable of translating the raw physical forces modeled in computational biophysics into the global, systemic genome architectures mapped by single-cell genomics.

This proposal outlines a community-scale synthesis project specifically designed to bridge this divide, perfectly aligning with the mandate of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We will synthesize multi-omic and polymer physics data to uncover how IDP-driven phase separation, cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, and pioneer factor cooperativity mechanically coordinate large-scale chromatin reorganization. By utilizing solely existing datasets, we bypass data generation to focus entirely on deep, transdisciplinary integration. 

We focus our synthesis on the neuro-immune axis, analyzing the profound cellular plasticity required in complex brain phenotypes (such as psychiatric disorders) and severe systemic immune responses (such as post-sepsis inflammation). Both contexts are characterized by rapid, widespread epigenetic reprogramming and transcriptional adaptation. Understanding how local biophysical forces transmit mechanical signals to restructure the entire 3D genome—and how this topology goes awry in disease—represents a long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. 

By leveraging AI-driven data synthesis, coarse-grained polymer physics, and systems-level network theory, this Working Group will establish the fundamental biophysical rules of mesoscale chromatin emergence. The significance of this project lies not only in answering how linear DNA folds into a functional organelle, but in providing a predictive, physics-grounded model of genome regulation that spans from nanometer-scale entropic forces to complex human disease phenotypes, fulfilling the bold scientific vision of NCEMS.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our transdisciplinary Working Group proposes three interrelated research questions and corresponding hypotheses to uncover the biophysical rules governing emergent 3D genome architectures. By synthesizing diverse computational models with massive public datasets, we aim to solve fundamental mysteries regarding mesoscale chromatin regulation.

Research Question 1: How do localized biophysical forces—specifically the steric pressures generated by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and pioneer transcription factors—mechanically transmit across the polymer to dictate emergent mesoscale 3D genome topologies in distinct cell states?

Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the entropic and electrostatic steric pressures exerted by IDPs and pioneer factors at chromatin domain boundaries serve as primary mechanical drivers of targeted chromatin decompaction and loop reconfiguration. By synthesizing structural bioinformatics with high-resolution single-cell chromatin conformation maps (e.g., Dip-C) and scATAC-seq, we predict that these biophysical parameters form a universal scaling law. This law can be computationally extracted from existing multi-omic data to explain the liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and targeted mechanical remodeling required for cell-type-specific compartmentalization, circumventing the need for deterministic, locus-by-locus biochemical rules.

Research Question 2: Can structural and physical rules abstracted from coarse-grained polymer physics models be integrated with massive single-cell genomic and proteomic atlases to accurately predict the transcriptional dynamics of neuro-immune cells?

Hypothesis 2: We posit that global 3D genome architecture operates via foundational polymer physics principles that are modified by cell-type-specific epigenetic landscapes. By synthesizing quantitative polymer models (accounting for cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and linker histone dynamics) with systems-level transcriptomic networks, we can generate a predictive "Biophysical 3D-Omics" latent space. We hypothesize that machine learning models constrained by physical priors will significantly outperform purely statistical models in predicting how structural perturbations—such as the loss of loop domains or the decompaction of heterochromatin—cascade into genome-wide expression changes in human brain cells and circulating immune cells.

Research Question 3: How do systemic biological perturbations—such as severe infectious states or complex neurological stress—remodel the genome's mesoscale architecture to drive maladaptive, long-lived phenotypic signatures?

Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that chronic stress states, including prolonged inflammatory signatures post-infection or the multifactorial etiology of psychiatric phenotypes, fundamentally destabilize the established physical thresholds of the 3D genome. Specifically, systemic perturbations disrupt normal IDP interaction networks and histone modifications, leading to catastrophic shifts in mesoscale looping—such as cohesin-independent superenhancer coalescing or aberrant phase separations. We predict that mapping expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and TWAS data onto our synthesized biophysical topologies will reveal that many disease-associated variants do not simply ablate specific gene function, but rather alter the local mechanical landscape of the genome, trapping cells in maladaptive, self-reinforcing transcriptional programs.
methods_and_approach:
This project utilizes exclusively existing, publicly available data, adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate for community-scale synthesis without new experimental data generation. We will integrate datasets from the 4D Nucleome (Hi-C, Micro-C, single-cell Dip-C), the Human Cell Atlas (scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq for brain and immune subsets), GTEx (eQTLs and transcriptomics), and PRIDE (high-throughput clinical plasma and cellular proteomics).

Aim 1: AI-Driven Multi-Omic Data Harmonization and Latent Space Construction
The fundamental challenge of synthesizing multi-omics is the severe dimensionality and sparsity of single-cell data. We will employ advanced machine learning frameworks to construct a unified latent representation of cell-type-specific genome architectures. Using variational autoencoders (VAEs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), we will map 1D sequence features (scATAC-seq, TF binding motifs), 2D interaction maps (Hi-C/Dip-C contact matrices), and 3D expression readouts (scRNA-seq) into a shared topological space. This synthesis will focus heavily on diverse human brain cell populations (e.g., somatostatin interneurons) and peripheral immune compartments (e.g., NK cells, memory B cells), enabling us to correlate specific epigenetic profiles with emergent 3D architectures across thousands of individual cells.

Aim 2: Biophysical Parameter Extraction and Coarse-Grained Polymer Simulations
To bridge genomics with biophysics, we will extract structural boundary constraints from our multi-omic latent spaces to parameterize coarse-grained polymer physics models. We will simulate chromatin as a block copolymer, incorporating empirical data on linker histone density, cohesin binding sites, and pioneer factor localization. Crucially, we will integrate predictive biophysical models of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). By cross-referencing public structural databases (e.g., AlphaFold/DisProt) with transcription factors identified in our omics pipelines, we will calculate localized entropic and electrostatic steric pressures. These parameters will drive Langevin dynamics simulations to explicitly model liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and chromatin looping dynamics. This unique synthesis of single-cell genomics with polymer physics will reveal the mechanical transmission rules that dictate how local binding events trigger widespread chromatin opening or collapse.

Aim 3: Phenotype Mapping via Transcriptome-Wide Association Synthesis
Finally, we will map complex disease states onto our synthesized physical framework. Using existing clinical transcriptomic data—such as patient cohorts exhibiting long-lived pro-inflammatory profiles post-sepsis or brain-wide psychiatric genetics—we will evaluate how systemic perturbations alter 3D genomic mechanics. We will overlay eQTL and TWAS data onto our biophysical models to assess whether disease-associated SNPs alter the mechanical thresholds of the polymer (e.g., modifying IDP steric pressure or loop boundary stability). By running predictive biophysical simulations using "diseased" parameters, we will evaluate structural decompaction and aberrant enhancer-promoter coalescing, identifying specific mesoscale vulnerabilities that lock cells into maladaptive states.

Integration & Collaboration:
This approach inherently requires NCEMS support; no individual lab possesses the simultaneous expertise in single-cell genomics algorithms, coarse-grained polymer physics, AI-driven data harmonization, and clinical systems immunology. The Working Group will facilitate intensive cross-disciplinary synthesis, creating a collaborative nexus where biophysicists and systems biologists iteratively refine models against multi-layered public datasets.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed community-scale synthesis project will fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. By bridging the critical gap between nanometer-scale biophysics and genome-wide functional topology, we will deliver the following major outcomes:

1. The "Biophysical 3D-Omics" Analytical Suite: We will release a comprehensive, fully open-source computational framework capable of extracting biophysical parameters (steric pressure, phase separation propensity, loop extrusion dynamics) directly from publicly available multi-omic datasets. This tool will democratize the integration of polymer physics and systems biology, allowing researchers across disciplines to predict structural chromatin dynamics from standard transcriptomic and epigenetic data.

2. Mechanistic Insight into Mesoscale Emergence: We will answer the long-standing puzzle of how the genome uses localized physical forces, such as IDP-driven phase separations and mechanical loop transmission, to globally reprogram its 3D architecture. We expect to establish universal biophysical scaling laws that dictate chromatin folding, moving the field beyond descriptive contact mapping toward predictive physical modeling.

3. Resolving the Etiology of Complex Neuro-Immune Phenotypes: By mapping psychiatric and systemic inflammatory disease states onto our biophysical models, we anticipate uncovering a new class of "mechanical" genetic variants—eQTLs that drive pathogenesis not by ablating protein function, but by altering the local steric pressure and loop boundaries of the genome. This will provide profound insights into how cells become locked in maladaptive stress responses, potentially identifying novel therapeutic targets for conditions like severe sepsis or schizophrenia.

4. Workforce Development: This project will serve as a premier training ground for a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students. By embedding trainees in a highly transdisciplinary Working Group, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely fluent in both theoretical biophysics and computational multi-omics, ready to tackle the future of emergent biological complexity.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to the highest standards of open science and reproducibility is foundational to this Working Group. We are committed to making all findings, integrated datasets, and analytical workflows fully public, aligning with community-created policies on FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles.

Data and Code Sharing: Since this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, we will rigorously document all data provenance, versioning, and processing steps. All customized machine learning architectures, biophysical simulation scripts, and data integration pipelines will be developed openly on GitHub from day one. Upon publication, stable versions of the codebase will be archived in Zenodo to ensure permanent DOI minting and citable reproducibility.

Reproducible Workflows: To overcome the computational "reproducibility crisis" common in complex omics and physics simulations, our "Biophysical 3D-Omics" analytical suite will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. All multi-omic data harmonization pipelines will be built using workflow managers such as Nextflow, ensuring they can be seamlessly executed across different high-performance computing (HPC) clusters or cloud environments (e.g., AWS, Terra) with a single command.

Pre-registration and Transparent Analysis: To mitigate analytical bias, we will pre-register our primary computational hypotheses and synthesis protocols on the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to executing large-scale modeling. 

Community Engagement: We will actively disseminate our tools through comprehensive, user-friendly documentation and interactive Jupyter/Google Colab notebooks. By providing pre-configured tutorials that guide users through running polymer simulations on toy genomic datasets, we will ensure that our synthesis framework is accessible to the broader molecular biology community, regardless of their prior expertise in biophysics or data science.
budget_and_resources:
The requested budget is meticulously structured to support the community-scale synthesis mandate of NCEMS, focusing exclusively on personnel, computational infrastructure, and Working Group collaboration, with zero funds allocated for wet-lab data generation.

Personnel ($150,000/year): The primary budget allocation supports trainees, critical to the NCEMS mission of developing a data-savvy workforce. We request funding for two Postdoctoral Fellows and two Graduate Research Assistants. These positions will be explicitly cross-trained. For example, a postdoc with a background in systems immunology will be co-mentored in polymer physics modeling, ensuring the transfer of highly specialized, transdisciplinary skills.

Cloud Computing and Data Storage ($50,000/year): Synthesizing massive single-cell multi-omic atlases alongside computationally intensive Langevin dynamics simulations requires substantial computing power. Funds are allocated for cloud computing credits (AWS/GCP) to train machine learning models and host the immense harmonized latent spaces. This cloud-first approach guarantees that our pipelines remain scalable and accessible for open science distribution.

Working Group Meetings and Travel ($40,000/year): To catalyze multidisciplinary integration, we request support for bi-annual, intensive in-person synthesis meetings at the NCEMS hub. These multi-day workshops will bring together the diverse expertise of our team (single-cell genomics, chromatin biophysics, structural proteomics, and complex phenotypes) to collaboratively troubleshoot models and refine algorithmic approaches. Funds also support trainees to present findings at major computational biology and biophysics conferences.

Open Science and Publication Costs ($10,000/year): We request funds to cover Article Processing Charges (APCs) to ensure all resulting publications are immediate, gold-standard Open Access. Additionally, a small portion of the budget will support cloud-hosting fees for large-scale, interactive data visualization portals built for the community.

This resource allocation ensures our Working Group is optimally supported to synthesize vast datasets into groundbreaking insights regarding mesoscale 3D genome emergence.
