author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Mapping Emergent Mesoscale Architectures at the Host-Microbiome Interface: A Deep-Time Proteogenomic Synthesis
abstract:
The unexpected appearance of new biological properties often occurs at the mesoscale, where distinct biomolecules assemble into complex functional modules. While mesoscale organization within individual cells is increasingly well-characterized, the emergence of cross-species mesoscale architectures—specifically, the structural and functional protein-protein interaction networks between human hosts and their resident microbiomes—remains a profound mystery. Understanding how these emergent host-microbiome interfaces assemble and evolve is critical to deciphering human systemic adaptations, yet it has been severely limited by computational bottlenecks, the prevalence of uncharacterized 'dark' microbial taxa, and the historic siloing of human proteomics and microbial metagenomics.

We propose a multidisciplinary Working Group to conduct a community-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omic datasets, answering fundamental questions about the evolutionary emergence of mesoscale host-microbe protein networks. Our project integrates massive, disparate public databases: high-resolution human genomic and plasma proteomic cohorts (e.g., UK Biobank, providing data on thousands of circulating human proteins and their genetic regulators) alongside vast repositories of modern and ancient human metagenomic data (e.g., the Human Microbiome Project, ancient dental calculus, and paleofeces databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will deploy a novel, transdisciplinary analytical strategy using AI and data science to synthesize these existing resources.

To overcome the immense computational challenge of cross-kingdom alignment, we will leverage state-of-the-art, ultra-fast protein sequence alignment algorithms and advanced phylogenetic network modeling to process massive short-read datasets at a fraction of traditional computational costs. This infrastructure will map millions of microbial sequences—including those from understudied and ancestral microbial lineages—into a functionally annotated protein space. Crucially, by applying rigorous, gold-standard computational bio-filters derived from low-biomass microbiome research protocols, we will systematically exclude environmental contamination, ensuring that the inferred cross-species interactomes represent genuine biological interfaces.

We will then utilize AI-driven structural predictions and proteogenomic integration frameworks, such as cis-anchored protein mapping and Mendelian randomization, to model how these microbial proteins physically and functionally interact with the host systemic proteome. By comparing these proteogenomic networks across deep evolutionary time (ancient vs. modern humans) and diverse metabolic states (e.g., caloric restriction, multi-disease outcomes), we will uncover how emergent mesoscale properties—such as multi-protein metabolic sinks, host-mimicking immune complexes, and novel signaling hubs—have appeared and reorganized under evolutionary and environmental pressures.

This synthesis requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as it operates at a scale far beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. By bridging algorithmic phylogenetics, rigorous microbial ecology, and large-scale epidemiological proteomics, our Working Group will establish a new paradigm for studying biological emergence. The project strictly adheres to open science principles, committing to the FAIR release of all analytical pipelines, canonical network models, and integrated databases. Importantly, this initiative will cross-train a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists with the transdisciplinary expertise required to navigate complex multi-omic integration, algorithmic optimization, and rigorous contamination control.
background_and_significance:
Understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties requires an in-depth examination of the mesoscale—the critical spatial and organizational tier bridging individual biomolecules and complex cellular organelles. While significant progress has been made in mapping intracellular mesoscale organization, inter-organismal mesoscale architectures remain largely unexplored. Specifically, the structural and functional protein-protein interaction networks operating at the interface between human hosts and their resident microbiomes represent a profound biological frontier. These cross-species mesoscale complexes govern systemic physiological adaptations, immune modulation, and disease etiology, yet they are historically treated as a biological black box due to profound methodological and computational limitations.

Historically, the fields of human systemic proteomics, computational phylogenetics, and microbial ecology have operated in silos, generating vast but disconnected repositories of publicly available data. For example, massive epidemiological datasets now map thousands of circulating human proteins and their genetic regulators across hundreds of thousands of individuals. Simultaneously, extensive metagenomic databases archive the diverse microbial communities inhabiting modern humans, alongside emerging datasets characterizing ancient human microbiota from calcified dental plaque and paleofeces. Despite the sheer volume of these resources, integrating them into a cohesive model of mesoscale biological emergence has been stymied by three primary obstacles: the computational bottleneck of mapping billions of short sequencing reads across kingdoms, the pervasive challenge of contaminant DNA noise in low-biomass and ancient samples, and the lack of analytical frameworks capable of bridging microbial genomics with human systemic proteomics.

Our proposed community-scale synthesis project addresses these exact barriers, aligning perfectly with the NCEMS mission to catalyze transdisciplinary research that synthesizes existing molecular data without generating de novo experimental datasets. By assembling a collaborative Working Group comprising experts in advanced algorithmic development, rigorous microbiome ecology, and large-scale epidemiological proteomics, we aim to overcome these long-standing puzzles. We will synthesize massive, disparate multi-omic datasets using ultra-fast double-indexing protein alignment algorithms capable of processing metagenomic data at unprecedented speeds. This algorithmic power will be coupled with stringent, automated computational bio-filters specifically designed to mathematically subtract contaminant noise derived from low-biomass environments, ensuring that only genuine biological interfaces are analyzed.

The significance of this project lies in its potential to uncover how emergent mesoscale properties—such as microbial protein complexes that mimic host signaling molecules or multi-protein metabolic sinks—have evolved over deep time. By deploying AI-driven structural predictions and cutting-edge proteogenomic integration, we will construct the first comprehensive, deep-time host-microbiome interactome. This transdisciplinary synthesis will not only answer fundamental questions regarding human evolutionary adaptation and systemic disease mechanisms but will also establish innovative analytical strategies and gold-standard protocols for multi-omic integration. Ultimately, this effort will fundamentally transform our understanding of biological emergence across species boundaries while heavily investing in the training of a diverse, data-savvy scientific workforce equipped to tackle the next generation of biological complexities.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group will leverage publicly available, multi-omic data to address compelling, novel scientific questions regarding the emergence of mesoscale biological properties at the host-microbiome interface. Our research is structured around three primary, interrelated questions, each driving specific hypotheses that bridge deep evolutionary time, systemic physiology, and advanced computational methodology.

Question 1: How have mesoscale host-microbe protein networks structurally and functionally reorganized over deep evolutionary time? 
Despite the availability of rich ancient DNA (aDNA) datasets from sources like calcified dental calculus, we do not fully understand how ancestral microbial proteins interacted with ancient host physiologies compared to modern configurations. We hypothesize that the transition from ancient to modern environments, diets, and lifestyles induced a structural reorganization of cross-species mesoscale assemblies. Specifically, we predict that comparative ancestral vs. modern network modeling will reveal the evolutionary emergence of novel microbial metabolic sinks and host-mimicking immune complexes that compensate for or adapt to altered human dietary and environmental exposures over the last 50,000 years. 

Question 2: How do emergent host-microbiome mesoscale interactions dynamically reconfigure under extreme metabolic stress and across diverse disease states? 
Human systemic proteomes exhibit profound adaptations to metabolic perturbations, such as extreme caloric restriction, and form the basis for multi-disease risk stratification. However, the microbial contribution to these host proteomic shifts remains obscure. We hypothesize that distinct structural mesoscale modules transiently emerge during metabolic perturbations and precede the onset of common diseases. Utilizing cis-anchored proteogenomic mapping and Mendelian randomization on matched human-microbiome multi-omic datasets, we expect to demonstrate that specific circulating metabolic markers and plasma protein trajectories are directly modulated by underlying, highly conserved microbial protein complexes, identifying novel targets for complex disease intervention.

Question 3: Can the integration of ultra-fast algorithmic alignment with rigorous, mathematically derived bio-filters reliably resolve true inter-kingdom interactomes from inherently noisy, massive public datasets?
The synthesis of disparate metagenomic and proteomic data is plagued by computational bottlenecks and artifactual noise, particularly in low-biomass or ancient samples. We hypothesize that traditional cross-kingdom sequence alignments fail to distinguish transient environmental contaminants from true evolutionary host-microbe interfaces. We postulate that by coupling double-indexing alignment algorithms—capable of massive short-read translation at speeds far exceeding traditional methods—with automated minimal-standard contamination frameworks (e.g., dynamically implementing consensus biological checklists as mathematical subtractions), we can unmask previously 'dark' microbial taxa interactions. We expect this combined methodological innovation to successfully eliminate artifactual noise, yielding canonical phylogenetic networks with robust mathematical properties that accurately represent true biological emergence.

By systematically testing these hypotheses entirely through the synthesis of existing data, our project will resolve long-standing mysteries regarding human-microbial co-evolution and physiological adaptation, ultimately redefining mesoscale emergence through a rigorous, computational lens.
methods_and_approach:
Our transdisciplinary analytical strategy focuses exclusively on synthesizing publicly available data, demanding no new experimental generation. The project operates through a three-phase computational pipeline, integrating algorithmic phylogenetics, rigorous microbial ecology, and epidemiological proteomics.

Phase 1: Data Assembly and Ultra-Fast Metagenomic Processing
We will synthesize thousands of public datasets, including the UK Biobank (matched genomic and multi-omic data), the Human Microbiome Project (HMP), and comprehensive ancient DNA archives of dental calculus and paleofeces. The foundational computational challenge is the translation and alignment of billions of short and long metagenomic sequencing reads against massive protein reference databases (e.g., NCBI-nr). We will deploy state-of-the-art double-indexing sequence alignment algorithms, which accelerate protein alignment by orders of magnitude compared to traditional tools, while maintaining high sensitivity. This allows us to rapidly translate genomic data into a functionally annotated protein space. Crucially, to ensure data fidelity, we will engineer and apply automated computational bio-filters. Drawing upon minimal standards and consensus workflows developed for low-biomass microbiome studies, these bio-filters will mathematically subtract ubiquitous environmental contaminants, cross-contamination artifacts, and spurious alignments. This strict quality control ensures that subsequent structural analyses are built solely on biologically genuine microbial presence.

Phase 2: Canonical Network Modeling and AI-Driven Structural Prediction
Once the robust microbial protein catalog is established, we will resolve the complex evolutionary relationships of these microbial proteins using advanced phylogenetic network modeling. By applying mathematical transformation algorithms, we will simplify tangled, reticulate evolutionary histories into canonical networks that highlight conserved, host-interacting microbial protein families across modern and ancient lineages. To predict emergent mesoscale architectures, we will leverage scalable, AI-driven structural biology tools (e.g., adapted forms of AlphaFold-Multimer). By computing predicted structural interactomes between the filtered microbial proteins and highly expressed human host plasma proteins, we will identify stable, emergent protein-protein interfaces. We will map these predicted mesoscale complexes onto deep evolutionary timelines, visualizing how structural affinities have shifted in response to human behavioral and dietary evolution.

Phase 3: Proteogenomic Integration and Epidemiological Synthesis
To translate these predicted structural interactions into systemic functional insights, we will integrate them with human proteogenomic data. We will utilize genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to perform cis-anchored gene-protein mapping, linking host genetic variants to the expression of plasma proteins identified in our cross-species interactome. Utilizing Mendelian randomization and colocalization analyses, we will map the causal pathways between these emergent host-microbiome modules and diverse human metabolic states. Specifically, we will synthesize data from multi-disease epidemiological cohorts and intensive physiological interventions (e.g., continuous 7-day systemic proteome adaptations to extreme caloric restriction). This approach will illuminate how emergent inter-kingdom protein complexes act as signaling hubs or metabolic sinks, modulating individual risk for complex diseases and shaping physiological resilience. The synthesis of these methods will establish a comprehensive framework for exploring biology at the mesoscale.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative scientific outcomes, methodological innovations, and substantial workforce development, directly advancing the NCEMS mission to explore mesoscale biological emergence. 

Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the release of the first Deep-Time Host-Microbiome Interactome—a comprehensive, functionally annotated database of structurally predicted cross-species protein-protein interaction networks spanning thousands of years of human evolution. By detailing how mesoscale architectures rearrange under metabolic stress (such as caloric restriction) and across diverse disease states, this resource will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how human systemic adaptations are fundamentally driven by microbial symbiosis. Furthermore, the identification of emergent microbial protein complexes interacting with the human systemic proteome will highlight novel, uncharacterized biological targets for primary disease prevention and therapeutic intervention.

Methodologically, this project will yield open-source, highly scalable computational pipelines that resolve the historical bottlenecks of multi-omic synthesis. By integrating ultra-fast double-indexing alignment algorithms with automated, mathematically rigorous contamination filters tailored for low-biomass data, we will establish a new gold standard for robust cross-kingdom metagenomic analysis. These tools will enable the broader scientific community to confidently explore complex, noisy public datasets without the confounding artifacts of environmental contamination.

Broadly, the impact of this Working Group will shift the paradigm of microbiome research from mere taxonomic compositional surveys toward deep, structural, and functional characterizations of mesoscale emergence. By tapping into diverse scientific perspectives—spanning computational biology, microbial ecology, ancient DNA, and clinical epidemiology—this project will foster a vibrant, collaborative ecosystem. Additionally, by heavily integrating postdoctoral fellows and graduate students into all phases of the pipeline, we will explicitly train the future data-savvy workforce, ensuring they are uniquely equipped to navigate and synthesize the multi-omic, AI-driven landscape of modern biological sciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to the highest standards of open science, reproducibility, and ethical data stewardship is a foundational pillar of this Working Group. All methodologies, software, and synthesized datasets will be made strictly publicly available, adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles.

To ensure complete computational reproducibility, all analytical pipelines—from ultra-fast sequence alignments and bio-filtering to AI structural predictions and proteogenomic mapping—will be authored using industry-standard workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake or Nextflow). These workflows will be containerized (via Docker and Singularity) and published in open repositories such as GitHub and Bioconda, complete with extensive documentation and reproducible test datasets. The Deep-Time Host-Microbiome Interactome database will be hosted on an interactive, publicly accessible web portal, enabling researchers globally to intuitively query host-microbe structural networks, canonical phylogenetic models, and associated multi-disease proteomic risk scores.

Furthermore, because our synthesis leverages ancient DNA and global genomic cohorts, we recognize the critical importance of ethical bio-data stewardship. We are strictly committed to integrating bioethical frameworks, particularly concerning the utilization of microbiome data derived from Indigenous and diverse global populations. We will adhere to community-created guidelines that respect data ownership, sovereignty, and responsible stewardship, ensuring that our synthesis of ancestral and global data prevents extractive research practices. 

Finally, the Working Group will publish comprehensive Consensus Statements detailing minimal reporting standards for multi-omic integration and low-biomass algorithmic filtering, pushing the global research community toward enhanced rigor. All resultant manuscripts will be published in open-access journals, with preprints deposited on platforms like bioRxiv prior to peer review, maximizing immediate community benefit.
budget_and_resources:
The proposed community-scale synthesis requires infrastructural, computational, and collaborative resources far beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory, explicitly necessitating NCEMS support. The budget is rigorously structured to fund human capital, massive-scale cloud computing, and collaborative Working Group convenings, with zero funds allocated to wet-lab or de novo data generation.

First, personnel funding is critical for training the next-generation data-savvy workforce. The budget will support dedicated postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who will serve as the transdisciplinary bridge between the bioinformatics, ancient DNA ecology, and clinical proteomics experts. These trainees will receive unparalleled cross-training in AI-driven structural biology, algorithmic optimization, and rigorous bio-filtering, driving the day-to-day execution of the analytical pipelines.

Second, significant resources are allocated to High-Performance Computing (HPC) and cloud infrastructure. While our algorithmic approaches utilize ultra-fast indexing to minimize traditional bottlenecks, the sheer volume of integrating thousands of metagenomic datasets with AI-based structural predictions (e.g., AlphaFold-Multimer applied at scale) requires substantial, dedicated cloud computing credits and massive data storage solutions for the resultant interactome databases.

Finally, the budget supports the logistical, travel, and hosting costs for recurring, intensive Working Group meetings and hackathons at the NCEMS facility. These in-person convenings are vital for synthesizing the diverse scientific perspectives required to merge epidemiological proteomics with ancient microbial ecology. By bringing together experts from disparate fields and geographic locations, these funds will stimulate transdisciplinary problem-solving, ensure the rapid iterative refinement of our canonical network models, and foster a cohesive, collaborative partnership that directly drives the successful mapping of mesoscale biological emergence.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Mapping the Emergent Bacterial Condensome: Synthesizing Transcriptomic and Biophysical Data to Predict Mesoscale Organization in Pathogenesis and Stress Adaptation
abstract:
The mesoscale organization of bacterial cells represents a critical frontier in molecular and cellular biosciences. While eukaryotic cells heavily rely on membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), the role of these emergent mesoscale structures in bacteria is only beginning to be recognized. Recent evidence suggests that bacteria utilize transient biomolecular condensates to coordinate stress responses, compartmentalize RNA-protein networks, and regulate host-microbe interactions. However, a major puzzle remains: how do dynamic fluctuations in gene expression and evolutionary mutations act as biophysical switches to trigger or dissolve these mesoscale assemblies? Addressing this requires integrating the principles of soft matter biophysics with systems-level bacterial genomics.

We propose to form an NCEMS Working Group that synthesizes massive, publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and structural datasets to construct the first comprehensive atlas of the "bacterial condensome." This project strictly utilizes existing data, integrating thousands of bacterial RNA-seq datasets (from GEO and SRA) covering diverse physiological states—including antibiotic exposure, host colonization, and quorum sensing—with genome-wide structural predictions from AlphaFold DB and intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) databases. 

By leveraging AI-driven biophysical models and associative polymer theory, our cross-disciplinary team will computationally map the sequence-encoded interaction potentials of bacterial proteomes. We will then overlay dynamic monomer concentrations derived from publicly available transcriptomic and proteomic data. Because the internal architecture and formation of condensates are highly sensitive to instantaneous monomer concentrations and specific stoichiometry, combining expression flux data with biophysical phase-separation thresholds will allow us to predict the emergence of mesoscale structures across distinct bacterial cell states. 

Our synthesis approach will focus on three key objectives: (1) Answer novel questions regarding how global shifts in transcriptomic states drive the systems-level emergence of phase-separated networks during bacterial stress adaptation. (2) Solve long-standing puzzles regarding pathogenic evolution by analyzing how specific mutations—such as those altering virulence factors or disrupting multidrug efflux pumps—reprogram internal condensate architecture or stoichiometry to enhance pathogenesis. (3) Develop an open-source, reproducible computational platform that bridges evolutionary genomics and soft matter physics, allowing researchers to predict phase-separation events directly from RNA-seq and genomic isolate data.

This community-scale synthesis project fundamentally requires NCEMS support, as it transcends the capabilities of any single laboratory. It necessitates a deep transdisciplinary integration of bacterial evolutionary genomics, RNA-seq bioinformatics, and polymer biophysics. In adherence to open science principles, all resulting atlases, predictive AI models, and analytical pipelines will be freely distributed. Furthermore, the Working Group will provide intensive cross-training for postdocs and graduate students, cultivating a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely fluent in both complex population-level genomics and the biophysical principles of mesoscale cellular emergence.
background_and_significance:
The mesoscale organization of biological systems—the crucial spatial and functional realm between individual biomolecules and entire organelles—is an area of profound emergent complexity. Historically, bacterial cells were viewed as relatively unstructured bags of enzymes lacking the intricate spatial compartmentalization characteristic of eukaryotes. This paradigm has been radically overturned by the discovery of bacterial biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Despite this conceptual breakthrough, a significant knowledge gap persists: we do not yet fundamentally understand how the emergence of these mesoscale structures is dynamically regulated during bacterial life cycles, nor how evolutionary forces acting on microbial populations shape the biophysical properties of these condensates. 

Currently, the fields of soft matter biophysics and bacterial evolutionary genomics operate largely in silos. Biophysicists elegantly define how sequence-encoded interactions, structural disorder, and multivalent binding program the internal architecture of condensates using well-controlled model systems and associative polymer theory. Concurrently, evolutionary biologists and synthetic biologists leverage massive transcriptomic (RNA-seq) and genomic datasets to map global gene expression shifts in response to environmental stresses, antibiotic exposure, quorum sensing, and host-microbe interactions. Yet, the physical reality is that phase separation inside a cell is exquisitely sensitive to instantaneous monomer concentrations and precise stoichiometric ratios of client and scaffold proteins. By failing to integrate dynamic gene expression flux with structural biophysics, we are missing the central mechanistic link that governs mesoscale emergence in vivo.

Our proposal addresses this exact disconnect by executing a massive, community-scale synthesis of publicly available data. We aim to fuse transcriptomic snapshots of bacterial cell states with AI-driven structural predictions (e.g., AlphaFold DB, MobiDB) and polymer physics models. This synthesis represents a novel strategy to computationally predict when and where biomolecular condensates form across diverse physiological conditions and evolutionary trajectories. For example, during pathogenic stress, evolutionary adaptations—such as the loss of antibiotic efflux pumps or the tuning of quorum-sensing circuits—dramatically reprogram global transcription networks. We hypothesize that these global shifts serve as coordinated biophysical switches, pushing specific protein and RNA populations across critical interaction energy thresholds to trigger the rapid demixing of specialized survival condensates. 

By leveraging the transdisciplinary structure of an NCEMS Working Group, we will systematically synthesize these distinct data types to answer fundamental mysteries regarding bacterial survival, virulence, and spatial adaptation. This effort requires zero de novo experimental data generation; instead, it relies entirely on mining and integrating the petabytes of underutilized, publicly available omics and structural data. The resulting synthesis will not only elucidate the rules of emergent bacterial organization but will also provide a transformative, predictive framework enabling researchers to infer biophysical phenotypes directly from standard RNA-seq and genomic variant data, thereby fundamentally advancing both molecular biophysics and systems microbiology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is designed to answer three fundamental questions regarding the emergence and regulation of the bacterial mesoscale. 

Question 1: How do global shifts in transcriptomic states drive the emergence of phase-separated networks during bacterial stress adaptation?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that abrupt, systems-level changes in gene expression triggered by environmental stress (e.g., antibiotic exposure, nutrient deprivation) act as primary biophysical switches that drive specific subsets of multivalent proteins across critical concentration thresholds, thereby inducing liquid-liquid phase separation. By integrating instantaneous expression levels from public RNA-seq repositories with computational models of protein solubility and associative polymer networks, we predict that distinct 'stress condensomes' emerge to temporarily sequester, protect, or organize vital RNA-protein interaction networks until homeostasis is restored. 

Question 2: How do evolutionary mutations and lineage-specific adaptations alter internal condensate architecture to influence bacterial pathogenesis and host-microbe interactions?
Hypothesis 2: Evolutionary biology has cataloged numerous genetic mutations that confer pathogenic advantages, such as those that tune quorum sensing or deactivate specific efflux pumps. We hypothesize that these evolutionary trajectories often inadvertently or adaptively modify the interaction energies and valencies of intrinsically disordered regions within key virulence factors. Furthermore, changes in expression stoichiometry driven by these mutations can shift the multiphase architecture of existing condensates. We predict that synthesizing variant allele frequencies and mutant transcriptomes with associative polymer models will reveal that pathogenic isolates frequently harbor optimized biophysical thresholds for condensate formation, enabling enhanced survival within the hostile environment of a host.

Question 3: Can we establish a reliable computational framework to predict condition-specific mesoscale organization directly from standard genomic and transcriptomic isolate data?
Hypothesis 3: The principles of soft matter physics governing biomolecular condensation are fundamentally deterministic, relying on monomer concentrations, binding affinities, and sequence-encoded features. We hypothesize that by employing machine learning to bridge AlphaFold-derived structural metrics, sequence disorder profiles, and empirical transcriptomic quantification, we can develop a generalizable, predictive AI model. This model will accurately forecast the probability and compositional architecture of phase separation events for any given bacterial state without requiring bespoke in vitro biophysical assays.

To address these questions, the NCEMS Working Group will synthesize disparate data modalities. Question 1 focuses on state-dependent emergence, requiring massive integration of time-series and stress-response transcriptomes. Question 2 explores the evolutionary tuning of these mesoscale properties, merging genomic mutation databases with biophysical modeling of phase boundaries. Finally, Question 3 synthesizes these insights into an actionable, open-source tool. Together, these interconnected inquiries will resolve long-standing puzzles about how bacteria spatially organize their interiors in the absence of membrane-bound organelles, entirely through the transdisciplinary analysis of existing public data.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodology strictly adheres to the synthesis of existing, publicly available datasets, combining computational genomics, AI-driven structural biology, and associative polymer biophysics to construct the 'bacterial condensome.'

Aim 1: Data Acquisition and Transcriptomic Profiling
We will construct a massive, normalized compendium of bacterial expression data. We will query the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) to extract thousands of high-quality RNA-seq and ribosome-profiling datasets covering model organisms (e.g., E. coli, B. subtilis) and critical human pathogens (e.g., P. aeruginosa, S. aureus). Datasets will be stratified by physiological state: exponential growth, stationary phase, antibiotic stress, biofilm formation, and host colonization. Using scalable, open-source bioinformatics pipelines, we will process raw reads into normalized transcript abundances. To estimate absolute instantaneous monomer concentrations, we will integrate matching public quantitative proteomics data (e.g., from PRIDE) to establish translation rate scalars for our transcriptomic models. 

Aim 2: Biophysical Feature Extraction and Interaction Modeling
Concurrently, we will analyze the complete proteomes of our target species. We will utilize AlphaFold DB and MobiDB to computationally extract structural features, with a specific focus on intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), charge distribution, and multivalent domain architectures. Leveraging associative polymer theory, we will define the sequence-encoded interaction potentials for every protein. Using previously established mathematical models of polymer gelation and liquid-liquid phase separation, we will calculate the theoretical critical concentration threshold (C_sat) required for each protein—and defined multiprotein networks—to undergo phase separation. AI-driven algorithms will be deployed to identify likely scaffolding proteins versus transient client molecules based on valency and scaffold stoichiometry parameters.

Aim 3: Synthesis and Atlas Generation
The core synthesis occurs by merging the dynamic monomer concentration data (Aim 1) with the static biophysical thresholds (Aim 2). We will develop a computational engine that overlays condition-specific protein concentrations onto their respective C_sat phase boundaries. When the in vivo concentration of a protein or interacting network exceeds the predicted threshold under a specific stress condition, it will be flagged as an emergent condensate. We will further apply network theory to predict the compositional architecture (internal demixing) of these condensates based on varying expression stoichiometries across states.

Aim 4: Evolutionary Integration
To study evolutionary modifications, we will ingest genomic variant data from public repositories representing clinical and environmental isolates. We will model how specific missense mutations or regulatory shifts (e.g., altered quorum sensing regulons due to efflux pump mutations) perturb the biophysical thresholds or interaction energies established in Aim 3. 

This approach necessitates a Working Group combining profound expertise in bacterial genomics and host-microbe interactions with advanced soft matter biophysics and mathematically modeled condensate dynamics. No new experimental data will be generated; instead, robust statistical methods, AI validation protocols, and rigorous error-propagation models will ensure the reliability of our synthetic findings.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This NCEMS Working Group will deliver the world’s first comprehensive atlas of the bacterial condensome, shifting the paradigm of microbiology from a focus on well-mixed biochemical pathways to one of dynamic, spatially organized mesoscale biophysics. 

First, we expect to answer the novel question of how macroscopic cellular stresses coordinate microscopic phase transitions, identifying specific stress-response condensates that were previously hidden within bulk transcriptomic data. Second, by solving the long-standing puzzle of how certain evolutionary mutations seemingly act at a distance to increase virulence, we anticipate showing that these adaptations fundamentally tune the physical properties of emergent biomolecular networks to favor survival in host environments. 

Scientifically, this proposal pioneers an innovative analytical strategy bridging two previously disparate disciplines: evolutionary genomics and polymer biophysics. By mathematically linking genetic variance and transcriptomic flux to critical concentration thresholds, we establish a robust framework for evaluating mesoscale emergence across all domains of life. 

Crucially, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. The Working Group will rigorously train a diverse cohort of postdoctoral researchers and graduate students. These trainees will navigate a unique, transdisciplinary intersection, gaining highly sought-after expertise in high-performance computing, AI-driven structural biology, transcriptomic data science, and soft matter physics. They will emerge as quintessential "data-savvy scientists" capable of leading the next generation of systems biology.

Ultimately, the public release of our predictive models will empower the broader scientific community to predict biomolecular condensation directly from routine RNA-seq and genomic sequencing, accelerating discovery in synthetic biology, antibiotic development, and infectious disease research without the immediate need for complex biophysical assays.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is intrinsically committed to the principles of Open, Team, and Reproducible Science. Because our project is entirely synthetic and reliant on publicly available data, ensuring the provenance and reproducibility of our analyses is paramount. 

All analytical workflows—from RNA-seq processing pipelines to associative polymer modeling and AI predictions—will be developed using Nextflow or Snakemake to guarantee scalable and highly reproducible execution across diverse computational environments. All source code, mathematical models, and machine learning architectures will be maintained in public, heavily documented GitHub repositories under an OSI-approved open-source license (e.g., MIT or GNU GPL). 

To ensure FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, the intermediate and finalized datasets, including the completed Bacterial Condensome Atlas, will be deposited in persistent repositories such as Zenodo and Figshare with DOIs assigned prior to publication. Furthermore, we will develop a user-friendly, open-access web portal—modeled after successful community tools—allowing researchers worldwide to visualize condition-specific condensate predictions, input their own transcriptomic data, and query the biophysical properties of bacterial proteomes interactively.

We will strictly adhere to community-created policies for open team science, implementing comprehensive data management plans and transparent authorship guidelines from the project's inception. All findings resulting from this synthesis will be published in open-access journals and immediately uploaded to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv). By providing full access to our raw code, containerized computing environments (Docker/Singularity), and synthesized datasets, we ensure our methodological innovations are seamlessly adopted and validated by the broader scientific community.
budget_and_resources:
This community-scale synthesis project inherently transcends the capabilities and resources of any single laboratory, making NCEMS support critical. The project requires the integration of deep expertise in bacterial evolutionary genomics and bioinformatics with specialized knowledge in soft matter biophysics and associative polymer modeling.

NCEMS funding is primarily requested to support the human capital and collaborative infrastructure necessary for this transdisciplinary effort. We request support for two full-time postdoctoral scholars and two graduate students, who will be co-mentored by our cross-disciplinary team. This intensive training environment will ensure the trainees develop a rare, hybrid fluency in both computational genomics and biophysics, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train the next-generation data-savvy workforce. 

To foster genuine intellectual synthesis, funds are requested to host bi-annual, intensive Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These multi-day collaborative workshops are essential to bridge the conceptual and vocabulary gaps between evolutionary biologists, physicists, and data scientists, ensuring cohesive integration of transcriptomic data with biophysical models. 

Furthermore, while we rely exclusively on public data, the computational burden of synthesizing thousands of RNA-seq datasets and integrating them with genome-wide AlphaFold structural predictions is substantial. We request resources for high-performance cloud computing and secure data storage to process, model, and host the petabyte-scale data required to construct and serve the Bacterial Condensome Atlas and its accompanying AI platforms. By centralizing these computational resources and personnel through NCEMS, we ensure the robust, reproducible execution of this transdisciplinary vision.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Dynamics from Molecular Thermodynamics: Synthesizing Protein Mutational Landscapes and Single-Cell Interactomes
abstract:
A central challenge in the molecular and cellular biosciences is bridging the gap between single-molecule biophysics and systems-level cellular behavior. While the thermodynamic constraints governing the biosynthesis, folding, and trafficking of individual proteins—such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and ion channels—are increasingly well-characterized, we lack a predictive understanding of how these molecular-level energetic properties scale up to shape mesoscale protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties, such as robust cellular homeostasis or the sudden collapse into pathological states like misfolding diseases and senescence, often originates at this poorly understood mesoscale level. 

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize three previously disconnected domains of publicly available data to uncover the thermodynamic rules governing mesoscale network emergence. Specifically, we will integrate (1) large-scale Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) and biophysical datasets capturing sequence-to-function thermodynamic landscapes; (2) structural interactome repositories including AlphaFold-predicted multimeric interfaces and public PPI databases; and (3) cell-type-specific transcriptomic atlases derived from single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). By doing so, we aim to answer a fundamental question: How do localized energetic perturbations at protein interfaces propagate through complex cellular networks to drive emergent mesoscale phenotypes?

Our collaborative, transdisciplinary approach will proceed in three phases. First, we will aggregate and harmonize public DMS datasets with structural models to calculate how specific sequence variations alter the folding and binding free energies of membrane and intracellular proteins. Second, we will leverage advanced network science methodologies to map these energetic parameters onto mesoscale protein complexes. Rather than treating PPI networks as static binary connections, we will construct dynamically weighted, "energetic networks" that model the thermodynamic coupling between interacting proteins. Third, we will contextualize these biophysical networks using public scRNA-seq data. By applying gene regulatory network inference and cell-type-specific co-expression data, we will evaluate how the buffering capacity of different cellular environments modulates the penetrance of thermodynamic defects—explaining, for example, why identical mutations cause membrane supertrafficking in one cell type but induce targeted degradation or inflammatory stress responses in another.

This project requires the unique support of NCEMS, as it demands a synthesis of expertise in protein biophysics, structural biology, evolutionary dynamics, and computational systems biology that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory. The Working Group will adhere strictly to open science principles, releasing a novel, open-source analytical framework capable of predicting emergent cellular behaviors from primary sequence variation. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, providing postdocs and graduate students with cross-disciplinary expertise in synthesizing molecular thermodynamics, machine learning, and single-cell systems biology.
background_and_significance:
A fundamental puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences is understanding how precise, localized changes in single macromolecules propagate to alter systems-level mesoscale biology. While the biophysical rules governing individual proteins are increasingly well-characterized, living systems do not operate as collections of isolated macromolecules. Rather, emergent cellular properties—ranging from robust physiological homeostasis to pathological states such as cellular senescence, immune hyperactivation, and protein misfolding diseases—arise from complex, dynamically interacting networks of molecules operating at the mesoscale. Despite decades of intense study, our ability to predict how changes in molecular thermodynamics (such as a single amino acid substitution altering folding free energy) will influence mesoscale network topology and subsequent cellular phenotypes remains highly limited.

Currently, biological research is highly siloed across scales. Biophysicists and structural biologists generate vast amounts of data regarding protein folding, membrane trafficking, and thermodynamic stability. Simultaneously, systems biologists produce massive repositories mapping protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks and single-cell transcriptomic (scRNA-seq) atlases capturing cell-type-specific gene expression. The critical gap is the lack of a unifying synthetic framework that integrates these distinct data modalities. Traditional PPI networks are treated as static, binary graphs that fail to account for the thermodynamic binding affinities and conformational stabilities of their constituent nodes. Conversely, molecular biophysics rarely contextualizes mutational energetic defects within the variable stoichiometric environments of different cell types, which often dictate whether a biophysical defect is buffered by the cellular network or cascades into systems-level failure.

Synthesizing these disparate, publicly available datasets represents a unique opportunity to decipher the rules of mesoscale emergence. By mapping high-throughput mutational data onto structurally resolved interactomes, and further contextualizing these interactions with scRNA-seq data, we can model how energetic variations scale up to alter network dynamics. For example, membrane proteins like G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) or voltage-gated ion channels rely on precise thermodynamic balances for proper biosynthesis, translocon integration, and trafficking. Perturbations can lead to targeted degradation or anomalous "supertrafficking," phenomena that depend entirely on the cellular environment's buffering capacity, such as chaperone abundance and interacting partner stoichiometry. 

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will directly address this long-standing puzzle. By exclusively utilizing existing publicly available data—including Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) repositories, AlphaFold multimeric predictions, and massive single-cell transcriptomic atlases—we will construct the first "energetic networks" of the cell. This community-scale synthesis project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission, as it requires transdisciplinary collaboration spanning protein biophysics, evolutionary dynamics, and network biology to illuminate how molecular thermodynamics drive emergent properties at the mesoscale.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective of understanding how biophysical perturbations at the molecular level propagate through complex interaction networks to generate emergent mesoscale phenotypes. To achieve this, the Working Group will address three primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses, entirely through the synthesis of existing publicly available datasets.

Question 1: How do localized, mutation-induced changes in protein folding and binding free energies alter the functional topology of mesoscale protein-protein interaction networks?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that mesoscale PPI networks function as thermodynamically coupled systems where node stabilities and edge affinities are highly interdependent. By mapping biophysical parameters derived from Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) and structural databases onto PPI networks, we expect to reveal that energetic perturbations act as quantitative weights that predict either localized network rewiring (e.g., loss of a specific complex module) or catastrophic global destabilization. We predict that highly connected "hub" proteins possess distinct thermodynamic buffering capacities compared to peripheral nodes, allowing specific sub-networks to absorb substantial biophysical variation without triggering emergent structural collapse.

Question 2: How does cell-type-specific gene expression and interactome stoichiometry buffer or amplify molecular thermodynamic defects to produce distinct cellular phenotypes?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the phenotypic penetrance of a thermodynamic defect (such as those causing protein misfolding or supertrafficking) is fundamentally determined by the stoichiometric ratio of interacting partners and regulatory chaperones within a specific cellular context. By integrating single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data with our thermodynamically weighted PPI networks, we expect to demonstrate that the identical biophysical perturbation can yield drastically different emergent mesoscale outcomes—such as maintaining homeostasis in one cell type while triggering targeted degradation, cellular senescence, or localized inflammatory responses in another—due purely to mass-action effects driven by baseline transcriptomic landscapes.

Question 3: Can the integration of thermodynamic landscapes and single-cell regulatory networks yield predictive models of evolutionary adaptation and pathological state transitions?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that emergent, systems-level transitions—such as the sudden acquisition of antibiotic resistance profiles or the transition into immunopathogenic disease states—are threshold-like phenomena dictated by the energetic limits of mesoscale networks. We posit that by synthesizing variant-fitness landscapes with gene regulatory network dynamics, we can train machine learning models to accurately predict the boundary conditions under which neutral drift in single proteins suddenly forces a mesoscale network to adopt a novel, emergent state. This will elucidate the physico-chemical constraints on network evolution, bridging the scale from amino acid sequence space to cellular fitness.

By addressing these questions, the working group will shift the paradigm of network biology from static, binary association maps to dynamic, thermodynamically grounded models capable of explaining and predicting mesoscale emergence.
methods_and_approach:
The proposed research will be conducted entirely in silico, utilizing no new experimental data, and will proceed through three integrated synthesis phases that demand transdisciplinary expertise.

Phase 1: Thermodynamic Parameterization of Sequence Space
We will synthesize massive repositories of primary biophysical data to build thermodynamic landscapes for target proteins. Data sources will include MaveDB for Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) datasets, the Protein Data Bank (PDB), and AlphaFold-Multimer interactome predictions. We will computationally derive folding free energies (ΔG_fold) and binding free energies (ΔΔG_bind) for tens of thousands of variants across diverse protein classes, including GPCRs, ion channels, and transcription factors. Using established biophysical modeling frameworks and machine learning algorithms, we will map how specific primary sequence variations quantitatively alter these localized thermodynamic parameters. This phase bridges structural biology with evolutionary variation, providing the numerical basis for energetic network construction.

Phase 2: Construction of Dynamically Weighted "Energetic Networks"
Standard PPI network analyses utilize binary edges to denote the presence or absence of an interaction. We will radically advance this approach by leveraging graph theory and network analysis tools (e.g., Python's NetworkX library) to construct continuous, thermodynamically weighted mesoscale networks. Using publicly available interactome databases (such as STRING and BioGRID), we will reconstruct protein complexes. However, rather than treating these edges uniformly, we will parameterize the edges using the ΔΔG_bind values derived in Phase 1, and parameterize the nodes using ΔG_fold stabilities. This synthetic approach transforms static interactomes into dynamic biophysical models, allowing us to simulate how localized energetic shocks—such as a destabilizing variant—propagate through the mesoscale network to alter binding equilibria and complex formation.

Phase 3: Single-Cell Contextualization and Systems-Level Simulation
To understand how these biophysical networks behave in living systems, we will integrate large-scale transcriptomic data from the Human Cell Atlas and other public scRNA-seq repositories. Utilizing computational pipelines such as pySCENIC, we will infer cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks and extract absolute and relative transcript abundances for the proteins comprising our energetic networks. By overlaying this transcriptomic data onto the biophysical network, we will establish mass-action models that account for local concentrations of interacting partners, competitive binders, and molecular chaperones. We will perform computationally intensive simulations to observe how specific cell types buffer energetic defects. For example, we will investigate whether high native expression of specific regulatory elements masks a folding defect, or if low expression in a distinct cell type forces a critical mesoscale complex below the threshold required for cellular homeostasis, triggering emergent phenotypes like senescence or immunopathogenic signaling.

Throughout all phases, rigorous statistical modeling and machine learning classifications will be employed to ensure the robustness of our synthesized outputs, fully relying on cross-disciplinary methodologies to fuse single-molecule physics with whole-cell transcriptomics.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This NCEMS Working Group will deliver several transformative outcomes that directly address fundamental puzzles in molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will create and publish the first comprehensive "Thermodynamic Interactome Atlas," a synthesized, publicly accessible database that maps quantitative biophysical parameters (derived from DMS and structural models) onto human mesoscale protein networks. Second, we will release an open-source, mathematically rigorous software framework capable of predicting how primary sequence variants perturb these energetic networks under varied, cell-type-specific transcriptomic contexts. 

The scientific impact of this work is profound. By bridging the critical gap between single-molecule biophysics and systems-level network biology, we will solve the long-standing mystery of "incomplete penetrance" and context-dependent phenotypic variation. Our synthesis will explain how identical biophysical defects can result in diverse emergent outcomes—from harmless buffering to devastating misfolding diseases or cellular senescence—based purely on the mesoscale network architecture of different cell types. This provides a entirely novel analytical strategy for the biological sciences, moving the field past static interaction maps toward dynamic, predictive models of emergent mesoscale behavior.

Furthermore, this project will have an immense impact on the scientific workforce. It will serve as an unprecedented training environment for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars. Trainees embedded within this Working Group will gain highly sought-after, transdisciplinary expertise spanning structural biophysics, single-cell data science, computational network analysis, and machine learning. By tackling this community-scale synthesis project, the next generation of data-savvy scientists will be equipped with the collaborative and technical skills necessary to lead the future of computational systems biology and data-driven molecular sciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to Open Science principles is foundational to this Working Group. We are committed to gold-standard practices that ensure all synthesized data, analytical workflows, and resulting findings are completely transparent, reproducible, and accessible to the global scientific community. 

Data and Code Accessibility: All public datasets utilized in this study (e.g., DMS datasets, scRNA-seq atlases, structural models) will be cataloged with persistent digital object identifiers (DOIs). Our synthesized databases, specifically the Thermodynamic Interactome Atlas, will be hosted on stable, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad, fully adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles. All custom computational pipelines, scripts, and machine learning models developed during this project will be maintained in public GitHub repositories under an open-source license (e.g., MIT or GNU GPL). 

Reproducibility and Community Engagement: To guarantee reproducibility, our computational environments will be containerized using Docker and Singularity, allowing any researcher to precisely replicate our software dependencies and analytical environments. We will produce comprehensive documentation, including interactive Jupyter and Google Colab notebooks, designed as tutorials to lower the barrier of entry for researchers wishing to apply our thermodynamic-network framework to their own biological questions. 

Open Access Dissemination: We pre-commit to publishing all findings in open-access (OA) peer-reviewed journals and will deposit preprints of all manuscripts on bioRxiv prior to peer review. Furthermore, the Working Group will host open virtual workshops to disseminate our analytical strategies and solicit feedback, fostering a broader community of practice centered on the rigorous synthesis of molecular and cellular data.

The proposed community-scale synthesis project requires NCEMS support because the computational resources, collaborative infrastructure, and transdisciplinary synthesis exceed the capacity of any single lab or traditional grant mechanism. We request funding to support three primary areas critical to the Working Group's success:

1. Personnel and Training: The majority of the budget will support postdoctoral fellows and graduate students who will serve as the primary engines of data synthesis. This funding provides dedicated time for these trainees to immerse themselves in cross-disciplinary research, bridging molecular thermodynamics and systems biology. Funds will also cover intensive training workshops for these personnel in advanced computational techniques, directly contributing to the NCEMS mandate of training the future data-savvy workforce.

2. Collaborative Infrastructure and Travel: To foster true transdisciplinary integration, funds are requested for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS hub. These meetings will bring together structural biophysicists, single-cell transcriptomics experts, and network biologists to synthesize data, refine analytical pipelines, and troubleshoot methodological challenges. Virtual collaboration tools and platforms will also be supported to maintain continuous integration between the physical meetings.

3. Computational Resources and Open Science: Given the massive scale of the data being integrated—including hundreds of thousands of structural models, high-throughput DMS arrays, and millions of single-cell transcriptomes—we require significant cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud) and high-performance computing (HPC) allocations for data storage, harmonization, and machine learning model training. Additionally, the budget includes explicit line items to cover Open Access publication fees and the long-term hosting of our public databases and interactive containerized tutorials, ensuring full compliance with our open science commitments.
