title: Decoding the Structural and Network Grammar of RNA-Driven Emergence in Biomolecular Condensates
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a canonical example of mesoscale emergence in biology, where non-stoichiometric assemblies of RNAs and proteins phase separate to form dynamically regulated, membraneless organelles. While the compositional landscape of condensates—such as stress granules and nuclear speckles—is increasingly well-documented, a fundamental mechanistic gap remains: we lack a predictive understanding of how atomic-scale RNA-protein interactions and protein sequence determinants scale up to dictate emergent, mesoscale material properties like viscoelasticity, interfacial tension, and dynamic subcellular trafficking. Currently, a massive amount of disconnected, publicly available data exists across diverse domains. These include high-resolution structural repositories (PDB, EMDB) capturing RNA-protein complexes, high-throughput pooled imaging datasets linking protein sequences to condensate phenotypes, and extensive dynamic spatial proteomics (e.g., BioID, APEX, and proximity-labeling networks) tracking proteome trafficking. 

We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize these disparate, multi-modal datasets into a unified, predictive computational framework of mesoscale condensate emergence. Relying entirely on existing publicly available data, our transdisciplinary team will bridge computational structural biology, RNA modeling, soft matter physics, and cellular proteomics. First, we will leverage advanced macromolecular modeling (e.g., Rosetta-based frameworks) and deep learning algorithms to extract high-confidence structural signatures—such as RNA-protein interaction interfaces, multivalent valency maps, and RNA folding architectures—from existing cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps and structural databases. Second, we will map these structural metrics onto dynamic, spatial interactomes derived from public proximity-labeling proteomics datasets. This synthesis will allow us to reconstruct the precise spatiotemporal trafficking networks of phase-separating proteins and their RNA scaffolds across varying cellular conditions, such as oxidative stress and environmental fluctuations.

Finally, we will integrate soft matter physics principles to correlate these derived structural networks with the tunable, emergent material properties documented in public high-throughput imaging screens. By identifying the underlying "grammar" of multi-component condensate networks, we aim to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how specific sequence properties and chaperone interactions dictate the assembly, maintenance, and dissolution of these mesoscale compartments. 

This synthesis project requires the unique collaborative environment of NCEMS, as it extends beyond the computational or biological capacity of a single lab. It will yield an open-access, integrated database and predictive analytical pipeline linking atomic structures to emergent cellular phenotypes. Furthermore, it will directly address the NCEMS mission by developing a new analytical strategy for understanding mesoscale biological systems, while providing a rich, collaborative training ground for postdocs and graduate students in the integration of structural bioinformatics, AI-driven macromolecular modeling, and spatial omics data.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates constitute a frontier in our understanding of mesoscale biological organization. Emerging through liquid-liquid phase separation, these membraneless organelles—such as stress granules, nucleoli, and P-bodies—spatially and temporally organize cellular matter in response to internal cues and environmental stressors. The defining characteristic of condensates is their emergence: non-stoichiometric collections of individual proteins and nucleic acids self-assemble into higher-order fluid and gel-like states exhibiting complex properties such as viscoelasticity and distinct interfacial tension. While recent advances have cataloged the compositional components of various condensates, a critical scientific void remains. The field lacks a unified framework that bridges the gap between atomic-level structural interactions (e.g., RNA folding, RNA-protein binding interfaces) and mesoscale physical behaviors. Consequently, it remains a long-standing puzzle how specific alterations at the sequence or atomic structural level propagate up to perturb condensate trafficking, dynamics, and function—a gap that limits both our fundamental understanding of cell biology and our ability to address age-related protein-aggregation diseases.

Simultaneously, the biological sciences are experiencing an unprecedented proliferation of publicly available, high-dimensional datasets. Structural biology repositories (PDB, EMDB) house vast collections of RNA-protein complexes and moderate-resolution cryo-EM maps. Large-scale spatial proteomics and proximity-labeling datasets (e.g., BioID, APEX, TransitID-derived networks) capture dynamic proteome trafficking across cellular compartments under stress. Additionally, high-throughput pooled imaging platforms have recently generated massive phenotypic datasets linking thousands of unique protein sequences to their nuclear and cytoplasmic condensation behaviors. Despite their immense potential, these rich datasets are fundamentally siloed within their respective sub-disciplines: computational structural biology, proteomics, and soft matter physics.

This proposal aligns perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We seek to aggregate, harmonize, and computationally synthesize these disparate datasets to decode the 'grammar' of mesoscale condensate emergence. By refusing to generate new experimental data, our effort will focus entirely on novel data integration. This synthesis holds profound significance. First, it will establish the missing link between atomistic models and soft matter physics, allowing researchers to predict how sequence variants alter macromolecular valency and drive physical phase transitions. Second, it shifts the paradigm from static composition lists to dynamic, structurally annotated interactomes, illuminating how cellular stress remodels complex RNA-protein architectures. By bridging these distinct scales through synthesis, this project will catalyze innovative analytical strategies, redefine our conceptual understanding of mesoscale biological phenomena, and provide a unified, predictive engine for the broader biomolecular community.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our Working Group will systematically address fundamental questions regarding the multiscale emergence of biomolecular condensates by integrating structural models, spatiotemporal proteomics, and soft matter physics. Our inquiry is organized around three synergistic research questions and corresponding hypotheses, designed to yield novel insights through deep data synthesis.

Research Question 1: What are the conserved atomic and sequence-level structural signatures that dictate the emergent mesoscale properties of distinct classes of biomolecular condensates?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that context-independent structural features—specifically the geometry of multivalent RNA-binding interfaces and intrinsic RNA folding architectures—serve as a universal 'grammar' for condensate formation. By applying advanced macromolecular modeling (such as Rosetta-based energy functions) to existing cryo-EM and small-molecule datasets, we anticipate identifying structural nodes where localized valency directly dictates bulk mesoscale behaviors, such as the transition from highly fluid aqueous two-phase systems to dense water-in-water emulsions.

Research Question 2: How do dynamic subcellular trafficking networks and specific chaperone proteins coordinate the assembly and dissolution of condensates under physiological stress?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the integration of spatiotemporal proximity-labeling proteomics with structural interaction maps will reveal specialized nodes functioning as active regulators of phase separation. Specifically, we expect synthesis to uncover that unconventional RNA-dependent chaperones—such as poly(A)-binding proteins—actively tune the valency networks of core condensate drivers (e.g., prion-like proteins). We predict that these chaperone networks reorganize across subcellular compartments (e.g., from nucleus to cytosol) in response to stressors like oxidation or hydration changes, preventing pathological transition into solid-like aggregates.

Research Question 3: Can we develop a predictive, multi-modal computational framework that maps atomic-scale compositional networks directly to the emergent material properties of non-stoichiometric assemblies?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that machine learning models, trained on a synthesized dataset merging high-throughput pooled imaging screens (condensate-forming propensities) with our derived structural valency maps, can accurately predict the emergent material properties of unknown sequences. By borrowing concepts from soft matter physics and evolutionary aptamer modeling, this predictive model will decode how nuanced changes in RNA-protein affinity modify bulk interfacial tension and viscoelasticity.

Together, these questions target the core of NCEMS’s mesoscale mandate. Answering them through purely public data synthesis will solve long-standing puzzles about the biophysical regulation of membraneless organelles. Moreover, mapping structural interaction energies onto massive spatial proteomics networks requires a unified, cross-disciplinary strategy that has never before been attempted in phase separation research.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve a predictive understanding of RNA-driven emergence in biomolecular condensates, our transdisciplinary Working Group will utilize a three-phase computational approach. This methodology relies entirely on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets from structural biology, spatial proteomics, and high-throughput cellular imaging, generating no new experimental data.

Phase 1: Extraction and Annotation of Structural Valency Maps
We will first synthesize atomic-scale data using public repositories (PDB, EMDB) alongside advanced computational modeling. Utilizing established macromolecular modeling suites (e.g., Rosetta, auto-DRRAFTER paradigms), we will systematically reconstruct and refine moderate-resolution cryo-EM density maps of key condensate-associated RNA-protein complexes. We will extract quantitative biophysical features—such as interaction energies, RNA folding architectures, multivalent binding site geometries, and intrinsically disordered region (IDR) conformations. This data will be synthesized into a standardized 'Structural Valency Matrix', categorizing specific sequence features and interaction interfaces capable of driving non-stoichiometric assembly.

Phase 2: Spatiotemporal Network Integration
In parallel, we will harvest dynamic spatial interactome data from public proteomics databases (e.g., PRIDE). Specifically, we will aggregate datasets derived from proximity-labeling mass spectrometry (BioID, APEX, TurboID) mapped across varied cellular compartments (nucleus, stress granules, mitochondria) and stress conditions (e.g., oxidative stress, hydration changes). Using graph-theoretic approaches, we will construct multilayered proteome trafficking networks. Crucially, we will overlay our Phase 1 Structural Valency Matrix onto these spatiotemporal graphs. This integration will illuminate how structural interaction potential fluctuates dynamically as proteins transit through the cell, and will identify active chaperone nodes that regulate RNA-protein complex disassembly or sequestration.

Phase 3: Machine Learning and Soft Matter Physics Synthesis
To link atomic structures to mesoscale emergence, we will integrate public high-throughput pooled imaging datasets (e.g., CondenSeq screens) that catalog the macroscopic properties of thousands of phase-separating proteins. We will apply soft matter physics frameworks (modeling condensates as aqueous two-phase systems and viscoelastic fluids) to extract proxy metrics for interfacial tension and material state from the imaging data. We will then train deep learning models (adapted from evolutionary modeling architectures like DAPTEV) to correlate the structural/network parameters from Phases 1 and 2 with the emergent phenotypic behaviors from Phase 3. The objective is a predictive algorithm capable of outputting a mesoscale material property based solely on sequence and structural network inputs.

Collaboration and Rigor
This synthesis necessitates continuous, integrated feedback between computational structural biologists, RNA biophysicists, proteomics experts, and soft-matter physicists. The Working Group will employ iterative hackathons and agile computational workflows. AI pipelines and energy function parameters will be rigorously validated against orthogonal public datasets to prevent overfitting, ensuring that the final analytical strategy is both biologically rigorous and mathematically robust.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence. By uniting structural biology with soft matter physics and spatial omics, our Working Group will yield the first multiscale 'grammar' of biomolecular condensates. 

Scientific Impact:
Our synthesis will solve long-standing mysteries regarding how molecular sequence dictates macroscopic cellular states. We will elucidate how RNA chaperones and localized interaction valencies guard against pathological protein aggregation, opening new avenues for understanding age-related neurodegenerative diseases. By mapping atomic features onto dynamic trafficking networks, we will transition the field from descriptive phenomenology to predictive biophysics, fundamentally reshaping our understanding of membraneless organelles.

Deliverables:
1. Open-Access Database: A fully integrated, multimodal database mapping the structural valency, spatiotemporal trafficking, and soft-matter physical properties of condensate proteins.
2. Predictive Analytical Framework: A novel machine-learning pipeline capable of predicting mesoscale material properties of RNA-protein complexes directly from primary sequences and structural topologies.
3. High-Impact Publications: Dissemination of fundamental insights regarding phase separation, RNA architecture, and condensate trafficking through open-access, peer-reviewed journals.

Workforce Development and Training:
The project provides an unprecedented training environment for early-career scientists. Two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students will be cross-trained in AI-driven structural bioinformatics, large-scale proteomics network analysis, and physical modeling. Working within a highly transdisciplinary environment, these trainees will develop the exact computational and collaborative skills required to become leaders in the future data-savvy bioscience workforce. Their integration into the Working Group ensures that novel analytical strategies are not only developed but effectively transmitted to the next generation of researchers.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to Open Science and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles is a foundational pillar of this proposal, ensuring that all findings, data, and analytical workflows empower the broader scientific community.

Data and Code Sharing:
Because this project relies exclusively on public data, all input data provenance will be strictly documented. All extracted structural valency maps, harmonized interactome networks, and machine learning models will be deposited in Zenodo and continuously updated on GitHub. To guarantee reproducibility, we will utilize containerized computing environments (e.g., Docker/Singularity) to distribute the multi-modal analytical pipeline. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local computing infrastructure, can reproduce our structural modeling and network synthesis results.

Platform Development:
We will develop an interactive, web-based portal to host the integrated Structural-Network Condensate Database. This interface will allow structural biologists and cell biologists alike to query specific RNA-protein complexes, visualize their spatiotemporal trafficking patterns, and predict their mesoscale phase separation properties using our derived machine-learning models.

Transparent Publishing and Team Science:
All manuscripts generated by the Working Group will be posted to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to formal peer review, accelerating knowledge dissemination. We will publish exclusively in open-access journals. Furthermore, we will adopt the CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) system to ensure transparent and equitable recognition of all team members, particularly trainees. Working Group meeting summaries, hackathon protocols, and lab notebooks will be made openly available to foster community engagement and establish best practices for large-scale, transdisciplinary data synthesis.
budget_and_resources:
The proposed synthesis project requires structural, computational, and collaborative resources that transcend the capabilities of any single laboratory, making NCEMS support indispensable. Our budget focuses on the personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative networking essential for transdisciplinary data synthesis.

Personnel:
The primary budget allocation will support two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. The postdocs will lead the cross-disciplinary integration—one specializing in AI-driven macromolecular modeling (Rosetta suite, auto-DRRAFTER pipelines), and the other in spatial proteomics network analysis and soft matter physics. Graduate students will be fully funded to execute data harvesting, harmonization, and database architecture development. This structure directly aligns with NCEMS’s workforce training mandate.

Computational Infrastructure:
Synthesizing moderate-resolution cryo-EM data and modeling thousands of RNA-protein interactions requires substantial computational power. Funds are requested for access to high-performance computing (HPC) clusters equipped with advanced GPU nodes for training the deep learning evolutionary models and running high-throughput Rosetta energy functions. Additionally, we request funding for secure, scalable cloud storage to host the integrated database and support the public-facing web portal.

Collaborative Networking and Travel:
Transdisciplinary synthesis relies on intensive, synchronous collaboration. We request support for biannual in-person Working Group meetings (hackathons) at the NCEMS hub to bring together our structural biologists, cell biologists, and biophysicists. These intensive sprints are crucial for resolving methodological bottlenecks and ensuring theoretical alignment. Additional funds will support trainees' travel to major national conferences to present the synthesized findings and host workshops on the newly developed predictive tools, maximizing community impact.

title: Decoding the Mesoscale Molecular Grammar: Synthesizing Physical Principles of Condensate Ultrastructure and Emulsion Stability
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a primary mode of mesoscale spatial organization across all domains of life, governing processes ranging from eukaryotic stress adaptation to bacterial subcellular compartmentalization. While recent years have seen an explosion of data cataloging phase-separating proteins, predicting the emergent physical properties of these assemblies—such as ultrastructural organization, emulsion stability, and tunable viscoelasticity—from primary sequence remains a critical frontier. Current efforts largely focus on binary predictions of liquid-liquid phase separation, failing to capture the intricate biophysical rules that dictate how condensates dynamically respond to environmental fluctuations, resist coalescence, and maintain complex multiphase architectures within the crowded cellular milieu.

This working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the pan-domain molecular grammar underlying condensate ultrastructure and mesoscale emergence. By aggregating and synthesizing disparate, publicly available datasets—including curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence repositories (DisProt), structural data (AlphaFold DB, EMDB for cryo-ET maps), and thousands of published in vitro biophysical measurements (phase diagrams, zeta potentials, and rheological parameters)—we will construct a unified, predictive framework of condensate physics. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, our approach relies entirely on the integration of existing multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data, requiring no new experimental generation.

To achieve this, we will combine artificial intelligence with physics-driven multiscale computational modeling. First, we will develop a machine-learning pipeline to mine sequence features, specifically mapping the 'stickers-and-spacers' valency and electrostatic charge patterning of IDPs across diverse biological kingdoms. We will correlate these specific sequence grammars with documented emergent behaviors, such as RNA-induced conformational switching, multiphase coexistence, and hydration-dependent structural transitions. Second, we will leverage these synthesized datasets to parameterize high-throughput, sequence-dependent coarse-grained molecular models. This will allow us to simulate mesoscale phenomena—such as long-ranged electrostatic repulsion, surface charge-driven size control, and fusion propensity—at an unprecedented scale. By triangulating these physical simulations with published ultrastructural readouts, we will determine how localized structural transitions and net charge within dense phases dictate higher-order cellular functions.

This transdisciplinary effort uniquely bridges structural biology, computational biophysics, and soft matter physics. The project requires the NCEMS infrastructure to facilitate the large-scale integration of highly heterogeneous data types (from atomic coordinates to rheological values) and to support the collaborative computational demands of parameterizing pan-domain physical models. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how intrinsically disordered sequences encode mesoscale architecture, generating predictive tools that map the physical rules of cellular adaptation. Furthermore, the project will train a diverse new generation of data-savvy biophysicists equipped to navigate the intersection of machine learning, polymer physics, and structural biology, fully embracing open science principles by releasing all analytical workflows, trained AI models, and coarse-grained parameters to the global community.
background_and_significance:
The unexpected emergence of novel biological properties at the mesoscale is one of the most compelling frontiers in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Biomolecular condensates—non-stoichiometric assemblies lacking a surrounding membrane—represent a fundamental mechanism of mesoscale spatial organization. These dynamic structures coordinate a vast array of physiological processes, from adaptive stress responses and cellular information processing in eukaryotes to the spatial localization of key machineries in bacterial systems. Driven largely by the phase separation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and multivalent macromolecules, condensates exhibit complex, tunable physical properties including viscoelasticity, multiphase coexistence, and precise emulsion stability. 

Over the past decade, the rapid expansion of molecular and cellular research has generated a massive volume of publicly available data on these systems. Extensive repositories catalog the sequences of phase-separating proteins (e.g., PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), structural insights (AlphaFold DB, EMDB), and empirical phase diagrams. However, our ability to interpret this wealth of data remains significantly constrained. The field currently excels at cataloging binary outcomes—predicting whether a protein will undergo liquid-liquid phase separation—but fails to decipher the continuous biophysical rules governing the emergent properties of the resulting condensates. Crucial phenomena, such as how surface electrostatics regulate condensate sizing, how molecular 'stickers' and 'spacers' dictate internal rheology, and how conformational switching within dense phases produces complex ultrastructures, remain elusive. The knowledge fragmentation across structural biology, soft matter physics, and computational biophysics has prevented a unified understanding of how mesoscale architecture is encoded at the molecular level.

This proposal addresses these long-standing puzzles by conducting a community-scale synthesis of existing data. Guided by the strategic vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), we will combine thousands of disjointed experimental measurements—including cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) maps, single-molecule fluorescence readouts, zeta potentials, and sequence-based metadata—into a cohesive analytical framework. We argue that the lack of understanding of mesoscale condensate phenomena is not due to a shortage of experimental data, but rather a lack of systematic integration and cross-disciplinary theoretical synthesis. 

By leveraging artificial intelligence and data science, this project will synthesize these heterogeneous data to construct the first comprehensive, physics-driven molecular grammar of condensates. This grammar will explicitly link primary sequence attributes—such as the distribution of charged residues, pi-pi interactions, and hydration-dependent regions—to mesoscale properties like electrostatic repulsion, structural transitions, and fusion propensity. The significance of this synthesis is twofold: fundamentally, it will reveal the universal biophysical principles underlying condensate ultrastructure across biological scales, from molecular interactions to cellular phenotypes; methodologically, it will provide the community with a fully predictive, multi-layered modeling platform that translates sequence data into soft matter physics profiles. Through the unprecedented transdisciplinary integration supported by NCEMS, this work will catalyze new paradigms in understanding cellular adaptation, driving innovation while strictly adhering to synthesis methodologies.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our transdisciplinary synthesis project is structured around three compelling, well-defined scientific questions that aim to decipher the rules of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. By interrogating publicly available sequence, structural, and biophysical data, we aim to bridge the gap between atomic-level features and cellular-scale architectural properties.

Question 1: What is the sequence-encoded molecular grammar governing the emulsion stability and size control of biomolecular condensates across diverse biological kingdoms? 
Despite extensive characterization of IDPs, the precise mechanisms by which condensates resist coalescence and maintain specific size distributions remain poorly defined. We hypothesize that long-ranged electrostatic repulsion, dictated by the patterning of net charge and multivalent interactions (the 'stickers-and-spacers' architecture), fundamentally controls droplet coarsening. By synthesizing single-condensate zeta potential measurements, literature-derived phase diagrams, and sequence repositories, we expect to demonstrate that distinct electrostatic profiles act as an intrinsic, passive stabilization mechanism to regulate condensate size and fusion propensity, allowing cells to dynamically tune their mesoscale organization in response to environmental cues.

Question 2: How do localized conformational transitions within dense phases dictate higher-order condensate ultrastructure and function? 
Biomolecular condensates are not homogeneous liquids; they frequently exhibit complex, multi-layered internal structures. We hypothesize that specific environmental triggers—such as RNA binding, hydration shifts, or ion fluctuations—induce conformational switching in intrinsically disordered domains that alters the network topology of the dense phase. We will test this by integrating high-resolution cryo-ET maps from EMDB, AlphaFold predictions, and molecular dynamics datasets. We anticipate that phase-dependent conformational changes expose cryptic interaction sites or drive hierarchical filamentation, revealing that cellular function and multiphase architectures are direct consequences of ultrastructural transitions rather than bulk liquid properties alone.

Question 3: Can machine learning and coarse-grained molecular models synthesize highly heterogeneous datasets to reliably predict the emergent viscoelasticity and thermodynamic stability of condensates? 
Currently, predicting the rheological and material properties of condensates from primary sequence is an unsolved challenge, primarily due to data fragmentation. We hypothesize that by utilizing artificial intelligence to scrape and aggregate thousands of in vitro biophysical parameters (e.g., critical temperatures, radii of gyration, viscosity metrics), we can parameterize physics-driven, coarse-grained multiscale models with near-quantitative accuracy. We posit that capturing subtle energetic contributions—such as cation-pi and pi-pi interactions—within these models will successfully recapitulate experimental energy landscapes, providing a unified predictive tool that accurately maps primary sequence to emergent mesoscale soft matter properties.

Through addressing these questions, our Working Group will validate the hypothesis that a universal molecular grammar underpins condensate behavior. Rather than generating new empirical data, our approach uses the NCEMS framework to cross-pollinate analytical strategies from structural biology, polymer physics, and computational biophysics, delivering a transformative, multi-layered understanding of how cells harness disorder for functional adaptation.
methods_and_approach:
To decode the mesoscale molecular grammar of biomolecular condensates, our Working Group will employ a purely synthetic, transdisciplinary approach, integrating artificial intelligence, soft matter physics, and computational biophysics. Our methodology strictly utilizes existing publicly available data and is divided into three interconnected, data-driven aims.

Aim 1: Automated Data Harvesting and Curation Pipeline
We will construct an advanced natural language processing (NLP) and data-mining pipeline to extract heterogeneous quantitative measurements from public databases and published literature. We will target sequence repositories (PhaSepDB, DisProt, CD-CODE), structural databases (AlphaFold DB, EMDB, PDB), and scrape biophysical parameters—including saturation concentrations, zeta potentials, critical temperatures, rheological data, and radii of gyration—from over 10,000 published articles. This step requires the computational infrastructure of NCEMS to unify multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data into a first-of-its-kind, relational 'Condensate Physics Database'. This database will standardize disparate data formats into a common ontology mapping primary sequences to their emergent physical readouts.

Aim 2: Machine Learning for Sequence Grammar Extraction
Leveraging the synthesized database, we will apply deep learning architectures (e.g., transformer-based neural networks) to mine sequence features. We will specifically map the 'stickers-and-spacers' architecture, evaluating the valency, spacing, and spatial distribution of aromatic and charged residues. By applying clustering algorithms, we will correlate these specific sequence grammars with documented emergent behaviors—such as RNA-induced conformational switching, stress-dependent viscoelasticity, and hydration-mediated phase separation. This AI-driven analysis will uncover the statistical rules connecting IDP charge patterning with macroscopic emulsion stability, allowing us to generate testable mathematical models of condensate size control and long-range electrostatic repulsion.

Aim 3: High-Throughput Coarse-Grained Molecular Modeling
The correlative insights generated by our AI models will be causally validated using physics-driven computational simulations. We will leverage the synthesized biophysical data to parameterize high-throughput, sequence-dependent coarse-grained molecular models (building upon frameworks like Mpipi). Utilizing GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and equilibrium field theory, we will model mesoscale phenomena across thousands of sequences. We will simulate droplet fusion, surface charge acquisition, ion expulsion, and the thermodynamic stability of multifunnel energy landscapes. Crucially, the outcomes of these simulations will be systematically triangulated against the synthesized ultrastructural data (cryo-ET maps and structural ensembles) to determine how phase-dependent conformational changes dictate higher-order mesoscale architecture. 

Integration and Synthesis Strategy: 
This approach requires the collaboration of multiple labs spanning diverse expertise: AI/machine learning experts to build the data pipelines, soft matter physicists to define the theoretical field models, and computational biophysicists to execute multiscale simulations. The synthesis of atomic coordinates, bulk rheological values, and sequence metadata is beyond the capability of any single laboratory. By harmonizing these distinct layers of biological information through the NCEMS collaborative framework, we will generate robust, predictive biophysical models that directly answer our formulated research questions without generating a single new experimental data point.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project will fundamentally advance the molecular and cellular biosciences by producing a unified, predictive framework for mesoscale emergent phenomena. The primary outcome will be the 'Condensate Physics Database' and its associated suite of machine-learning and physics-driven computational models. For the first time, researchers will have access to a tool that maps primary intrinsically disordered protein sequences directly to predictive biophysical properties—such as ultrastructural organization, emulsion stability, multiphase architecture, and tunable viscoelasticity.

Scientifically, this project will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells autonomously control the size, stability, and selective client recruitment of membraneless organelles. By demonstrating how net charge, surface electrostatics, and localized structural transitions dictate higher-order architecture, we will provide the biophysical missing link in our understanding of cellular adaptation. This paradigm shift—from qualitative observation of liquid-liquid phase separation to the quantitative prediction of soft matter physics in biological systems—will ripple across fields studying eukaryotic stress granules, bacterial mesoscale organization, and seed hydration.

Broadly, the impact of this project aligns seamlessly with the NCEMS mission. It demonstrates the immense, untapped potential of synthesizing dispersed, heterogeneous, publicly available data to drive transdisciplinary discoveries. Furthermore, this working group will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers involved in this project will receive unique, cross-disciplinary training at the nexus of artificial intelligence, structural biology, and polymer physics. They will acquire high-demand skills in data synthesis, coarse-grained molecular dynamics, and open science practices. By fostering a diverse workforce capable of traversing traditional disciplinary boundaries, we will cement a legacy of collaborative, computational innovation in the biological sciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to gold-standard Open Science principles is central to this synthesis project. We are fully committed to making all data, analytical workflows, and computational models openly accessible, ensuring reproducibility and broad utility for the scientific community. 

Data Availability and FAIR Principles: All scraped literature data, extracted biophysical parameters, and curated relational databases will be strictly aligned with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. The complete 'Condensate Physics Database' will be deposited in Zenodo with comprehensive, machine-readable metadata. We will establish a user-friendly, open-access web portal hosted via NCEMS to allow biologists to query sequences and retrieve predicted biophysical properties and coarse-grained parameters seamlessly.

Code and Workflow Transparency: To guarantee full computational reproducibility, all source code for the natural language processing pipelines, machine learning models, and molecular dynamics simulation scripts will be hosted on a public GitHub repository under an MIT license. We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, to encapsulate all computing environments, dependencies, and analytical pipelines. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local operating system, can independently reproduce our sequence mining and simulation workflows.

Community Engagement and Pre-registration: We will pre-register our core hypotheses and AI modeling protocols on the Open Science Framework (OSF) to prevent analytical bias. All resulting manuscripts will be submitted to open-access preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) concurrently with peer review. Furthermore, our Working Group will develop open-access Jupyter Notebook tutorials and host virtual community workshops in collaboration with NCEMS to train the broader biological community in utilizing our predictive models and datasets, democratizing access to cutting-edge computational biophysics tools.
budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this ambitious, transdisciplinary synthesis project, we request funding and resources that are uniquely provided by the NCEMS infrastructure, as the scope of this work far exceeds the capabilities of any individual laboratory. 

Personnel and Training: The core budget will support three postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students distributed across the collaborating institutions. These trainees will be strategically recruited to ensure diversity in both scientific background (spanning AI, computational biophysics, and structural bioinformatics) and demographic representation. Funds are requested to support their full-time focus on data aggregation, AI pipeline development, and coarse-grained parameterization, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train a diverse, data-savvy future workforce.

Working Group Meetings and Collaboration: We request travel and logistical support for bi-annual, week-long intensive Working Group meetings to be hosted at the NCEMS headquarters. These in-person convenings are essential to facilitate the deep intellectual cross-pollination required to merge soft matter physics theories with structural biology datasets, ensuring that AI-driven insights are robustly anchored in biophysical reality.

Computational Resources and Cyberinfrastructure: A critical component of our budget involves high-performance computing (HPC) allocations. We require NCEMS cyberinfrastructure and cloud-computing support for training deep learning models on large aggregated datasets and running highly parallelized GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, we request modest funds for cloud-hosting the 'Condensate Physics Database' and its associated web portal to guarantee long-term open access for the scientific community.

Broader Impacts: Finally, we request funding to host an annual, open-access virtual summer school on 'Data-Driven Approaches to Biomolecular Condensates,' leveraging NCEMS resources to disseminate our analytical workflows and train external researchers in synthesizing existing data for mesoscale discovery.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: AI-Driven Synthesis of Mesoscale Chromatin and Protein Networks to Decode Emergent Cellular Plasticity and Immune Evasion
abstract: The emergence of complex cellular phenotypes—such as tumor immune evasion and rapid therapeutic resistance—is fundamentally driven by interactions at the mesoscale. Rather than arising from isolated molecular events, these adaptive traits emerge from the dynamic reorganization of 3D chromatin architectures (e.g., enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA assemblies) and the subsequent rewiring of mesoscale protein-protein interaction networks. Despite the sheer volume of public multi-omics data, understanding how distributed genetic variations and secondary genetic modifiers synergistically perturb these mesoscale assemblies to drive variable disease expressivity remains a long-standing mystery. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the multiscale mechanisms underlying cancer plasticity and immune-checkpoint efficacy. By synthesizing vast, publicly available datasets—including ENCODE, TCGA, CCLE/DepMap, DICE, and large-scale CRISPR/Cas9 cellular screens—we will build an AI-driven computational framework that connects 1D sequence variation to emergent cellular outcomes. Importantly, this project relies exclusively on existing data and requires a transdisciplinary integration of machine learning, computational structural biology, 3D genomics, and tumor immunology. Our synthesis approach is structured across three integrated aims. First, we will map how primary driver mutations and secondary genetic modifiers dictate lineage-specific 3D genome organization. By leveraging single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell eQTL data, and 3D chromatin conformation maps, we will employ advanced sequence-to-function statistical learning to model the assembly of mesoscale regulatory hubs. We will specifically focus on how extrachromosomal DNA and structural variants override traditional topological boundaries to drive oncogenic and immunosuppressive transcriptional programs. Second, we will bridge the gap between 3D chromatin dysregulation and mesoscale protein complex dynamics. Using positive-unlabeled (PU) machine learning and ensemble-based scoring functions for protein-protein docking, we will predict how altered gene expression profiles and variant-driven misfolding events reshape protein interaction networks. This will allow us to map the hierarchy of protein complex stability and identify interaction nodes that act as functional hubs during cellular adaptation. Finally, we will link these mesoscale reconfigurations to emergent cellular outcomes, specifically the variable expressivity of immune escape in T cell subsets and breast cancer models. By analyzing transcriptomic and structural tumor-immune interaction networks, we will pinpoint the epigenetic and structural determinants that curtail targeted therapy and immunotherapy efficacy. This project directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to investigate emergent mesoscale phenomena through AI and data synthesis. The collaboration merges expertise in single-cell regulatory genomics, precision oncology, evolutionary genetic modifiers, and computational structural biology—a synergy beyond the scope of any single laboratory. Adhering to gold-standard open science practices, all predictive models, ensemble classifiers, and annotated multiscale networks will be distributed via public web portals. Furthermore, this Working Group will provide rigorous, cross-disciplinary training for a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists to lead multiscale biological synthesis.
background_and_significance:
Understanding the emergence of complex biological phenotypes from fundamental molecular components is one of the most pressing challenges in the molecular and cellular biosciences. At the heart of this challenge is the mesoscale—the intermediate spatial and temporal domain bridging individual biomolecules and organelles. In the context of cancer plasticity and tumor-immune dynamics, emergent cellular behaviors such as therapeutic resistance and immune evasion cannot be adequately explained by single genetic mutations or isolated signaling cascades. Instead, these phenomena emerge from the dynamic reorganization of mesoscale structures, particularly three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architectures, including enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) assemblies, alongside the consequential rewiring of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. 

While the scientific community has generated unprecedented volumes of public multi-omics data—spanning large-scale genomic repositories (e.g., TCGA, ENCODE), deep mutational scanning databases, single-cell transcriptomics, and massive cellular screens (e.g., CCLE/DepMap)—these datasets remain largely siloed by discipline. Genomic structural variations are rarely modeled in concert with mesoscale protein complex stability, and immunological single-cell profiles are infrequently mapped back to their underlying 3D chromatin drivers. Consequently, a critical knowledge gap persists regarding how distributed sequence variations, interacting with secondary genetic modifiers, synergistically perturb mesoscale assemblies to drive the variable expressivity of disease phenotypes. 

This proposal outlines a community-scale data synthesis initiative directly aligned with the NCEMS mission to elucidate emergent mesoscale phenomena through advanced artificial intelligence and data science. By exclusively leveraging existing, publicly available data, we aim to construct a unified, multiscale computational framework. This framework will seamlessly connect 1D genomic sequence variations to the 3D reorganization of chromatin, trace these effects through the altered thermodynamics of mesoscale protein complexes, and ultimately predict emergent cellular outcomes in tumor immune microenvironments. 

The significance of this work is multifold. First, it directly addresses long-standing puzzles concerning how cancers rapidly adapt to targeted therapies and why immune checkpoint blockade exhibits extreme variable expressivity across patient cohorts. Second, it shifts the analytical paradigm from reductionist, single-molecule studies to a holistic, systems-level understanding of mesoscale emergence. By identifying the critical topological boundaries and protein interaction nodes that function as structural linchpins during cellular adaptation, we will uncover fundamental principles of biological plasticity. Finally, this synthesis necessitates a level of transdisciplinary integration—merging computational structural biology, single-cell genomics, evolutionary genetics, and systems immunology—that exceeds the capacity of any individual laboratory. Through this NCEMS-supported Working Group, we will not only generate novel scientific insights but also pioneer innovative machine learning strategies capable of handling highly heterogeneous, multi-scale biological data, ultimately charting a new course for precision medicine and predictive cellular engineering.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The central objective of this Working Group is to decode how genetic variations cascade through mesoscale biological organizations to produce emergent, adaptable cellular phenotypes. To achieve this, our synthesis relies on advanced AI models to interrogate publicly available data across three multiscale dimensions. The research is driven by three primary questions and their corresponding hypotheses:

Research Question 1: How do primary driver mutations, structural variants, and secondary genetic modifiers interact to dynamically reconfigure mesoscale 3D chromatin architectures, such as enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA assemblies?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the variable expressivity of cancer cell plasticity is fundamentally driven by the synergistic interactions between primary genomic drivers and an underlying network of secondary genetic modifiers. Rather than acting strictly through linear transcriptional pathways, these genomic alterations disrupt traditional topological associating domains (TADs) and facilitate the formation of aberrant mesoscale regulatory hubs. Specifically, structural variants such as ecDNA bypass chromosomal constraints to assemble localized, high-density enhancer networks that hyper-activate oncogenic and immunosuppressive gene expression programs.

Research Question 2: In what ways do variant-driven disruptions in 3D chromatin architecture and altered transcriptomic profiles cascade into the proteome to reshape the stability and hierarchy of mesoscale protein-protein interaction networks?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that altered transcriptional outputs and concurrent missense mutations do not simply change protein abundance, but fundamentally alter mesoscale protein folding and interaction landscapes. We propose that specific genomic variants induce misfolded states and kinetic traps that reorganize the hierarchy of protein-protein interaction networks. By systematically predicting the binding affinities and structural conformations of these altered complexes, we anticipate identifying 'vulnerability hubs'—mesoscale protein assemblies that become structurally essential only under the specific evolutionary pressures of targeted therapy or immune attack.

Research Question 3: How do the reconfigured mesoscale chromatin hubs and rewired protein networks dictate emergent cellular outcomes, specifically the capacity of tumors to evade immune surveillance and resist checkpoint blockade therapies?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the efficacy of anti-tumor immunity is heavily curtailed by specific, predictable reconfigurations at the mesoscale within both the tumor and the infiltrating immune compartments. Specifically, we posit that the dysregulation of lineage-specific 3D chromatin organization in follicular regulatory T cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes leads to an emergent immunosuppressive cellular state. By linking mesoscale chromatin/protein alterations to single-cell immune profiles, we expect to demonstrate that the failure of therapies (e.g., anti-PD-1) is a direct consequence of emergent mesoscale properties that reinforce mutually suppressive tumor-immune interaction networks. 

By testing these hypotheses through the synthesis of disparate public datasets, this project will formulate a predictive model of cellular emergence. We will transition from describing static molecular states to mapping the dynamic, multiscale trajectories that cells navigate to survive therapeutic bottlenecks, fulfilling the NCEMS directive to unlock the rules of mesoscale biological organization.
methods_and_approach:
To investigate these multiscale emergent phenomena, our Working Group will strictly utilize existing, publicly available datasets, employing innovative AI and machine learning strategies to synthesize data across domains. No new experimental data will be generated. The methodology is structured across three integrated aims.

Aim 1: Mapping Mesoscale 3D Chromatin Reorganization via Statistical Learning.
We will aggregate whole-genome sequencing, single-cell RNA-seq, and single-cell eQTL datasets from TCGA, ENCODE, and CCLE. To model 3D genome organization, we will utilize available Hi-C, ChIA-PET, and CRISPR/Cas9 perturbation screen data. Our AI approach will involve developing a statistical sequence-to-function framework utilizing sequence and subsequence kernels to predict aberrant enhancer-promoter interactions. To address extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), we will synthesize genomic copy number data and publicly available metaphase FISH imaging repositories using deep learning-based image analysis and automated post-processing pipelines. By utilizing network analysis algorithms, we will map synergistic interactions between primary structural variants and secondary single nucleotide variants (SNVs), isolating the genetic contexts that trigger the breakdown of topological boundaries and the emergence of oncogenic chromatin hubs.

Aim 2: Predicting Mesoscale Protein Complex Dynamics with Ensemble Machine Learning.
To connect chromatin dysregulation to protein network dynamics, we will process massive deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets and interactome databases. A central challenge is inferring sequence-function relationships from large-scale experimental data that frequently lacks definitive negative examples. We will deploy Positive-Unlabeled (PU) machine learning frameworks to accurately pinpoint key structural residues driving altered protein functions. Furthermore, to evaluate the structural integrity of altered protein-protein interactions, we will adapt ensemble-based Random Forest classifiers—trained on physicochemical properties, energy terms, and evolutionary conservation—to score protein docking conformations. This strategy will allow us to in silico extrapolate the stability and binding kinetics of rewired mesoscale protein complexes under the precise mutational burdens identified in Aim 1.

Aim 3: Decoding Emergent Immune Evasion via Multimodal Single-Cell Synthesis.
To link mesoscale reconfigurations to cellular immune escape, we will synthesize datasets from the Database of Immune Cell Expression (DICE) with public single-cell transcriptomes of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and breast cancer models. We will apply multiplexed eQTL-inspired analytical frameworks to identify activation-dependent effects of disease-risk variants in distinct T cell subsets (e.g., CD4+ follicular regulatory T cells and CD8+ cytotoxic cells). Using advanced clustering and graph neural networks, we will model the cross-talk between the tumor's rewired mesoscale protein interaction networks (from Aim 2) and the infiltrating immune cells' transcriptomic states. This will enable the identification of specific mesoscale structural determinants that curtail the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade (e.g., anti-PD-1) and targeted kinase inhibitors.

Throughout the project, we will employ rigorous computational statistical approaches, including spatial and fixed-effects modeling, to ensure robustness. High-performance cloud computing environments will be utilized to handle the massive dimensionality of these synthesized multi-omics datasets, culminating in a robust, AI-driven framework for predicting mesoscale cellular emergence.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will deliver transformative insights into the principles governing mesoscale emergence in cancer and immunology, directly addressing the core mission of NCEMS. By seamlessly integrating 1D sequence data, 3D genomic architecture, and protein interactomics, we will produce a comprehensive, predictive map of cellular plasticity. 

Scientifically, our expected outcomes include: (1) The identification of novel enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA networks driven by synergistic primary and secondary genetic variations. (2) A refined library of variant-driven protein-protein interaction vulnerabilities, validated in silico through advanced ensemble scoring and positive-unlabeled machine learning frameworks. (3) The delineation of precise mesoscale architectural states in tumor-infiltrating T cells that dictate the variable expressivity of immune checkpoint blockade resistance. These discoveries will solve long-standing puzzles regarding why tumors with similar mutational burdens exhibit vastly different therapeutic trajectories and immune microenvironments.

Methodologically, this project will produce a suite of robust, scalable AI algorithms capable of synthesizing highly disparate, publicly available multi-omics datasets without the need for de novo experimental validation. This addresses the NCEMS goal of developing innovative research and analytical strategies. The computational frameworks developed herein will be adaptable to numerous other complex diseases beyond cancer.

Broadly, the impact of this Working Group will be a fundamental shift in how the biological community approaches the mesoscale. By demonstrating that macroscopic cellular outcomes like immune evasion are emergent properties of mesoscale network reconfigurations, we establish a new paradigm for therapeutic intervention—shifting focus from single-molecule inhibitors to mesoscale network disruptors. Furthermore, this initiative will bridge isolated scientific communities, fostering an enduring transdisciplinary ecosystem that maximizes the utility of the world’s existing biological data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to Open Science principles is foundational to this Working Group's operational framework. Recognizing that community-scale synthesis relies on the trust and transparency of the data ecosystem, we are committed to making all findings, models, and workflows completely accessible, adhering strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data standards.

All analytical pipelines, machine learning models, ensemble classifiers, and statistical frameworks developed during this project will be open-source. Codebases will be version-controlled via GitHub and permanently archived with DOIs using Zenodo. To ensure uncompromising reproducibility, we will utilize containerization technologies (Docker and Singularity) for all computational environments, allowing the broader scientific community to execute our exact sequence-to-function and protein-docking algorithms on their local infrastructure or cloud environments without dependency conflicts.

Furthermore, to maximize the accessibility of our synthesized mesoscale networks, we will develop a comprehensive, user-friendly web portal—conceptually similar to established centralized registries in genomics and structural biology. This portal will allow researchers to interactively query how specific genetic modifiers alter 3D chromatin architectures, visualize the projected structural shifts in protein-protein interactions, and explore the predicted downstream cellular impacts on immune evasion. All generated intermediate datasets, including annotated interaction networks and single-cell eQTL mappings, will be deposited in appropriate public repositories (e.g., dbGaP, Synapse) well ahead of publication. 

We will also adopt a collaborative, open-notebook science approach, openly sharing our meeting protocols, training materials, and negative results. By embedding these practices deeply into the project's lifecycle, we ensure our synthesis efforts serve as an enduring, reliable resource for the global biological community.
budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this ambitious community-scale synthesis project, significant support from NCEMS is required to facilitate collaboration, secure computational infrastructure, and train the next generation of data scientists. The proposed scale and transdisciplinary nature of this endeavor are inherently beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory.

First, funding is requested for robust cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS/GCP). The synthesis of massive public datasets—including petabytes of genomic, transcriptomic, and deep mutational scanning data from ENCODE, TCGA, and DICE—alongside the training of advanced deep learning and ensemble Random Forest classifiers, demands substantial, high-performance computational bandwidth and scalable storage solutions.

Second, NCEMS support is essential to fund the Working Group’s collaborative activities. We request budget allocations for semi-annual, in-person collaborative summits and regular virtual meetings. These gatherings are critical for bridging the distinct vocabularies and methodologies of experts spanning tumor immunology, 3D genomics, machine learning, and structural biology, ensuring a truly unified synthesis approach rather than parallel, siloed analyses.

Finally, a significant portion of the budget will be dedicated to personnel, specifically the support and cross-training of early-career researchers, including postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. These trainees will be immersed in a highly transdisciplinary environment, gaining expertise at the intersection of AI, multi-omics, and mesoscale biology. Funding will also support cross-training workshops organized by the Working Group to teach these advanced data synthesis methodologies. By investing heavily in trainee development, this budget directly supports the NCEMS mandate to tap diverse new talent and build a resilient, forward-looking workforce equipped to tackle the future of multiscale, data-driven biological discovery.
