author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Uncovering Mesoscale Emergence in Microbial Dark Matter through AI-Driven Synthesis of Metagenomic and Mass Spectrometry Data
abstract: Microbial communities exhibit remarkable emergent properties, orchestrating complex biochemical dialogues that shape host and environmental systems. These behaviors emerge primarily at the mesoscale, where diverse operons dictate the assembly of multi-enzyme protein complexes. These mesoscale structures subsequently synthesize heavily modified, highly diverse specialized metabolites. However, the vast majority of this biochemical repertoire remains hidden as biological "dark matter," largely because traditional analytical approaches rely on heavily biased reference databases. Consequently, our understanding of how novel mesoscale complexes emerge and drive chemical diversity remains fundamentally fragmented. To solve this long-standing puzzle, we propose the Working Group for Multi-Omic Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence. This project will execute a community-scale synthesis of massive, publicly available but currently siloed datasets: uncultured metagenomic sequences and billions of untargeted mass spectrometry (MS/MS) proteomics and metabolomics spectra. Because this synthesis requires advanced cross-disciplinary data science spanning microbial evolutionary genomics and computational mass spectrometry, it fundamentally necessitates the collaborative environment and computational infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our working group will pioneer a reference-free computational ecosystem to link the genetic blueprints of uncultured microbiomes to their emergent mesoscale assemblies and resulting chemical outputs. First, we will utilize alignment-free deep learning architectures—such as Siamese neural networks—to analyze global public metagenomes. This will enable the identification of shared functional domains and the evolutionary reconstruction of complex ancestral operons, bypassing the limitations of known functional annotations. Second, we will deploy expressive pattern-matching algorithms and mass spectrometry query languages to mine over a billion public MS/MS spectra. This computational search will identify structural patterns of uncharacterized metabolites and peptide fragments produced by these previously hidden operon-encoded assemblies. By synthesizing these independent multi-omic data streams, the working group will construct a unified "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph." This integrated network will answer fundamental questions regarding how novel multi-protein structures emerge across microbial lineages and how variations in these mesoscale assemblies translate into unappreciated chemical diversity, such as complex lipid or polyamine modifications. This synthesis will directly link primary molecular sequence data to emergent community-level biochemical phenotypes. The working group is entirely committed to open science principles; all unified data structures, predictive neural network models, and MS/MS querying workflows will be published as open-source computational tools. Furthermore, this initiative emphasizes vital workforce development, providing dedicated training for a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of computational multi-omics, deep learning, and mesoscale biology. By bridging disparate biological disciplines, this project will reveal the structural and chemical emergence of microbial ecosystems while maximizing the latent value of public omics data.
background_and_significance: Microbial communities govern global biogeochemical cycles, shape host health, and drive environmental adaptation through intricate, emergent biochemical dialogues. At the heart of these complex systems is emergence at the mesoscale: the organizational level bridging fundamental molecular sequences to observable cellular and community-level phenotypes. In microbial ecosystems, mesoscale emergence is prominently characterized by the evolution of highly complex operons that encode multi-enzyme protein assemblies. These structural complexes act as modular cellular factories, collaborating to synthesize heavily modified, structurally diverse specialized metabolites—ranging from novel lipid derivatives to complex polyamine conjugates—that mediate microbial interaction and environmental adaptation. Despite the vast amount of publicly available sequencing and metabolomic data generated over the past decade, a profound disconnect remains. Traditional bioinformatics and mass spectrometry data analysis workflows are intrinsically anchored to reference databases. However, these databases represent only a minute fraction of Earth's biological diversity, heavily biased toward a handful of culturable model organisms. Consequently, the vast majority of environmental genetic blueprints and untargeted mass spectrometry (MS/MS) spectra remain unannotated, relegated to the status of biological "dark matter." This reliance on known annotations critically impedes our ability to understand how novel mesoscale multi-protein structures emerge and how they dictate unexplored chemical diversity. Our understanding of microbial emergence is further fragmented by the historical siloing of multi-omic data. Uncultured metagenomic sequences (genomic potential) and untargeted mass spectrometry data (realized chemical output) are typically analyzed in isolation. To solve this long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences, a massive synthesis of these distinct data modalities is urgently required. Advancements in artificial intelligence, specifically alignment-free deep learning architectures like Siamese neural networks, now allow us to detect shared functionality among highly divergent microbial homologs without relying on reference markers. Concurrently, the development of expressive mass spectrometry query languages permits the rapid, pattern-based mining of billions of untargeted mass spectra to find hidden structural motifs, regardless of whether the exact molecule exists in a database. Synthesizing these computational innovations presents an unprecedented opportunity to transcend reference-based limitations. By integrating global metagenomic repositories with massive public MS/MS datasets, we can reconstruct the ancestral evolution of complex operons and directly correlate these emergent multi-enzyme assemblies with uncharacterized biochemical outputs. This community-scale data synthesis will answer fundamental questions about how biochemical complexity arises at the mesoscale. It is highly significant because it shifts the analytical paradigm from piecemeal, database-restricted observations to a holistic, reference-free mapping of the genomic-to-chemical landscape, ultimately unlocking a vast, untapped reservoir of biological dark matter to advance the molecular and cellular sciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is structured around three compelling, interrelated research questions aimed at decoding mesoscale emergence through multi-omic data integration. 

Question 1: How do novel multi-enzyme mesoscale assemblies evolve from ancestral operons across highly divergent, uncultured microbial lineages? 
We hypothesize that by utilizing reference-free, deep-learning-based functional classification on global metagenomic data, we can identify convergent evolutionary trajectories wherein standalone functional genes are recruited into complex, multi-component operons. By mapping these unannotated genetic clusters using maximum parsimony frameworks, we predict we will uncover previously unrecognized vertical evolution models demonstrating how simple genetic elements systematically assemble into emergent, higher-order mesoscale protein complexes capable of novel catalytic functions. 

Question 2: What is the cryptic chemical output of these uncharacterized mesoscale multi-enzyme assemblies, and how do variations in operon architecture translate into structural chemical diversity? 
We hypothesize that untargeted MS/MS spectra housed in public repositories contain robust, predictable structural patterns—such as specific ion fragmentation signatures indicating unique lipid conjugations or polyamine modifications—that map directly to the catalytic capacities of uncharacterized operons. We anticipate that by querying over a billion MS/MS spectra using highly expressive pattern-matching languages, we will discover thousands of unrecognized specialized metabolites and structural modifications whose synthesis is dependent upon the specific architectural variations of emergent multi-protein complexes. 

Question 3: Can we mathematically and computationally synthesize independent genomic and mass spectrometry data streams to accurately predict emergent biochemical phenotypes directly from raw environmental sequence data? 
We hypothesize that the co-occurrence of predicted mesoscale operon assemblies in uncultured metagenomes correlates strongly with the presence of distinct, uncharacterized spectral families in paired or environmentally similar meta-metabolomic datasets. By leveraging AI to synthesize these data types, we will construct a unified "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph." We propose that this integrated network will not only establish definitive links between genetic dark matter and chemical dark matter but will also enable predictive modeling of a microbial community's emergent chemical phenotype based solely on its metagenomic profile. 

Collectively, these research questions challenge the current reliance on annotated molecular data and address long-standing mysteries regarding the origins of biochemical diversity. By exploring these hypotheses through the synthesis of strictly pre-existing data, the Working Group will elucidate the fundamental rules of mesoscale structural assembly and its resulting chemical emergence. This approach pushes the boundaries of our understanding of molecular evolution and the vast, unmapped chemical space generated by uncultured microbiomes.
methods_and_approach:
To answer our proposed research questions, the Working Group will employ a purely data-driven synthesis strategy, exclusively utilizing publicly available datasets and developing a novel, transdisciplinary computational ecosystem. No new experimental data will be generated. 

Data Sources: 
We will harvest terabytes of raw sequence data from environmental and host-associated uncultured metagenomes via the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and MG-RAST. Concurrently, we will synthesize chemical data by accessing over 1.2 billion untargeted proteomics and metabolomics MS/MS spectra from global community repositories, such as GNPS and PRIDE. 

Phase 1: Reference-Free Genomic Discovery of Mesoscale Assemblies 
To bypass the limitations of heavily biased functional annotations, we will process massive metagenomic datasets using alignment-free deep learning models. Specifically, we will deploy Siamese Neural Networks capable of identifying shared nucleic acid functionalities across divergent homologs by recognizing complex sequence embeddings rather than simple sequence identity. Once novel functional groups are clustered, we will map their genomic neighborhoods to identify putative operons. We will then employ evolutionary reconstruction algorithms utilizing maximum parsimony models to trace the ancestry of these operons, delineating how individual ancestral genes iteratively combined to form emergent mesoscale multi-enzyme complexes across microbial lineages. 

Phase 2: Pattern-Based Mining of the Mass Spectrometry Universe 
Parallel to genomic analysis, we will analyze the colossal corpus of public MS/MS data. We will utilize advanced Python-based data processing frameworks to standardize, clean, and unify the diverse spectral datasets. Crucially, we will implement expressive Mass Spectrometry Query Languages (MassQL) to execute complex, pattern-based searches across the 1.2 billion spectra. Rather than searching for known exact molecular masses, we will query for conserved structural motifs—such as predictable mass shifts associated with novel bile acid modifications or previously undiscovered polyamine conjugations. This approach will group fragmented "chemical dark matter" into cohesive structural families derived from shared enzymatic modifications. 

Phase 3: Multi-Omic Synthesis and Graph Construction 
The crux of the project lies in the synthesis of Phase 1 and Phase 2 outputs. We will perform large-scale co-occurrence analyses, integrating metadata from paired multi-omic studies where both metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics were performed on the same biological samples. We will utilize machine learning association models to link the evolutionary appearance of specific mesoscale operon structures (Phase 1) with the emergence of distinct uncharacterized spectral families (Phase 2). This integration will populate the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," a multi-layered network directly linking previously unannotated genomic features to their corresponding cryptic chemical outputs. 

Validation and Rigor: 
The computational models will be iteratively refined using a subset of highly characterized datasets (e.g., well-documented secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters and their known MS/MS spectra) to validate the precision of the reference-free alignment and query architectures before deploying them on entirely unannotated biological dark matter. All models will incorporate robust statistical bootstrapping to ensure confidence in the synthetic linkages.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will deliver the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," an unprecedented public resource that maps the evolutionary trajectories of uncharacterized mesoscale multi-enzyme complexes directly to their emergent chemical outputs. We expect to identify thousands of novel structural linkages, significantly reducing the proportion of data categorized as biological "dark matter."

Second, the project will result in the discovery of entirely new classes of specialized metabolites, such as previously unrecognized lipid-conjugates and complex polyamine modifications. These discoveries will illuminate the hidden biochemical dialogue of uncultured microbiomes, providing novel insights into community-scale resilience, host-microbiome interactions, and potential biotechnological applications.

Third, we will release a suite of innovative, validated AI and pattern-matching software tools. By proving that alignment-free deep learning and expressive MS/MS query languages can successfully bypass the limitations of biased reference databases, we will provide the scientific community with a new blueprint for reference-free multi-omic discovery.

The impact of this project aligns perfectly with the core mission of NCEMS. By resolving long-standing puzzles surrounding the emergence of structural and chemical complexity, this work shifts the paradigm of omics research. Furthermore, the collaborative framework of this project will foster deep cross-pollination between evolutionary genomics and computational mass spectrometry. Importantly, this initiative will profoundly impact workforce development. By immersing graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists fluent in deep learning, massive data integration, and mesoscale biology, equipping them to lead the next frontier of computational biosciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The Working Group is unequivocally committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science. Given that this project synthesizes vast arrays of public data, it is imperative that our methodologies, code, and resulting data structures are rigorously transparent and accessible to the broader community.

Code and Software Accessibility: 
All computational pipelines—including the alignment-free Siamese Neural Networks, the evolutionary maximum parsimony scripts, and the Python-based MassQL query algorithms—will be developed entirely in the open. Source code will be hosted in version-controlled public GitHub repositories under an open-source license (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker, to encapsulate the entire data-processing environment, ensuring that any researcher can perfectly reproduce our computing ecosystems irrespective of their local hardware configuration.

Data Availability and Standards: 
Following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, all intermediate and final outputs, most notably the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," will be made publicly available. Annotated spectral networks and newly discovered chemical motifs will be directly integrated into community data repositories like GNPS (Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking), allowing immediate use by the global mass spectrometry community. Synthesized genomic annotations and operon models will be deposited in platforms such as Zenodo with clear, standardized metadata.

Documentation and Community Engagement: 
To maximize the utility of our generated tools, we will provide exhaustive documentation, including step-by-step Jupyter Notebook tutorials demonstrating how to apply our reference-free AI models to new datasets. Furthermore, the Working Group will host open virtual workshops to instruct the scientific community on utilizing these new analytical strategies, thereby democratizing access to massive-scale synthesis research.
budget_and_resources:
The proposed research requires NCEMS support because synthesizing global metagenomic repositories with over 1.2 billion MS/MS spectra is fundamentally beyond the capabilities, both computational and intellectual, of any single laboratory. This project demands a transdisciplinary merger of microbial evolutionary genomics, high-performance computational proteomics, and advanced deep learning—a convergence only possible through a dedicated, Center-supported Working Group.

Working Group Meetings and Collaboration: 
Funding is requested to support bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at NCEMS facilities. These intensive synthesis sessions will assemble our diverse team of mass spectrometry bioinformaticians, microbial ecologists, software engineers, and evolutionary biologists to actively integrate the distinct omics data streams, refine the "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph," and troubleshoot complex transdisciplinary challenges.

Workforce Development and Personnel: 
A significant portion of the budget will be allocated to support early-career researchers, specifically two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students. These trainees will serve as the operational bridge between the disparate disciplines, receiving invaluable cross-training in uncultured genomics, computational mass spectrometry, and AI-driven data synthesis, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train a diverse, data-savvy scientific workforce.

Computational Infrastructure: 
The scale of data requires substantial computational resources. While we will utilize public datasets, processing terabytes of metagenomic data and training Siamese Neural Networks requires access to high-performance GPU clusters. Similarly, querying billions of spectra demands significant memory and parallel processing capabilities. We request budget allocations for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or GCP) and dedicated storage to house intermediate data structures, ensuring smooth and rapid execution of our deep learning and pattern-matching algorithms. NCEMS infrastructure support is critical to establishing this highly scalable, reproducible computational ecosystem.

title: Evolutionary Origins of Mesoscale Signaling: An AI-Driven Synthesis of Exascale Dynamics and Ancestral Allosteric Networks
abstract: The unexpected emergence of complex cellular behaviors from biomolecular interactions remains a central challenge in molecular biology. At the mesoscale, modular signaling hubs—such as nuclear receptors (NRs) and multi-domain kinases—translate diverse metabolic and environmental cues into precise transcriptional cascades. Although the community has generated vast amounts of isolated structural and functional data, the dynamic mechanisms by which atomic-scale ligand binding allosterically dictates the recruitment of massive, multimeric co-regulator complexes at the mesoscale remain obscured. We hypothesize that this mesoscale emergence is governed by conserved, dynamic 'wiring diagrams' sculpted over evolutionary time. Currently, thousands of static structures, petabytes of open-access exascale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, and deep phylogenomic sequence alignments exist across disparate public repositories. However, they have never been systematically integrated. This Working Group will synthesize public structural data (PDB), open-source MD trajectories (leveraging distributed computing repositories like Folding@home), and expansive phylogenomic databases to elucidate the evolutionary and dynamic origins of mesoscale signaling. We will construct a transdisciplinary, AI-driven pipeline that maps atomic-level conformational fluctuations to emergent cellular transcriptional outputs. Our project is structured around three integrated synthesis aims. First, we will fuse phylogenomic databases with structural ensembles to reconstruct the ancestral sequence space of key modular proteins, including nuclear receptors and Src-family kinases. Leveraging machine learning models, we will synthesize open-access structural data to predict ancestral conformational ensembles, bridging evolutionary history with structural biophysics. Second, we will mine distributed computing datasets to calculate network-based dynamic metrics, specifically adapting the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI), across these evolutionary trajectories. This massive data synthesis will reveal how functionally critical rigid hinges and flexible active sites migrate, couple, and co-evolve to support novel ligand specificities and enable mesoscale complex formation. Third, we will develop machine learning models that link these dynamic coupling architectures directly to publicly available transcriptomic and high-throughput functional assay datasets (e.g., GEO, ChEMBL). This framework will predict how specific mutation- or ligand-induced shifts in allosteric networks cascade into emergent phenotypic states, such as metabolic reprogramming or disease pathologies. This community-scale synthesis relies exclusively on existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental generation in strict accordance with the NCEMS mandate. By bridging evolutionary protein dynamics, receptor pharmacology, and exascale computational biophysics, this project demands a transdisciplinary collaboration far surpassing the capacity of any single lab. The initiative champions open science by committing to publish all AI models, dynamic network maps, and synthesized phylogenetic trajectories in robust, open-access portals. Furthermore, it addresses the NCEMS mission by providing rich cross-training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs, equipping the next generation of researchers with essential skills in data science, generative AI, and multi-scale biological synthesis. Ultimately, this work will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the structural basis of evolution and establish a predictive framework for allosteric emergence in cellular systems.
background_and_significance: The unexpected appearance of new biological properties at the mesoscale—the critical interface between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular organelles—remains one of the most fundamental mysteries in the molecular and cellular biosciences. At this scale, the transmission of information involves highly complex, emergent phenomena, wherein atomic-level perturbations such as ligand binding or point mutations cascade through a protein's architecture to govern the assembly of massive, multimeric signaling complexes. Prototypical examples of this mesoscale emergence include modular signaling hubs, such as nuclear receptors (NRs) and Src-family kinases. These biomolecular machines function as allosteric switches, translating extracellular and metabolic cues into profound transcriptional cascades and cellular responses. Despite their biological importance and therapeutic relevance, the precise physical principles and evolutionary trajectories that dictate how allosteric signals propagate across these modular domains to mediate mesoscale complex formation remain obscured. Over the past two decades, the global scientific community has amassed an unprecedented volume of publicly available data. We now possess deep phylogenomic alignments capturing billions of years of evolutionary history, tens of thousands of static crystallographic and cryo-EM structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB), petabytes of exascale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories hosted in distributed computing archives (e.g., Folding@home), and exhaustive transcriptomic and functional datasets residing in repositories like GEO and ChEMBL. However, these massive datasets exist in isolated silos. Evolutionary biologists analyze sequence conservation, biophysicists study localized atomistic dynamics, and systems biologists map transcriptomic outputs. Consequently, a unified theoretical and computational framework connecting evolutionary sequence space to atomistic dynamics, and ultimately to mesoscale emergent phenotypes, has not yet been established. The synthesis of these disparate data streams represents a profound opportunity to solve the long-standing puzzle of protein allostery and mesoscale regulation. We hypothesize that mesoscale signaling complexes are governed by conserved, dynamically coupled 'wiring diagrams' that have been finely sculpted by evolution. By identifying how functionally critical rigid hinges and highly flexible recognition sites migrate and co-evolve over evolutionary time, we can understand the physical basis of how proteins adapt to bind new ligands and recruit novel co-regulators. Aligning with the core mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), our proposed Working Group seeks to execute a community-scale synthesis project utilizing exclusively publicly available data. We will integrate AI and data science with principles of evolutionary biophysics to link deep evolutionary time with exascale molecular dynamics. By synthesizing structural ensembles, simulated trajectories, and transcriptomic data, we aim to map the dynamic order parameters of allostery. This transdisciplinary approach will fundamentally shift the paradigm from viewing proteins as static entities to understanding them as dynamic, evolving networks. The significance of this project lies not only in addressing fundamental questions regarding the physical basis of biological emergence but also in pioneering novel analytical strategies that can be generalized to other complex mesoscale systems, ultimately establishing a predictive engine for synthetic biology, protein engineering, and precision pharmacology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our transdisciplinary synthesis project is driven by three fundamental research questions that bridge evolutionary history, atomistic dynamics, and mesoscale cellular phenotypes. These questions are designed to challenge our current understanding of allostery and modular protein regulation by leveraging the vast expanse of unintegrated, publicly available structural, dynamic, and functional data. 

Research Question 1: How do ancestral allosteric networks evolve to support the emergence of novel mesoscale signaling complexes? Current evolutionary analyses largely focus on sequence conservation, neglecting the physical dynamics that enable function. We hypothesize that the emergence of novel mesoscale interactions—such as the recruitment of distinct multimeric co-regulators by nuclear receptors or the modular autoinhibition mechanisms of Src-family kinases—is driven by the evolutionary migration of critical dynamic 'wiring diagrams.' Specifically, we hypothesize that the spatial distribution of highly rigid hinges and highly flexible active sites is not static; rather, it co-evolves to accommodate new ligand specificities and facilitate altered complex formations. By synthesizing ancestral sequence reconstruction with predicted structural ensembles, we aim to map the evolutionary trajectories of these allosteric networks, testing the hypothesis that dynamic flexibility is a highly evolvable trait crucial for mesoscale adaptation.

Research Question 2: Can emergent mesoscale properties of modular signaling hubs be quantitatively predicted from atomistic dynamic coupling indices derived from exascale datasets? The gap between microsecond atomistic fluctuations and macroscopic cellular function is historically difficult to bridge. We hypothesize that network-based dynamic metrics—specifically the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI)—extracted from synthesized petabyte-scale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories can serve as definitive 'order parameters' for large-scale conformational states. By mining open-source exascale MD archives generated via distributed computing (e.g., Folding@home), we hypothesize that these dynamic indices will reveal hidden, long-range allosteric communication channels. We expect to demonstrate that specific patterns of dynamic coupling dictate the thermodynamic probability of adopting active versus inactive mesoscale assemblies, effectively bridging the atomic and mesoscale regimes.

Research Question 3: How do ligand-induced or mutational perturbations in fundamental dynamic wiring diagrams cascade into systems-level phenotypic changes? To connect physical biophysics with biological emergence, it is necessary to link dynamic changes to actual cellular outputs. We hypothesize that machine learning models can be trained to recognize specific DFI/DCI network signatures and accurately predict corresponding transcriptional or functional outcomes. By synthesizing our dynamic network maps with publicly available high-throughput transcriptomic datasets (GEO) and biochemical assay databases (ChEMBL), we predict that specific perturbations (e.g., a disease-associated point mutation or an allosteric ligand) will induce quantifiable shifts in the dynamic coupling index. We hypothesize that these shifts can be mathematically correlated with emergent phenotypic states, such as metabolic reprogramming or altered immune signaling, thus providing a predictive AI framework for mesoscale emergence.

These interconnected questions directly align with the NCEMS mandate by demanding the synthesis of massive, disparate datasets to solve long-standing puzzles in molecular biology, far exceeding the capability of a single laboratory or traditional experimental approach.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve our objectives, we will construct a robust, AI-driven computational pipeline structured around three integrated specific aims, utilizing exclusively existing, publicly available data in strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate. Our transdisciplinary methodology integrates phylogenomics, exascale molecular dynamics (MD) mining, network theory, and machine learning (ML).

Aim 1: AI-Enabled Reconstruction of Ancestral Structural Ensembles. We will systematically mine phylogenomic databases (e.g., Pfam, UniProt) to extract deep sequence alignments for modular signaling hubs, primarily targeting Nuclear Receptors (NRs) and Src-family kinases. Using established maximum likelihood phylogenetic tools, we will infer the ancestral sequence space of these protein families. Because empirical structures of these ancestral nodes are largely absent, we will employ state-of-the-art AI-based structural prediction algorithms (e.g., AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold) coupled with generative conformational sampling. By synthesizing available structural data from the PDB, we will generate robust ensembles of structural models for thousands of modern and ancestral nodes. This synthesis will map the evolutionary drift of three-dimensional topology alongside primary sequence evolution.

Aim 2: Mining Exascale Trajectories to Map Dynamic Coupling Networks. We will pivot from static structures to functional dynamics by tapping into massive, open-access MD repositories, such as those generated by distributed computing platforms (e.g., Folding@home datasets, MoDEL). For trajectories that are unavailable, we will leverage publicly available Markov State Models to sample conformational space. From these petabytes of atomic coordinates, we will compute network-based dynamic metrics—specifically the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI). DFI quantifies the resilience of individual residues to random force perturbations, acting as a metric for local flexibility, whereas DCI measures the mechanical coupling between distal functional sites. By mapping DFI and DCI values onto the structural ensembles generated in Aim 1, we will construct evolutionary dynamic network graphs. Graph theory analyses will be applied to trace how rigid allosteric hinges and flexible recruitment interfaces have migrated through evolutionary time to support the emergence of novel mesoscale complex assemblies.

Aim 3: Machine Learning Synthesis for Phenotypic Prediction. To connect biophysical dynamics with emergent cellular functions, we will develop deep learning architectures (e.g., Graph Neural Networks, GNNs). We will construct a synthesized database integrating our DFI/DCI network maps with high-throughput functional data extracted from ChEMBL (binding affinities, transcriptional activity assays) and GEO (ligand- and mutation-specific transcriptomic profiles). The GNNs will use the dynamic network graphs as input features to predict transcriptomic signatures and functional activity states. Recognizing the inherent noise in biological datasets, we will employ sophisticated uncertainty quantification techniques—such as evidential deep learning or Bayesian neural networks—to assign confidence intervals to our phenotypic predictions. This rigorous validation step ensures our models provide actionable, high-confidence insights into how atomic-level perturbations cascade through the allosteric network to dictate mesoscale signaling outputs. This methodology relies entirely on the transdisciplinary synthesis of public data, creating a novel analytical strategy for the broader scientific community.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence. By successfully integrating evolutionary biology, exascale biomolecular simulations, and functional genomics through an AI-driven framework, we expect to deliver a unified, multi-scale model of allosteric regulation. 

Scientifically, this project will yield the first comprehensive maps of evolutionary dynamic coupling for critical modular signaling hubs, specifically nuclear receptors and Src-family kinases. These 'wiring diagrams' will resolve long-standing puzzles surrounding how proteins evolve to accommodate new ligands and recruit diverse, massive co-regulator complexes without disrupting their fundamental folds. Furthermore, the development of Graph Neural Networks that predict transcriptomic outputs directly from atomistic Dynamic Coupling Indices (DCI) will establish a groundbreaking predictive paradigm. This will illuminate how specific mutations or pharmacological interventions at the atomic level precipitate complex cellular behaviors, such as metabolic reprogramming and altered gene transcription.

Methodologically, we will create an innovative suite of analytical strategies that synthesize previously siloed data modalities—spanning PDB structures, Folding@home exascale MD trajectories, and GEO/ChEMBL functional databases. This pipeline will be highly generalized, providing the broader scientific community with the tools to investigate mesoscale phenomena in entirely different protein systems.

Broader impacts include a profound contribution to workforce development, directly answering the NCEMS call. The Working Group will fund and cross-train a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students. Trainees will gain rare, highly sought-after expertise at the intersection of generative AI, high-performance distributed computing, and multi-scale biological data synthesis. They will become the vanguard of the next-generation, data-savvy workforce capable of navigating petabyte-scale biological problems. Ultimately, the predictive framework generated by this synthesis effort will catalyze future breakthroughs in protein engineering, synthetic biology, and the development of next-generation allosteric modulators for precision medicine.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is unequivocally committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science, adhering to the highest FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data standards. Because this project is entirely computational and synthesizes existing public datasets, ensuring the transparency and reproducibility of our AI models and analytical pipelines is paramount.

All synthesized datasets, including our reconstructed ancestral sequence alignments, predicted structural ensembles, and compiled dynamic indices (DFI/DCI), will be hosted on stable, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad. To facilitate community access and exploration, we will develop and deploy the 'Mesoscale Dynamics Atlas,' an interactive, web-based portal where researchers can visualize evolutionary dynamic networks and query mutational impacts on allosteric coupling.

All software, machine learning architectures, and data-processing pipelines developed during this project will be open-source. Codebases will be version-controlled via GitHub, extensively documented, and released under a permissive MIT or Apache 2.0 license. To guarantee reproducibility across different computing environments, all computational workflows will be containerized using Docker and Singularity, and orchestration will be managed via Nextflow. This ensures that any researcher worldwide can seamlessly download our containers and reproduce the calculation of DFI/DCI metrics or the training of our transcriptomic prediction models from raw data inputs.

Furthermore, we commit to disseminating our findings rapidly through open-access channels. All manuscripts will be deposited in preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) concurrently with journal submission. We will also publish our data curation and processing protocols on platforms like Protocols.io. By embedding these rigorous open science practices into the core of our operations, we will maximize the value of NCEMS funding, ensuring our methodological innovations and biological insights serve as a permanent, accessible resource for the global molecular and cellular biosciences community.

title: Emergent Topologies at the Mesoscale: Synthesizing Protein Entanglement and 3D Genome Architecture through AI and Polymer Physics
abstract:
The physical organization of the mesoscale—the critical nexus between single biomolecules and large-scale organelles—relies on complex topological constraints to drive emergent biological functions. A long-standing puzzle in cellular biophysics is how intricate entanglements at the individual protein level (such as knots, slipknots, and theta-curves) scale up to influence the mesoscale architecture and mechanical properties of massive cellular assemblies like the 3D genome. While recent advances in deep learning have unveiled thousands of previously uncharacterized knotted proteins across the human proteome, and data-driven polymer physics models have successfully mapped chromosomal loop extrusion by multi-protein SMC (Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes) complexes, these domains of study have largely remained isolated. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to construct the first unified framework of biological topology, from individual polypeptide entanglements to macroscopic chromatin networks.

By integrating vast, publicly available datasets—spanning the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, the Protein Data Bank (PDB), high-resolution Hi-C chromosomal contact maps, and large-scale coevolutionary sequence alignments—our multi-disciplinary Working Group will trace the flow of topological information across biological scales. First, we will develop and deploy advanced topological algorithms and convolutional neural networks to comprehensively catalog entanglements, theta-curves, and pierced lassos specifically within chromatin-associated proteins, condensin/cohesin complexes, and mesoscale phase-separated condensates. This structural synthesis will yield a comprehensive, genome-wide map of protein entanglement in the nucleus, classifying structures based on predicted topological complexity, chaperone-dependency, and coevolutionary constraints.

Next, we will fuse these topological structural maps with data-driven, coarse-grained polymer physics models to understand mesoscale emergence. Utilizing maximum entropy approaches and large-scale conformational sampling, we will simulate how topologically complex protein hubs mechanically interact with chromatin arrays. We seek to test the hypothesis that intricately folded proteins and highly constrained topological motifs act as specialized architectural ratchets and viscoelastic anchors. By acting as topological roadblocks or highly stable scaffolding hubs, these proteins may fundamentally direct the emergent 3D spatial organization, loop-extrusion dynamics, and mechanical stress responses of interphase and mitotic chromosomes.

This project strictly leverages existing open-access data, requiring no new experimental generation, but instead relying on the transdisciplinary synthesis of physical knot theory, structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and computational genomics. Support from NCEMS is critical, as mapping the interplay between structural topology and genomic organization far exceeds the capacity of isolated labs. The initiative will culminate in the 'MesoTopo Atlas,' an open-access AI-driven platform integrating protein entanglement data directly with genomic architecture models. Adhering strictly to FAIR open-science principles, this Working Group will also provide unparalleled training opportunities, equipping the next generation of data-savvy biophysicists with the computational and theoretical tools necessary to explore the frontier of multi-scale biological topology.
background_and_significance:
The molecular and cellular biosciences are currently undergoing a paradigm shift, transitioning from the study of isolated biomolecules to the investigation of mesoscale assemblies. The mesoscale—the spatial and functional regime spanning nanometers to micrometers—is where fundamental molecular interactions orchestrate the emergence of complex, systems-level biological properties. Among the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence is the three-dimensional organization of the genome. Chromatin architecture dictates gene regulation, cellular differentiation, and mechanical stability, driven by the dynamic action of structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes, transcription factors, and phase-separated condensates. Concurrently, structural biology has revealed a previously hidden layer of complexity within individual biomolecules: topological entanglement. Over recent years, structural bioinformatics has demonstrated that a significant portion of the proteome contains deep topological features, including open knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and theta-curves formed by covalent or ionic linkages. 

Despite an explosion of publicly available data in both genome architecture (e.g., high-resolution Hi-C contact maps, microscopy datasets) and protein structure (e.g., the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold predictions), these two fields remain profoundly siloed. A critical, unanswered question in cellular biophysics is how the intrinsic topological complexity of individual proteins scales up to influence the mesoscale physical properties of chromatin networks. While polymer physics and data-driven computational models have successfully described chromosomal loop extrusion and chromatin compartment formation, these models typically treat interacting proteins as simple, topologically trivial nodes or generic bridging constraints. Conversely, studies characterizing intricate protein folding pathways, topological stability, and chaperone-dependent knotting rarely consider how these immense structural barriers function when integrated into macro-molecular chromosomal machines under extreme mechanical stress.

This proposal addresses this critical knowledge gap by catalyzing a transdisciplinary synthesis of physical knot theory, structural bioinformatics, AI-driven structure prediction, and polymer physics. Our overarching objective is to synthesize disparate, publicly available datasets to uncover how protein-level topological entanglements dictate the emergent 3D structural and viscoelastic properties of the genome. By integrating the vast repositories of structural data with chromosomal contact maps, we will determine whether knotted and topologically complex proteins are preferentially enriched within genomic scaffolding and whether their intricate folds serve as mechanical ratchets, viscoelastic anchors, or topological roadblocks during loop extrusion.

The significance of this NCEMS-supported synthesis project lies in its potential to entirely redefine our understanding of mesoscale mechanics in the nucleus. By building a unified, multi-scale framework, we will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the structural stability of the genome under axial stress and uncover new evolutionary principles governing protein folding. This community-scale initiative will transcend the capabilities of any single research lab, uniting mathematicians, computer scientists, structural biologists, and genomicists. In doing so, we will not only derive novel biological insights from existing open-access data but also establish innovative analytical strategies and computational pipelines that will train the next generation of researchers to navigate the converging frontiers of AI, topology, and mesoscale biology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project aims to bridge the gap between individual molecular topology and mesoscale genomic architecture through a coordinated, multi-scalar investigation. By synthesizing public structural, genomic, and evolutionary data, our Working Group will address three compelling research questions, each driven by a central hypothesis.

Question 1: What is the topological landscape of the nuclear proteome, and how are complex entanglements distributed within chromatin-interacting networks?
We currently lack a comprehensive understanding of how topological features are distributed among proteins that govern 3D genomic architecture. We will synthesize structural data from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and the PDB to systematically catalog knots, slipknots, and theta-curves in nuclear proteins. 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that chromatin-associated proteins—specifically subunits of SMC-kleisin complexes, DNA-binding response regulators, and hub proteins in phase-separated genomic condensates—exhibit a statistically significant enrichment in complex topological motifs compared to the general proteome. We further predict that these specific entanglements correspond to regions of high coevolutionary coupling, functioning to lock these proteins into extraordinarily stable, long-lived functional states that are strictly dependent on molecular chaperones (e.g., Hsp90) for their initial folding and assembly.

Question 2: How do protein-level topological constraints structurally modulate the dynamics of large-scale chromosomal loop extrusion?
The spatial organization of the genome is actively maintained by loop extrusion mechanisms, yet the physical barriers that control and limit this extrusion remain poorly characterized at the molecular-mechanical level. By integrating topological data with high-resolution Hi-C maps and data-driven polymer physics models, we will simulate loop extrusion across structurally heterogeneous chromatin.
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that intricately folded proteins and highly constrained topological networks act as specialized mechanical ratchets or architectural 'speed bumps' during DNA loop extrusion. Rather than merely occupying space, the rigid, knotted cores of these proteins possess distinct mechanical resistance properties that stall or redirect condensin and cohesin complexes, thereby deterministically shaping the boundaries of topologically associating domains (TADs) and genomic compartments.

Question 3: In what ways do co-evolved protein topologies dictate the emergent viscoelastic properties of the entire mesoscale chromosome?
Chromosomes behave as viscoelastic solids, altering their stiffness dramatically between interphase and mitosis. The molecular origins of these distinct mechanical states are not fully explained by DNA composition alone. We will synthesize coevolutionary landscape models with large-scale coarse-grained simulations to analyze stress responses across different cell lines.
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the mesoscale viscoelasticity of mitotic and interphase chromosomes emerges directly from the collective mechanical integration of topological protein hubs and dynamic chromatin loops. We propose that the exceptional tensile strength and stiffness observed in mitotic chromosomes are structurally dependent on a coordinated network of specific, knot-stabilized anchor proteins. The coevolution of these topological features represents a hidden physical code that ensures chromosomal integrity during the extreme mechanical stress of cellular division.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve our community-scale synthesis goals, the Working Group will deploy a transdisciplinary methodological framework strictly utilizing existing, publicly available datasets. Our approach integrates machine learning, mathematical knot theory, coevolutionary landscape modeling, and polymer physics through a three-phase computational pipeline.

Phase 1: AI-Driven Topological Cataloging and Structural Synthesis
We will first construct a high-throughput computational pipeline to mine the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (covering diverse proteomes, including the human and primary model organisms). Utilizing advanced algorithms based on the uniform closure method and genus trace analysis, we will calculate the topological complexity of all nuclear and chromatin-associated proteins. To handle the scale of this data and filter out prediction artifacts, we will modify custom Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)—originally designed for pattern recognition in complex medical imaging—to automatically detect, classify, and validate intricate topologies (knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and theta-curves) based on structural coordinates and prediction confidence (pLDDT) scores. This phase will yield the foundational dataset of our project: a genome-wide, confidence-weighted map of nuclear protein entanglement.

Phase 2: Coevolutionary and Genomic Data Integration
Once nuclear topological motifs are mapped, we will synthesize these structural insights with vast evolutionary and genomic datasets. By analyzing deep bacterial and eukaryotic sequence alignments, we will build coevolutionary landscape models using maximum entropy approaches. This will allow us to quantify the inter-domain residue interactions and energetic barriers required to stabilize these complex topological nodes. Concurrently, we will cross-reference the genomic loci of these topologically complex proteins with high-resolution Hi-C chromosomal contact maps from multiple distinct human cell lines. We will employ statistical machine learning techniques to correlate the presence of knotted protein hubs with the spatial boundaries of topologically associating domains (TADs) and A/B genomic compartments, identifying statistically significant colocalizations.

Phase 3: Data-Driven Polymer Physics Simulations
To test how these microscopic topologies drive mesoscale emergence, we will incorporate our structural and genomic synthesis into advanced, coarse-grained polymer physics models of the 3D genome (e.g., MiChroM and MEGABASE frameworks). We will assign distinct biophysical parameters—derived from the structural stability and coevolutionary constraints of the knotted motifs identified in Phase 1 and 2—to specific chromatin-interacting nodes within the simulation environment. Through large-scale molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo conformational sampling, we will simulate the process of DNA loop extrusion and apply simulated axial stretching to the modeled chromosomes. This will allow us to quantitatively observe how the topological resistance of specific protein hubs influences the emergent spatial organization, phase separation (hydrophobic-like collapse), and overall viscoelastic stiffness of the chromosome during both interphase and mitosis.

Collaboration and Feasibility:
This methodology inherently requires the collective expertise of knot theorists, AI specialists, computational biologists, and polymer physicists. By operating exclusively in the computational domain using open-access data, the project bypasses experimental bottlenecks, ensuring a high degree of feasibility and directly aligning with NCEMS's mandate to foster synthesis-based discoveries.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The primary outcome of this synthesis project will be the creation of the 'MesoTopo Atlas,' the first comprehensive, AI-driven open-access database that directly maps protein-level topological entanglements onto 3D genomic architecture. This platform will provide the global scientific community with a novel resource to visualize and interrogate how molecular knots, slipknots, and theta-curves correlate with chromosomal looping, TAD boundaries, and gene regulatory networks across multiple species and cell lines.

Scientifically, this project will resolve critical, long-standing puzzles regarding the mechanical stability of the genome. By demonstrating that specific knotted or topologically complex proteins function as critical architectural ratchets and viscoelastic anchors, we will provide a fundamentally new, physics-based paradigm for understanding chromosomal compaction and mesoscale cellular organization. The integration of polymer physics with structural topology will pioneer innovative analytical strategies that can subsequently be applied to other massive mesoscale assemblies, such as the cytoskeleton or biomolecular condensates.

Furthermore, this Working Group will have a profound impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees (postdoctoral scholars and graduate students) into a highly transdisciplinary environment, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy biophysicists fluent in both abstract mathematics (knot theory) and high-performance computational genomics. These scientists will be uniquely positioned to lead the future of AI-driven structural biology.

Ultimately, this research will demonstrate how synthesizing disparate layers of publicly available biological data—from atomic coordinates to macroscopic chromosomal contact maps—can uncover the hidden physical rules governing emergent mesoscale phenomena, fully realizing the strategic scientific vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of Open, Team, and Reproducible Science, strictly adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data standards. Because this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring complete transparency of our analytical pipelines and computational models is paramount.

All raw inputs synthesized during this project (e.g., specific subsets of the PDB, AlphaFold databases, Hi-C maps, and coevolutionary alignments) will be thoroughly documented with persistent digital object identifiers (DOIs). The 'MesoTopo Atlas' database generated by this project will be hosted on an open-access web server and mirrored on community repositories such as Zenodo or Dryad to ensure long-term accessibility.

To guarantee the absolute reproducibility of our methodological approaches, all custom software, topological algorithms, convolutional neural networks, and coarse-grained polymer physics simulation scripts will be developed openly via GitHub and GitLab under an MIT or GNU General Public License. We will deploy our workflows using containerization technologies such as Docker and Singularity, allowing any researcher globally to download and execute our exact computational environments, effectively eliminating the "works on my machine" barrier.

We will practice rapid dissemination of our findings by submitting all manuscripts to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv or arXiv) prior to rigorous peer review, ensuring immediate access for the broader scientific community. All final publications will be released under Open Access (CC-BY) licenses. Furthermore, detailed Jupyter Notebooks detailing our statistical methodologies, machine learning training regimes, and data visualization protocols will be published alongside all manuscripts, ensuring that our innovative analytical strategies are fully transparent and adaptable for future synthesis research.

The proposed research requires NCEMS support because the scope of multi-scale synthesis—bridging knot theory, structural AI, and polymer physics—far exceeds the computational and financial resources of any single investigator's laboratory. 

Personnel Support: The primary budget allocation will fund two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate research assistants. These trainees will serve as the crucial integrative links between the disparate disciplines of the Working Group. Funds will provide competitive stipends and tuition remission, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will benefit from dual-mentorship, gaining expertise in both structural topology and genomic modeling.

Computational Resources: A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to securing high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. Developing and training convolutional neural networks on vast structural databases, computing topological invariants across entire proteomes, and running large-scale, molecular dynamics and polymer physics simulations require substantial computational power. We request funding for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS, GCP) and dedicated time on national supercomputing clusters to guarantee rapid processing and data storage for the 'MesoTopo Atlas.'

Working Group Meetings and Dissemination: To stimulate genuine cross-disciplinary collaboration, we require funding for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS headquarters, alongside regular virtual hackathons. These face-to-face interactions are essential for translating mathematical topology concepts into genomic physics parameters. Additionally, the budget includes travel funds for PIs and trainees to present findings at major national and international biophysics and computational biology conferences.

By leveraging existing open-access data, the budget completely eschews costs associated with wet-lab reagents or experimental equipment, ensuring that all NCEMS funds are highly optimized and directly invested into synthesis, computation, and workforce training.

title: Deciphering the Mesoscale Emergence of Skeletal Muscle Adaptation: A GPU-Accelerated Multi-Omic and Mathematical Synthesis of Ribosome Dynamics under Competing Stresses
abstract:
Skeletal muscle plasticity—specifically its capacity to undergo hypertrophy or atrophy—is an emergent cellular property strictly governed by mesoscale phenomena: the dynamic assembly, biogenesis, and regulatory control of the ribosome. While individual molecular pathways (e.g., mTORC1 signaling) and systemic influences (e.g., inflammatory cytokines) are well documented, a fundamental mystery remains regarding how competing systemic signals—such as mechanical overload from exercise and systemic inflammatory stress from rheumatic conditions—spatiotemporally integrate at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive opposing phenotypic outcomes. Although individual transcriptomic, translatomic (Ribo-seq), and proteomic studies have profiled these states in isolation, the resulting vast repositories of publicly available data remain fragmented. 

To solve this long-standing puzzle, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project leveraging massive, publicly available human and rodent multi-omic datasets to map the mesoscale emergence of muscle adaptation. We will integrate transcriptomic, Ribo-seq, phosphoproteomic, and structural data across healthy exercise cohorts and patients with inflammatory conditions. Because aligning and synthesizing such divergent, high-dimensional multi-omic datasets is computationally prohibitive for traditional bioinformatics pipelines, we will develop ultra-fast, GPU-accelerated algorithms and Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. These AI-driven tools will efficiently align divergent sequences, reconstruct dynamic translational networks, and predict the interaction structures of mesoscale molecular assemblies in real time.

To bridge the gap from GNN-derived molecular networks to emergent cellular phenotypes, we will couple our AI frameworks with advanced mathematical modeling. We will construct spatiotemporal systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) with free boundaries to model the physical expansion of the muscle fiber cross-sectional area (hypertrophy) as a direct mathematical consequence of mesoscale ribosome biogenesis and translational output. This hybrid AI-mathematical framework will allow us to simulate how localized mechanical stimuli promote ribosomal assembly, and precisely how inflammatory stress acts as a molecular roadblock to dampen this translational capacity.

This transdisciplinary approach perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. The project relies entirely on the computational synthesis of existing public repositories, generating no new experimental data. It demands the integration of three distinct scientific domains—high-performance GPU computing, continuous mathematical modeling, and molecular exercise physiology—a synergy fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. All developed GPU-accelerated pipelines, GNN architectures, PDE models, and integrated datasets will be open-sourced, adhering to the highest standards of reproducible team science. Furthermore, our Working Group will cross-train a new generation of data-savvy postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of AI, computational mathematics, and cellular biology. By decoding the mesoscale logic of translational control under competing biological stresses, this synthesis will uncover profound insights into the emergent nature of cellular growth and adaptation.
background_and_significance:
Skeletal muscle plasticity exemplifies a classic problem of biological emergence, where mesoscale interactions dictate macroscale cellular and organismal phenotypes. The dynamic assembly, biogenesis, and regulatory control of the ribosome form the core of this mesoscale machinery, dictating whether a muscle fiber will undergo hypertrophy in response to mechanical overload or atrophy under pathological conditions. Although decades of research have charted isolated signaling cascades, such as mTORC1 activation or the role of inflammatory cytokines, a profound knowledge gap persists. We still lack a cohesive, multiscale understanding of how competing systemic signals—specifically, mechanical stress from resistance exercise versus systemic inflammation from rheumatic diseases—integrate simultaneously at the ribosomal interface to dictate translational output and subsequent changes in cell size.

Currently, vast repositories of publicly available omics data—spanning transcriptomics, translatomics (Ribo-seq), proteomics, and structural biology—capture these distinct physiological states. However, these datasets remain largely siloed by discipline. Synthesizing these data into a unified, predictive model of mesoscale emergence is hindered by two major bottlenecks. First, the computational demand of aligning and analyzing high-dimensional, multi-omic data across diverse cohorts exceeds the capabilities of standard bioinformatics pipelines, requiring novel GPU-accelerated architectures. Second, establishing a causal, predictive bridge from dynamic molecular interactions (mesoscale) to physical cellular expansion (macroscale) requires sophisticated mathematical frameworks capable of accommodating shifting physiological boundaries, a challenge rarely addressed in biological data science.

This proposal addresses these critical limitations through a highly collaborative, data-driven synthesis project. By leveraging high-performance computing, we will synthesize publicly available datasets representing healthy individuals undergoing mechanical overload alongside datasets from individuals experiencing systemic inflammatory stress. We introduce a novel synthesis approach that combines GPU-accelerated sequence alignment, advanced Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for structural pose-prediction, and complex mathematical modeling utilizing partial differential equations (PDEs) with free-boundary conditions. 

The significance of this project is threefold. Biologically, it resolves long-standing questions regarding how the translational machinery parses competing anabolic and catabolic signals to modulate muscle cross-sectional area. Computationally, it pioneers the application of advanced AI and GPU acceleration to significantly reduce the time required to reconstruct multi-omic biological networks. Mathematically, it introduces free-boundary PDE models to cellular biology, effectively treating the growing cell membrane as a mathematical boundary driven by mesoscale translational output. In strict alignment with the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission, this Working Group relies exclusively on the integration of existing public data, transcends the boundaries of any single discipline, and yields generalized AI and mathematical frameworks that will broadly benefit the molecular and cellular biosciences community.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our Working Group aims to decode the mesoscale control of cellular adaptation through three interrelated, interdisciplinary research questions, driven by the synthesis of multi-omic data.

Question 1: How do competing systemic signals (mechanical overload vs. inflammatory stress) spatiotemporally integrate at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive divergent cellular phenotypes? 
We hypothesize that inflammatory stress acts as a molecular roadblock at the mesoscale, physically disrupting the dynamic assembly of ribosomal subunits and dampening the enhanced translational capacity normally induced by mechanical overload. By synthesizing existing transcriptomic, Ribo-seq, and phosphoproteomic data, we predict that distinct 'stress-specific' ribosome interactomes emerge, fundamentally altering translation efficiency. Testing this hypothesis requires mapping these fragmented datasets onto unified biological networks to uncover the hidden regulatory logic governing ribosome biogenesis under conflicting physiological pressures.

Question 2: Can GPU-accelerated Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) accurately and rapidly reconstruct the dynamic structural conformations of the translational machinery from integrated multi-omic data? 
We hypothesize that by coupling ultra-fast diagonal partitioning parallelization strategies on multi-GPU architectures with GNNs, we can predict mesoscale ribosomal interactions and docking structures up to two orders of magnitude faster than conventional simulation approaches. Existing structural docking algorithms are computationally prohibitive for large-scale, multi-omic synthesis. By training GNNs on publicly available structural datasets (e.g., PDB) and contextualizing them with Ribo-seq data, we expect to successfully generate high-throughput, pose-prediction models that capture the transient protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions underlying translational control in both healthy and inflamed muscle states.

Question 3: How does the mathematical translation of mesoscale ribosomal output govern the macroscopic physical boundaries of the muscle cell during hypertrophy or atrophy? 
We hypothesize that a spatiotemporal system of partial differential equations (PDEs) utilizing free-boundary conditions can accurately predict emergent cellular structural changes (e.g., muscle fiber cross-sectional area) by mapping molecular translational rates directly to structural protein accumulation. While AI and GNNs map the molecular networks, they do not inherently capture physical cellular expansion. By utilizing the GNN-derived translational capacities as forcing functions within a PDE framework, we predict that the shifting sarcolemma boundary can be computationally modeled and validated against historically reported, publicly available histological measurements. 

These interconnected questions directly address the NCEMS objective of elucidating emergent properties at the mesoscale. They demand a synthesis strategy where computational predictions of mesoscale molecular structures directly feed into macroscopic mathematical equations, a synthesis impossible to achieve without the collaborative expertise of computer scientists, mathematicians, and molecular physiologists.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodology is strictly computational and synthetic, relying entirely on publicly available data. The workflow is designed as a collaborative pipeline across three distinct disciplines: molecular exercise physiology, high-performance computing, and continuous mathematical modeling.

Data Curation and Multi-Omic Harmonization: 
We will first comprehensively mine public repositories (e.g., GEO, SRA, PRIDE, PDB) for human and rodent transcriptomic, translatomic (Ribo-seq), phosphoproteomic, and structural datasets. The inclusion criteria will focus on skeletal muscle tissues subjected to mechanical overload (e.g., resistance exercise paradigms) and systemic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, myositis). Curated data will undergo rigorous quality control and normalization to create a unified, multi-omic metadata repository. 

GPU-Accelerated Sequence Alignment and AI-Driven Structural Prediction: 
To overcome the computational bottlenecks inherent in aligning divergent omic datasets, we will develop optimized parallel algorithms utilizing multi-GPU architectures. By employing diagonal partitioning strategies, we will dramatically reduce the computational overhead for pairwise and multiple sequence alignments, maintaining high sensitivity while accelerating throughput by orders of magnitude compared to traditional CPU-bound tools. 
Once harmonized, this data will feed into custom Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. The GNNs will be designed to predict mesoscale macromolecular interactions—specifically, the assembly of the ribosomal complex and its interaction with translational regulators under various stress conditions. By treating biomolecules as nodes and interactions as edges, the pose-prediction models within the GNN will generate dynamic, flexible molecular docking structures in real time, yielding a highly resolved picture of the translational machinery's functional state under mechanical versus inflammatory stress.

Mathematical Modeling of Emergent Phenotypes: 
To transition from mesoscale molecular interactomes to macroscopic cellular outcomes, we will construct a robust mathematical framework. We will design a system of partial differential equations (PDEs) to model the intracellular diffusion and reaction kinetics of newly synthesized structural proteins. Crucially, we will employ free-boundary problems to simulate the physical boundaries of the muscle cell (the sarcolemma). 
The output from the GNNs—representing the effective translational capacity of the ribosome under specific conditions—will serve as the primary forcing function in the PDEs. As structural protein concentrations increase or decrease within the model, the free-boundary condition will dynamically expand (hypertrophy) or contract (atrophy). 

Validation and Retrospective Synthesis: 
The AI-mathematical hybrid model's predictions will be rigorously validated against distinct, held-out historical datasets containing quantitative phenotypic measurements, such as muscle fiber cross-sectional area and type I/type II fiber ratios. This retrospective synthesis ensures that our predictive models are biologically accurate and generalize across multiple independent public cohorts. Through iterative collaboration, the physiologists will biologically contextualize the mathematical outputs, ensuring the synthesis generates novel insights into muscle adaptation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will deliver a comprehensive, multi-scale molecular map of skeletal muscle adaptation, explicitly defining how competing systemic stresses are resolved at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive macroscopic cellular emergence. By identifying the specific mechanisms by which inflammatory signaling dampens mechanical overload-induced ribosome biogenesis, this synthesis will solve a long-standing puzzle in muscle physiology and rheumatology.

Beyond biological discovery, the methodological impact of this Working Group will be transformative for the wider scientific community. We will produce and release novel, ultra-fast GPU-accelerated algorithms capable of processing complex multi-omic data at unprecedented speeds. Our Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks will establish a new benchmark for structural interaction prediction, allowing researchers to model dynamic biological assemblies without relying on computationally prohibitive molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, the development of our free-boundary PDE framework will provide the biomedical community with a scalable mathematical tool for modeling cellular size and structural adaptation across varying tissue types.

Crucially, this project will fulfill the NCEMS mandate to train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows embedded in this Working Group will receive transdisciplinary cross-training. Trainees with backgrounds in biology will learn high-performance GPU computing and AI utilization, while trainees from computational and mathematical backgrounds will gain deep expertise in molecular cell biology and physiological data interpretation. Ultimately, this transdisciplinary synthesis will lower the barrier to entry for community-scale data integration, driving innovative research strategies in molecular and cellular biosciences well beyond the lifespan of this specific funding mechanism.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of open, reproducible, and team science. All research outputs—data, AI models, mathematical frameworks, and analytical workflows—will be made publicly available in strict adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles.

The unified multi-omic dataset generated from public repositories will be thoroughly annotated with comprehensive metadata and hosted on open platforms such as Zenodo and specific NCEMS data portals. This will allow researchers globally to independently query our synthesized cohorts of healthy and inflamed tissues. 

All source code developed for GPU-accelerated alignments, Graph Neural Network training architectures, and PDE simulations will be maintained on public GitHub repositories under open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or GNU GPL). To ensure computational reproducibility regardless of local hardware configurations, we will deploy our full analytical pipeline as containerized environments using Docker and Singularity. Jupyter notebooks documenting the step-by-step synthesis—from raw public data ingestion to the final cellular phenotype prediction—will be included in the repositories to serve as educational and reproducible templates.

Furthermore, we commit to pre-registering our major analytical protocols, publishing all findings in open-access journals, and depositing preprints on servers such as bioRxiv prior to formal peer review. By operating with radical transparency and providing comprehensive documentation, our Working Group will ensure that the tools and insights generated can be seamlessly adopted, validated, and expanded upon by the broader molecular and cellular science community.
budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we request funding to support an integrated, transdisciplinary Working Group in alignment with NCEMS resource guidelines. The primary allocation of the budget will support human capital, specifically the funding of two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. These trainees will be intentionally recruited across disciplines to form the core data-science workforce of the project, receiving cross-training in molecular biology, GPU computing, and mathematical modeling.

A critical portion of the budget will be allocated for high-performance computing resources necessary for the project's success. While we will leverage existing institutional infrastructure where possible, we request funds for dedicated cloud computing instances and multi-GPU node access (e.g., NVIDIA A100 architectures) to facilitate the rapid training of the Graph Neural Networks and the high-throughput, GPU-accelerated sequence alignments required by our synthesis pipeline. This computational support goes far beyond the standard capabilities of a single biology laboratory and is essential for realizing our AI-driven objectives.

Finally, we request travel and administrative support to facilitate robust collaborative partnerships. Funds will cover bi-annual in-person meetings at the NCEMS hub, bringing together the diverse expertise of our Working Group spanning physiology, computer science, and mathematics. These intensive synthesis meetings will be supplemented by regular virtual workshops. The budget will also cover open-access publication fees and the costs associated with long-term public data hosting, ensuring full compliance with our open science and reproducible research commitments.
