title: Mapping the Emergent Collapse of Mesoscale Proteostasis Networks in Aging and Stress
abstract:
Cellular survival during physiological stress and aging depends on the delicate balance of protein synthesis, folding, and degradation. While the kinetic rates of individual biomolecules are increasingly characterized, a critical long-standing puzzle remains: how do these microscale dynamics integrate to determine the emergent stability and function of mesoscale macromolecular assemblies, such as the nuclear lamina, sarcomeres, and stress granules? Traditional single-lab approaches often treat transcriptomics and proteomics in isolation, failing to capture the discordant, dynamic buffering—governed by translation rates and protein turnover—that sustains these mesoscale structures under duress. 

To address this gap, we propose a community-scale data synthesis Working Group to map the emergent properties of mesoscale proteostasis networks under environmental stress (e.g., hypoxia, metabolic perturbation) and biological aging. This project will strictly utilize the vast repository of publicly available multi-omics datasets, generating no new experimental data. We will integrate transcriptomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq), translatomics (ribosome profiling), global proteomics, in vivo protein turnover rates (pulsed SILAC and dynamic SILAM), and structural databases quantifying protein disorder. By harmonizing disparate datasets across mammalian tissues, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, and large-scale biobanks, we will build a unified computational framework to decode how multi-level regulation dictates mesoscale structural integrity.

Our collaborative synthesis will employ machine learning and dynamic systems modeling to answer fundamental questions about molecular emergence. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that the intrinsic structural disorder of component proteins and their highly regulated turnover rates act as a buffer during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR). We will mathematically model how the uncoupling of mRNA and protein abundances reaches a “tipping point” where this buffering capacity fails, leading to the abrupt pathological disassembly or aggregation of mesoscale complexes. We will focus our analytical pipelines on cardiovascular and vascular aging models, using LMNA-linked cardiomyopathies and stress-induced endothelial dysfunction as prototypical examples of mesoscale failure translating to cellular collapse.

This project requires the unique transdisciplinary environment provided by NCEMS. The synthesis demands a fusion of expertise spanning translation dynamics, protein misfolding, cardiovascular disease modeling, systems biology, and big data precision medicine—perspectives perfectly aligned with our team’s background. By moving beyond isolated analyses of transcript-protein correlations, our Working Group will uncover the universal network principles governing protein turnover dynamics and mesoscale complex stability.

In strict adherence to NCEMS open science principles, all unified databases, AI-driven predictive models, and analytical workflows will be open-source and freely disseminated to the community. Furthermore, this initiative will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral and graduate trainees integrated into the Working Group will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship in multi-omics integration, computational biophysics, and reproducible team science, equipping them to lead the future of synthetic biology and molecular data science.
background_and_significance:
The fundamental processes of cellular life depend on the emergent properties of mesoscale structures—supramolecular assemblies such as the nuclear lamina, sarcomeres, and stress granules that exist temporally and spatially between individual biomolecules and whole organelles. While recent decades have seen an explosion in omics data characterizing microscale molecular events, the mechanisms governing how these individual kinetic rates (transcription, translation, folding, degradation) coalesce to maintain or destabilize mesoscale assemblies remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap is particularly acute in the context of physiological stress and biological aging, where cellular environments undergo drastic, system-wide perturbations. Under these conditions, the classic assumption of tight correlation between mRNA abundance and steady-state protein levels frequently fails. Instead, cellular survival hinges on complex, multi-layered regulatory networks that buffer mesoscale structures against proteotoxic insults. Understanding this buffering capacity is a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

Traditionally, single-investigator laboratories have generated critical but siloed datasets. Transcriptomic studies reveal stress-induced gene expression programs, while translatomic (ribosome profiling) and proteomic studies document variations in synthesis and steady-state abundances. Furthermore, specialized approaches utilizing in vivo isotopic labeling (e.g., SILAC, SILAM) have charted the diverse turnover rates of individual proteins. Despite this wealth of publicly available data, there has been no comprehensive, community-scale effort to synthesize these disparate modalities into a unified dynamic model of mesoscale structural integrity. The absence of such synthesis prevents us from recognizing the emergent thresholds—the exact kinetic 'tipping points'—where the uncoupling of protein synthesis and degradation precipitates the abrupt collapse or pathological aggregation of mesoscale complexes.

This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by catalyzing a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize vast amounts of existing, publicly available data. We focus on the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) and aging-related cardiovascular degeneration as quintessential models of mesoscale failure. For example, in cardiomyopathies linked to LMNA mutations or in stress-induced endothelial dysfunction, the architectural integrity of the nuclear lamina and cytoskeletal network degrades over time. By integrating single-cell transcriptomics, translation dynamics, turnover rates, and biophysical metrics of protein disorder, we aim to uncover how intrinsic molecular plasticity and regulated turnover collectively act as a shock absorber for the cell. 

Our synthesis approach will shift the scientific paradigm from static correlative analyses to a dynamic systems perspective of molecular emergence. By rigorously applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, and dynamic modeling to integrated data sourced from public repositories such as GEO, PRIDE, and the UK Biobank, this project promises to reveal universal network principles governing mesoscale proteostasis. Crucially, this initiative strictly adheres to the mandate of utilizing only existing data to answer novel biological questions, leveraging transdisciplinary expertise to yield deeper, broader insights into cellular vulnerability and resilience without the generation of new experimental data. The significance lies in creating a universally applicable predictive framework for mesoscale biological emergence.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our Working Group will leverage community-scale data synthesis to address three compelling scientific questions regarding the emergent dynamics of mesoscale proteostasis networks. By integrating vast publicly available datasets, we aim to uncover how microscale kinetics dictate the stability of supramolecular assemblies during stress and aging.

Question 1: How do translation dynamics and intrinsic protein turnover rates interact to buffer the structural integrity of mesoscale complexes during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR)?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the structural stability of mesoscale assemblies, such as stress granules and the nuclear lamina, is not maintained by steady-state transcript abundance, but by a precise, emergent equilibrium between dynamic translation rates and post-translational degradation. Specifically, we posit that subunits of these complexes characterized by high intrinsic structural disorder possess highly tuned, rapid turnover rates that allow for immediate, adaptive stoichiometric remodeling upon ISR activation. This discordance between mRNA and protein half-lives provides a quantifiable buffering capacity that sustains mesoscale functionality when transcriptional pathways are transiently disrupted by hypoxia or metabolic stress.

Question 2: What are the mathematical and kinetic determinants that define the “tipping point” of mesoscale complex collapse during chronological aging and prolonged physiological duress?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that biological aging progressively erodes the translational and degradative buffering capacity of the cell, leading to a mathematically definable phase transition—or tipping point—where mesoscale proteostasis fails. Through dynamic systems modeling of synthesized multi-omics data, we anticipate identifying specific kinetic thresholds where the uncoupling of mRNA abundance, ribosome occupancy, and protein degradation inevitably precipitates pathological disassembly or toxic aggregation. We expect to demonstrate that this kinetic divergence is the primary driver of emergent mesoscale failure rather than a single deterministic genetic mutation or linear pathway alteration.

Question 3: Are the principles of mesoscale network failure conserved across diverse models of aging-related cardiovascular and vascular disease?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that despite differing etiologies, diverse cardiovascular pathologies—such as LMNA-related dilated cardiomyopathy and stress-induced endothelial dysfunction—share a universal kinetic signature of mesoscale collapse. By integrating in vitro iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte models with large-scale human proteomic biobanks (e.g., UK Biobank), we will test the hypothesis that the systemic uncoupling of the proteostasis network converges on a highly conserved set of molecular vulnerabilities within the sarcomere and nuclear envelope. We anticipate that machine learning models trained on integrated omics data will reveal these shared network nodes, linking microscale kinetic instability to emergent phenotypic failure.

These research questions cannot be addressed through localized, isolated experiments. They require the transdisciplinary integration of proteomics, translational dynamics, computational biophysics, and large-scale precision medicine datasets. By exclusively employing data synthesis and advanced computational modeling, our collaborative effort will decode the long-standing mysteries of emergent mesoscale stability, fundamentally advancing our understanding of cellular survival under stress and providing a robust conceptual foundation for future therapeutic interventions.
methods_and_approach:
Our analytical framework relies entirely on the synthesis of publicly available datasets, integrating multi-omic information to map mesoscale emergence. The approach is structured into three integrated phases: Data Acquisition and Harmonization, Computational Systems Modeling, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Driven Pattern Recognition.

Phase 1: Multi-Omic Data Acquisition and Harmonization
We will systematically harvest matching and highly comparable datasets from public repositories including the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE), and large-scale population resources like the UK Biobank. The synthesis will specifically target: 1) Transcriptomics (bulk and scRNA-seq) to capture baseline and stress-induced mRNA abundance; 2) Translatomics (Ribosome profiling/Ribo-seq) to quantify subcodon translation efficiencies and active translons; 3) Global Proteomics for steady-state protein abundances; 4) In vivo/in vitro protein turnover datasets (pulsed SILAC, dynamic SILAM) to define precise synthesis and degradation kinetics; and 5) Structural databases (e.g., MobiDB, AlphaFold) to quantify intrinsic protein disorder. To enable cross-study integration, we will develop an automated harmonization pipeline using standard identifiers and applying robust batch-correction algorithms (e.g., ComBat, Harmony) to mitigate technical variations across disparate studies. This pipeline will map all kinetic data onto predefined mesoscale assemblies (e.g., nuclear lamina, sarcomeres) using established ontology networks (Gene Ontology, Reactome).

Phase 2: Dynamic Systems Modeling of Mesoscale Buffering
To test our hypotheses regarding the buffering capacity of proteostasis networks, we will transition from static correlative analyses to dynamic kinetic modeling. We will construct Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) models that represent the flux of synthesis, folding, and degradation for individual subunits of mesoscale complexes. By populating these models with our synthesized kinetic parameters (translation efficiency, protein half-lives), we will simulate the dynamic response of these complexes to simulated ISR perturbations (e.g., simulated hypoxic or metabolic stress). We will perform bifurcation analysis to mathematically identify the “tipping points”—the critical thresholds of kinetic uncoupling where buffering capacity is overwhelmed, leading to simulated complex disassembly or aggregation.

Phase 3: AI-Driven Pattern Recognition in Cardiovascular Models
To apply our framework to physiological aging and disease, we will utilize machine learning algorithms to uncover conserved signatures of mesoscale collapse. Using Random Forest and Gradient Boosting architectures, we will train predictive models on our integrated multi-omics matrices derived from iPSC-cardiomyocyte stress models and endothelial cell arrays. The objective is to predict the emergent stability of the LMNA and sarcomeric complexes based purely on upstream microscale kinetic features. These models will subsequently be validated against population-scale plasma proteomic data (e.g., UK Biobank) to confirm whether the kinetic vulnerabilities identified in vitro manifest as systemic proteomic signatures in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and vascular dysfunction. 

By leveraging the diverse scientific perspectives of our Working Group—spanning translation dynamics, cardiovascular precision medicine, and computational systems biology—this approach moves far beyond the capabilities of a single lab. It provides a robust, transdisciplinary method for decoding mesoscale emergence using purely synthetic, community-scale data.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group project will deliver transformative insights into the emergent properties of molecular and cellular biology, producing outcomes with broad utility across multiple disciplines. 

First, we will produce the first comprehensive, multi-omic kinetic atlas of mesoscale proteostasis networks, documenting the interconnected rates of translation, turnover, and degradation for structural complexes across healthy, stressed, and aging states. By shifting the paradigm away from static snapshots of mRNA-protein correlations toward dynamic kinetic modeling, we will provide the scientific community with a fundamentally new understanding of how molecular buffering systems function during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR).

Second, our dynamic systems models will deliver mathematically defined “tipping points” that predict when mesoscale complexes—such as the nuclear lamina and sarcomeres—will undergo pathological collapse or aggregation. This addresses a major long-standing puzzle in cellular biology: why certain molecular assemblies fail catastrophically under chronic stress while others adapt. These predictive models will establish a robust foundation for identifying novel, emergent vulnerabilities in cardiovascular diseases, including LMNA-linked cardiomyopathies and age-related vascular dysfunction.

Finally, the impact of this synthesis will extend far beyond the immediate findings. By creating an open-source, standardized computational pipeline for integrating disparate transcriptomic, translatomic, proteomic, and structural datasets, we will provide an invaluable analytical strategy for the broader biosciences community. This methodological innovation directly supports the NCEMS mission to develop innovative analytical strategies. Furthermore, the cross-disciplinary collaborative nature of this project will forge new conceptual bridges between systems biology, cardiovascular precision medicine, and structural proteomics, ensuring that our insights catalyze a new wave of transdisciplinary research into emergent mesoscale phenomena.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the gold standard principles of open, reproducible, and team-based science, strictly aligning with NCEMS community policies. To ensure maximum transparency, we will pre-register all analytical protocols, data inclusion criteria, and hypotheses on the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to the execution of computational analyses.

All harmonized, multi-omic datasets generated through our data synthesis efforts will be fully annotated utilizing FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. These curated datasets will be deposited in public repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad upon manuscript submission. To ensure computational reproducibility, all code, machine learning architectures, and ODE models will be version-controlled and hosted in public GitHub repositories under an MIT open-source license. We will utilize containerization technologies (e.g., Docker, Singularity) to package our analytical pipelines, ensuring that external researchers can identically reproduce our computational environments and results regardless of their local computing infrastructure.

To facilitate broad accessibility, we will develop an interactive, web-based R-Shiny application. This portal will allow researchers without extensive computational expertise to query the synthesized kinetic atlas, visualize translation and turnover dynamics, and simulate stress-induced network tipping points for their mesoscale complexes of interest.

Furthermore, all research outcomes will be disseminated as preprints on bioRxiv concurrently with submission to open-access, peer-reviewed journals. By embedding these rigorous open science practices into the core of our operations, we ensure that our synthetic methodologies, codebases, and data products serve as enduring, accessible resources that empower the global scientific community.

title: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework for Predicting the Emergence of Mesoscale Ribonucleoprotein Compartmentalization from Public Spatial Transcriptomic and Single-Molecule Datasets
abstract:
The unexpected appearance of mesoscale biological properties—such as the formation of localized subcellular translational hubs and membrane-less ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates—bridges the critical gap between stochastic single-molecule interactions and deterministic cellular phenotypes. Despite vast amounts of publicly available data at both ends of this spatial spectrum, our understanding of mesoscale emergence remains deeply fragmented. Single-molecule biophysical studies capture the high-resolution kinetic, stoichiometric, and reaction-diffusion properties of multivalent protein-RNA and protein-DNA interactions. Conversely, highly multiplexed spatial transcriptomics maps the subcellular compartmentalization of thousands of RNA species across whole cells and tissues. Currently, these two disjoint data modalities are rarely synthesized, leaving a crucial analytical blind spot in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize publicly available single-molecule tracking (SMT), single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), and multiplexed spatial transcriptomics (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH) datasets to elucidate the biophysical rules governing the emergence of mesoscale RNP compartmentalization. We propose to develop a transdisciplinary predictive framework that merges rigorous Bayesian single-molecule inference with large-scale spatial multi-omics integration algorithms. Our collaborative approach strictly leverages existing public data to solve the long-standing puzzle of how transient, multivalent microscale interactions scale up to form stable mesoscale structures across diverse physiological and disease states, such as neurodevelopment and cancer microenvironments.

Our methodology proceeds in three integrative phases. First, utilizing advanced probabilistic modeling and Bayesian inference tools originally designed for single-photon and single-particle tracking, we will extract fundamental kinetic parameters, dissociation constants, and multivalent stoichiometric profiles of key RNA-binding proteins from public biophysical data repositories. Second, we will embed these microscale biophysical priors into a unified, scalable predictive algorithm—extending existing embedding and integration frameworks like Harmony—to analyze broad public spatial transcriptomic datasets. Third, we will calculate in situ thermodynamic probability landscapes to model how dynamically forming multivalent complexes drive specific RNAs into mesoscale compartments, effectively mapping single-molecule reaction-diffusion kinetics onto whole-cell spatial transcriptomic coordinates.

This community-scale synthesis relies fundamentally on NCEMS support, as it goes far beyond the scope of a single laboratory. It demands the deep integration of diverse scientific domains: computational multi-omics, single-molecule tracking, statistical optics, and biophysical chemistry. By bringing together researchers across these fields, we will deliver an open-source computational platform that uncovers how localized molecular biophysics dictates higher-order cellular architecture.

In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized multi-scale datasets, Bayesian models, and deep integration pipelines will be made freely available. Furthermore, the Working Group is deeply committed to training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, learning to bridge the analytical divide between the physics of photon-arrival statistics and the computational scale of genome-wide spatial omics. Ultimately, this project will pioneer innovative analytical strategies to decode the physical emergence of mesoscale biological organization from publicly available data.
background_and_significance:
The fundamental challenge in molecular and cellular biology today is understanding how molecular parts list spontaneously organize into functionally complex, emergent architectures. At the heart of this challenge lies the mesoscale: the structural tier existing between individual biomolecules (nanometers) and whole organelles (micrometers). Among the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence is the compartmentalization of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes into specialized membrane-less organelles, such as stress granules, processing bodies, and localized translational hubs. These mesoscale domains are critical for regulating gene expression, cellular stress responses, and developmental trajectories. Aberrations in these structures are frequently implicated in severe pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases and malignant tumor microenvironments. 

Despite their biological importance, our predictive understanding of RNP condensation remains severely limited by a profound analytical divide. On one hand, single-molecule biophysics offers remarkable insights into the fundamental interactions driving RNP formation. Public repositories of single-molecule tracking (SMT) and single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) data harbor vast amounts of underutilized information regarding the fast, stochastic reaction-diffusion dynamics, valency, and concentration-facilitated unbinding events of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). On the other hand, the genomics community has produced massive, high-dimensional spatial transcriptomics datasets using highly multiplexed in situ hybridization techniques (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH). These datasets map the static, steady-state subcellular localization of thousands of RNA species but lack biophysical depth. 

Currently, these two powerful fields—statistical optics-based biophysics and computationally driven spatial genomics—operate in silos. There is no existing mathematical or computational framework that synthesizes stochastic single-molecule kinetics with whole-cell spatial RNA coordinate mapping. As a result, a critical analytical blind spot persists: we cannot yet predict how specific biophysical microscale rules scale up to generate the mesoscale RNA compartmentalization observed in spatial transcriptomic atlases. 

This proposal addresses this gap by directly aligning with the NCEMS mission to leverage artificial intelligence and data science for community-scale data synthesis. We propose the first comprehensive, multi-scale synthesis framework that utilizes only existing, publicly available data to unify single-molecule probabilistic inference with high-dimensional spatial omics embedding. By systematically integrating these disjoint datatypes, we will uncover the biophysical principles driving the emergence of mesoscale properties. 

The significance of this work is twofold. First, it solves a long-standing puzzle regarding how multivalent protein-RNA interactions manifest as stable, compartmentalized cellular phenotypes. Second, it develops an entirely novel, cross-disciplinary analytical strategy that projects fundamental thermodynamic and kinetic constants onto genomic-scale structural maps. This transdisciplinary synthesis is beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. It necessitates a Working Group that seamlessly integrates expertise in single-cell and spatial computational biology, single-molecule biophysical chemistry, and rigorous statistical optics. Ultimately, this predictive framework will allow researchers to mathematically link nanometer-scale single-photon arrival statistics to the micrometer-scale subcellular geography of the transcriptome, redefining our understanding of cellular organization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our Working Group will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available data to address three critical research questions regarding the physical emergence of mesoscale RNP compartmentalization. These questions are designed to bridge the analytical gap between molecular biophysics and spatial omics, testing explicit hypotheses derived from statistical mechanics and systems biology.

Research Question 1: How do the microscale kinetic parameters of RNA-binding proteins predict the steady-state mesoscale spatial distribution of the transcriptome?
Hypothesis 1: The subcellular compartmentalization of RNA species observed in multiplexed spatial transcriptomics is not random but governed by the reaction-diffusion kinetics of multivalent regulatory proteins. We hypothesize that by employing Bayesian inference models on public single-molecule reaction-diffusion (smRD) data, we can extract biophysical priors (e.g., binding affinities, off-rates, diffusion coefficients) that accurately predict the clustering and compartmentalization of target RNAs in corresponding public MERFISH and seqFISH datasets. We posit that high-affinity, slow-diffusing RBP states correlate directly with dense mesoscale transcriptomic hubs.

Research Question 2: What is the role of multivalent stoichiometry and concentration-facilitated unbinding in driving cell-state-specific RNA compartmentalization?
Hypothesis 2: Multivalency-enabled ternary complexes act as thermodynamic sinks that drive the phase separation and mesoscale organization of RNPs. Drawing on public single-molecule tracking and localization data, we hypothesize that changes in the stoichiometric ratio and multivalent interactions of RBPs across different physiological states (e.g., neurodevelopmental stages or cancer microenvironments) shift the thermodynamic probability landscape. By computationally integrating this biophysical data with state-specific spatial transcriptomics, we predict we can model concentration-facilitated unbinding events that explain how specific transcripts are dynamically recruited to or released from mesoscale compartments during cellular state transitions.

Research Question 3: Can we map continuous single-molecule reaction-diffusion dynamics onto discrete, high-dimensional spatial transcriptomic coordinates to create a unified 'in situ thermodynamic landscape'?
Hypothesis 3: High-dimensional multi-omics integration algorithms can be adapted to co-embed biophysical kinetic profiles with spatial transcriptomic mapping. We hypothesize that extending dimensionality reduction and data integration frameworks (such as the Harmony algorithm) to incorporate probabilistic biophysical parameters will enable the construction of an 'in situ thermodynamic landscape.' In this landscape, local transcript density acts as the boundary condition for the Bayesian reaction-diffusion model. This will allow us to calculate the probability of RNP compartment emergence at any given sub-cellular coordinate, effectively linking the stochastic nature of photon-arrival biophysical measurements to the spatial certainty of transcriptomic maps.

By addressing these questions solely through the synthesis of existing data, we aim to validate a predictive model of mesoscale emergence. The successful proof of these hypotheses will demonstrate that complex, higher-order cellular structures are mathematically predictable emergent properties arising from localized single-molecule thermodynamic and kinetic rules. This framework will provide the molecular and cellular biology communities with a transformative theoretical tool capable of inferring dynamic biophysical states from static transcriptomic snapshots.
methods_and_approach:
Our community-scale synthesis project strictly utilizes publicly available datasets, involving no new experimental generation. The methodology is organized into three integrative phases requiring deep transdisciplinary collaboration across computational genomics, single-molecule biophysics, and probabilistic modeling.

Phase 1: Bayesian Inference of Microscale Kinetics from Public SMT/SMLM Data
We will curate a comprehensive repository of publicly available single-molecule tracking (SMT) and single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) datasets from databases such as SMTracker, Zenodo, and the NIH 4D Nucleome Data Portal. Focusing on key multivalent RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) implicated in phase separation (e.g., FUS, TDP-43, G3BP1), we will apply advanced probabilistic modeling to extract kinetic parameters. Leveraging tools related to Bayesian single-molecule reaction-diffusion (Bayes-smRD) and single-photon single-particle tracking (SP2T), we will analyze raw photon arrival data and discrete coordinate trajectories to infer robust biophysical priors. This computational step will quantify diffusion coefficients, kinetic on/off rates, and the stoichiometric distributions of RBP complexes without the artifactual bulk averaging present in standard biochemical assays. These parameters will serve as the microscale foundation for our synthesis.

Phase 2: Spatial Integration and High-Dimensional Embedding
Simultaneously, we will harmonize publicly available subcellular spatial transcriptomics data (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH+) sourced from the SpaceTx consortium and the Brain Initiative Cell Census Network (BICCN). Because these datasets exist across highly varied formats and biological states (e.g., murine neurodevelopment, human glioblastoma), we require robust algorithmic integration. We will extend computationally efficient integration architectures, conceptually similar to the Harmony algorithm, to project these diverse spatial transcriptomic coordinates into a shared embedding space. However, instead of integrating solely across technological modalities, we will implement a novel co-embedding strategy that registers local spatial RNA density with the stoichiometric and multivalent binding probability distributions extracted in Phase 1. 

Phase 3: Thermodynamic Mapping and Predictive Modeling
In the final synthesis phase, we will map the microscale biophysics onto the mesoscale transcriptomic geography. We will treat the spatially resolved RNA counts from Phase 2 as steady-state endpoints driven by the reaction-diffusion processes quantified in Phase 1. By developing an 'in situ thermodynamic landscape' model, we will calculate the localized probability of multivalent ternary complex formation across the cellular volume. This involves constructing a non-equilibrium statistical mechanics framework where local transcript density dictates the concentration-facilitated unbinding and recruitment rates of regulatory proteins. We will validate our predictive framework by computationally predicting the location and density of specific RNP compartments (e.g., stress granules or nucleoli) based solely on transcript coordinates and biophysical priors, comparing our predictions against independent publicly available multiplexed immunofluorescence and transcriptomic co-staining datasets.

Feasibility and Rigor: Our approach is entirely computational and data-driven, leveraging the distinct but complementary expertise of our Working Group. Rigor will be ensured through cross-validation against withheld public datasets and the application of strict, standardized quality control metrics for both the biophysical inference and spatial integration pipelines. NCEMS support is vital to provide the computational infrastructure and collaborative environment necessary to execute this transdisciplinary synthesis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver a suite of transformative outcomes that address the fundamental biological puzzle of mesoscale emergence while fundamentally advancing computational methodology in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

First, we will produce a unified computational synthesis framework that successfully bridges the gap between single-molecule biophysics and spatial genomics. This framework will be the first of its kind to mathematically link the stochastic, microsecond-scale dynamics of protein-RNA interactions with the static, whole-cell subcellular spatial mapping of the transcriptome. 

Second, we will generate a massive, synthesized multi-scale dataset. By annotating existing public spatial transcriptomic atlases with high-resolution thermodynamic and kinetic biophysical parameters, we will provide the scientific community with a novel 'in situ thermodynamic map' of the cell. This resource will allow researchers to predict dynamic molecular behavior directly from static, highly multiplexed genomic imaging data. 

The broader impacts of this project are substantial. By elucidating the biophysical rules governing RNP compartmentalization, our findings will offer critical insights into cell-state transitions underlying both normal physiology (e.g., neural differentiation) and pathology (e.g., cancer cell states, neurodegenerative proteinopathies). 

Furthermore, this project will significantly impact the scientific workforce. By executing this project through a collaborative NCEMS Working Group, we will cross-train a cohort of postdoctoral and graduate trainees. These early-career researchers will develop a highly unique, dual-fluency in statistical optics/biophysics and high-dimensional computational genomics. This training will address a critical shortage in the data-savvy scientific workforce, equipping the next generation to pioneer holistic, multi-scale approaches to biological complexity.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is resolutely committed to gold-standard Open Science principles, ensuring that all synthesized data, code, and analytical pipelines generated during this project are completely transparent, accessible, and reproducible.

Code and Software Availability: The entirety of our novel Bayesian inference frameworks, integration algorithms, and thermodynamic predictive models will be written in open-source languages (Python, R, and C++ for GPU-accelerated steps). All code will be actively maintained on a public GitHub repository under an MIT open-source license. To guarantee computational reproducibility, we will package our multi-scale integration pipelines into Docker and Singularity containers, allowing any researcher to deploy our environment with identical dependencies.

Data Accessibility: Following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles, all harmonized intermediate datasets and the final multi-scale synthesized atlases will be deposited into public repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF). These deposits will be accompanied by exhaustive metadata detailing the provenance of the original public datasets (SMT/SMLM and Spatial Transcriptomics), the specific preprocessing steps applied, and the versioning of the analytical tools utilized.

Documentation and Protocols: We will provide rigorous documentation, including extensive Jupyter Notebook and RMarkdown tutorials that step users through the analytical workflow—from raw photon-arrival statistics and transcript spatial coordinates to the final localized probability landscapes. 

Team Science: We will adopt an open, collaborative team science approach. Working Group meeting notes, decision logs regarding data inclusion criteria, and preliminary synthesis models will be made publicly available on our OSF project page, fostering real-time community engagement and external peer review throughout the project lifecycle.
budget_and_resources:
This community-scale synthesis fundamentally requires NCEMS support, as the computational demands and transdisciplinary integration vastly exceed the resources of any single investigator or existing bilateral collaboration.

Personnel and Training Support: A significant portion of the budget will support two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate trainees. These trainees will be co-mentored by Working Group members, facilitating deep cross-pollination between the computational genomics, Bayesian biophysics, and single-molecule microscopy domains. NCEMS funding ensures dedicated time for these early-career scientists to focus entirely on dataset synthesis and multi-scale algorithmic development, serving as the core drivers of our workforce training mandate.

Computational Resources: Synthesizing millions of single-photon biophysical traces with billions of spatial transcriptomic coordinates requires substantial computational power. Funds are requested for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud) equipped with high-performance GPU clusters. This infrastructure is essential for running the computationally intensive Bayesian reaction-diffusion inferences and the high-dimensional spatial embedding algorithms at scale.

Working Group Convenings: To effectively integrate these disparate scientific disciplines, we request support for bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS hub. These multi-day intensive collaborative sessions are critical for bridging field-specific vocabularies, troubleshooting analytical bottlenecks in the synthesis pipeline, and ensuring cohesive team science practices. 

Dissemination and Open Science Costs: Modest funds are allocated to support open-access publication fees, the hosting of large synthesized datasets on robust repositories, and the organization of a virtual community workshop in Year 2 to train external researchers on how to utilize our newly developed multi-scale integration software. 

By centralizing these resources through NCEMS, we will efficiently catalyze a transdisciplinary synergy that maximizes the value of existing public data to solve fundamental mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence.

title: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Structural Data to Decode the Emergent Mesoscale Organization of Epigenetic and Epitranscriptomic Networks
abstract:
Mesoscale biological phenomena—such as the higher-order organization of chromatin clutches and the coordinated assembly of translational ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes—emerge from dynamic networks of molecular-level modifications. While specific epigenetic and epitranscriptomic marks (e.g., histone acetylation, lysine lactylation, and tRNA modifications) are known to respond to metabolic and environmental cues, the rules governing how these multi-layered modifications collectively interact to remodel mesoscale architectures and drive cellular-level phenotypic heterogeneity remain a critical unknown. This NCEMS Working Group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to answer a fundamental question: How do coordinated epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications cooperatively drive the emergent mesoscale organization of chromatin and translational machineries to control cellular state transitions?

To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team will synthesize massive amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic atlases (e.g., Human Cell Atlas, GEO), multi-omic disease and aging cohorts (e.g., TCGA), epitranscriptomic maps, and structural databases (PDB, EMDB). Because interpreting this multi-layered data transcends the capabilities of a single discipline, we will integrate diverse expertise in structural biophysics, single-cell AI algorithms, multi-omic proteomics, and RNA bioinformatics.

Our methodological strategy comprises three integrated phases. First, we will employ advanced AI and graph-based analytical strategies—specifically bi-level feature propagation and similarity network fusion clustering—to harmonize, impute, and integrate highly sparse single-cell epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data. This will allow us to define distinct, multi-omic cellular states and map concurrent alterations in chromatin marks and RNA modifications across diverse biological conditions, such as aging and metabolic stress. Second, the extracted modification profiles will serve as boundary conditions to parameterize residue-resolution, coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By bridging atomistic details to the mesoscale, these simulations will model how specific combinations of modifications alter electrostatic and thermodynamic landscapes, thereby dictating chromatin fiber destacking, nucleosome interactomes, and the structural coupling of RNP networks. Third, using extensive bioinformatic data mining and interactome mapping, we will link these emergent mesoscale structural states to downstream cellular functional outputs. Specifically, we will decode how modified chromatin architectures and RNP assemblies influence translation dynamics—such as global ribosome pausing—and ultimately rewire intercellular ligand-receptor communication networks.

Aligned with the core mission of NCEMS, this project relies exclusively on the integration and synthesis of existing public datasets without generating new experimental data. The transdisciplinary nature of coupling single-cell multi-omic AI imputation with coarse-grained structural modeling necessitates a highly collaborative Working Group approach. We are committed to open science principles; all generated multi-omic interactome maps, AI frameworks, and MD simulation pipelines will be deposited in public repositories with reproducible workflows. Furthermore, this initiative will prioritize the training of a diverse, next-generation workforce of data-savvy scientists, equipping postdocs and graduate students with highly interdisciplinary skills at the intersection of AI, computational biophysics, and systems biology. By revealing how molecular modifications percolate upward to dictate mesoscale structure and cellular fate, this synthesis will yield novel, transformative insights into the fundamental principles of biological emergence.
background_and_significance:
The fundamental principles governing how atomic-level biological modifications translate into complex, cellular-scale behaviors remain one of the most compelling mysteries in the molecular and cellular biosciences. At the center of this mystery is the concept of emergence at the mesoscale—the critical spatial domain bridging individual biomolecules and functional organelles. While modern molecular biology has exhaustively cataloged distinct chemical modifications, such as histone acetylation, lysine lactylation, and tRNA modifications, these marks do not operate in isolation. Instead, they form a vast, interconnected network that collectively orchestrates mesoscale phenomena. Examples include the formation of higher-order chromatin structures (e.g., chromatin clutches) and the dynamic assembly of translational ribonucleoprotein (RNP) machineries. 

Despite an explosion of publicly available high-throughput sequencing and structural data, we currently lack a synthesized understanding of how coordinated multi-omic modifications cooperatively remodel these mesoscale architectures. Current research typically isolates either epigenetic or epitranscriptomic mechanisms, investigating single datasets in highly specialized silos. Consequently, the field struggles to answer how global networks of molecular modifications act synergistically to define robust cellular states, such as those observed in aging, tissue regeneration, or metabolic stress. Understanding this interplay is essential to deciphering how cells translate environmental or metabolic cues into lasting phenotypic changes through structural reorganization at the mesoscale.

This gap represents an unparalleled opportunity for data synthesis. Over the past decade, the global scientific community has generated a staggering volume of publicly available data. We now possess massive single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic atlases via the Human Cell Atlas and GEO, deep multi-omic cohorts spanning the proteome and transcriptome through resources like TCGA, precise epitranscriptomic maps, and high-resolution structural repositories including the PDB and EMDB. However, this wealth of data remains fragmented. Transforming these disparate datasets into a cohesive understanding of biological emergence requires computational synthesis on a scale that transcends the capabilities of any individual laboratory.

Addressing this synthesis challenge aligns seamlessly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). This Working Group proposes to synthesize these isolated datasets using a fundamentally novel, transdisciplinary approach. We will merge advanced artificial intelligence (AI) methodologies tailored for highly sparse single-cell data with sophisticated, residue-resolution coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. By doing so, we can bridge the scale gap—using statistical genomics to define the molecular boundary conditions and biophysics to model the emergent mesoscale outcomes.

The significance of this proposal lies in its capacity to generate a unified, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. By synthesizing existing data to map how modifications like H4K16 acetylation or tRNA dihydrouridylation interact, we will uncover hidden structural dynamics, such as chromatin fiber destacking and ribosome pausing. Ultimately, this community-scale synthesis will resolve long-standing puzzles regarding molecular synergy, offering transformative insights into cellular biology without the need to generate a single new experimental dataset.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The central objective of this NCEMS Working Group is to synthesize vast, disconnected multi-omic and structural datasets to decode how molecular-level modifications drive the emergent mesoscale organization of biological systems. To structure this extensive data synthesis, our research is guided by three interconnected research questions (RQs) and hypotheses that span from statistical genomics to structural biophysics and cellular phenotyping.

RQ1: How do concurrent epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications co-vary to define distinct, multi-omic cellular states across diverse physiological conditions?
Existing single-cell datasets are notoriously sparse and noisy, making it difficult to observe simultaneous epigenetic and transcriptomic states in single cells. We hypothesize that by applying bi-level feature propagation and similarity network fusion clustering to massive, publicly available multi-omic datasets, we can successfully impute missing data and identify robust, co-varying patterns of histone modifications (e.g., acetylation, lactylation) and RNA modifications. We predict that specific environmental and metabolic perturbations consistently induce distinct 'molecular boundary conditions'—stereotyped profiles of multi-omic modifications that represent highly coordinated functional states rather than stochastic noise.

RQ2: What are the biophysical rules by which these synthesized multi-omic modification profiles govern the emergent mesoscale architecture of chromatin and ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes?
While statistical correlations can link modifications to cell states, the physical mechanism of emergence resides at the mesoscale. We hypothesize that specific combinations of epigenetic and epitranscriptomic marks, extracted from our AI-driven synthesis in RQ1, act as thermodynamic and electrostatic drivers that predictably alter mesoscale structures. Specifically, we hypothesize that simulated environments parameterized with these exact modification profiles will reveal distinct biophysical behaviors in coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. For instance, specific hyperacetylation patterns will drive emergent chromatin fiber destacking and clutch formation under tension, while mapped RNA modifications will fundamentally alter the structural stability and coupling dynamics of translational RNP assemblies.

RQ3: How do these emergent mesoscale structural transitions propagate outward to rewire downstream cellular phenotypes, specifically translation dynamics and intercellular signaling networks?
Emergent mesoscale structures do not merely exist; they dictate cellular function. We hypothesize that the structural reorganization of chromatin and translational machinery ultimately governs downstream cellular outputs by modulating translation speed and cell-cell communication. By integrating our structural models with transcriptomic and proteomic interactome databases, we predict we will find that epitranscriptomic-driven structural changes in RNP complexes directly correlate with global ribosome pausing events in specific metabolic states. Concurrently, we hypothesize that the chromatin reorganization identified via MD simulations will systematically map to the dysregulation of specific intercellular ligand-receptor networks (e.g., altered secretory profiles affecting local cellular microenvironments).

By answering these questions, this project will fulfill the NCEMS mandate to address fundamental puzzles of mesoscale emergence. Our hypotheses are entirely testable through the advanced computational synthesis, AI imputation, and predictive physical modeling of existing public datasets, requiring no new experimental data generation.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve our synthesis objectives, we have designed a rigorous, three-phase computational methodology that integrates AI-driven data harmonization, biophysical modeling, and systems-level bioinformatics. Our approach relies exclusively on the integration of existing, publicly available data.

Phase 1: Multi-Omic Data Harmonization and AI-Driven Imputation
The primary challenge in multi-omic synthesis is data sparsity and technical noise, particularly in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell epigenomics. We will source massive datasets from the Human Cell Atlas, GEO, and multi-omic cohorts like TCGA. To overcome dropout events and technical noise, we will deploy single-cell bi-level feature propagation (scBFP), an advanced two-step graph-based AI algorithm that leverages both gene-gene and cell-cell relationships to impute missing values without distorting biological signals. Following imputation, we will utilize similarity network fusion clustering to integrate proteomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic profiles. This phase will yield high-resolution, multi-omic maps detailing concurrent epigenetic (e.g., acetylation, lactylation) and epitranscriptomic modifications across distinct cellular states and biological conditions.

Phase 2: Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Mesoscale Architectures
To understand the mesoscale emergence driven by these modifications, we will bridge statistical genomics with structural biophysics. The modification profiles defined in Phase 1 will serve as direct parameter inputs for residue-resolution, coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By extracting atomistic structures of nucleosomes, chromatin fibers, and RNP complexes from the PDB and EMDB, we will construct coarse-grained models capable of simulating large mesoscale assemblies over extended biological timescales. We will apply enhanced sampling techniques to simulate how specific modification patterns alter charge-neutralization and thermodynamic landscapes. Specifically, we will compute force-extension curves to model chromatin fiber destacking and nucleosome interactions under varying degrees of crowding and tension. Simultaneously, we will simulate the structural coupling of RNP complexes to determine how specific RNA modifications (e.g., dihydrouridylation) stabilize dynamic translational machinery at the mesoscale.

Phase 3: Intercellular Interactome and Phenotypic Data Mining
The final phase links the structural mesoscale phenomena to cellular functional outputs. We will employ extensive bioinformatic data mining to map the downstream consequences of our simulated structural states. First, we will evaluate translation dynamics by integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data to measure global ribosome pausing parameters, determining how simulated RNP structural instabilities correspond to observed translation speed deficits in public datasets. Second, we will project the functional outputs of our chromatin structural models onto intercellular communication networks. Utilizing custom ligand-receptor databases and spatial transcriptomic datasets, we will perform intercellular interactome mapping. This will allow us to mathematically model how the mesoscale reorganization of chromatin in a given cellular subpopulation alters the secretion of signaling molecules, thereby rewiring the broader tissue microenvironment.

This strictly computational approach synthesizes data across disparate biological scales. By seamlessly connecting AI imputation, molecular biophysics, and bioinformatics, our methodology perfectly aligns with the NCEMS call to develop innovative analytical strategies to resolve complex mesoscale phenomena using only existing public data.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project is expected to deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences, firmly aligning with the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence. 

First, we will produce a comprehensively imputed, harmonized multi-omic atlas detailing the co-occurrence of epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications across diverse cellular states. By overcoming the sparsity of existing public data through advanced AI algorithms, this resource will serve as a foundational tool for researchers exploring the molecular drivers of aging, cellular stress, and disease progression. 

Second, we will deliver an open-source suite of parameterized, residue-resolution coarse-grained molecular dynamics models. These models will mathematically establish the biophysical rules by which distinct molecular modifications cooperatively orchestrate the mesoscale emergence of higher-order chromatin assemblies and translational RNP networks. This addresses a major long-standing puzzle in structural biology: how local chemical changes dynamically percolate to alter massive molecular machines.

Third, we will generate predictive interactome maps linking these emergent mesoscale structures to systems-level phenotypes, such as global ribosome pausing events and the rewiring of intercellular ligand-receptor networks. 

The broader impacts of this work are substantial. By shifting the paradigm from siloed single-omics research to a unified biophysical and multi-omic framework, we will stimulate novel cross-disciplinary research strategies. Furthermore, the Working Group will directly train the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will gain unique, highly sought-after expertise at the intersection of AI, computational biophysics, and systems biology. By maximizing the utility of existing public data, this community-scale synthesis project will provide fundamental insights into the mesoscale rules of life, establishing a scalable computational blueprint for future emergence research.
open_science_and_reproducibility:

Codebases will be extensively documented, and we will provide containerized environments using Docker and Singularity. This will allow external researchers to instantiate our exact computational environments, ensuring that our AI imputations and similarity network fusions can be seamlessly reproduced on diverse high-performance computing (HPC) clusters.

Similarly, all molecular dynamics simulation parameters, topologies, custom force fields, and analysis scripts will be open-sourced. We will provide tutorial Jupyter notebooks detailing the step-by-step parameterization of the coarse-grained models, empowering structural biologists to apply our mesoscale modeling techniques to their own systems of interest.

Finally, we are committed to rapid and open dissemination of our findings. All manuscripts generated by the Working Group will be uploaded to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to formal peer review, and all final peer-reviewed publications will be published in open-access journals. Through these comprehensive open science practices, we ensure that our methodologies and findings will act as a durable, highly accessible resource for the global scientific community.

title: Synthesizing the Global Repertoire of Microbial Mesoscale Compartments: Emergence, Pathogenesis, and Bioengineering Potential from Public Omics Data
abstract:
The emergence of organized mesoscale structures—such as lipid-bounded ferrosomes, magnetosomes, and protein-bounded bacterial microcompartments (BMCs)—from individual molecular components represents a critical evolutionary leap in prokaryotic biology. These structures allow bacteria to achieve localized metabolic reactions, sequester toxic metabolites, facilitate electrochemical cofactor recycling, and resist host immune clearance. While experimental studies have elucidated a handful of these bacterial organelles, the vast diversity of mesoscale compartmentalization remains hidden within fragmented public databases. Our multidisciplinary working group proposes a large-scale data synthesis project to map the genetic, structural, and functional landscape of prokaryotic organelles. This project brings together expertise in bacterial cell biology, structural modeling, host-pathogen dynamics, and large-scale computational genomics to synthesize publicly available metagenomic, transcriptomic, and structural datasets.

First, we will apply advanced machine-learning algorithms to mine public genomic and metagenomic repositories (e.g., MG-RAST, NCBI SRA) for novel loci encoding structural shell proteins, cytoskeletal elements, and membrane-remodeling factors. Leveraging approaches analogous to genomic signature analysis used in complex disease profiling, we will develop "compartment signatures" to identify both canonical assemblies and atypical, minimal functional loci. Second, we will integrate these genomic sequences with public structural databases (PDB) and predictive tools (AlphaFold-Multimer) to model the emergent self-assembly of these newly discovered components into enclosed mesoscale architectures. We will specifically focus on identifying structural features that enable targeted molecular gating and cofactor recycling, extracting design principles for programmable metabolic functions.

Third, to understand the physiological impact of these mesoscale phenomena, we will synthesize dual host-pathogen RNA-seq data and clinical microbiome datasets. By correlating the expression of mesoscale compartment genes with pathogen survival metrics in host environments, we will uncover how these structures provide emergent stress responses—such as desiccation tolerance and evasion of host nutritional immunity via trace metal sequestration—and how their dynamic regulation contributes to chronic infection pathogenesis.

This purely computational, synthesis-driven approach leverages existing data to solve long-standing puzzles about the evolutionary origins and biochemical necessities of bacterial compartmentalization. The primary deliverable will be a publicly accessible "Mesoscale Compartment Atlas" detailing genetic signatures, structural models, and predicted functional states. Furthermore, by characterizing these bacterial organelles as natural analogues to therapeutic nanoparticle delivery systems, our synthesis will directly inform downstream synthetic biology and translational drug delivery efforts. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative project will cross-pollinate structural microbiology, pathogenesis, and data science, providing a robust, transdisciplinary training ground for a new generation of scientists focused on multi-scale biological emergence.
background_and_significance:
The classical paradigm of bacteria as structurally simplistic, uncompartmentalized "bags of enzymes" has been thoroughly overturned. It is now well established that prokaryotes employ a diverse array of mesoscale compartments—ranging from lipid-bounded organelles like magnetosomes and ferrosomes to protein-bounded architectures such as bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) and encapsulins. The self-assembly of these individual biomolecular components into organized, higher-order structures represents a profound instance of biological emergence at the mesoscale. These emergent properties enable vital cellular functions that are impossible in a homogeneous cytoplasm: the spatial isolation of toxic intermediates, the localized concentration of volatile substrates, the facilitation of sophisticated electrochemical cofactor recycling, and the biomineralization of critical trace elements to evade host nutritional immunity.

Despite the fundamental importance of these mesoscale phenomena in microbial ecology, pathogenesis, and biogeochemical cycling, our current understanding is derived from a limited subset of model organisms. Experimental characterization of novel bacterial organelles is inherently low-throughput and frequently hindered by the difficulty of cultivating diverse environmental and clinically relevant microbes in vitro. However, an untapped reservoir of biological information exists within exponentially growing, publicly available databases of metagenomic, transcriptomic, and structural data. The global scientific community has sequenced tens of thousands of diverse microbiomes, yet this "dark matter" of the microbial world has rarely been systematically mined for the specific genetic and structural signatures of mesoscale compartmentalization.

Our project addresses this critical gap by synthesizing highly diverse, publicly available omics datasets to systematically map the global repertoire of microbial mesoscale compartments. This community-scale synthesis requires overcoming substantial analytical bottlenecks. It demands the integration of advanced machine-learning-driven genomic signature analysis—traditionally utilized in precision oncology and chronic disease profiling—with comparative microbial genomics, 3D structural modeling, and host-pathogen transcriptomics. By translating the conceptual frameworks of genomic mutational signatures into "compartment signatures," we can rapidly identify atypical or minimal genetic loci that encode uncharacterized organelles. 

This proposal aligns perfectly with the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission. It utilizes strictly existing, publicly available data to solve long-standing mysteries regarding the evolutionary origins and functional diversity of bacterial organelles. Furthermore, the significance of this work extends beyond fundamental biology. The mesoscale architectures we aim to catalog act as naturally evolved analogues to synthetic therapeutic nanoparticles. Understanding the emergent biophysical principles governing their targeted molecular gating, selective payload encapsulation, and structural stability under physiological stress will directly inform next-generation synthetic biology applications and nanoparticle-based drug delivery strategies. Through NCEMS support, we will unite disparate fields—computational oncology, bacterial cell biology, structural bioinformatics, and pathogenesis—to illuminate how mesoscale organization dictates cellular survival and host interactions.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is structured around three compelling research questions that address the discovery, structural emergence, and physiological function of bacterial mesoscale compartments. Each question is paired with specific hypotheses that will be rigorously tested utilizing publicly available datasets.

Question 1: Can computational "compartment signatures" derived from known prokaryotic organelles accurately predict the existence and distribution of novel, uncharacterized mesoscale structures across global metagenomes?
We hypothesize that the genetic loci encoding both lipid-bounded and protein-bounded mesoscale compartments possess conserved, architecturally distinct sequence signatures—even when sequence homology of individual structural genes is low. We further hypothesize that by employing machine-learning algorithms on existing metagenomic repositories (e.g., MG-RAST, NCBI SRA), we can identify these signatures to uncover novel organelle-forming gene clusters, including minimal, atypical loci that provide distinct, localized functional advantages to diverse microbial lineages. This addresses the long-standing puzzle of organelle evolution by mapping the transition from minimal essential parts to highly complex mesoscale assemblies.

Question 2: What are the emergent biophysical and structural principles that govern the self-assembly, molecular gating, and cofactor recycling capabilities of highly diverse bacterial compartments?
We hypothesize that despite vast primary sequence divergence, the structural constraints required for mesoscale self-assembly and selective permeability converge on a defined set of 3D architectural motifs. By synthesizing public structural databases (PDB) and leveraging AI-driven predictive modeling tools (AlphaFold-Multimer) on newly discovered loci, we expect to demonstrate that emergent properties—such as the formation of selective pores for NAD+/NADH recycling or specific metal ion channels—are dictated by the quaternary arrangement of repeating homooligomeric units. We hypothesize that modeling these assemblies will reveal a standardized, programmable "grammar" of modular shell proteins and membrane-remodeling factors that can be co-opted for synthetic biology applications.

Question 3: How does the dynamic regulation of mesoscale compartments dictate pathogen survival, stress tolerance, and evasion of host defenses during chronic infections?
We hypothesize that the expression of mesoscale compartments is highly responsive to the specific biochemical stresses of the host environment, functioning as a primary mechanism of pathogenesis and persistence. Specifically, we hypothesize that dual host-pathogen RNA-seq data from publicly available clinical infection models will reveal a strong positive correlation between the upregulation of iron-sequestering ferrosomes, stress-mitigating BMCs, and bacterial survival under conditions of host-mediated nutritional immunity and desiccation. By integrating this transcriptomic data with established survival metrics, we will show that the emergent property of compartmentalization is statistically inextricably linked to the mechanisms driving chronic disease pathogenesis.

These hypotheses necessitate a transdisciplinary approach that integrates the logic of complex disease genomics with bacterial structural biology. They can only be addressed through the community-scale synthesis of fragmented public datasets, bringing together expertise that vastly exceeds the capabilities of any single research laboratory.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodology is entirely computational and synthesis-driven, adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. The project is structured into three interconnected analytical aims, executed by a transdisciplinary Working Group integrating expertise in comparative genomics, structural modeling, host-pathogen transcriptomics, and large-scale data science.

Aim 1: AI-Driven Mining of Global Metagenomes for Compartment Signatures.
We will aggregate existing genomic and metagenomic datasets from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA), the JGI Integrated Microbial Genomes & Microbiomes (IMG/M) system, and MG-RAST. We will train Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and deep-learning-based genomic classifiers on the canonical loci of known bacterial organelles (e.g., magnetosomes, ferrosomes, carboxysomes). Leveraging analytical frameworks adapted from complex mutational signature profiling, we will extract multigenic "compartment signatures" based on synteny, operon structure, and the presence of cytoskeletal anchoring domains or shell protein homologs. This pipeline will be deployed across global environmental and clinical metagenomes to identify both canonical and atypical, minimized loci. The output will be a comprehensive catalog of predicted mesoscale organelle clusters, cross-referenced with phylogenetic and ecological metadata.

Aim 2: Emergent Structural Modeling and Functional Prediction.
To understand how these linear genetic sequences encode emergent 3D properties, we will synthesize sequence data with structural information from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). For high-confidence novel loci identified in Aim 1, we will utilize AlphaFold-Multimer and Rosetta to model the quaternary self-assembly of predicted shell proteins and membrane-remodeling complexes. We will map biophysical parameters onto these multi-subunit models, specifically calculating electrostatic surface potentials, pore sizes, and internal volume constraints. By conducting predictive structural analyses—such as simulating the docking of electrochemical cofactors (e.g., NAD+/NADH) and metal ions—we will map potential molecular gating and recycling pathways. This in silico structural synthesis will define the physical parameters that allow these compartments to function as modular, programmable metabolic units.

Aim 3: Meta-Analysis of Organelle Dynamics in Host-Pathogen Transcriptomes.
To decipher the physiological roles of these structures in disease, we will acquire publicly available dual host-pathogen RNA-seq datasets and clinical microbiome profiles representing various chronic infection states and host stress environments (e.g., iron starvation, desiccation, reactive oxygen species exposure). We will perform large-scale differential gene expression meta-analyses using DESeq2 and limma-voom to correlate the transcriptional activation of identified compartment loci with specific host responses and pathogen survival outcomes. Network analysis (WGCNA) will be employed to identify co-expression modules linking organelle biogenesis with known virulence factors, toxin export systems, and stress tolerance pathways.

Data Integration and Workflow:
All three data streams (genomic signatures, structural models, and transcriptomic correlations) will be integrated into a unified relational database. Our multidisciplinary Working Group will meet quarterly at NCEMS to iteratively refine analytical parameters, interpret emergent patterns, and synthesize the findings into our final deliverable, utilizing cloud-computing infrastructure to manage the massive scale of the combined omics datasets.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The primary outcome of this project will be the creation and deployment of the "Mesoscale Compartment Atlas," a publicly accessible, interactive, and fully annotated database integrating the genetic signatures, predicted structural models, and transcriptomic profiles of prokaryotic organelles. This resource will fundamentally transform the scientific community’s understanding of bacterial compartmentalization, shifting the paradigm from a handful of experimentally isolated novelties to a globally distributed, systematically categorized structural necessity of microbial life.

Scientifically, this synthesis will resolve critical questions regarding the evolutionary trajectory of mesoscale emergence. By identifying minimal functional loci, we will provide the community with evolutionary stepping-stones that bridge the gap between simple protein assemblies and complex, multi-layered organelles. The meta-analysis of dual host-pathogen transcriptomes will establish new mechanistic links between mesoscale compartmentalization and bacterial pathogenesis, specifically highlighting how dynamic organelle regulation enables pathogens to circumvent host nutritional immunity and survive extreme physiological stress, such as desiccation and oxidative bursts.

Translational and biotechnological impacts are equally profound. The structural rules and modular "grammar" derived from our AlphaFold-Multimer syntheses will act as a foundational blueprint for synthetic biologists engineering programmable metabolic microcompartments. Furthermore, identifying the design principles that allow bacterial organelles to target, selectively import, and protect sensitive biological payloads will directly inspire the engineering of novel therapeutic nanoparticle delivery systems, improving the safety and efficacy of targeted disease treatments.

Finally, this NCEMS-supported Working Group will serve as a premier training environment. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will be immersed in a truly transdisciplinary setting, mastering cutting-edge machine learning, large-scale omics integration, and structural bioinformatics, thereby forging the data-savvy scientific workforce required for the future of molecular biosciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of Open Science, FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data practices, and computational reproducibility. Given that our project relies entirely on the synthesis of publicly available data, ensuring that our analytical pipelines and outputs are completely transparent is paramount to our mission.

First, all custom code, machine-learning algorithms, and data processing scripts developed for genomic signature mining, structural modeling, and transcriptomic meta-analysis will be version-controlled and hosted on a publicly accessible GitHub/GitLab repository under an MIT open-source license. To guarantee reproducibility across different computational environments, all data processing workflows will be containerized using Docker/Singularity and orchestrated via Nextflow or Snakemake pipelines.

Second, the core deliverable—the Mesoscale Compartment Atlas—will be hosted on a robust, open-access web platform. The underlying integrated datasets, including compiled metagenomic loci, AlphaFold-Multimer PDB models, and normalized RNA-seq count matrices, will be deposited in stable, community-recognized repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad, each assigned a persistent Digital Object Identifier (DOI).

Third, we will preregister our core hypotheses and analytical protocols on the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to executing the large-scale computational runs to mitigate analytical bias. All scientific manuscripts resulting from this work will be submitted as preprints to bioRxiv prior to peer review, and final publications will be strictly Open Access. We will comprehensively document our metadata standards using established ontologies to ensure that future researchers can seamlessly integrate our synthetic findings into new studies of cellular emergence.
budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we request NCEMS funding tailored to support extensive computational infrastructure, multidisciplinary collaborative integration, and comprehensive workforce training.

1. Personnel and Training ($140,000/year): 
The majority of the budget is dedicated to training the next-generation data-savvy workforce. We request support for two full-time postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. These trainees will be cross-mentored by the multidisciplinary PI team, ensuring they gain expertise spanning computational genomics, structural modeling, and host-pathogen interactions. Funds will cover stipends, benefits, and tuition remission.

2. Cloud Computing and Data Storage ($45,000/year):
The massive scale of global metagenomic mining, RNA-seq meta-analysis, and AlphaFold-Multimer structural predictions far exceeds standard institutional clusters. We request funds for high-performance cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud) specifically optimized for GPU-intensive machine-learning tasks and large-memory structural simulations. This also includes costs for hosting the "Mesoscale Compartment Atlas" and long-term secure data storage of synthesized results.

3. Working Group Collaboration and Travel ($35,000/year):
A critical requirement of this project is the integration of diverse scientific perspectives. We request funds to support biannual, intensive, week-long Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These funds will cover travel, lodging, and per diem for all PI team members, postdocs, and graduate trainees. These immersive sessions are vital for iterative data analysis, pipeline troubleshooting, and conceptual synthesis.

4. Open Science and Publication Costs ($10,000/year):
To adhere to our stringent open science commitments, we request funds for open-access publication fees, software licensing (if open-source alternatives are temporarily insufficient), and cloud-hosting fees for community-facing open data repositories.

This focused resource allocation guarantees the computational power and transdisciplinary collaboration required to unlock emergent insights from existing public omics data.
