author: gpt-5.5
title: Circadian Control of Heat-Sensitive Mesoscale Assembly During Plant Cell Division
abstract:
Plant growth under episodic high temperature depends not only on stress-responsive transcription but also on whether dividing cells can assemble a functional cytokinetic apparatus at the right time. The central question of this synthesis project is: how do time of day and heat stress jointly alter the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis, including microtubule arrays, endomembrane trafficking, cell plate formation, and nascent cell wall deposition? We propose that cytokinetic failure under heat is an emergent systems property arising from misalignment among circadian-regulated stress pathways, vesicle sorting capacity, cytoskeletal reorganization, and cell wall biosynthesis, rather than from disruption of any single gene or organelle.

This NCEMS Working Group will use only publicly available datasets to build a cross-scale synthesis of heat-sensitive plant cell division. We will integrate public RNA-seq time courses from Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other plant systems exposed to temperature perturbations at different times of day; root and shoot single-cell transcriptomic atlases enriched for proliferative tissues; public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interactome, and subcellular localization resources; and archived fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets containing dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, Golgi/trans-Golgi network markers, cell plate markers, and cell wall biosynthetic reporters. Existing resources such as GEO, SRA, ENA, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Expression Atlas, SUBA, and plant orthology databases will be harmonized into a reproducible analysis framework.

The project has three synthesis aims. First, we will create a shared ontology and data model linking cytokinetic structures, endomembrane compartments, cell wall assembly processes, heat-response regulators, and circadian phase information across plant species and experimental platforms. Second, we will construct confounder-aware, context-specific gene and protein networks that distinguish heat-responsive modules that are constitutive from those gated by time of day, tissue identity, developmental stage, or genotype. These networks will prioritize conserved and lineage-specific modules connecting calcium signaling, heat shock regulation, vesicle trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, and polysaccharide deposition. Third, we will apply standardized image-analysis workflows to public microscopy data to extract mesoscale phenotypes such as phragmoplast geometry, cell plate expansion symmetry, vesicle-marker distribution, microtubule array coherence, and spatial relationships among organelles during cytokinesis. Network features will then be linked to image-derived phenotypes to identify candidate molecular configurations that predict robust versus heat-vulnerable cytokinetic assembly.

The expected outcome is an open, community-curated atlas of plant cytokinetic heat sensitivity that connects molecular state, cellular architecture, circadian timing, and species-level variation. This effort requires NCEMS support because it depends on coordination among plant cell biologists, circadian and stress biologists, endomembrane specialists, computational genomicists, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees across institutions. No individual laboratory could assemble, standardize, and interpret these heterogeneous public datasets at the necessary scale. The Working Group will release containerized workflows, harmonized metadata, image-analysis notebooks, network models, and training materials. By synthesizing public molecular and cellular data, the project will reveal how environmental timing reshapes mesoscale cellular organization and will provide a general framework for studying emergent stress sensitivity in eukaryotic cell division.
background_and_significance:
Plant productivity during heat waves depends on the ability of meristems and developing tissues to continue producing viable cells. Although heat-stress biology has been studied extensively at the level of transcription factors, chaperones, hormones, and membrane stability, a critical unresolved problem is how high temperature affects the mesoscale machinery that physically completes plant cell division. Plant cytokinesis requires coordinated organization of the phragmoplast microtubule array, targeted vesicle trafficking through Golgi and trans-Golgi network compartments, cell plate membrane maturation, callose and cellulose-related wall deposition, and eventual fusion of the new cross wall with the parental wall. These structures are larger than individual macromolecular complexes but smaller than whole organelles or tissues, placing them directly within the NCEMS focus on emergent mesoscale properties.

The proposed Working Group addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: why do dividing plant cells become heat vulnerable at particular times, in particular tissues, or in particular genotypes? Public data suggest that the answer cannot be reduced to a single heat shock pathway. Temperature responses are gated by the circadian system, and the magnitude and composition of heat-responsive transcriptional programs vary with time of day. Separately, plant cytokinesis depends on temporally ordered interactions among cytoskeletal proteins, vesicle coats, tethering factors, small GTPases, phosphoinositide metabolism, autophagy-related remodeling, and cell wall biosynthetic enzymes. The emergent behavior of this system is successful partitioning of one cell into two daughters. Heat may disrupt that outcome when circadian phase, stress signaling, membrane trafficking capacity, and wall assembly demand become poorly aligned.

This question is now tractable through synthesis research because large, heterogeneous public resources have accumulated across molecular, cellular, and organismal scales. Time-resolved RNA-seq datasets exist for Arabidopsis and several crops under heat and temperature-shift regimes, including experiments that explicitly vary time of day. Single-cell and single-nucleus atlases identify proliferative root and shoot cell populations and allow cytokinesis-relevant gene programs to be placed in tissue and developmental context. Proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interaction, localization, and orthology databases provide complementary evidence for protein modules and conserved cellular functions. Public light microscopy and electron microscopy repositories include images of dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, endomembrane compartments, cell plates, and cell wall reporters, but these data have not been jointly analyzed for heat-sensitive mesoscale phenotypes.

The project is significant because it will transform dispersed datasets into a community resource for explaining how environmental timing influences cellular architecture. It directly meets NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, requiring a multidisciplinary team, integrating data types beyond the reach of a single laboratory, and targeting emergence across scales from gene regulation to mesoscale cytokinetic organization. The work will also generate reusable methods for confounder-aware network construction, cross-species metadata harmonization, and image-derived phenotype extraction. These outputs will benefit plant biology, cell biology, climate-resilience research, and the broader study of stress-sensitive cell division in eukaryotes.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The central research question is how circadian phase and heat stress jointly influence the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis. We will address this question through three interlocking synthesis questions that connect molecular state, cellular architecture, and evolutionary conservation.

Question 1: Which cytokinesis-associated molecular modules are heat responsive, circadian gated, or both? We hypothesize that heat-responsive regulation of plant cell division is partitioned into at least three classes: constitutive heat-response modules active across time points; circadian-gated modules whose response amplitude or direction depends on time of day; and cell-cycle- or tissue-restricted modules detectable primarily in proliferative cell populations. We expect core heat shock and protein-folding genes to behave more broadly, whereas modules involving vesicle sorting, microtubule remodeling, calcium signaling, callose deposition, and wall-polysaccharide trafficking will show stronger dependence on circadian phase and developmental context.

Question 2: Do heat-vulnerable cytokinetic states arise from misalignment among interacting mesoscale subsystems rather than from failure of a single pathway? We hypothesize that cytokinetic breakdown under heat reflects loss of coordinated timing among cytoskeleton dynamics, endomembrane delivery, membrane remodeling, and nascent cell wall construction. Under this hypothesis, vulnerability will be predicted by network configurations in which heat-stress regulators are activated but trafficking, microtubule-associated, or wall-synthesis modules are delayed, suppressed, or uncoupled from one another. Robust cytokinesis should instead correspond to coordinated activation of stress-protection and assembly modules at compatible circadian phases.

Question 3: Which aspects of heat-sensitive cytokinesis are conserved across plant lineages, and which are species- or genotype-specific? We hypothesize that conserved modules will include calcium-dependent signaling, chaperone-mediated proteostasis, cytoskeletal regulators, vesicle tethering and fusion components, and core cell plate maturation factors. Lineage-specific or genotype-sensitive modules are expected in expanded gene families involved in cell wall biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription, hormone signaling, and endomembrane specialization. Cross-species synthesis across Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and additional public plant datasets will distinguish broadly conserved principles from crop-specific adaptation.

Question 4: Can image-derived mesoscale phenotypes be predicted from public molecular data? We hypothesize that extracted features such as phragmoplast expansion symmetry, microtubule array coherence, cell plate curvature, vesicle-marker concentration near the division plane, and cell wall reporter distribution will correlate with context-specific network states. For example, reduced coherence of phragmoplast arrays may associate with altered expression or phosphorylation of microtubule regulators and stress-associated kinases, while abnormal cell plate expansion may associate with endomembrane sorting and polysaccharide deposition modules.

Question 5: What metadata standards are necessary to make time-of-day, heat-treatment, cell-cycle, tissue, and imaging information interoperable? We hypothesize that many currently public datasets are scientifically valuable but underused because key contextual variables are recorded inconsistently. A shared ontology linking circadian phase, thermal regime, cytokinetic structures, subcellular compartments, and developmental identity will enable analyses that are not possible using dataset-specific metadata alone.

Together, these questions test the overarching hypothesis that heat sensitivity in dividing plant cells is an emergent property of cross-scale coordination. The project will not seek a single master regulator. Instead, it will define combinations of molecular and mesoscale features that predict when cytokinesis is buffered against heat and when it becomes a bottleneck for growth.
methods_and_approach:
This Working Group will conduct a synthesis study using only existing publicly available data. No new experimental data will be generated. The work will be organized into three integrated aims supported by shared data governance, reproducible workflows, and recurring cross-disciplinary analysis meetings.

Aim 1 will build a harmonized cytokinesis-heat-circadian data framework. We will identify and curate public datasets from GEO, SRA, ENA, Expression Atlas, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Gramene, PLAZA, OrthoDB, SUBA, BioGRID, IntAct, and related plant resources. Transcriptomic datasets will include bulk RNA-seq time courses under heat, temperature shifts, diel cycles, and constant-condition circadian experiments in Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other species where metadata are adequate. Single-cell and single-nucleus atlases will be used to annotate proliferative tissues and cell-cycle states. Proteomic, phosphoproteomic, localization, and interaction resources will provide protein-level support. Image datasets will be screened for dividing cells and markers of microtubules, Golgi, trans-Golgi network, cell plate, plasma membrane, callose, cellulose-related processes, and cell wall assembly. We will develop a lightweight ontology and metadata schema covering species, genotype, tissue, developmental stage, thermal regime, Zeitgeber time or circadian phase, assay type, cell-cycle stage, cytokinetic structure, and imaging modality.

Aim 2 will infer context-specific molecular networks. Public RNA-seq reads will be reprocessed where feasible through containerized workflows using consistent quality control, alignment or pseudoalignment, gene quantification, and orthology mapping. Existing count matrices will be incorporated when raw data are impractical, with provenance recorded. We will model heat response while controlling for confounders including species, genotype, tissue, batch, developmental stage, time after treatment, and time of day. Differential expression, rhythmicity analysis, phase-aware regression, and interaction models will identify genes whose heat response depends on circadian context. Co-expression and protein-supported networks will be constructed using confounder-aware methods, with context-specific edges tested for robustness by resampling, dataset holdout, and comparison across species. Network modules will be annotated for cytokinesis, endomembrane trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, calcium signaling, heat response, and cell wall biosynthesis.

Aim 3 will extract and integrate mesoscale image phenotypes. Public fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets will be processed using standardized notebooks and open image-analysis tools. When sufficient annotations exist, supervised or semi-supervised segmentation will identify dividing cells, phragmoplasts, cell plates, vesicle-rich zones, and relevant organelle markers. Where image heterogeneity limits automation, curated benchmark subsets will be analyzed with transparent quality scoring. Extracted features will include phragmoplast length and width, expansion symmetry, microtubule orientation coherence, cell plate continuity, marker enrichment at the division plane, spatial proximity among endomembrane compartments, and wall reporter distribution. Metadata will link image phenotypes to species, genotype, tissue, temperature, and sampling time.

Finally, molecular network features and image-derived phenotypes will be integrated using multilevel statistical models and interpretable machine learning. The goal is not black-box prediction, but identification of reproducible molecular configurations associated with robust or disrupted cytokinetic assembly. Regular NCEMS-supported workshops will bring plant cell biologists, circadian specialists, computational genomics experts, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees together to validate assumptions, refine terminology, troubleshoot metadata gaps, and prioritize community-useful outputs.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The primary outcome will be an open atlas of heat-sensitive plant cytokinesis that connects circadian timing, stress-responsive molecular networks, proliferative cell identities, protein localization, and mesoscale image phenotypes. This atlas will provide curated links among genes, proteins, structures, compartments, and phenotypes across Arabidopsis and major crop species, allowing researchers to query which cytokinetic processes are predicted to be heat vulnerable at specific times of day or in particular tissues.

A second outcome will be a set of conserved and lineage-specific network modules associated with robust or vulnerable cytokinetic assembly. These modules will clarify whether heat sensitivity is driven mainly by proteostasis, calcium signaling, vesicle trafficking, cytoskeletal reorganization, wall biosynthesis, or by failures of coordination among these processes. The project will generate prioritized hypotheses for future experimental laboratories, while the Working Group itself will remain entirely within synthesis research.

A third outcome will be reusable methodology. The metadata schema, ontology, confounder-aware network workflow, cross-species orthology framework, and public microscopy analysis notebooks will be applicable to other mesoscale cellular systems. These tools will help the community analyze emergence where cell behavior cannot be inferred from transcript abundance alone.

The broader impact is timely and substantial. Heat waves increasingly threaten plant development and agricultural productivity, yet cellular bottlenecks in dividing tissues remain poorly synthesized across available data. By revealing how environmental timing reshapes cytokinetic organization, the project will advance fundamental molecular and cellular biology and provide a conceptual framework for climate-relevant plant resilience. The Working Group will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in open data synthesis, reproducible computation, network analysis, and quantitative cell biology. Because the work requires integration across data modalities, species, institutions, and disciplinary cultures, NCEMS support will enable discoveries that would be unattainable through isolated laboratory efforts.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from inception. All datasets used will be publicly available, and every accession, download date, license condition, processing decision, and quality-control outcome will be recorded in a public data inventory. Because the project synthesizes existing data rather than generating new experiments, transparency of provenance and analysis decisions is central to scientific rigor.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories, with stable releases archived through Zenodo or an equivalent repository. Workflows for RNA-seq processing, metadata harmonization, orthology mapping, network construction, statistical modeling, and image analysis will be containerized using Docker or Apptainer and orchestrated with reproducible workflow systems such as Nextflow or Snakemake. Computational environments will be documented with locked software versions. Analysis notebooks will include executable examples using small test datasets so that users can verify installation and reproduce core steps without specialized infrastructure.

The Working Group will release harmonized metadata tables, derived count matrices where redistribution is permitted, network edge lists, module annotations, image feature tables, ontology files, and documentation under permissive open licenses whenever compatible with source repositories. Large files will be stored through appropriate community repositories rather than informal file sharing. Public microscopy annotations generated during synthesis will be deposited in formats compatible with community image archives.

Reproducibility will be strengthened through preregistered analysis plans for major comparisons, explicit criteria for dataset inclusion and exclusion, sensitivity analyses, and independent code review by team members not responsible for the original implementation. Trainees will participate in reproducibility checks as part of structured training.

Community engagement will include open virtual tutorials, issue-tracking for ontology refinement, and short training modules on circadian metadata, plant cytokinesis terminology, confounder-aware co-expression analysis, and quantitative image analysis. These practices will ensure that the outputs are not merely publications but reusable resources for molecular and cellular synthesis research.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis across disciplines, data types, and institutions rather than conventional single-laboratory research. Funds will be used to support Working Group convenings, trainee participation, data curation, computational analysis, open-science dissemination, and community training. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

The largest resource need is collaborative time. We request support for two in-person NCEMS meetings per year, supplemented by monthly virtual working sessions. In-person meetings will focus on ontology development, dataset triage, cross-disciplinary interpretation of network and image results, and manuscript and resource planning. Travel support will prioritize participation by graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career investigators, and collaborators from institutions with varied research capacity.

A second budget category is personnel effort for synthesis tasks. Partial support for trainees or research staff will enable public dataset discovery, metadata cleaning, accession tracking, quality-control review, orthology table construction, image annotation, documentation, and reproducibility testing. These tasks are labor-intensive and require coordination but are central to the proposed scientific contribution.

A third category is computation and data management. Although much work can use institutional and NCEMS infrastructure, modest cloud or high-performance computing allocations will be needed for reprocessing large RNA-seq collections, storing intermediate files, running network resampling analyses, and processing public microscopy data. Container registries, repository archiving, and persistent identifiers will support long-term accessibility.

A fourth category is training and dissemination. Funds will support open workshops, tutorial preparation, community feedback sessions, and publication or repository costs where needed to ensure public access. NCEMS staff expertise in synthesis facilitation, data science, team science, and reproducible workflows will be as important as direct financial support.

The requested resources are proportionate to a synthesis Working Group. They enable a geographically distributed, multidisciplinary team to produce shared infrastructure, rigorously integrated analyses, and trainee training that no individual laboratory or existing collaboration could achieve at comparable scale.

title: Cross-Scale Synthesis of Emergent Chromatin Microenvironments in Human Brain Cell Types
abstract:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular neuroscience is how molecular features of chromatin regulators, transcription factors, histone modifications, and architectural proteins combine to produce mesoscale genome structures that differ across brain cell types and alter cellular phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define the “chromatin microenvironment grammar” of human brain cells: the rules by which local molecular interactions give rise to emergent 3D regulatory neighborhoods, enhancer hubs, and compartmental domains that influence gene expression and psychiatric disease risk. The project will use only publicly available data, integrating single-cell and bulk chromatin conformation datasets, brain single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq atlases, epigenomic maps, proteomic resources, transcription factor binding data, genetic association studies, and public annotations of intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, and chromatin-binding proteins.

The working group will address three linked questions. First, which classes of mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods recur across human brain cell types, developmental stages, and disease-relevant genomic loci? Second, can these neighborhoods be predicted from molecular features such as nucleosome positioning, histone marks, CTCF/cohesin occupancy, transcription factor motif density, RNA-binding protein expression, and the disorder or multivalency of chromatin-associated proteins? Third, do psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disease variants preferentially perturb particular emergent chromatin microenvironments rather than individual genes or linear regulatory elements?

To answer these questions, we will assemble a harmonized atlas from public datasets including human and mouse brain single-cell 3D genome maps, PsychENCODE and related brain transcriptomic and epigenomic resources, ENCODE/Roadmap chromatin annotations, public proteomic and protein-domain databases, and genome-wide association summary statistics for schizophrenia, autism, bipolar disorder, major depression, cognition, and neurodegenerative traits. We will develop open computational workflows that align regulatory elements across modalities, infer cell-type-specific 3D regulatory neighborhoods, quantify mesoscale features of chromatin organization, and test whether these features are enriched for disease heritability. A key innovation will be the integration of polymer-inspired and biophysical descriptors—loop density, contact anisotropy, domain compaction, predicted multivalent binding capacity, and disorder-associated interaction potential—with machine learning models trained to predict expression and disease-relevant regulatory disruption.

This project is well matched to NCEMS because it focuses on emergence at the mesoscale: how molecular-scale interactions among DNA, histones, transcription factors, architectural proteins, and disordered chromatin regulators generate higher-order genome structures with consequences for cellular identity and disease. It requires expertise beyond any single laboratory, combining single-cell genome architecture, chromatin structural biology, polymer physics, statistical genetics, proteomics, transcriptomics, and open data engineering. The synthesis will produce a public atlas of brain cell chromatin microenvironments, reusable software for cross-scale genome-structure integration, benchmark datasets for trainees, and testable models for how disease variants alter emergent regulatory architecture. Trainees will participate through collaborative code sprints, reproducibility workshops, and cross-disciplinary analysis teams, gaining experience in public data synthesis, biophysical modeling, and responsible open science.
background_and_significance:
Brain cell identity emerges from interactions among genomic sequence, chromatin state, nuclear organization, regulatory proteins, and transcriptional programs. Although each layer has been studied extensively, the field lacks an integrated understanding of how molecular-scale features combine to create mesoscale chromatin microenvironments: regulatory neighborhoods, enhancer clusters, loop domains, compartments, and locally compacted or decompacted chromatin regions that influence gene expression. This gap is especially consequential in the human brain, where neurons, glia, progenitors, and regionally specialized cell states share nearly identical DNA sequences but differ profoundly in morphology, physiology, developmental history, and disease vulnerability.

A large and rapidly expanding public data landscape now makes it possible to address this problem through synthesis rather than new data generation. Public resources include single-cell and bulk chromatin conformation maps, brain single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq atlases, histone modification and DNA methylation profiles, transcription factor occupancy maps, chromatin accessibility datasets, protein interaction and domain databases, proteomic atlases, and genome-wide association studies for psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and neurodegenerative traits. These datasets were generally generated to answer modality-specific questions. Their combined value lies in the possibility of identifying emergent organizational principles that are invisible in any one dataset.

The proposed working group addresses a central NCEMS priority: understanding how new biological properties arise across scales of composition, space, time, information, and motion. Chromatin microenvironments are mesoscale systems in which molecular components such as nucleosomes, histone marks, CTCF, cohesin, transcription factors, RNA-associated proteins, and intrinsically disordered or multivalent chromatin regulators can collectively produce domains, hubs, and compartments. These structures are not simple sums of individual binding events. They exhibit nonlinear relationships with transcription, developmental timing, cell-type specificity, and disease-associated genetic variation.

Current genome annotation frameworks still emphasize linear regulatory elements and nearest-gene assignments. This is inadequate for brain disorders, where most associated variants are noncoding, distributed across many loci, and enriched in cell-type-specific regulatory regions. A disease variant may alter the activity of an enhancer, but it may also perturb the stability, composition, or connectivity of a 3D regulatory neighborhood. Testing this possibility requires simultaneous consideration of genome architecture, epigenomic state, regulatory protein features, cell type, and statistical genetics.

This project is significant because it will convert heterogeneous public data into a cross-scale atlas and analytical framework for studying emergent chromatin organization in human brain cell types. It will establish reusable definitions of chromatin microenvironment classes, identify molecular predictors of mesoscale genome architecture, and determine whether psychiatric and neurodevelopmental risk variants are concentrated in specific 3D regulatory contexts. The work requires expertise in single-cell genomics, chromatin biology, structural and polymer biophysics, proteomics, machine learning, open data engineering, and human genetics, making it well suited for NCEMS support as a community-scale synthesis effort.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will pursue three integrated research questions designed to identify, model, and interpret emergent chromatin microenvironments in human brain cell types.

Question 1: What classes of mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods recur across brain cell types, developmental stages, and disease-relevant genomic loci? We hypothesize that the human brain contains a finite set of recurrent chromatin microenvironment classes that can be defined by combinations of 3D contact structure, regulatory element composition, chromatin state, and transcriptional output. These classes may include insulated loop neighborhoods, active enhancer hubs, Polycomb-enriched repressive domains, lamina-associated or compartmentalized regions, highly transcribed decompacted domains, and mixed regulatory neighborhoods at lineage-transition genes. We further hypothesize that these classes are conserved in part across species and developmental stages but are redeployed in cell-type-specific ways in excitatory neurons, inhibitory interneurons, oligodendrocyte lineage cells, astrocytes, microglia, and progenitor populations.

Question 2: Can mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods be predicted from molecular and biophysical features? We hypothesize that local genome architecture is predictable from multi-layer features that include nucleosome occupancy, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, CTCF and cohesin binding, transcription factor motif density and expression, CpG and repeat composition, enhancer-promoter density, and protein-level properties of chromatin-associated regulators. In addition to standard genomic features, we will test whether biophysical descriptors improve prediction. These descriptors include predicted multivalency, intrinsically disordered region content, DNA-binding and RNA-binding potential, low-complexity sequence content, phase-separation propensity, and polymer-inspired measures such as loop density, contact anisotropy, contact decay, and local compaction. The central hypothesis is that emergent 3D regulatory neighborhoods reflect both sequence-encoded regulatory information and collective physical interaction potential among chromatin-bound molecules.

Question 3: Do disease-associated variants preferentially perturb chromatin microenvironments rather than isolated genes or linear elements? We hypothesize that variants associated with schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, major depression, cognition, and neurodegenerative traits are enriched in specific classes of brain-cell chromatin microenvironments. For example, schizophrenia risk may concentrate in neuronal enhancer hubs active during cortical development, while neurodegenerative risk may involve microglial or glial regulatory neighborhoods. We further hypothesize that incorporating 3D microenvironment annotations will improve heritability enrichment, variant-to-gene mapping, and prediction of disease-relevant regulatory disruption compared with analyses based only on linear chromatin accessibility or promoter proximity.

Together, these questions test a cross-scale model of chromatin emergence. Molecular features define a local interaction landscape; the interaction landscape gives rise to mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods; and these neighborhoods shape cell-type-specific gene regulation and disease susceptibility. The project will generate falsifiable outputs: microenvironment classes, quantitative feature weights, predictive models, enrichment estimates, and prioritized disease loci where public data support specific mechanisms of architectural disruption.
methods_and_approach:
This project will use only existing publicly available datasets and will generate no new experimental measurements. The work will proceed through five coordinated synthesis activities.

Activity 1: Public data inventory and harmonization. We will assemble a curated compendium of human and mouse brain datasets, including single-cell and bulk Hi-C, Micro-C, Dip-C and related chromatin conformation data; single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq atlases; PsychENCODE and related developmental brain resources; ENCODE, Roadmap, and other epigenomic maps; public transcription factor binding datasets; DNA methylation and histone modification profiles; protein domain and disorder annotations from public databases; proteomic resources; and GWAS summary statistics for psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and neurodegenerative traits. Metadata will be standardized for genome build, brain region, developmental stage, assay, cell type, donor context, and processing status. When necessary, coordinates will be lifted to common genome builds, and cell-type labels will be mapped to controlled vocabularies.

Activity 2: Cross-modal regulatory element alignment. We will define candidate regulatory elements using accessible chromatin peaks, promoters, enhancers, histone-marked regions, CTCF sites, and conserved noncoding elements. These elements will be linked to cell-type-specific expression profiles and 3D contacts. We will use reproducible pipelines for normalization, batch assessment, sparse contact processing, pseudobulk aggregation, and uncertainty estimation. Orthologous regulatory intervals between human and mouse will be used to evaluate conservation and developmental recurrence.

Activity 3: Inference of chromatin microenvironment classes. We will represent genomic regions as multiscale graphs in which nodes are regulatory elements, promoters, chromatin states, or genomic bins and edges are 3D contacts, co-accessibility links, enhancer-promoter predictions, or shared regulatory features. Community detection, graph embeddings, topic models, and probabilistic clustering will be used to identify recurrent microenvironment classes. Each class will be summarized by loop density, domain boundaries, compartment status, contact anisotropy, compaction, enhancer density, transcriptional activity, histone marks, and cell-type specificity.

Activity 4: Molecular and biophysical prediction. Machine learning models will predict microenvironment class and quantitative 3D features from molecular descriptors. Models will include interpretable regularized regression, gradient-boosted trees, graph neural networks where justified by data scale, and Bayesian hierarchical models to account for donor, assay, and cell-type uncertainty. Feature sets will include sequence composition, motif density, chromatin marks, accessibility, architectural protein occupancy, RNA-binding protein expression, protein multivalency, disorder-associated interaction potential, and polymer-inspired descriptors. Performance will be evaluated using chromosome holdout, dataset holdout, and cross-cell-type generalization tests.

Activity 5: Disease enrichment and variant interpretation. We will integrate GWAS summary statistics using stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression, fine-mapping annotations, transcriptome-wide association results, colocalization where public QTL data exist, and 3D variant-to-gene mapping. We will test whether microenvironment classes explain disease heritability beyond standard annotations. High-confidence loci will be prioritized when variants fall in disease-enriched microenvironments, contact relevant promoters, occur in active brain cell states, and alter predicted regulatory or biophysical features.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The project will deliver four major products. First, we will produce a public atlas of chromatin microenvironments across major human brain cell types, developmental contexts, and selected mouse comparative datasets. The atlas will provide standardized annotations for 3D regulatory neighborhoods, enhancer hubs, compartmental domains, loop-rich regions, repressive domains, and mixed or transitional chromatin states.

Second, we will release open computational workflows for harmonizing public 3D genome, single-cell transcriptomic, chromatin accessibility, epigenomic, proteomic, and genetic association data. These workflows will allow other investigators to reproduce our analyses, extend them to new cell types, and apply the same framework to other tissues or diseases.

Third, we will generate predictive models linking molecular features to mesoscale genome architecture. By combining chromatin-state annotations with protein disorder, multivalency, architectural protein occupancy, and polymer-inspired descriptors, the project will provide testable hypotheses for how local molecular interactions produce emergent regulatory neighborhoods.

Fourth, we will produce disease-focused maps that identify chromatin microenvironment classes enriched for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental risk. These results may improve variant interpretation by shifting analysis from isolated noncoding elements to the 3D regulatory systems in which variants act.

The impact extends beyond any individual dataset. The project will create a synthesis framework for studying emergence in genome regulation, provide benchmark data for methods development, and train early-career scientists in cross-disciplinary data integration. The work is feasible because all required datasets are public, the analytical tasks can be partitioned across expert subgroups, and NCEMS working group support will enable the sustained coordination, shared infrastructure, and community standards needed for rigorous synthesis.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from the outset. All datasets used will be publicly available, and each dataset will be documented with accession numbers, licensing information, genome build, processing history, and quality-control metrics. We will maintain a living data inventory that distinguishes raw public inputs, harmonized intermediate files, derived annotations, and final analysis products.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories under a permissive open-source license. Workflows will be implemented using reproducible workflow managers and containerized software environments to ensure portability across NCEMS computing resources, institutional clusters, and cloud platforms. Major analyses will include executable notebooks, configuration files, test datasets, and automated checks. We will use continuous integration for core software components and maintain stable release versions linked to manuscripts and data products.

The working group will establish shared standards for authorship, contribution tracking, data citation, documentation, code review, and conflict resolution. Analytical decisions will be recorded in public issue trackers or project logs when appropriate. Predefined analysis plans will be used for major enrichment and prediction analyses to reduce selective reporting. Sensitivity analyses will test robustness to cell-type labels, dataset inclusion, contact normalization, genomic resolution, and model class.

Training will be integrated with project execution. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will participate in code sprints, reproducibility workshops, cross-lab analysis teams, and short tutorials on 3D genome data, statistical genetics, protein feature annotation, and biophysical modeling. Trainees will be assigned leadership roles for defined analysis modules and will receive mentoring in collaborative software development, data stewardship, responsible AI use, and scientific communication.

Final products will include public data tables, genome browser tracks, interactive visualizations, software packages, workflow documentation, and preprints or peer-reviewed manuscripts. Outputs will be deposited in durable community repositories with persistent identifiers, enabling reuse by molecular, cellular, neuroscience, and computational biology communities.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination across disciplines, institutions, data modalities, and analytical traditions. The requested resources will support working group meetings, trainee participation, shared computation, open-science infrastructure, and community dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

A major budget category will be collaborative meetings. We propose an initial in-person launch meeting to finalize data standards, assign analysis modules, and define reproducibility policies; two focused working meetings for model development and disease enrichment analyses; and a final synthesis meeting to complete manuscripts, data releases, and training materials. Between meetings, monthly virtual sessions and smaller analysis subgroup calls will maintain progress.

A second category will support trainees and early-career researchers. Funds will enable graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to attend NCEMS meetings, participate in code sprints, lead reproducible analysis modules, and receive cross-disciplinary mentoring. This investment directly addresses NCEMS goals of recruiting diverse talent and training a data-savvy workforce.

A third category will cover computational and data-management needs. Although all source data are public, harmonizing single-cell, 3D genome, epigenomic, proteomic, and GWAS datasets requires storage, workflow execution, versioned releases, and secure collaborative workspaces. NCEMS cyberinfrastructure and staff expertise will accelerate standardization, containerization, workflow testing, and dissemination.

A fourth category will support open-science products, including documentation, website or portal development, interactive visualization, long-term repository deposition, and community tutorials. Funds may also support limited professional assistance for project management, accessibility of training materials, and coordination of cross-institutional deliverables.

The participating investigators will contribute complementary expertise in single-cell genome architecture, chromatin structure, polymer and mesoscale biophysics, proteomics, transcriptomics, statistical genetics, and open data integration. NCEMS resources will transform these complementary capabilities into a coherent community-scale synthesis effort that exceeds what any single laboratory or informal collaboration could accomplish.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Contamination-Aware Synthesis of Microbiome Functional Modules Linked to Emergent Human Proteome and Metabolome States
abstract: Human-associated microbial communities generate metabolites, antigens, and extracellular molecules that can reorganize host cellular signaling, yet it remains unclear when these effects arise from individual microbial species versus emergent community-level functional modules. This working group will synthesize publicly available metagenomic, metabolomic, proteomic, and genetic datasets to test whether reproducible microbial gene modules across oral and gut ecosystems predict host circulating protein and metabolite states better than taxonomic profiles alone. The central hypothesis is that host molecular phenotypes associated with inflammation, cardiometabolic risk, and immune regulation are coupled to mesoscale microbial community structures: combinations of genes, strains, and biochemical pathways that emerge from microbial consortia and cannot be inferred from single taxa in isolation. We will integrate open shotgun metagenomes from modern oral and gut microbiome studies, public ancient dental calculus datasets that preserve historical oral community functions, paired host metabolomic and proteomic datasets from public repositories, and publicly released proteogenomic and disease-association summary statistics. A major innovation will be a contamination-aware synthesis framework that explicitly models low-biomass and ancient DNA artifacts, batch effects, reference database bias, and cross-study metadata heterogeneity before biological interpretation. Metagenomes will be reprocessed through a standardized protein-level annotation workflow using fast translated alignment, functional binning, strain-aware profiling, and phylogenetic network methods to identify recurrent microbial gene constellations. These modules will then be linked to host proteins and metabolites using multilevel models, network propagation, and genetic triangulation where public pQTL, mQTL, and disease GWAS summary statistics are available. Rather than asking whether a named microbe is associated with a disease, the project asks whether convergent microbial biochemical capacities produce emergent host molecular states across populations, body sites, and time. The project is well suited to NCEMS because it requires coordinated expertise that no single laboratory is likely to possess: scalable metagenomic algorithm development, ancient and low-biomass microbiome quality control, microbial ecology, plasma proteomics, metabolomics, epidemiology, and causal inference. NCEMS support would enable community standards for harmonizing microbiome multi-omics metadata, convene domain experts to evaluate contamination and provenance policies, and train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in reproducible synthesis workflows spanning sequence analysis, molecular epidemiology, and open science. Deliverables will include an openly documented workflow, reusable contamination and metadata scoring tools, harmonized feature tables, interactive microbial gene-module networks, and a public atlas linking microbial functional emergence to host proteome and metabolome signatures. By combining modern and ancient microbiome data with human molecular phenotype resources, this project will clarify which microbial community functions are stable, recently altered, or disease-linked, and will provide a generalizable strategy for studying emergent molecular phenotypes generated by complex microbial consortia.
background_and_significance:
Human microbiomes are increasingly recognized as dynamic molecular systems that influence host biology through metabolites, surface molecules, secreted proteins, immunogenic fragments, and modifications of diet-derived or host-derived substrates. Yet many microbiome associations remain difficult to interpret because they are framed around named taxa rather than the distributed biochemical capacities of communities. Different strains and species can encode overlapping functions, while the same species can have divergent gene content across individuals and environments. As a result, host molecular outcomes may be driven less by the presence of a single organism than by mesoscale microbial functional modules: recurrent combinations of genes, pathways, strains, and ecological interactions that generate emergent biochemical properties at the community level.

This question is central to molecular and cellular emergence. Microbial communities sit between individual molecules and host tissues, producing molecular outputs that can alter immune signaling, epithelial barrier function, inflammatory tone, and systemic metabolism. Circulating proteins and metabolites provide an experimentally grounded readout of these effects, capturing host pathway activation, cardiometabolic state, immune regulation, and disease risk. Public investments have generated large, complementary datasets relevant to this problem, including shotgun metagenomes from oral and gut ecosystems, paired metabolomic and proteomic cohorts, ancient dental calculus metagenomes, microbial genome and protein reference databases, pQTL and mQTL maps, and disease GWAS summary statistics. However, these data have rarely been synthesized in a contamination-aware, function-centered framework that compares microbial modules with host molecular phenotypes across populations, body sites, and historical time.

The oral and gut microbiomes are ideal systems for this synthesis. Both are dense, taxonomically complex communities with strong links to inflammation, cardiometabolic disease, immune modulation, and nutritional status. Oral communities are also represented in ancient dental calculus, providing rare access to historical microbial functions that predate modern industrialized diets, antibiotics, and current health behaviors. Integrating ancient and modern datasets can distinguish stable human-associated functions from recently altered modules, but it also requires rigorous treatment of DNA damage, environmental contamination, reagent contaminants, low-biomass artifacts, and reference database bias.

The proposed working group addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do microbiome disease associations replicate poorly at the taxonomic level, while mechanistic studies often implicate conserved biochemical activities. We will test whether functionally defined microbial modules provide a more reproducible and biologically interpretable bridge between microbiome composition and host proteome and metabolome states. The work requires expertise in scalable metagenomic algorithms, ancient DNA authentication, low-biomass contamination control, microbial ecology, proteomics, metabolomics, epidemiology, genetic triangulation, and open data synthesis. NCEMS is uniquely suited to support this effort because the project is not a conventional single-cohort analysis; it is a community-scale synthesis that will harmonize public data, define reusable quality standards, and train researchers to study emergent molecular phenotypes using reproducible computational workflows.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The central research question is whether recurrent microbial functional modules across human-associated ecosystems predict host molecular states more robustly than taxonomic profiles alone. We define a microbial functional module as a statistically reproducible and biologically interpretable constellation of genes, protein families, pathways, strains, or phylogenetically distributed functions that co-occur across samples and jointly encode a potential biochemical activity. We define host molecular states as coordinated patterns in circulating proteins and metabolites that reflect inflammation, immune regulation, cardiometabolic risk, tissue remodeling, nutrient handling, or disease-linked physiology.

Question 1 asks: Do microbial gene and pathway modules recur across independent oral and gut metagenomic datasets after correction for contamination, batch effects, and reference bias? Hypothesis 1 is that a subset of microbial functions will form conserved modules across studies even when taxonomic composition differs, because ecological redundancy and horizontal gene transfer allow multiple community configurations to produce similar biochemical capacities. We expect these modules to include functions related to short-chain fatty acid metabolism, sulfur and nitrogen metabolism, bile acid transformation, amino acid fermentation, cell envelope biosynthesis, oxidative stress tolerance, and immunogenic surface structures.

Question 2 asks: Do these functional modules explain variation in host proteomic and metabolomic signatures better than species-level or genus-level abundance profiles? Hypothesis 2 is that function-centered modules will outperform taxonomic features in cross-cohort prediction of host inflammatory proteins, metabolic biomarkers, and disease-associated molecular signatures. This hypothesis follows from the expectation that host cells respond to molecular products and biochemical activities rather than to taxonomic labels. We will evaluate predictive value using held-out cohorts, body-site stratification, and models that compare taxonomic, pathway, strain, and module-level feature spaces.

Question 3 asks: Which microbial modules show evidence of historical stability or recent perturbation when modern oral metagenomes are compared with authenticated ancient dental calculus datasets? Hypothesis 3 is that core oral biofilm functions involved in adhesion, carbohydrate utilization, and anaerobic metabolism will be detectable across time, whereas modules linked to modern diet, antimicrobial exposure, and inflammatory disease risk will show altered prevalence or network context in contemporary populations. Ancient data will not be treated as direct disease cohorts; rather, they will provide a temporal reference for the persistence and reorganization of community-level functions.

Question 4 asks: Can public human genetic resources help distinguish correlation from plausible causal pathways linking microbial modules to host molecular phenotypes and disease risk? Hypothesis 4 is that modules associated with host proteins or metabolites that are themselves genetically linked to disease will prioritize biologically coherent pathways, such as microbial metabolites influencing inflammatory mediators or cardiometabolic proteins. We will use pQTL, mQTL, and GWAS summary statistics for triangulation, colocalization-informed annotation, and sensitivity analyses, not as definitive proof of causality.

Collectively, these questions test an emergence-oriented model: host molecular phenotypes arise from interactions among microbial genes, community structure, biochemical outputs, and host regulatory networks. The project will identify when microbial effects are reducible to individual taxa and when they require a mesoscale community explanation.
methods_and_approach:
The working group will synthesize existing publicly available datasets only. Candidate data sources will include shotgun metagenomes from oral and gut microbiome studies in repositories such as NCBI SRA, ENA, MG-RAST, Qiita, and curated microbiome resources; public ancient dental calculus shotgun datasets with available authentication information; cohort datasets with paired microbiome and metabolomic or proteomic measurements where access terms permit reuse; public metabolomic resources such as MetaboLights, GNPS-associated datasets, and cohort summary data; public plasma proteomic datasets; and open pQTL, mQTL, and disease GWAS summary statistics. No new biospecimens, sequencing, or experimental measurements will be generated.

Aim 1 will create a harmonized metadata and quality framework. We will extract sample provenance, body site, extraction method, library preparation, sequencing platform, geography, host age and sex when available, disease status, antimicrobial exposure, diet-related fields, negative controls, and data-use restrictions. A contamination and provenance score will be assigned to each sample and study. For modern low-biomass datasets, the score will incorporate negative control availability, expected microbial biomass, reagent-associated taxa and genes, index hopping risk, and batch structure. For ancient datasets, it will incorporate DNA fragment length, damage patterns, deamination profiles, excavation context, laboratory processing history, environmental microbial signatures, and authentication metrics. These scores will be used in sensitivity analyses rather than as simple exclusion rules.

Aim 2 will reprocess metagenomes using a standardized protein-level workflow. Reads will undergo adapter trimming, quality filtering, host read removal where permitted, duplicate assessment, and contamination screening. Functional annotation will use fast translated alignment against versioned protein databases, complemented by gene family and pathway mapping to resources such as UniRef, KEGG Orthology, eggNOG, MetaCyc, and antimicrobial resistance or virulence databases where appropriate. Taxonomic profiling, strain-aware profiling, and assembly-based recovery of gene neighborhoods will be performed when data quality supports it. Phylogenetic network methods will be used to visualize and quantify conflicting signals, strain relationships, and functional convergence across taxa.

Aim 3 will infer microbial functional modules. We will build study-aware co-abundance and co-occurrence networks using compositional data methods, sparse latent factor models, graph clustering, and stability selection. Modules will be required to replicate across independent datasets or show coherent body-site or time-stratified specificity. We will compare modules to taxonomic features, individual pathways, and random gene sets. Batch effects and database bias will be assessed through leave-study-out validation, reference subsampling, alternative annotation databases, and negative control features.

Aim 4 will link microbial modules to host proteome and metabolome states. Multilevel models will account for cohort, body site, sequencing depth, demographic covariates, disease status, medication, and technical platform. Predictive performance will be assessed using nested cross-validation and external validation when possible. Network propagation will connect microbial modules to metabolite classes, protein pathways, and disease-associated molecular signatures. Genetic triangulation will integrate public pQTL, mQTL, and GWAS evidence to prioritize host proteins and metabolites plausibly involved in disease pathways. Throughout, the group will emphasize effect stability, uncertainty quantification, and transparent reporting over single-study discovery.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The project will produce a public atlas of microbial functional modules linked to host circulating proteins and metabolites across oral and gut ecosystems. The atlas will distinguish modules that are robust across modern cohorts, modules that are body-site specific, modules that appear historically persistent in authenticated ancient dental calculus, and modules that are associated with contemporary inflammatory or cardiometabolic molecular states. By explicitly comparing module-level, pathway-level, strain-level, and taxonomic models, the project will clarify when microbial effects on host biology are reducible to named organisms and when they emerge from distributed community functions.

Scientific outcomes will include testable hypotheses about microbial biochemical capacities that shape host immune and metabolic regulation, prioritized host proteins and metabolites for future mechanistic work, and a framework for integrating microbiome data with proteogenomic and metabolomic disease resources. The project will also generate practical advances: harmonized feature tables, contamination and provenance scoring tools, standardized metadata templates, reproducible metagenomic annotation workflows, and interactive network visualizations that can be reused by the broader community.

The impact aligns directly with NCEMS priorities. The work addresses an emergent mesoscale biological phenomenon, integrates public molecular and cellular data at community scale, and requires expertise spanning computational biology, microbial ecology, ancient DNA, contamination control, proteomics, metabolomics, epidemiology, and statistical genetics. It will help move microbiome research beyond fragile taxonomic associations toward mechanistic, reproducible synthesis of molecular functions. Training outcomes will include hands-on experience for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in scalable sequence analysis, multi-omics integration, uncertainty-aware modeling, and open collaborative science. The final products will serve both as a discovery resource and as a generalizable model for studying emergent host phenotypes generated by complex microbial consortia.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The working group will operate under open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from project initiation. All datasets will be drawn from public repositories or controlled-access resources with explicit reuse permissions; derived products will be released only in forms consistent with source data terms, participant privacy, Indigenous data governance considerations, and community standards for ancient and human microbiome data. The group will maintain a public project registry describing datasets considered, inclusion and exclusion criteria, quality metrics, analysis plans, deviations from plans, and versioned deliverables.

Computational workflows will be implemented in portable workflow systems such as Nextflow or Snakemake and distributed through public version-controlled repositories. Software environments will be containerized using Docker or Apptainer, with dependency locks, test datasets, continuous integration, and documented compute requirements. All reference databases will be versioned, checksummed, and accompanied by scripts that recreate mapping tables. Statistical notebooks and analysis scripts will be organized to separate raw data acquisition, preprocessing, feature generation, modeling, visualization, and manuscript figures.

Reproducibility will be strengthened through multiple validation layers: leave-study-out testing, alternative annotation databases, negative control features, contamination-score sensitivity analyses, randomization tests, and independent code review within the working group. The project will publish harmonized metadata schemas, feature matrices where permitted, contamination and provenance scores, module definitions, model coefficients, uncertainty intervals, and interactive networks through stable repositories with persistent identifiers.

Training will be embedded in the open science plan. Trainees will participate in code review, documentation sprints, reproducibility audits, and cross-disciplinary tutorials on metagenomics, ancient DNA authentication, proteomics, metabolomics, and genetic triangulation. Authorship, contribution tracking, data stewardship, and conflict resolution policies will be established at the first NCEMS meeting and revisited throughout the project.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires coordinated synthesis infrastructure, repeated cross-disciplinary convening, trainee integration, and computational resources beyond a typical single-laboratory effort. The proposed budget will support a two-year working group organized around three in-person NCEMS meetings, regular virtual analysis sessions, focused hackathons, trainee exchanges, cloud or high-performance computing time, open repository maintenance, and dissemination activities.

Personnel support will prioritize graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and research software contributors who will implement workflows, harmonize metadata, curate public datasets, and perform reproducibility checks. Funds will support trainee participation across institutions and career stages, including travel to NCEMS meetings and short collaborative visits that pair computational trainees with domain experts in microbiome ecology, ancient DNA, proteomics, metabolomics, and statistical genetics. A modest allocation will support professional data management and software engineering consultation to ensure that deliverables are reusable by the broader community.

Computational costs will cover storage and reanalysis of large public shotgun metagenomic datasets, protein-level translated alignment, functional annotation, network inference, model fitting, and workflow testing across alternative databases. Because no new experimental data will be generated, no funds are requested for sequencing, sample collection, wet-lab reagents, or participant recruitment. Instead, resources are concentrated on synthesis: data acquisition, standardization, scalable computation, and open dissemination.

NCEMS convening resources will be used to establish community standards for contamination-aware microbiome synthesis, develop metadata recommendations, and evaluate ethical and provenance issues around ancient and human-associated microbiome data. Final dissemination will include an open workshop, public documentation, archived workflows, interactive module networks, and a synthesis manuscript. This allocation directly supports the NCEMS mission to catalyze multidisciplinary teams, leverage public data, train data-savvy scientists, and discover emergent principles in molecular and cellular biosciences.
