title: Predicting Emergent Mesoscale Organization in Bacteria from Public Multi-Omics, Sequence Features, and Cellular Phenotypes
abstract:
Bacteria exhibit coordinated physiological states that cannot be understood from single genes alone: stress bodies assemble, nucleoids compact, secretion and virulence programs switch on, plasmids alter host resource allocation, and quorum-sensing networks synchronize population behavior. Many of these transitions likely depend on mesoscale organization—multivalent protein, RNA, DNA, and metabolite interactions that create spatially and dynamically distinct cellular environments. Yet bacterial transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, genome-variation, and imaging datasets are usually analyzed separately, leaving a central question unresolved: can emergent bacterial cell states be predicted from the combined expression and sequence-encoded interaction properties of their molecular components?

This working group will synthesize existing public data to build a cross-species computational framework for identifying bacterial mesoscale organization states and linking them to phenotypic outcomes such as antibiotic tolerance, virulence, host association, plasmid maintenance, and evolutionary adaptation. We will integrate publicly available RNA-seq, proteomics, metabolomics, Tn-seq/fitness profiling, genome variation, plasmid annotations, and cell-imaging datasets from model bacteria and clinically or ecologically important systems, including Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus subtilis, Vibrio species, and insect-associated symbionts where sufficient public data exist. These data will be harmonized with protein sequence features relevant to mesoscale assembly, including intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, low-complexity regions, oligomerization domains, nucleic-acid-binding capacity, predicted interaction networks, and known bacterial compartment or condensate-associated proteins.

The project will ask whether bacterial conditions cluster into reproducible “mesoscale organization regimes” that cut across species and perturbations. For example, do antibiotic stress, efflux-pump disruption, quorum-sensing activation, phage or plasmid carriage, nutrient limitation, and host-associated growth produce common signatures of nucleoid remodeling, RNA-protein granule formation, metabolic compartment use, or envelope-associated assembly? We will develop machine-learning and statistical-physics-inspired models that combine gene-expression modules with sequence-encoded interaction propensities to infer latent organizational states. These states will then be tested computationally for their ability to explain higher-level outcomes: growth-rate tradeoffs, evolutionary repeatability, virulence-factor expression, horizontal gene transfer compatibility, and persistence under stress.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise across bacterial evolution, synthetic and plasmid biology, host-microbe systems, biophysics of multivalent assembly, machine learning, omics harmonization, and open-science infrastructure. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will create interoperable public resources: a curated bacterial multi-omics compendium, a catalog of predicted mesoscale-organizing proteins and RNAs, reusable workflows for cross-study normalization and uncertainty tracking, and interactive maps linking molecular features to emergent cell-state phenotypes. Trainees will participate in data curation sprints, model-building workshops, and reproducible workflow development.

By connecting bacterial physiology and evolution to principles of mesoscale molecular organization, this project will provide a new synthesis framework for understanding how collective cellular properties emerge from molecular interactions. The resulting resource will help researchers predict when genetic or environmental perturbations are likely to rewire bacterial organization, alter pathogenic potential, destabilize engineered circuits, or constrain evolutionary trajectories.
background_and_significance: Bacterial cells exhibit organized, dynamic physiological states despite lacking many membrane-bound organelles characteristic of eukaryotes. Stress granule-like assemblies, biomolecular condensates, nucleoid domains, chemosensory clusters, metabolic microcompartments, secretion platforms, plasmid partitioning systems, and envelope-associated complexes all demonstrate that mesoscale organization is central to bacterial function. These structures arise from collective interactions among proteins, RNAs, DNA, metabolites, membranes, and ions. Their behavior is emergent: it cannot be predicted by measuring one gene, one protein, or one metabolic pathway in isolation. Instead, bacterial cell states reflect coordinated changes in expression, molecular interaction capacity, biophysical assembly properties, and environmental context. Public molecular and cellular datasets now provide an unprecedented opportunity to synthesize these dimensions across species and perturbations. Thousands of bacterial RNA-seq datasets describe responses to antibiotics, nutrient shifts, host environments, quorum-sensing signals, phage exposure, plasmid acquisition, and engineered genetic constructs. Proteomic and metabolomic resources quantify changes in molecular abundance and pathway usage. Tn-seq and other fitness-profiling datasets identify genes required under specific conditions. Genome sequencing of clinical, laboratory-evolved, environmental, and host-associated isolates reveals recurrent mutations and mobile genetic elements. Public microscopy datasets increasingly capture nucleoid morphology, cell shape, reporter activity, and spatial organization. However, these resources are fragmented by species, platform, annotation standard, and disciplinary focus. Most analyses remain confined to one data type or one organism, limiting the ability to identify general principles of emergent bacterial organization. The central gap addressed by this proposal is the lack of a synthesis framework connecting sequence-encoded interaction features to organism-level and population-level phenotypes through mesoscale cellular states. Proteins enriched for intrinsic disorder, charged regions, low-complexity motifs, oligomerization domains, and nucleic-acid-binding capacity are plausible drivers of phase separation, clustering, scaffolding, and dynamic compartmentalization. RNAs, plasmid loci, metabolites, and membrane surfaces can further tune these assemblies. Yet bacterial systems biology has rarely integrated such biophysical features with transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, genotype-phenotype maps, and imaging. As a result, fundamental questions remain unresolved: why do diverse stresses induce similar growth-arrest or persistence phenotypes; when do plasmids impose manageable versus destabilizing burdens; how do quorum-sensing and virulence programs reorganize the cell; and why do some evolutionary trajectories repeatedly alter regulatory and transport functions? This project is well aligned with NCEMS because it addresses emergence at the mesoscale using only existing public data, requires a multidisciplinary working group, and will generate reusable community resources. The proposed synthesis combines bacterial evolution, synthetic biology, host-microbe biology, plasmid annotation, statistical biophysics, machine learning, and reproducible data engineering. By comparing model bacteria, pathogens, and symbionts, the project will move beyond organism-specific catalogs toward predictive principles. The significance is both fundamental and practical: identifying bacterial mesoscale organization regimes will clarify how molecular interactions produce coherent cell states and will improve prediction of antibiotic tolerance, virulence activation, engineered circuit instability, plasmid persistence, and adaptation in changing environments.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will address a focused set of synthesis questions that connect molecular features to emergent bacterial cell states. Question 1: Do public multi-omics and imaging datasets contain reproducible signatures of mesoscale organization that recur across bacterial species, growth conditions, and perturbations? We hypothesize that conditions such as antibiotic exposure, nutrient limitation, oxidative stress, quorum-sensing activation, phage challenge, plasmid carriage, and host-associated growth will cluster into a finite number of latent organization regimes. These regimes will not simply mirror taxonomy or growth rate; instead, they will reflect coordinated changes in nucleoid-associated proteins, RNA metabolism, chaperones, membrane and envelope proteins, secretion machinery, metabolite pools, and stress-responsive interaction networks. Question 2: Can sequence-encoded molecular interaction properties improve prediction of bacterial phenotypes beyond expression abundance alone? We hypothesize that gene modules enriched for intrinsically disordered proteins, charge-patterned regions, low-complexity sequences, coiled-coil or oligomerization domains, RNA-binding domains, DNA-binding domains, and multivalent interaction motifs will be disproportionately informative for predicting shifts in cellular organization and downstream outcomes. A stress response in which these features are strongly induced should be more likely to involve condensate-like or scaffolded assemblies than a response dominated by purely catalytic enzymes. Question 3: Are there conserved and species-specific bacterial proteins, RNAs, and mobile genetic elements that act as mesoscale organizers? We hypothesize that some organizers are deeply conserved, such as nucleoid-associated factors, translation-associated proteins, RNA chaperones, and cell-envelope assembly factors, whereas others are lineage-specific, condition-specific, or encoded on plasmids, prophages, pathogenicity islands, and symbiosis-associated elements. This distinction will help explain why related perturbations can produce shared physiological outcomes while relying on different molecular components. Question 4: Can inferred mesoscale organization regimes explain higher-level phenotypes relevant to evolution, pathogenesis, and engineering? We hypothesize that latent organizational states will predict antibiotic tolerance, persistence, virulence-factor expression, biofilm-associated transitions, host colonization programs, plasmid maintenance costs, horizontal gene transfer compatibility, and the repeatability of evolutionary adaptation. For example, conditions that induce nucleoid compaction and translational repression may align with tolerance and slow growth, whereas conditions that induce secretory and quorum-sensing assemblies may align with virulence activation. Question 5: What methodological strategies are needed to integrate heterogeneous public datasets without overinterpreting batch effects or incomplete metadata? We hypothesize that robust synthesis will require hierarchical models, orthology-aware feature mapping, uncertainty propagation, negative controls, and benchmarking against held-out datasets. The project will therefore treat mesoscale regimes as probabilistic latent variables rather than fixed labels. These questions are designed for community-scale synthesis because no single laboratory can curate the required breadth of public data, combine the needed biophysical and bacterial expertise, and build interoperable workflows spanning omics, sequence features, imaging, plasmid annotation, and phenotypic metadata.
methods_and_approach: The project will proceed through coordinated synthesis activities organized around data assembly, feature engineering, model development, validation, and dissemination. No new experimental data will be generated. First, the working group will build a curated bacterial multi-omics compendium from public repositories including NCBI Sequence Read Archive, Gene Expression Omnibus, ArrayExpress, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, MetaboLights, BioCyc-associated resources, public Tn-seq and fitness-profile collections, RefSeq, GenBank, PATRIC or BV-BRC, and image repositories where suitable metadata and licensing permit reuse. Initial focal taxa will include Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus subtilis, Vibrio species, and selected insect-associated symbionts with adequate public coverage. Datasets will be prioritized when they include interpretable perturbations, biological replication, accessible raw or processed files, and links to phenotypes such as growth, virulence, persistence, host association, or plasmid carriage. Second, the group will harmonize annotations across species. Ortholog groups, gene families, regulatory categories, plasmid features, mobile elements, and pathway assignments will be mapped using public genome annotations and reproducible pipelines. Expression data will be reprocessed or normalized using study-appropriate workflows, with batch structure, platform, strain background, and condition metadata recorded explicitly. Proteomic and metabolomic values will be converted to comparable feature spaces where direct cross-study normalization is not justified. Fitness data will be represented as condition-specific gene importance profiles. Imaging data will be transformed into quantitative descriptors such as cell size, nucleoid morphology, reporter localization, and population heterogeneity when published segmentations or analyzable images are available. Third, sequence-derived mesoscale features will be computed for proteins and, where feasible, structured and regulatory RNAs. Features will include intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, low-complexity regions, prion-like or aggregation-prone regions, coiled-coils, oligomerization domains, nucleic-acid-binding motifs, membrane association, signal peptides, predicted protein interactions, domain valence, and homology to known bacterial condensate, compartment, cytoskeletal, partitioning, or nucleoid-associated proteins. Plasmids will be annotated for replication, partitioning, conjugation, toxin-antitoxin, regulatory, and burden-associated modules. Fourth, models will infer latent mesoscale organization regimes. We will compare matrix factorization, topic models, variational latent-variable models, graph neural networks, multi-view learning, and hierarchical Bayesian models. Statistical-physics-inspired features will summarize multivalent interaction potential, scaffold-client imbalance, charge complementarity, and concentration-dependent assembly propensity at the module level. Models will be evaluated by cross-validation across studies, species, perturbation classes, and data modalities. Predictive targets will include antibiotic tolerance, virulence-related expression, quorum-sensing activation, plasmid stability proxies, growth-rate tradeoffs, fitness profiles, and evolutionary recurrence of mutations. Fifth, the working group will hold NCEMS-supported data curation sprints, model comparison workshops, trainee hackathons, and synthesis meetings. Domain experts will define biological interpretation standards, while data scientists will maintain reusable workflows and uncertainty reports. Feasibility will be maintained by staged milestones: an initial E. coli and P. aeruginosa pilot compendium, extension to additional taxa, release of feature catalogs, benchmark modeling, and final synthesis maps.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will deliver four major outcomes. First, it will produce a curated public compendium linking bacterial multi-omics, genome variation, plasmid features, fitness profiles, imaging-derived descriptors, and phenotypic metadata across diverse public studies. This resource will reduce barriers for researchers who currently must repeatedly locate, reformat, and reconcile fragmented datasets. Second, it will generate a catalog of candidate bacterial mesoscale organizers, including proteins, RNAs, gene modules, plasmid-encoded systems, and mobile-element-associated features predicted to influence compartmentalization, scaffolding, nucleoid structure, or dynamic assembly. Third, it will provide open workflows for integrating expression modules with sequence-encoded interaction properties and for inferring probabilistic mesoscale organization regimes. Fourth, it will create interactive maps that connect perturbations, molecular features, latent organizational states, and phenotypic outcomes. The scientific impact will be a new synthesis framework for bacterial cell states. Instead of treating stress responses, virulence, plasmid burden, persistence, and adaptation as separate phenomena, the project will test whether they share recurring organizational principles. This perspective can clarify why unrelated perturbations produce similar physiological states and why similar genetic changes have different effects across strains or environments. Practical impacts include improved prediction of antibiotic tolerance and virulence-associated transitions, better understanding of plasmid compatibility and engineered circuit instability, and new hypotheses about evolutionary constraints in pathogens and symbionts. The project will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in public-data synthesis, cross-domain communication, reproducible computational biology, and responsible machine learning. By aligning bacterial physiology with NCEMS priorities in emergent mesoscale organization, the working group will create resources and conceptual tools that remain useful well beyond the initial focal taxa.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The working group will operate under open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from project initiation. All code, workflow definitions, metadata schemas, documentation, analysis notebooks, model specifications, benchmark results, and derived nonrestricted datasets will be released through public version-controlled repositories. Stable releases will be archived with persistent identifiers through Zenodo or an equivalent service. Data products will include provenance records identifying original repositories, accession numbers, licenses, processing steps, software versions, quality-control decisions, and known limitations. When raw public data are too large to redistribute, the group will provide scripts and containerized workflows that regenerate derived outputs from original accessions. Reproducibility will be supported through workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or comparable systems; container environments; continuous integration tests for core code; standardized file formats; and machine-readable metadata. Analyses will include uncertainty estimates, batch-effect diagnostics, sensitivity tests, and negative-control tasks to reduce the risk of overinterpreting correlations. Model cards and dataset cards will describe intended uses, limitations, taxonomic coverage, missing-data patterns, and biases arising from uneven public-data availability. The group will develop community guidelines for responsible interpretation of inferred mesoscale states, emphasizing that predictions identify synthesis-derived hypotheses rather than direct experimental proof of physical assemblies. NCEMS meetings will include open documentation sessions so that trainees and external contributors can understand decisions and reuse outputs. Preprints, peer-reviewed manuscripts, tutorials, and workshop materials will be made openly available. Interactive visualizations will allow users to inspect evidence behind predicted organizers, regimes, and phenotype links. The project will invite feedback through public issue trackers, virtual community demonstrations, and targeted outreach to bacterial systems biology, biophysics, microbiology, and synthetic biology communities. This approach ensures that the products are transparent, reusable, extensible, and aligned with community-created standards.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Predicting Emergent Proteostasis Network Rewiring from the Energetic Landscapes of Human Membrane Protein Variants
abstract:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how small energetic changes in individual proteins propagate into mesoscale cellular outcomes such as altered trafficking, interactome rewiring, stress-response activation, and disease phenotypes. This working group will test the hypothesis that membrane protein variants produce emergent cellular behavior when their effects on folding, translocon insertion, and interaction energetics cross context-dependent thresholds that redirect proteins through the proteostasis and signaling networks. We will address this question entirely through synthesis of public data, integrating molecular biophysics, protein interaction networks, variant interpretation, and single-cell regulatory-state analysis.

The project will focus on human membrane proteins with unusually rich public data: CFTR, GPCRs, potassium and other ion channels, transporters, and disease-associated receptors. We will assemble a harmonized atlas linking ClinVar and gnomAD variants, deep mutational scanning and multiplexed expression datasets, public cell-surface trafficking and abundance measurements, AlphaFold and experimental structures, predicted stability and membrane-insertion energetics, BioPlex/IntAct/STRING protein interaction networks, proteostasis-factor annotations, public drug-response and pharmacological chaperone datasets, and disease- or tissue-relevant single-cell RNA-seq atlases. This integrated resource will allow us to ask when molecular perturbations remain locally buffered and when they instead generate higher-order changes in cellular network state.

Analytically, we will construct a multilayer graph in which nodes represent variants, protein structural regions, proteostasis components, interaction partners, regulatory programs, and cellular phenotypes. Edges will encode physical contacts, predicted energetic coupling, genetic or clinical associations, co-expression, protein-protein interactions, and regulatory relationships inferred from public single-cell data. We will develop open workflows that combine structure-aware variant effect prediction, thermodynamic modeling, network propagation, community detection, and regulon activity inference. A key innovation will be to search explicitly for nonlinear thresholds: regions of sequence and structural space where gradual changes in predicted folding or interaction energy are associated with abrupt changes in trafficking efficiency, interactome connectivity, or activation of stress and inflammatory programs.

This synthesis will produce three major outcomes. First, it will identify general biophysical rules that explain why some variants primarily reduce protein abundance, others alter signaling or channel function without strong expression defects, and others unexpectedly increase surface delivery or network connectivity. Second, it will define tissue- and cell-type-specific vulnerability maps showing where the same molecular defect is predicted to have different consequences because proteostasis capacity, interaction partners, or regulatory circuits differ across cellular contexts. Third, it will nominate classes of variants most likely to be rescued by pharmacological chaperones or other proteostasis-modulating interventions based on energetic mechanism rather than gene identity alone.

The project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can integrate the necessary expertise across membrane protein biophysics, disease variant interpretation, large-scale interaction networks, single-cell regulatory analysis, and reproducible data engineering. The working group will include computational and experimental domain experts, trainees, and community contributors who will co-develop open standards for representing energetic variant effects in network models. All curated datasets, analysis pipelines, benchmark tasks, interactive visualizations, and training modules will be released publicly. By connecting atomic-scale energetic perturbations to emergent mesoscale network states, this project will provide a generalizable framework for understanding how molecular variation becomes cellular phenotype.
background_and_significance:
Membrane proteins account for a large fraction of therapeutic targets and inherited disease genes, yet the cellular consequences of their variation remain difficult to predict. A single amino acid substitution can reduce folding efficiency, alter membrane insertion, change ligand or partner binding, perturb channel gating, or modify trafficking through the secretory pathway. In many cases these molecular effects do not translate linearly into phenotype. Some variants with modest destabilization cause severe loss of function because they are retained by quality-control systems. Others show substantial molecular defects but are buffered by redundant pathways or high expression. Still others unexpectedly increase surface delivery, network connectivity, or signaling output. These observations point to emergence: new cellular properties arise when molecular perturbations interact with proteostasis, trafficking, and regulatory networks at the mesoscale.

The proposed working group addresses a fundamental gap between atomic-scale variant interpretation and systems-scale cellular behavior. Existing resources provide unusually rich, but fragmented, information relevant to this gap. Public variant databases capture population frequency and clinical annotations. Deep mutational scanning, multiplexed expression assays, and receptor-scale measurements quantify variant effects on abundance, surface expression, trafficking, or function for selected membrane proteins. AlphaFold models, cryo-EM structures, and homology models enable residue-level structural interpretation. Public interaction databases map physical and functional protein associations, including many proteostasis factors, signaling adaptors, and trafficking components. Single-cell atlases reveal tissue- and cell-type-specific expression of folding machinery, receptors, channels, inflammatory programs, and stress-response regulators. Drug-response and pharmacological chaperone datasets provide additional information about which molecular defects can be rescued.

Individually, these datasets have advanced variant classification, network biology, and cell-state analysis. However, they have rarely been synthesized to ask whether energetic perturbations produce predictable network-level transitions. This is precisely the type of question that requires community-scale synthesis rather than new experimental data. The relevant information spans protein biophysics, membrane insertion, disease genetics, interactome modeling, transcriptional regulation, single-cell biology, and therapeutic mechanism. No single laboratory can curate, harmonize, and interpret these data sources at the necessary scale while developing reusable standards for the broader community.

The project is strongly aligned with the NCEMS mission because it focuses on emergent mesoscale phenomena: the redirection of membrane protein variants through cellular proteostasis and signaling networks. The central premise is that folding energy, insertion efficiency, and interaction energetics form local molecular landscapes, but cellular outcomes appear when those landscapes intersect with network thresholds. These thresholds may differ across cell types because proteostasis capacity, partner availability, and regulatory states are not uniform. By synthesizing public data across proteins and contexts, the working group will identify generalizable rules that explain when variants remain locally buffered, when they trigger quality-control responses, and when they reshape higher-order cellular networks. The resulting framework will support basic discovery, improve interpretation of rare disease variants, and guide mechanism-based therapeutic hypotheses without generating new experimental data.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project is organized around four linked research questions that connect molecular energetics to emergent cellular outcomes. First, what energetic features best distinguish membrane protein variants that reduce abundance or surface trafficking from those that primarily alter function or signaling? We hypothesize that variants affecting core folding stability, transmembrane insertion, and domain-interface packing will be enriched among abundance- and trafficking-defective alleles, whereas variants in ligand-binding, gating, or signaling interfaces will more often preserve expression while rewiring downstream activity. We further hypothesize that the predictive value of any single energetic feature will be protein-family dependent, requiring models that include topology, domain architecture, and quality-control route.

Second, do membrane protein variants exhibit nonlinear thresholds between predicted molecular perturbation and cellular phenotype? We hypothesize that gradual changes in folding free energy, membrane insertion score, or interaction energy will be associated with abrupt changes in observable outcomes such as surface delivery, interaction-network degree, or stress-program activation. These thresholds are expected to occur near decision points in biosynthesis and trafficking, including translocon insertion, endoplasmic reticulum quality control, ER-associated degradation, Golgi export, plasma membrane retention, and ligand-dependent stabilization. The working group will test whether threshold positions can be inferred from public variant-effect data and whether they recur across unrelated membrane protein families.

Third, how does cellular context modify the consequences of the same molecular perturbation? We hypothesize that cell-type-specific expression of chaperones, degradation factors, trafficking adaptors, signaling partners, and transcriptional regulators shifts the boundary between buffered and pathological states. For example, a variant with borderline folding stability may be tolerated in a cell type with high proteostasis capacity but produce disease-relevant loss of expression in a cell type where key folding or trafficking factors are limiting. Similarly, a receptor or channel variant may cause network rewiring only in cells that co-express the appropriate partners and regulatory circuits. Public single-cell atlases provide the data needed to estimate these context-dependent vulnerability maps.

Fourth, can integrated energetic-network models identify classes of variants likely to respond to pharmacological chaperones or related proteostasis-modulating interventions? We hypothesize that rescuable variants will occupy a specific region of the landscape: energetically impaired enough to be recognized by quality-control systems, but not so structurally disrupted that ligand binding, channel activity, or essential interactions are eliminated. In contrast, variants that primarily perturb active-site chemistry, gating, or obligatory interaction interfaces may require function-specific interventions rather than generalized stabilization. Public drug-response, modulator, and chaperone datasets will be used to benchmark this hypothesis.

Across all questions, the overarching hypothesis is that emergent proteostasis network rewiring can be predicted when variant energetics are interpreted within a multilayer cellular network. The group will explicitly evaluate competing explanations, including purely additive molecular models, gene-specific empirical models, and network-only models lacking energetic information. Success will be defined not by perfect prediction for every variant, but by demonstrating that integrated synthesis reveals reproducible thresholds, context dependencies, and mechanistic classes that are invisible when datasets are analyzed separately.
methods_and_approach:
The working group will conduct a synthesis-only project using public datasets and reproducible computational workflows. The first phase will build a harmonized membrane protein variant atlas. Target proteins will include CFTR, GPCRs, voltage-gated and ligand-gated ion channels, solute carriers, transporters, and disease-associated receptors for which public variant, structure, expression, trafficking, functional, or clinical data exist. Variants will be mapped to canonical UniProt sequences and protein isoforms, annotated with ClinVar significance, gnomAD frequency, disease association, residue conservation, topology, domain membership, and structural location. Public deep mutational scanning, multiplexed expression, surface abundance, receptor biosynthesis, channel function, and rescue datasets will be curated with provenance, assay metadata, and measurement uncertainty.

The second phase will generate standardized energetic and structural features without producing new experimental data. AlphaFold structures, Protein Data Bank entries, membrane topology annotations, and predicted transmembrane segments will be integrated. Variant effects on folding stability, local packing, interface energetics, membrane insertion, disorder, and post-translational modification motifs will be estimated using established open tools and compared across tools to quantify robustness. Where multiple structures or conformations exist, analyses will retain ensemble information rather than forcing a single model. Features will be calibrated against public abundance and function measurements using cross-validation that separates proteins and protein families to test generalization.

The third phase will construct a multilayer network representing the mesoscale system. Nodes will include variants, residues, structural regions, membrane protein genes, proteostasis factors, trafficking adaptors, interaction partners, transcription factors, regulons, cell types, disease terms, and therapeutic compounds. Edges will represent physical contacts, predicted energetic coupling, co-complex membership, protein-protein interactions from BioPlex, IntAct, STRING, and related resources, genetic or clinical associations, co-expression, ligand or drug relationships, and regulatory links inferred from public single-cell RNA-seq atlases. Single-cell datasets will be selected from disease- and tissue-relevant public repositories, processed using consistent quality-control criteria, and analyzed to estimate cell-type-specific expression of proteostasis, trafficking, and signaling modules. Regulon activity inference and co-expression analysis will identify regulatory programs associated with unfolded protein response, ER stress, inflammatory activation, epithelial differentiation, neuronal excitability, and other relevant states.

The fourth phase will test for nonlinear emergence. We will apply segmented regression, generalized additive models, Bayesian change-point analysis, survival-style threshold models, network propagation, graph embeddings, and community detection to determine where continuous energetic variation predicts abrupt changes in trafficking, abundance, connectivity, or regulon activation. Models will be benchmarked against additive baselines, sequence-only predictors, structure-only predictors, and network-only predictors. Generalization will be evaluated by leaving out protein families, assay types, or disease areas. Uncertainty will be propagated from source data, energetic predictions, and network confidence scores.

The working group will meet through NCEMS-supported virtual and in-person synthesis sessions. Subteams will focus on data standards, energetic annotation, network construction, single-cell context modeling, benchmarking, and visualization. Trainees will rotate across subteams to gain experience in protein biophysics, graph analysis, and reproducible data science. External community contributors will be invited to critique data models, nominate additional public datasets, and test workflows on independent proteins.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The project will deliver a public, analysis-ready atlas linking human membrane protein variants to structural features, predicted energetic effects, proteostasis and interaction networks, cellular contexts, clinical annotations, and therapeutic-response information. This resource will be valuable beyond the initial proteins because it will establish reusable schemas for representing variant energetics in network models. Interactive visualizations will allow users to inspect how a residue or variant connects to folding constraints, trafficking routes, interaction partners, cell-type expression, and disease relevance.

Scientifically, the working group expects to identify general principles governing how molecular perturbations become mesoscale cellular outcomes. These principles may explain why some variants are primarily abundance defects, why others alter signaling or channel activity while retaining expression, and why a subset produces unexpected increases in trafficking or connectivity. A major outcome will be the identification of threshold regions where small energetic changes are associated with sharp transitions in surface expression, interaction rewiring, or stress-regulatory state. Such thresholds would provide direct evidence for emergent behavior arising from the coupling of molecular energetics to cellular networks.

The project will also produce tissue- and cell-type-specific vulnerability maps. These maps will predict where variants with similar energetic defects may have different consequences because cells differ in chaperone levels, degradation capacity, trafficking machinery, interaction partners, or regulatory programs. This will improve interpretation of rare variants in diseases involving epithelia, neurons, immune cells, endocrine tissues, and other contexts in which membrane protein function is central.

Finally, the work will inform therapeutic hypothesis generation. By classifying variants by energetic mechanism and network context, the project will nominate variants most likely to respond to pharmacological chaperones, stabilizing ligands, trafficking modulators, or pathway-specific interventions. The impact will be both conceptual and practical: a general synthesis framework for emergence in molecular and cellular biology and a community resource for variant interpretation, network analysis, and trainee education.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from initiation through dissemination. All datasets used will be publicly available, and each source will be documented with accession numbers, download dates, licenses, preprocessing steps, assay descriptions, and known limitations. Curated derivative tables will be released under permissive licenses when compatible with source terms. When redistribution of a source dataset is restricted, workflows will provide automated instructions for users to retrieve the data directly and reproduce the processed outputs.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, and documented release tags. Workflows will be implemented with portable workflow managers and containerized environments so that analyses can be rerun on laptops, institutional clusters, or cloud resources. Computational notebooks will be used for exploration, but final analyses will be converted into scripted pipelines with explicit inputs, outputs, and parameters. Model training, benchmark splits, random seeds, and evaluation metrics will be preserved to support transparent comparison and reuse.

The working group will create community-facing data standards for representing variant-level energetic annotations, membrane topology, assay outcomes, network edges, and cell-type context. These standards will be developed iteratively with feedback from structural biologists, network scientists, clinicians, single-cell analysts, and trainees. Metadata will follow FAIR principles, and outputs will be deposited in stable repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, and relevant domain repositories.

Training is integral to the open science plan. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will participate in data curation sprints, reproducibility checks, software documentation, and cross-disciplinary tutorials. Training modules will cover membrane protein variant annotation, graph construction, single-cell regulon analysis, uncertainty-aware modeling, and ethical use of clinical variant information. Public webinars and workshop materials will enable broader community adoption. Authorship and contribution policies will be established at project launch to ensure transparent recognition of intellectual, technical, and training contributions.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordination, shared infrastructure, and sustained synthesis activity across scientific communities that do not routinely operate within a single laboratory framework. Funds will be allocated to working group meetings, trainee participation, computational resources, data engineering, open science dissemination, and community engagement. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data; all effort will focus on public data synthesis, integration, analysis, benchmarking, and release.

Meeting support will enable two in-person synthesis workshops and regular virtual working sessions. The first workshop will finalize data standards, assign curation responsibilities, and define benchmark tasks. The second will integrate results across subteams, evaluate models, prepare community releases, and plan manuscripts. Travel funds will prioritize participation by trainees, early-career scientists, researchers from institutions with varied research capacities, and contributors whose expertise fills critical gaps in protein biophysics, network science, single-cell analysis, disease genetics, or software engineering.

Personnel resources will support part-time effort for data harmonization, workflow development, and project coordination. A dedicated data-science coordinator will maintain repositories, enforce metadata standards, manage release schedules, and assist subteams with reproducibility. Trainee support will provide short-term fellowships or stipends for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who lead curated dataset modules, benchmarking analyses, visualization tools, or training materials.

Computational resources will include cloud storage, scalable compute for structure-based feature calculation and graph modeling, container registries, and web hosting for interactive dashboards. The project will use open-source software whenever possible to minimize long-term costs and maximize reuse. Requested resources also include accessibility support for hybrid meetings, transcription of training sessions, and production of reusable educational materials.

The anticipated deliverables are a harmonized public atlas, documented workflows, benchmark datasets, model outputs, visualization portals, training modules, and open manuscripts. NCEMS provides the necessary convening power and synthesis infrastructure to transform fragmented public data into a coherent framework for understanding emergent proteostasis network rewiring.

author: gpt-5.5
title: A Multiscale Atlas Linking RNA-Protein Binding Grammar to Condensate Identity, Dynamics, and Cellular Routing
abstract: Biomolecular condensates arise from many weak, context-dependent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet we still lack a predictive framework for how molecular binding features give rise to mesoscale condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes. This working group will synthesize public datasets to test the hypothesis that distinct classes of cellular condensates are specified by a combinatorial RNA-protein grammar: RNA sequence and structure features tune the effective valency, spacing, and competition among RNA-binding proteins, thereby shaping condensate composition, material state, exchange kinetics, and trafficking connections across the cell. The project will not generate new data. Instead, it will integrate existing eCLIP and related RNA-binding maps, stress granule and nuclear body proteomes, public proximity-labeling datasets, high-content imaging screens, RNA structure probing data, disorder and low-complexity annotations, AlphaFold and experimental structural models, public condensate databases, and transcriptome-wide localization and abundance measurements. The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate identity can be predicted more accurately from an integrated RNA-protein interaction network than from protein sequence features or RNA abundance alone. We will build a harmonized atlas connecting RNAs, RNA-binding proteins, condensate-associated factors, subcellular compartments, and perturbation contexts. Computational structural biology will be used to annotate interaction modules, including folded RNA-binding domains, intrinsically disordered regions, short linear motifs, predicted RNA secondary structure, base-composition patterns, and multivalent binding architectures. Network science and machine learning will then identify recurring molecular motifs that distinguish condensates with different behaviors, such as rapid exchange versus persistent retention, nuclear versus cytoplasmic localization, stress-inducible versus constitutive assembly, and trafficking-linked versus compartment-restricted composition. A key innovation is to treat RNAs not simply as clients or scaffolds, but as programmable multivalent polymers whose structural ensemble and binding-site organization can remodel protein interaction networks. The working group will compare candidate grammars across public datasets from human cells, yeast, plants, and disease-relevant perturbations to determine which principles are conserved and which are lineage- or context-specific. We will also evaluate whether disease-associated mutations and repeat expansions alter predicted RNA-protein network topology in ways that favor aberrant mesoscale assemblies. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in RNA structure, condensate biophysics, proteomics, imaging, network inference, machine learning, and open data engineering, and because the relevant datasets are fragmented across communities that rarely use common standards. Deliverables will include a public, versioned RNA-protein-condensate knowledge graph; reproducible workflows for dataset harmonization and feature extraction; benchmark tasks for predicting condensate association and dynamic class; and interpretable models that nominate molecular design principles for condensate regulation. Trainees will participate in cross-lab code sprints, data annotation jamborees, and collaborative model-evaluation workshops, gaining experience in reproducible synthesis science. By linking molecular-scale binding determinants to mesoscale condensate properties and cellular routing, this project will provide a general framework for understanding how new cellular behaviors emerge from distributed RNA-protein interaction networks.
background_and_significance: Membraneless condensates provide a major example of emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak interactions among many biomolecules generate mesoscale compartments with properties not evident from any single component. Stress granules, processing bodies, nucleoli, Cajal bodies, paraspeckles, transcriptional condensates, and plant hydration-responsive assemblies differ in composition, kinetics, material state, stimulus sensitivity, and connections to trafficking pathways. Yet the field still lacks a general framework that links molecular binding determinants to these higher-order behaviors. Many studies emphasize protein low-complexity regions, prion-like domains, folded interaction modules, and post-translational modification. These features are important, but they cannot fully explain why related RNA-binding proteins partition into different condensates, why the same protein can behave differently across RNA contexts, or why specific transcripts strongly influence assembly, dissolution, retention, and transport. RNAs are abundant, structured, chemically heterogeneous polymers that contain repeated sequence motifs, structured and unstructured binding sites, variable spacing, and competitive binding opportunities. These features can alter effective valency, recruit or exclude RNA-binding proteins, and reshape interaction networks. Public data now make it possible to test this idea at community scale. ENCODE and related consortia provide eCLIP and orthogonal RNA-binding maps for hundreds of RNA-binding proteins. Transcriptome-wide RNA structure probing datasets, RNA localization resources, single-cell and bulk abundance measurements, ribonucleoprotein interaction studies, and disease variant catalogs provide RNA-centered context. Proteomic studies define components of stress granules, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, processing bodies, and other assemblies across conditions. Proximity-labeling datasets, including compartmental and trafficking-focused experiments, reveal dynamic exchange between condensates and adjacent cellular regions. High-content imaging screens quantify condensate morphology, number, intensity, persistence, and perturbation response. Structural resources, including AlphaFold models, RNA-binding domain annotations, low-complexity and disorder predictors, and experimentally determined structures, support mechanistic annotation of interaction modules. However, these datasets are distributed across repositories, processed with inconsistent identifiers, and rarely analyzed together. This fragmentation prevents the field from asking whether condensate identity is predictable from an integrated RNA-protein network and whether common design rules operate across compartments, organisms, and disease states. The proposed working group directly addresses NCEMS priorities by synthesizing existing public data, focusing on mesoscale emergence, and requiring expertise that exceeds a single laboratory. The central significance is conceptual and practical. Conceptually, the project will treat condensates as emergent network states controlled by combinatorial RNA-protein grammar rather than as lists of components or isolated phase-separating proteins. Practically, it will produce harmonized data structures, benchmarks, and interpretable models that allow researchers to evaluate how sequence, structure, valency, competition, localization, and trafficking jointly shape condensate behavior. This synthesis can clarify long-standing puzzles in RNA granule biology, reveal conserved and context-specific principles, and create a reusable foundation for future predictive studies of condensate regulation and dysfunction.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will organize its synthesis around one overarching question: can mesoscale condensate identity, dynamics, and cellular routing be predicted more accurately from integrated RNA-protein interaction grammar than from protein sequence features, RNA abundance, or condensate proteome membership alone? We define RNA-protein grammar as the joint organization of RNA sequence composition, RNA secondary structure, binding-site number, spacing, accessibility, transcript localization, RNA abundance, RNA modifications when public data are available, and the protein features that recognize or compete for those RNAs, including folded RNA-binding domains, intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity tracts, short linear motifs, oligomerization modules, and post-translationally regulated segments. Question 1 asks which molecular features distinguish condensate classes. We hypothesize that condensates with similar dynamics share network-level motifs, such as high RNA-mediated multivalency for rapidly exchanging granules, stable protein-protein cores with RNA-tuned recruitment for persistent nuclear bodies, and sequence-specific RNA hubs for stimulus-inducible assemblies. We predict that feature sets combining RNA binding maps, transcript structure, and protein disorder will outperform models based only on protein low-complexity scores or RNA abundance. Question 2 asks how RNA architecture tunes material and kinetic behavior. We hypothesize that binding-site valency, spacing, and structural accessibility modulate the balance between bridging, competition, and client displacement. Transcripts with clustered accessible motifs for multiple compatible RNA-binding proteins should promote network condensation, whereas transcripts with overlapping motifs for competing proteins or highly structured inaccessible regions should reduce effective connectivity. Question 3 asks whether condensate routing is encoded in RNA-protein network topology. We hypothesize that trafficking-linked condensates contain bridge factors and RNAs connecting localization modules, translation regulation, stress response, and organelle-proximal proteomes, whereas compartment-restricted condensates show more insulated networks. Public proximity-labeling and localization datasets provide a direct test by linking condensate components to movement between cytosol, nucleus, mitochondria-proximal regions, stress granules, and other compartments. Question 4 asks which grammar elements are conserved across human cells, yeast, plants, and disease-relevant perturbations. We hypothesize that broad principles, such as multivalency, disorder-coupled RNA recognition, and competition among RNA-binding proteins, are conserved, but the specific motifs and regulatory modules differ by lineage, cell state, and environmental context. Question 5 asks whether pathogenic mutations and repeat expansions perturb predicted condensate grammars. We hypothesize that disease-associated variants alter network topology by increasing local valency, changing motif accessibility, weakening chaperone-like RNA-protein interactions, or redirecting proteins into aberrant assemblies. These hypotheses are falsifiable through held-out prediction tasks, cross-dataset replication, negative controls using randomized binding sites and expression-matched transcripts, and comparison of integrated models to simpler baselines. The result will be not only a catalog of associations but a tested framework for predicting emergent condensate properties from molecular-scale information.
methods_and_approach: The project will be conducted entirely through synthesis of existing public datasets. Aim 1 will build a harmonized RNA-protein-condensate atlas. We will collect eCLIP and related binding datasets from ENCODE, POSTAR, doRiNA, GEO, SRA-derived processed tables when public, and organism-specific resources. Condensate component lists will be drawn from public condensate databases, stress granule and nuclear body proteomes, curated literature tables with reusable licenses, and proteomic repositories. Proximity-labeling and trafficking datasets will be incorporated from public mass spectrometry repositories, including studies mapping compartment exchange and stress-dependent relocalization. Imaging-derived phenotypes will be assembled from public high-content screens and databases reporting condensate number, size, localization, persistence, intensity, and perturbation response. RNA structure, abundance, localization, and isoform information will be obtained from public transcriptome-wide structure probing, RNA atlas, single-cell, and bulk transcriptomic datasets. All entities will be mapped to stable identifiers, including Ensembl, UniProt, RefSeq, Gene Ontology, Sequence Ontology, and controlled vocabulary terms for condensates and compartments. Aim 2 will extract mechanistic features. For proteins, we will annotate folded domains, RNA-binding domains, predicted disorder, low-complexity regions, prion-like composition, charged patterning, aromatic and glycine-rich segments, short linear motifs, oligomerization domains, phosphorylation sites, and structural confidence from AlphaFold and experimental models. For RNAs, we will compute motif density, motif clustering, binding-site accessibility, predicted and experimentally supported secondary structure, repeat content, base composition, length, isoform-specific untranslated region architecture, abundance, localization, and conservation. Where public perturbation datasets exist, we will encode stress, mutation, knockdown, overexpression, and disease context. Aim 3 will construct multilayer networks and knowledge graphs. Nodes will include RNAs, proteins, domains, motifs, condensates, compartments, conditions, phenotypes, and datasets. Edges will represent binding, co-partitioning, proximity, trafficking, co-expression, localization, structural compatibility, and perturbation effects, with provenance and confidence scores. Network analyses will identify hubs, bridges, communities, motif-rich subgraphs, and condition-specific rewiring. Aim 4 will develop predictive and interpretable models. Benchmark tasks will include predicting condensate association, condensate class, dynamic category, stress inducibility, nuclear versus cytoplasmic partitioning, and trafficking linkage. Models will include regularized regression, graph neural networks, random forests, gradient boosting, matrix factorization, and interpretable rule-learning approaches. Performance will be evaluated with strict train-test splits by dataset, condensate type, organism, and protein family to prevent leakage. Baselines will include protein sequence features alone, RNA abundance alone, and proteome membership alone. Aim 5 will perform cross-species and disease analyses. Orthology mapping, conserved domain architectures, and comparable condensate phenotypes will be used to identify shared grammar elements across human, yeast, and plants. Disease variants, repeat expansions, and mutation datasets will be projected onto the knowledge graph to predict how network topology changes. The working group will meet through NCEMS-supported workshops, code sprints, trainee-led annotation jamborees, and model review sessions, with milestones for data freeze, feature release, benchmark release, model release, and synthesis manuscripts.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The primary outcome will be a public, versioned RNA-protein-condensate knowledge graph that links molecular interaction features to mesoscale condensate behaviors and cellular routing. This resource will allow users to query which RNAs, proteins, domains, motifs, structures, compartments, perturbations, and phenotypes support a proposed condensate mechanism. A second outcome will be reproducible workflows for harmonizing heterogeneous public datasets, extracting RNA and protein features, generating multilayer networks, and benchmarking predictive models. A third outcome will be a set of interpretable models and benchmark tasks that quantify when integrated RNA-protein grammar improves prediction over simpler alternatives. Scientifically, the project will test whether condensate identity is an emergent property of distributed RNA-protein networks rather than a direct consequence of individual phase-separating proteins. It will identify candidate molecular design principles, such as motif spacing, RNA structural accessibility, multivalent binding architectures, competitive binding, and trafficking bridge nodes, that distinguish dynamic, persistent, inducible, and compartment-restricted condensates. Cross-species comparisons will separate conserved physical principles from organism-specific regulatory implementations. Disease-focused analyses will nominate mechanisms by which mutations, repeat expansions, or altered RNA-binding landscapes promote aberrant assemblies. The impact extends beyond condensate biology. The atlas and workflows will provide a reusable model for synthesis research in mesoscale cell biology, linking structural biology, proteomics, imaging, RNA biology, and machine learning. Because the project uses only public data, it will amplify prior investments, expose gaps in metadata and standards, and create community benchmarks for future studies. Trainees will gain practical experience in open, team-based data science and will help carry these standards into the next generation of molecular and cellular research.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from the start. All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories under a permissive open-source license. Workflows for data acquisition, identifier mapping, feature extraction, network construction, model training, and evaluation will be implemented with reproducible workflow managers and containerized software environments. Each data release will include machine-readable provenance, source accession numbers, processing parameters, software versions, quality-control metrics, and known limitations. The knowledge graph will be released in multiple interoperable formats, including tabular edge lists, RDF-compatible exports, and analysis-ready graph objects, with persistent identifiers assigned through public repositories. We will not redistribute restricted data; instead, we will prioritize public, reusable datasets and provide scripts that regenerate derived features from primary accessions whenever licensing allows. Model development will emphasize transparency. Benchmark definitions, train-test splits, negative controls, baseline models, hyperparameter ranges, and evaluation metrics will be frozen before final model comparison. We will report failures and dataset biases, including cell-type imbalance, assay-specific ascertainment, protein-family leakage, missing negative examples, and uncertainty in condensate labels. Interpretable feature attribution and network explanations will accompany predictive models to support mechanistic evaluation rather than black-box classification alone. Collaborative practices will include a written authorship and contribution policy, code review, issue tracking, open meeting notes when appropriate, and trainee-accessible documentation. Community engagement will occur through public tutorials, annotation jamborees, and feedback periods before major releases. Training materials will cover reproducible workflow design, responsible machine learning, metadata standards, graph analysis, and FAIR data principles. These practices will ensure that the project produces not only conclusions but reusable infrastructure that other researchers can inspect, rerun, extend, and challenge.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination across RNA biology, condensate biophysics, computational structural biology, proteomics, imaging analysis, network science, machine learning, and open data engineering. Requested resources will support working group meetings, trainee participation, collaborative computing, data curation, software engineering, and dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. Meeting funds will enable two in-person synthesis workshops and regular virtual working sessions. The first workshop will finalize dataset inclusion criteria, ontology mappings, benchmark definitions, and division of labor. The second will focus on model interpretation, cross-species synthesis, disease analyses, manuscript planning, and community release. Travel support will prioritize trainees, early-career researchers, and participants from institutions with limited research infrastructure, strengthening the geographic and career-stage diversity expected by NCEMS. Personnel and trainee support will fund graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and a part-time data engineer or research software specialist to maintain workflows, implement quality control, and ensure robust documentation. Computing resources will cover cloud storage, versioned data hosting, graph database deployment, container building, and model training. The project will use public repositories, institutional high-performance computing, and NCEMS cyberinfrastructure where available, avoiding duplicative local infrastructure. Curation funds will support structured annotation of condensate labels, perturbation contexts, imaging phenotypes, proteomic evidence, and RNA-protein binding confidence. Dissemination resources will support public tutorials, documentation, open workshops, and archival deposition of releases and training materials. The budget is designed around synthesis-specific needs: bringing fragmented public resources into a common framework, enabling collaboration beyond any single lab, training data-savvy researchers, and producing durable community assets. NCEMS resources will convert a collection of disconnected public datasets into an integrated platform for studying emergent mesoscale organization.
