author: gpt-5.5
title: A Cross-Kingdom Atlas of Sequence-to-Mesoscale Rules for Stress-Responsive Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: Cells often respond to environmental change by reorganizing disordered proteins, RNA, and multivalent interaction networks into mesoscale assemblies whose properties cannot be inferred from any single molecule alone. Yet the field lacks a unified, quantitative framework for predicting when sequence-encoded disorder produces adaptive condensates, maladaptive aggregates, or spatially organized non-phase-separated assemblies across cellular contexts. This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, cellular, and biophysical datasets to define generalizable rules connecting intrinsically disordered protein sequence features, RNA context, cellular environment, and emergent condensate properties during stress adaptation. The central question is: which combinations of sequence grammar, interaction valence, charge patterning, expression state, and client composition predict the mesoscale material state, spatial organization, and functional reversibility of stress-responsive condensates across bacteria, plants, yeast, and animals? The project will integrate existing data from condensate and phase-separation databases, proteome-wide disorder annotations, public mutational and saturation-concentration datasets, in vitro phase diagrams, protein-RNA interaction resources, stress-induced transcriptomic and proteomic datasets, AlphaFold-derived structural annotations, public microscopy image repositories, and cryo-electron tomography or volume electron microscopy datasets where available. We will build an open, harmonized data model that links molecular descriptors—stickers, spacers, aromatic and cationic motifs, charge patterning, predicted compaction, folded-domain valence, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification sites—to mesoscale observables such as condensate number, size distribution, coarsening behavior, localization, client enrichment, reversibility, and inferred material state. A major analytical innovation will be the development of physics-informed machine learning models that combine associative-polymer concepts, coarse-grained interaction potentials, image-derived condensate phenotypes, and cellular abundance estimates. Rather than treating condensate formation as a binary annotation, the models will infer context-dependent phase behavior and emergent mesoscale regimes: dispersed networks, dynamic droplets, arrested emulsions, gels, fibrillar condensates, and spatially patterned assemblies. Comparative analyses across taxa and stress conditions will test whether evolution repeatedly uses similar disorder-encoded design principles for adaptation, or whether distinct cellular milieus impose different solutions. This synthesis is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in disordered protein biophysics, molecular simulation, soft matter theory, image analysis, bacterial and eukaryotic cell organization, evolutionary genomics, and FAIR data engineering. NCEMS support would enable a community working group to establish shared vocabularies, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and uncertainty standards for condensate-related data, addressing a current bottleneck in the field: heterogeneous measurements that are difficult to compare or reuse. The anticipated outcomes are an open cross-kingdom atlas of stress-responsive disordered proteins and condensates, validated predictive models for sequence-to-mesoscale behavior, and a set of community guidelines for integrating condensate imaging, biophysical, and omics data. Trainees will participate through collaborative hackathons and model-building sprints focused on reproducible data curation, physics-aware machine learning, and open software development. By synthesizing existing data rather than generating new experiments, this project will reveal how molecular disorder gives rise to adaptive mesoscale organization and will provide a reusable framework for predicting emergent cellular responses from protein sequence and context.
background_and_significance: Environmental stress changes the physical and biochemical state of cells. Heat, osmotic shifts, starvation, oxidative stress, desiccation, infection, and developmental transitions can rapidly alter RNA availability, protein solubility, post-translational modification, crowding, pH, ionic strength, and energy-dependent remodeling. Across bacteria, plants, fungi, and animals, these changes are frequently accompanied by reorganization of intrinsically disordered proteins, RNA-binding proteins, folded multivalent scaffolds, and client molecules into mesoscale assemblies. Some assemblies are liquid-like condensates that concentrate clients and remain reversible; others are gels, fibrillar states, arrested emulsions, spatially patterned networks, or aggregates associated with dysfunction. These states are emergent because their properties arise from collective interactions among many molecules and cannot be predicted by inspecting a single sequence, structure, or binding event in isolation. A central challenge in molecular and cellular biosciences is to determine when sequence-encoded disorder supports adaptive organization and when similar molecular features lead to pathological or maladaptive material states. The field now has a remarkable quantity of public information relevant to this challenge. Databases describe proteins implicated in condensates, phase separation, stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, bacterial organizing bodies, plant stress assemblies, and disease-associated aggregates. Public repositories contain proteome-wide disorder predictions, low-complexity annotations, AlphaFold-derived structural models, mutational scans, saturation concentration measurements, in vitro phase diagrams, protein-RNA interaction maps, post-translational modification catalogs, transcriptomic and proteomic measurements across stress conditions, microscopy images, and ultrastructural data. However, these datasets were generated for different purposes, use inconsistent terminology, and rarely connect molecular grammar to cellular mesoscale outcomes. A protein may be labeled phase separating in one resource, stress-associated in another, disordered in a third, and aggregation-prone in a fourth, with little information about context, stoichiometry, RNA state, cellular abundance, or reversibility. This fragmentation prevents community-scale inference. Existing predictive approaches often reduce condensate biology to binary classifiers, despite the fact that cellular assemblies occupy a continuum of material and organizational regimes. A synthesis effort is therefore timely and necessary. By harmonizing public data across kingdoms and modalities, this working group will establish quantitative links between sequence features, interaction valence, cellular context, and emergent mesoscale phenotypes. The project directly addresses NCEMS priorities by focusing on emergence at the mesoscale between molecules and organelles, using only existing public data, requiring expertise beyond any single laboratory, and developing reusable analytical strategies. The significance extends beyond condensate biology. The resulting atlas and models will provide general principles for how molecular disorder, RNA, and cellular environment encode adaptive responses, thereby advancing understanding of cellular organization, stress tolerance, disease mechanisms, and evolutionary innovation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: The overarching research question is: which combinations of molecular grammar and cellular context predict the mesoscale state, spatial organization, and functional reversibility of stress-responsive condensates and related assemblies across bacteria, plants, yeast, and animals? We will address this question through four integrated aims. Aim 1 asks whether sequence features of intrinsically disordered regions are sufficient to define broad classes of stress-responsive mesoscale behavior. We hypothesize that sticker identity, sticker spacing, aromatic and cationic motif density, charge patterning, hydropathy, predicted compaction, low-complexity composition, and short linear interaction motifs provide a conserved but incomplete grammar for assembly. We expect these features to distinguish many dispersed, droplet-forming, gel-like, and aggregation-prone systems, but we predict that identical sequence grammars can yield different outcomes depending on abundance, RNA, partners, and stress state. Aim 2 asks how RNA and multivalent folded domains alter sequence-to-mesoscale relationships. We hypothesize that RNA-binding potential and folded-domain valence act as context-sensitive modifiers that tune percolation thresholds, client selectivity, material aging, and reversibility. In some systems, RNA will buffer or chaperone condensation by competing with self-association; in others, RNA will promote network formation by increasing effective valence. We will test whether these alternative regimes can be inferred from public binding maps, transcript abundance, RNA length and composition, and known domain architectures. Aim 3 asks whether cellular environment explains cross-kingdom differences in condensate organization. We hypothesize that bacteria, plants, yeast, and metazoan cells use overlapping polymer-physics principles but implement them under distinct constraints imposed by cell size, compartmentalization, cytoplasmic crowding, hydration, ionic conditions, stress duration, and proteostasis capacity. Thus, evolution may repeatedly select similar disorder-encoded modules while deploying them in different mesoscale architectures, including polar localization in bacteria, hydration-sensitive assemblies in plants, and RNA-rich granules in eukaryotic cytoplasm. Aim 4 asks whether public heterogeneous data can support quantitative prediction of emergent regimes rather than binary phase-separation labels. We hypothesize that physics-informed machine learning models constrained by associative-polymer theory, coarse-grained interaction potentials, and abundance-aware cellular features will outperform sequence-only classifiers. Predicted outputs will include probability distributions over mesoscale regimes, confidence intervals, and explanatory feature contributions. Key hypotheses will be evaluated by cross-validation across taxa, leave-one-system-out benchmarking, comparison with held-out mutational and phase-diagram datasets, and retrospective prediction of known stress-induced transitions. Success will be defined not only by predictive accuracy but by mechanistic interpretability: models should reveal combinations of valence, patterning, RNA context, and expression state that shift assemblies among dispersed networks, dynamic droplets, arrested emulsions, gels, fibrillar condensates, aggregates, and spatially organized non-phase-separated structures.
methods_and_approach: This working group will conduct a synthesis-only project using publicly available data and will not generate new experimental measurements. The approach has five linked components. First, we will construct a FAIR data model for stress-responsive mesoscale assemblies. The schema will capture proteins, isoforms, intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, RNA partners, organism, cell type, stress condition, measurement modality, perturbation, observed assembly state, localization, reversibility, and uncertainty. We will map existing terms from condensate, phase-separation, aggregation, protein-disorder, RNA-binding, and microscopy resources into a controlled vocabulary developed with community input. Second, we will assemble molecular descriptors. Protein sequences will be obtained from UniProt and reference proteomes; disorder, low-complexity, charge patterning, aromatic and cationic motif organization, hydropathy, predicted compaction, prion-like composition, short motifs, and post-translational modification sites will be computed using reproducible open pipelines. AlphaFold-derived models will be used to annotate folded-domain valence, accessible interaction surfaces, and disorder-to-order boundaries. RNA-binding potential will be integrated from public CLIP, RIP, interactome capture, domain annotation, and sequence motif resources. Third, we will curate mesoscale observables from existing datasets. Public in vitro phase diagrams, saturation concentrations, mutational scans, rheological or diffusion measurements where available, and coarse-grained simulation benchmarks will be harmonized with cellular observations from microscopy repositories, published image supplements, and ultrastructural datasets. Image-derived features will include condensate number, size distribution, morphology, localization, coarsening behavior, intensity partitioning, and recovery or dissolution after stress relief when metadata permit. Automated segmentation and feature extraction will be performed only on public images, with manual review for benchmark subsets. Cryo-electron tomography and volume electron microscopy data will be used, where available, to annotate ultrastructural classes such as filamentous networks, porous assemblies, or dense bodies. Fourth, we will develop physics-informed predictive models. Baseline models will include sequence-only classifiers and regression models. Advanced models will combine graph representations of multivalent molecules, polymer-inspired features, cellular abundance estimates from public proteomics and transcriptomics, RNA context, and stress-specific environmental proxies. Outputs will be probabilistic assignments to emergent regimes and quantitative predictions such as saturation concentration ranges, droplet coarsening propensity, client enrichment, and reversibility likelihood. Model constraints will be informed by stickers-and-spacers concepts, associative-polymer percolation, charge-regulated coarsening, and available coarse-grained interaction potentials. Fifth, we will perform comparative analyses across kingdoms and stress types. We will identify convergent design principles, lineage-specific solutions, and outlier systems that reveal limits of current theory. The working group will operate through NCEMS-supported workshops, data-curation sprints, virtual analysis meetings, and trainee-led software hackathons. Expertise in disordered protein biophysics, soft matter theory, molecular simulation, image analysis, bacterial organization, eukaryotic stress biology, evolutionary genomics, and FAIR engineering is essential for feasibility.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will deliver three major products. First, we will release a cross-kingdom atlas of stress-responsive disordered proteins, RNAs, clients, and mesoscale assemblies. The atlas will connect molecular descriptors to experimentally observed or inferred cellular states and will include evidence codes, provenance, uncertainty, and links to source datasets. Second, we will produce benchmark datasets and validated predictive models for sequence-to-mesoscale behavior. Rather than reporting only whether a protein forms condensates, the models will estimate context-dependent probabilities for dispersed networks, dynamic droplets, arrested emulsions, gels, fibrillar assemblies, aggregates, and spatially patterned structures. Third, we will publish community guidelines for describing condensate-related data, including minimal metadata for stress conditions, abundance, RNA context, imaging modality, perturbation history, and reversibility. The scientific impact will be to transform a fragmented literature into a quantitative framework for emergence in molecular and cellular systems. The project will clarify which features of disordered proteins are broadly conserved predictors of adaptive organization and which depend strongly on organismal or cellular context. It will help resolve long-standing confusion caused by inconsistent use of terms such as condensate, aggregate, granule, body, gel, and phase-separated assembly. By integrating sequence grammar, biophysical measurements, public omics, and image-derived phenotypes, the project will create a reusable strategy for studying other mesoscale cellular systems. The broader impact includes improved interpretation of stress adaptation, neurodegenerative disease mechanisms, microbial organization, plant environmental resilience, and synthetic design of biomolecular assemblies. NCEMS support will make possible a community-scale synthesis that no single group could complete alone and will train trainees in open, quantitative, collaborative bioscience.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All project activities will follow open science, team science, and reproducible research practices consistent with NCEMS goals. The working group will use only publicly available data and will document dataset inclusion criteria, licensing, provenance, versioning, and quality-control decisions. A public project repository will host data dictionaries, controlled vocabularies, curation templates, code, notebooks, model configurations, analysis workflows, benchmark splits, and documentation. Stable releases of the atlas, software, and models will be archived with persistent identifiers through community repositories such as Zenodo, Dryad, GitHub releases, and appropriate biological data archives. Workflows will be implemented in containerized and environment-locked formats, using workflow managers where practical, so that analyses can be rerun by users outside the team. Each derived feature will be traceable to source records and computational parameters. The team will report negative results, ambiguous annotations, and uncertainty rather than forcing all systems into a single category. Model evaluation will use transparent train-test splits, cross-validation, held-out organism and held-out protein-family tests, calibration analysis, and interpretable feature attribution. Public issue trackers and discussion forums will allow community members to suggest corrections, contribute annotations, and request features. Trainees will receive structured training in FAIR data stewardship, reproducible coding, statistical validation, responsible AI use, and collaborative authorship norms. Authorship and contribution policies will be established at project launch and will recognize curation, software, analysis, and conceptual contributions. Preprints, open-access publications, conference tutorials, and recorded workshops will disseminate results broadly. The group will also produce lightweight educational modules so that graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and new users can learn how to analyze condensate-related public data without specialized local infrastructure.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is requested because the project requires sustained coordination, shared computational infrastructure, data engineering, and cross-disciplinary synthesis beyond the capacity of an individual laboratory or existing collaboration. Funds and center resources will support three in-person working group meetings, regular virtual meetings, trainee participation, data-curation sprints, model-building hackathons, cloud computing, software maintenance, and public dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. Personnel effort will focus on synthesis roles: a part-time data engineer to implement the harmonized schema and data pipelines; trainee stipends or travel support for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers contributing to curation, image analysis, and modeling; and limited support for domain experts who will lead annotation standards, benchmarking, and interpretation. Travel funds will enable participation by researchers from different geographic regions, institution types, career stages, and disciplinary backgrounds, including molecular biophysicists, cell biologists, computational scientists, soft matter theorists, image analysts, bacterial and plant biologists, and evolutionary genomics researchers. Computational resources will include cloud storage for curated metadata and derived image features, CPU and GPU time for large-scale feature generation and model training, and continuous integration services for reproducible workflows. Meeting resources will be used for structured workshops on vocabulary alignment, uncertainty standards, public image reuse, physics-informed machine learning, and community guideline drafting. NCEMS staff expertise in synthesis facilitation, data management, open science policy, and collaborative project governance will be essential for keeping the project interoperable and community-facing. The budget will prioritize reusable products over one-time analyses: open datasets, documented software, benchmark models, tutorials, and archived workflows. This resource plan directly advances NCEMS goals by enabling multidisciplinary synthesis of public molecular and cellular data, training a data-savvy workforce, and producing infrastructure that the broader community can reuse.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Mapping Emergent Drug-Tolerant Cell States from Extrachromosomal DNA and 3D Regulatory Architecture in Cancer Cell Lines
abstract:
Cancer cell lines with rich public multi-omics profiles provide an unusual opportunity to ask how molecular parts combine into mesoscale structures that generate emergent phenotypes such as transcriptional heterogeneity, pathway plasticity, and drug tolerance. This working group will synthesize existing public data to test the hypothesis that drug response is shaped not only by individual mutations or gene expression programs, but by emergent regulatory assemblies formed through interactions among copy-number amplification, extrachromosomal DNA, enhancer rewiring, 3D chromatin contacts, and protein-coding variant effects. These assemblies can create variable oncogene dosage, altered enhancer accessibility, and heterogeneous single-cell states that are not predictable from any one data modality alone.

The project will integrate publicly available datasets across molecular and cellular scales, including DepMap/CCLE genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, CRISPR-dependency, and drug-sensitivity profiles; public single-cell RNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets from cancer cell lines; ENCODE, 4DN, and related chromatin accessibility, transcription factor occupancy, enhancer, Hi-C, Micro-C, and promoter-capture resources; TCGA and PCAWG-derived structural variation and amplification calls; public ecDNA and focal amplification annotations from resources such as AmpliconArchitect-based analyses; and available microscopy or image-derived ecDNA measurements where public. The synthesis will focus on well-profiled breast, melanoma, glioblastoma, colorectal, and lung cancer lineages where multi-omics, drug response, and genome-architecture data overlap sufficiently for cross-lineage comparison.

We will develop a multimodal graph-learning framework in which genes, enhancers, variants, regulatory motifs, chromatin contacts, amplified segments, proteins, pathways, metabolites, drugs, and single-cell states are represented as interacting layers. The model will combine supervised, semi-supervised, and positive-unlabeled learning to handle incomplete labels for ecDNA and drug-tolerant phenotypes. It will infer enhancer-gene and amplification-gene relationships, identify 3D regulatory neighborhoods associated with heterogeneous expression, and predict which mesoscale features best explain sensitivity, resistance, or adaptive plasticity across drug classes. Protein-structure and sequence-function annotations will be incorporated for coding variants in amplified or dependency-associated genes, allowing the group to distinguish regulatory dosage effects from altered protein function. Single-cell data will be used to quantify whether predicted mesoscale regulatory assemblies correspond to emergent subpopulations rather than bulk-average expression shifts.

The central scientific products will be: an open atlas of inferred cancer-cell-line mesoscale regulatory assemblies; interpretable models linking these assemblies to drug response and genetic dependency; benchmark datasets for multimodal prediction of emergent cellular phenotypes; and reusable workflows for integrating single-cell, 3D genome, cancer genomics, proteomics, and pharmacogenomic data. The project requires NCEMS support because it spans data types, algorithms, and biological expertise that exceed the scope of a single laboratory: cancer systems biology, 3D genome organization, machine learning, single-cell genomics, protein variant interpretation, and open-science software engineering. Trainees will participate through cross-institutional data-analysis sprints, reproducibility reviews, and open tutorials on multimodal biological graph modeling. By synthesizing existing data rather than generating new experiments, the working group will reveal how mesoscale genome organization and molecular variation combine to produce emergent cancer cell behaviors relevant to therapeutic response.
background_and_significance: Cancer therapy response is often modeled as a function of individual driver mutations, basal gene expression, or pathway activity. These predictors have produced important biomarkers, yet they frequently fail to explain why genetically similar cancer cells exhibit heterogeneous transcriptional states, reversible drug tolerance, and rapid pathway switching. A growing body of public data suggests that these phenotypes arise from mesoscale regulatory organization: focal amplifications and extrachromosomal DNA alter gene dosage; enhancer landscapes are rewired by structural variation and transcription factor redistribution; 3D chromatin contacts place genes in new regulatory neighborhoods; and coding variants change protein activities within dependency networks. The resulting assemblies are larger than single molecules but smaller than whole organelles or cells, making them a natural focus for NCEMS synthesis research on emergent biological properties. Cancer cell lines are uniquely suited for this question because they have been profiled repeatedly across public resources and perturbation platforms. DepMap and CCLE provide harmonized genomes, transcriptomes, copy-number profiles, proteomics, metabolomics, CRISPR dependency maps, and drug sensitivity data for hundreds of lines. Public single-cell RNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets reveal intraline heterogeneity and adaptive transcriptional responses. ENCODE, 4DN, Roadmap-derived resources, and individual studies provide chromatin accessibility, transcription factor occupancy, histone modification, Hi-C, Micro-C, and promoter-capture datasets in cancer and lineage-matched contexts. TCGA, PCAWG, and AmpliconArchitect-based analyses provide structural variation, focal amplification, and ecDNA annotations that can be mapped onto cell line genomes. Public microscopy-derived measurements of ecDNA, when available, add an orthogonal view of amplified DNA organization. Individually, these datasets answer modality-specific questions. Synthesized across scales, they can reveal how molecular components combine into regulatory structures that generate phenotypes not predictable from any one data layer. The significance of this working group lies in converting a fragmented public data ecosystem into a testable framework for emergence in cancer cells. Drug tolerance is a particularly compelling emergent phenotype because it is dynamic, heterogeneous, and clinically consequential. A cell line may harbor an amplified oncogene, but drug response depends on whether the amplified segment is chromosomally integrated or extrachromosomal, whether relevant enhancers contact the oncogene promoter, whether transcription factor motifs are accessible, whether protein-altering variants modify downstream signaling, and whether a rare single-cell state already expresses a bypass program. These relationships cross conventional boundaries among cancer genomics, 3D genome biology, single-cell biology, protein function, pharmacogenomics, and machine learning. No single laboratory can curate, harmonize, model, and interpret these data at community scale. NCEMS support will enable a collaborative synthesis effort that addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do interacting genomic, regulatory, and protein features self-organize into mesoscale assemblies that produce emergent cell states and drug responses?
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project is organized around four interlocking scientific questions. First, what mesoscale regulatory assemblies recur across cancer cell lines with focal amplification or ecDNA? We define a regulatory assembly as a connected set of amplified segments, genes, enhancers, transcription factor motifs, chromatin contacts, expressed proteins, pathway components, and single-cell states whose joint configuration is associated with altered expression or dependency. The working hypothesis is that amplified oncogenes do not act as isolated dosage events. Instead, their phenotypic effects depend on the regulatory context created by enhancer availability, 3D proximity, chromatin accessibility, and variant-modified protein interactions. We expect assemblies to be partly lineage-specific, reflecting developmental enhancer landscapes, and partly convergent, reflecting recurrent selection for drug-tolerant programs. Second, can these assemblies explain drug sensitivity, resistance, or adaptive plasticity better than conventional single-modality features? We hypothesize that multimodal mesoscale features will improve prediction of response to targeted therapies, epigenetic drugs, kinase inhibitors, DNA damage agents, and immunomodulatory pathway perturbations relative to models based only on mutations, expression, or copy number. We further hypothesize that certain drugs will be associated with distinct assembly classes: for example, amplified enhancer-rich oncogene neighborhoods may predict sensitivity to transcriptional or chromatin regulators, whereas assemblies involving altered signaling proteins may predict kinase dependency or pathway bypass. Third, do predicted regulatory assemblies correspond to heterogeneous single-cell states rather than simple bulk-average shifts? Bulk profiles can obscure rare or transient states that seed tolerance. We hypothesize that cell lines with ecDNA or complex focal amplification will show increased single-cell variance, multimodal oncogene expression, and subpopulations enriched for stress-response, epithelial-mesenchymal, stem-like, metabolic, or cell-cycle programs. We will test whether graph-inferred assemblies map onto these subpopulations using public single-cell and Perturb-seq data. A key prediction is that some assemblies will manifest as variable gene dosage and enhancer activity across cells, producing fractional populations that are disproportionately associated with resistance signatures. Fourth, how can coding variant effects be separated from regulatory dosage effects in amplified and dependency-associated genes? Many amplified loci contain both regulatory alterations and protein-altering variants. We hypothesize that integrating protein sequence, structural, conservation, and interaction annotations will clarify whether drug response is driven by increased abundance, altered activity, modified binding interfaces, or combinations of these mechanisms. This distinction is essential for interpreting dependencies and designing transferable models across lineages. Together, these questions test the central hypothesis that drug-tolerant cancer cell states emerge from interactions among genome architecture, regulatory rewiring, dosage variation, and protein function. The hypotheses are falsifiable through held-out prediction, cross-lineage replication, ablation of data layers, comparison to baseline models, and assessment of whether inferred assemblies reproduce known biology while also nominating new mechanisms. The project intentionally uses only publicly available data and prioritizes questions that require synthesis across datasets rather than new experimental generation.
methods_and_approach: The working group will implement a staged synthesis plan using existing public data. In Phase 1, we will define the study universe by selecting breast, melanoma, glioblastoma, colorectal, and lung cancer cell lines with sufficient overlap among DepMap/CCLE molecular profiles, drug response, dependency screens, public chromatin or 3D genome resources, and available amplification or ecDNA annotations. We will build a transparent data inventory that records source, release version, assay type, genome build, cell line identifiers, treatment status, lineage, and quality metrics. Cell line identity will be reconciled using common identifiers and known aliases, with exclusion or flagging of ambiguous samples. All genomic coordinates will be lifted to a common reference assembly, and feature matrices will be harmonized with documented normalization choices. In Phase 2, we will construct a multilayer biological graph. Nodes will include genes, enhancers, regulatory motifs, copy-number segments, ecDNA or focal amplicons, structural variants, proteins, metabolites, pathways, drugs, and single-cell states. Edges will represent chromatin contacts, enhancer-gene links, motif-to-factor relationships, gene-protein mappings, pathway membership, drug-target annotations, variant effects, co-expression, co-dependency, and shared amplicon membership. Enhancer-gene assignments will combine promoter capture, Hi-C, Micro-C, accessibility-expression correlation, distance-aware priors, and lineage-matched ENCODE or 4DN evidence. Amplicon and ecDNA calls will be mapped to genes and regulatory elements, and confidence labels will capture uncertainty. Protein-coding variants will be annotated using public structure, domain, conservation, interaction, and sequence-function resources. In Phase 3, we will develop interpretable multimodal learning models. Supervised models will predict drug sensitivity and CRISPR dependency where labels are available. Semi-supervised methods will propagate information across graph neighborhoods for sparsely labeled drugs and lineages. Positive-unlabeled learning will be used for ecDNA and drug-tolerant phenotypes because absence of annotation often reflects missing measurement rather than true absence. Graph neural networks, regularized generalized linear models, random forests, matrix factorization, and calibrated ensemble methods will be compared against baseline mutation-only, expression-only, and copy-number-only predictors. Interpretability will be emphasized through feature attribution, subgraph extraction, stability selection, and biological enrichment analysis. In Phase 4, we will test emergence at the single-cell level. Public scRNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets will be reprocessed or imported from standardized objects, batch-corrected where appropriate, and analyzed for expression heterogeneity, rare states, pathway activity, inferred copy-number variation, and perturbation-responsive programs. Predicted assemblies will be evaluated for association with single-cell variance, state transitions, and drug-response signatures. Rigor will be supported through pre-specified train-test splits by lineage and drug class, external validation in TCGA or PCAWG tumor data where appropriate, sensitivity analyses for batch effects, negative-control features, data-layer ablation, and reproducible workflow execution.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will produce four primary deliverables. First, we will release an open atlas of inferred mesoscale regulatory assemblies across well-profiled cancer cell lines. The atlas will link amplified regions, ecDNA annotations, enhancer landscapes, 3D contacts, affected genes, coding variants, protein and pathway features, and observed single-cell states. Each assembly will include evidence scores, lineage context, uncertainty estimates, and associated drug or dependency phenotypes. Second, we will deliver benchmark datasets for multimodal prediction of emergent cancer cell phenotypes. These benchmarks will include standardized feature matrices, documented labels, baseline models, and recommended evaluation splits, enabling the broader community to compare methods fairly. Third, we will provide interpretable predictive models that identify which combinations of genome architecture, regulatory dosage, protein function, and cellular state best explain sensitivity or resistance across drug classes. Fourth, we will publish reusable workflows and tutorials for integrating pharmacogenomic, single-cell, 3D genome, protein annotation, and cancer genomics data. The scientific impact will be to shift analysis of cancer drug response from isolated biomarkers toward mesoscale organization. By identifying regulatory assemblies that are reproducible across public resources, the project will clarify when focal amplification or ecDNA acts through gene dosage alone and when its effects depend on enhancer capture, chromatin topology, or variant-altered protein function. The work will also provide a general synthesis strategy for studying emergence in molecular and cellular systems: define interacting components, represent them in a cross-scale graph, test whether their collective organization predicts phenotypes beyond individual parts, and validate predictions using independent public data. The translational relevance is substantial but appropriately indirect. The project will not make clinical claims; instead, it will generate mechanistic hypotheses, data resources, and computational tools that can guide future experimental studies and improve interpretation of public cancer models.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The working group will operate under open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from project initiation. All input datasets will be public, and the data inventory will record accession numbers, download dates, licenses, processing decisions, quality filters, and provenance. Derived datasets that can be redistributed will be deposited in public repositories with persistent identifiers. When source licenses restrict redistribution, we will provide scripts, manifests, checksums, and instructions that allow users to reconstruct the processed data from the original public resources. Code will be developed in a public version-controlled repository using issue tracking, pull requests, code review, and tagged releases. Reproducibility reviews will be assigned to working group members who did not conduct the original analysis, with trainees participating as reviewers and maintainers. Open tutorials will introduce harmonization of public cancer multi-omics data, construction of biological knowledge graphs, positive-unlabeled learning for incomplete biological labels, and interpretation of multimodal graph models. Manuscripts, preprints, data descriptors, and software documentation will be released under permissive terms whenever possible. Community engagement will include public webinars, office hours, and mechanisms for external users to report errors, suggest datasets, or contribute improvements. author: gpt-5.5
title: A Public Multimodal Atlas for Predicting Cytoskeletal Control of Cellular Architecture and Ciliary State
abstract:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biosciences is how local cytoskeletal interactions generate cell-scale architectural outcomes such as organelle positioning, polarized surface domains, and the presence, length, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent: they cannot be inferred from any single filament, motor, or organelle, but arise from mesoscale organization across actin, microtubules, septins, centrioles, membranes, and transport pathways. We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate publicly available whole-cell imaging, ciliary and flagellar imaging, cytoskeletal perturbation datasets, and biophysical simulation outputs to determine whether shared quantitative rules link cytoskeletal organization to cellular architecture across organisms and imaging modalities.

The working group will build an open, analysis-ready atlas from public repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence, electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging datasets. We will include mammalian cells with primary cilia or centrosome-associated cytoskeletal structures, Chlamydomonas and related flagellated systems, and non-ciliated model systems such as yeast or dividing animal cells where cytoskeletal networks produce well-defined cellular-scale structures. Rather than treating these systems as separate case studies, we will represent them through common mesoscale features: filament-network anisotropy, cortical versus internal organization, organelle volumes and curvatures, basal body or centrosome position, membrane protrusion geometry, and time-dependent structural transitions.

The project will develop interoperable workflows for segmentation transfer, morphometric feature extraction, and cross-modal comparison. Deep learning models trained on curated volumetric datasets will be adapted to less annotated public images using transfer learning and human-in-the-loop validation. Extracted cellular and subcellular geometries will be represented as meshes, graphs, and time series. We will use optimal-transport-based methods to compare shapes and dynamics across different dimensionalities, sampling rates, and imaging modalities, enabling principled integration of static 3D cellular anatomy with live cytoskeletal dynamics. Agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubule, and motor-driven organization will be incorporated as synthetic reference data, allowing us to ask which physical mechanisms reproduce observed regions of cellular morphospace.

The primary scientific question is whether ciliary state and broader cellular architecture can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization. Specifically, we will test whether cells occupy a small number of recurrent architectural regimes defined by cytoskeletal geometry, organelle packing, and centrosome or basal body context; whether transitions among these regimes correspond to events such as ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, deciliation, cytokinetic ring formation, or large-scale organelle remodeling; and whether perturbations of motors, severing proteins, or cytoskeletal regulators move cells through this shared morphodynamic landscape in predictable ways.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, harmonize, and analyze the breadth of public imaging and simulation resources needed to compare mesoscale organization across cell types, organisms, and modalities. The working group will bring together cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, data curators, applied mathematicians, and trainees. All curated metadata, segmentation workflows, morphometric features, simulation interfaces, and analysis notebooks will be released openly. The outcome will be both a reusable public resource for cell anatomy synthesis and a mechanistic framework for explaining how cytoskeletal organization gives rise to emergent cellular structures.
background_and_significance:
Cells acquire architecture through interactions among many molecular components that are individually well studied but collectively difficult to predict. Actin networks, microtubules, septins, molecular motors, membrane trafficking pathways, centrioles, basal bodies, and organelles interact at the mesoscale to produce cell-scale outcomes: organelle placement, cell polarity, membrane protrusions, contractile rings, and the presence, length, maintenance, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent because they depend on spatial organization, mechanical coupling, transport, and dynamic feedback across scales rather than on the behavior of any single molecule. Understanding these relationships is a core challenge for molecular and cellular biosciences and directly matches the NCEMS goal of synthesizing public data to discover principles of emergence at the scale between biomolecules and organelles.

Cilia and flagella provide a powerful entry point into this problem. Their assembly and disassembly require coordination between microtubules, membrane domains, basal bodies, cytoplasmic transport, and the broader cytoskeleton. Mammalian primary cilia can appear, elongate, shorten, or be lost through rapid shedding, while motile flagella in unicellular organisms maintain length through transport and tubulin availability. Yet ciliary state is also embedded in whole-cell architecture: centrosome position, cortical organization, organelle crowding, actin structure, and membrane geometry may determine whether a cilium can form or persist. Similar principles may govern non-ciliary systems, including cytokinetic ring formation, actomyosin network reorganization, and organelle remodeling in yeast and animal cells. A synthesis spanning these systems can reveal whether different cellular structures occupy shared morphodynamic regimes.

The opportunity is timely because public imaging resources now contain diverse data suitable for cross-system synthesis. Whole-cell soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging, and curated cell atlases provide images of cellular anatomy, cytoskeletal organization, organelle morphology, and dynamic transitions. Public repositories such as the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, and Allen Cell Collection include datasets that were originally generated for separate purposes but can be harmonized around common features. In parallel, public or reproducible biophysical simulations of actin, microtubules, motors, and continuum cell mechanics provide synthetic reference systems for testing mechanistic explanations.

Despite this potential, current analyses remain fragmented by organism, imaging modality, annotation practice, and disciplinary community. Individual laboratories generally lack the capacity to curate many public datasets, standardize metadata, transfer segmentation models across modalities, compare shapes and time series on common mathematical grounds, and connect observations with mechanistic simulations. NCEMS support is therefore essential. This working group will integrate cell biology, imaging science, applied mathematics, machine learning, and biophysical modeling to build a public atlas and test whether cytoskeletal mesoscale organization predicts emergent cellular architecture and ciliary state.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The central research question is whether cell-scale architecture and ciliary state can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization using only existing public data. We will address this question through three linked aims that connect biological mechanism, quantitative representation, and cross-modal synthesis.

Aim 1 asks whether diverse cells occupy a limited set of recurrent architectural regimes. We will test the hypothesis that cells from mammalian, algal, yeast, and dividing animal systems can be mapped into a shared morphospace defined by measurable features including actin and microtubule anisotropy, cortical enrichment, centrosome or basal body position, cell shape, membrane protrusion geometry, organelle volumes, organelle curvature, and intracellular packing. We predict that this morphospace will not be random or organism-specific but will contain recurrent states corresponding to polarized ciliated cells, non-ciliated proliferative cells, compact flagellated cells, remodeling cells, and contractile or cytokinetic cells. This hypothesis treats cellular anatomy as a set of mesoscale patterns that can be compared across biological systems despite differences in molecular details.

Aim 2 asks whether transitions among architectural regimes correspond to known dynamic cellular events. We will test the hypothesis that ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, whole-cilium shedding, flagellar length changes, cytokinetic ring assembly, and organelle remodeling appear as trajectories through the shared morphospace. Public live-cell imaging and time-resolved perturbation datasets will be represented as time series of shape, cytoskeletal, and organelle features. We predict that different biological events will share transition motifs, such as movement of the centrosome or basal body toward a specialized surface domain, reorganization of cortical actin, redistribution of microtubule orientation, and changes in organelle crowding. We further predict that transition speed and direction will distinguish gradual remodeling from rapid state changes such as deciliation.

Aim 3 asks whether perturbations of cytoskeletal regulators move cells through the morphospace in predictable directions. We will test the hypothesis that motors, severing enzymes, actin regulators, tubulin transport factors, and cell-cycle regulators produce characteristic displacements in cellular architecture. For example, perturbations that alter microtubule severing or tubulin availability may shift cells toward ciliary shortening or shedding states, whereas altered motor activity may shift actin networks between isotropic, bundled, contractile, or polarized configurations. We will compare perturbation signatures across organisms to identify conserved and system-specific responses.

A final integrative question asks which physical mechanisms are sufficient to generate observed architectural regimes. We will use agent-based and continuum simulations as synthetic data to test whether local rules for filament growth, motor binding, severing, transport, and mechanical coupling reproduce observed regions of the empirical morphospace. We hypothesize that a small number of physical control parameters, including filament turnover, motor processivity, cortical anchoring, and transport capacity, can explain many observed transitions. Support for these hypotheses would establish a predictive framework linking molecular-scale cytoskeletal regulation to emergent cellular organization.
methods_and_approach:
This project will be conducted as a synthesis working group using only existing publicly available data and reusable computational outputs. No new experimental data will be generated. The work will proceed in five coordinated phases.

Phase 1 will identify, prioritize, and curate public datasets. We will survey repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published supplementary archives. Candidate datasets will include volumetric soft X-ray tomography of whole cells, fluorescence imaging of cytoskeletal and organelle markers, electron microscopy of cilia, centrioles, and flagella, live-cell imaging of ciliary dynamics, and perturbation studies involving cytoskeletal motors, severing proteins, actin regulators, tubulin transport, or cell-cycle state. Inclusion criteria will require public accessibility, sufficient metadata for biological interpretation, and image quality adequate for quantitative analysis. Each dataset will be annotated with organism, cell type, imaging modality, resolution, labels, perturbation, time sampling, licensing, and provenance.

Phase 2 will create interoperable segmentation and feature-extraction workflows. Existing annotations and segmentations will be reused when available. For unsegmented images, we will adapt public deep learning models through transfer learning, foundation model prompting, and human-in-the-loop validation by domain experts. Segmentation targets will include cell boundaries, nuclei, organelles, cilia or flagella, centrioles or basal bodies when resolvable, membranes, and cytoskeletal structures. Quality control will use benchmark subsets, inter-rater comparison, uncertainty maps, and failure-mode documentation. Outputs will be stored as standardized masks, meshes, point clouds, skeletons, graphs, and tabular features.

Phase 3 will define a common mesoscale feature vocabulary. Static images will yield features describing cell shape, organelle number and volume, organelle curvature, spatial adjacency, polarity axes, basal body or centrosome position, cytoskeletal anisotropy, cortical enrichment, and ciliary or flagellar geometry. Live images will yield trajectories of length, position, velocity, deformation, and structural transitions. Where raw image resolution differs, we will compute features at multiple confidence levels rather than forcing unsupported measurements.

Phase 4 will integrate heterogeneous data mathematically. We will use dimensionality reduction, graph-based embeddings, and optimal-transport methods to compare shapes, meshes, graphs, and time series across modalities and sampling rates. Gromov-Wasserstein and fused optimal-transport distances will allow comparison among objects with different point densities, dimensionalities, and feature annotations. Clustering and supervised prediction will test whether cytoskeletal features predict ciliary state, organelle organization, or transition class. Cross-validation will be stratified by dataset and organism to distinguish generalizable rules from repository-specific artifacts.

Phase 5 will incorporate simulation outputs as mechanistic references. Publicly available or openly reproducible agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubules, motors, and cell geometry will be converted into the same feature space as empirical data. Parameter ensembles will be compared with observed morphospace regions to identify mechanisms that are sufficient, insufficient, or ambiguous. The working group will meet regularly to review curation decisions, validate biological interpretations, train trainees, and release iterative atlas versions.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The project will produce three primary outcomes. First, it will deliver an open, analysis-ready multimodal atlas of cytoskeletal organization, cell architecture, and ciliary or flagellar state assembled from public datasets. The atlas will include harmonized metadata, curated links to original repositories, standardized segmentations where feasible, morphometric feature tables, meshes, graphs, time-series representations, and documented uncertainty. This resource will make previously disconnected imaging collections usable for community-scale synthesis.

Second, the project will produce a quantitative framework for comparing cellular architecture across organisms, modalities, and temporal resolutions. By representing cells through common mesoscale features and optimal-transport-based comparisons, we will enable principled integration of volumetric anatomy, live dynamics, and simulation outputs. The resulting methods will be reusable for many problems beyond cilia, including organelle inheritance, polarity, cytokinesis, and cytoskeletal remodeling.

Third, the project will test a mechanistic model of emergence in which local cytoskeletal interactions generate predictable cell-scale architectural regimes. If successful, we will identify feature combinations that predict ciliary presence, length class, loss, or transition state, and determine whether perturbations move cells through a shared morphodynamic landscape. Even negative results will be informative by defining where organism-specific mechanisms dominate or where current public datasets lack sufficient resolution.

The broader impact is a shift from isolated image analysis toward synthesis-driven cell anatomy. The working group will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in open data curation, reproducible image analysis, mathematical comparison of biological structures, and integration of simulations with public data. The atlas and workflows will lower barriers for investigators at institutions with varied resources and will support new hypotheses about how mesoscale organization gives rise to emergent cellular form and function.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open science is central to the project design. All work will use public datasets and will maintain explicit provenance linking each derived product to the original repository, publication, accession, license, and processing history. We will not redistribute restricted data in ways that violate repository terms; instead, we will provide metadata, derived features, code, and reproducible instructions for retrieving authorized source files. Dataset inclusion, exclusion, and quality-control criteria will be documented before analysis begins and updated transparently as living protocols.

All code for curation, segmentation adaptation, feature extraction, optimal-transport comparison, statistical modeling, visualization, and simulation conversion will be developed in public version-controlled repositories. Workflows will be packaged as reproducible notebooks and containerized environments using standard tools such as Python, napari, scikit-image, PyTorch, Docker or Apptainer, and workflow managers where appropriate. Each release will include tests, example datasets, environment files, and archived versions with persistent identifiers. Analysis notebooks underlying publications will be executable from processed public inputs whenever file sizes and licenses permit.

The atlas will follow FAIR principles. Metadata will use community standards where available, including structured fields for organism, cell type, imaging modality, resolution, perturbation, time sampling, segmentation class, and uncertainty. Derived tables will be released in open formats, and image-derived objects will be shared as masks, meshes, point clouds, graphs, and interoperable spatial data structures. We will solicit community feedback through working group meetings, open issue trackers, and public documentation.

Reproducibility will be strengthened through independent validation. Segmentation subsets will be reviewed by multiple participants, model performance will be reported by dataset and modality, and predictive analyses will use held-out datasets to test generalization. Trainees will participate in code review, documentation sprints, and reproducibility checks, creating a training environment aligned with NCEMS principles for open, team-based, data-savvy science.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is needed because the proposed synthesis requires coordinated expertise, shared computational infrastructure, structured meetings, and trainee participation beyond the capacity of a single laboratory. Funds will support working group coordination, data curation, analysis development, trainee training, and dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

Personnel resources will prioritize partial support for trainees and technical contributors who will curate public datasets, implement reproducible workflows, validate segmentations, construct metadata tables, and maintain documentation. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will receive structured mentorship from cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, and applied mathematicians. Their roles will include both scientific analysis and community resource development.

Meeting resources will support a combination of in-person synthesis workshops and regular virtual working sessions. Initial workshops will define dataset scope, metadata standards, feature vocabularies, and benchmarking plans. Mid-project meetings will evaluate segmentation transfer, morphospace construction, and simulation integration. Final meetings will focus on manuscript preparation, public release, training materials, and community adoption. Travel support will be allocated to ensure participation across geographic regions, career stages, and institution types.

Computational resources will support cloud storage, data transfer, GPU-enabled segmentation adaptation, large-scale feature extraction, and public hosting of derived products. Whenever possible, workflows will use existing NCEMS cyberinfrastructure and public repositories to minimize duplication. Budgeted resources will also include software engineering support for packaging workflows, assigning persistent identifiers, and ensuring long-term usability.

Dissemination resources will support open documentation, tutorial development, trainee-led workshops, and conference or community presentations. The requested investment will yield a durable public atlas, reusable analytical workflows, trained early-career scientists, and a collaborative network capable of extending synthesis approaches to additional mesoscale emergence problems in molecular and cellular biosciences.
