author: gpt-5.5
title: Emergent Regulatory Neighborhoods from Transposable-Element-Derived Transcription Factor Grammar Across Mammalian Cell States
abstract:
Transposable elements (TEs) have dispersed millions of potential transcription factor binding sites across mammalian genomes, yet only a minority become functional regulatory elements in any given cell type. A central unresolved question is whether TE-derived regulatory activity emerges primarily from individual insertions with favorable sequence features, or from collective mesoscale organization in which families of related repeats create dense, chromatin-compatible neighborhoods that recruit transcription factors, nucleosomes, cofactors, and 3D genome contacts in a coordinated manner. This working group will synthesize public epigenomic, genomic, and chromatin conformation data to test the hypothesis that TE families generate emergent regulatory properties when their sequence grammars, chromatin states, and spatial clustering cross cell-type-specific thresholds.

The project will integrate existing datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Cistrome, GEO/SRA, 4D Nucleome, FANTOM, and public single-cell atlases, focusing initially on human and mouse hematopoietic and immune differentiation because these systems provide unusually rich transcription factor ChIP-seq, chromatin accessibility, histone modification, transcriptomic, and 3D genome data. We will annotate TE insertions by family, age, conservation, genomic context, motif content, and orthology, then link them to matched chromatin accessibility, nuclease footprints, transcription factor occupancy, histone states, enhancer RNAs, promoter contacts, and nearby gene expression. Rather than treating repeats as nuisance sequence, the analysis will ask when groups of related insertions produce regulatory behavior that cannot be predicted by isolated motif matches alone.

The working group will develop a synthesis framework combining epigenome segmentation, high-resolution binding-site modeling, motif grammar analysis, graph-based chromatin neighborhood detection, and domain-adaptive neural networks that explicitly account for species-specific repeat landscapes. These models will separate three contributions to TE regulatory activity: intrinsic sequence affinity, local chromatin permissiveness, and mesoscale neighborhood effects such as enhancer clustering, contact frequency, and co-occupancy by cooperative transcription factors. Cross-species modeling will determine whether similar regulatory outcomes arise through shared ancestral insertions, lineage-specific TE expansions, or convergent sequence grammars embedded in distinct repeat families.

The expected outcome is an open atlas of TE-associated regulatory neighborhoods across cell states and species, along with predictive models that identify which repeat families are poised to seed new enhancers, insulators, or lineage-specific transcriptional programs. This synthesis will directly address emergence by defining how distributed molecular features—motifs, repeat copy number, chromatin accessibility, nucleosome positioning, and 3D proximity—combine to create higher-order regulatory properties at the mesoscale. The project requires NCEMS-scale coordination because no single lab can uniformly integrate the breadth of public datasets, repeat annotations, machine learning models, chromatin-state maps, and biological expertise needed to compare regulatory emergence across species and cell types. All workflows, harmonized metadata, model outputs, and training materials will be released openly through reproducible computational notebooks and containerized pipelines, with graduate students and postdoctoral researchers trained in collaborative genomic data synthesis, interpretable AI, and open-science practices.
background_and_significance: Transposable elements are a major source of regulatory sequence innovation in mammalian genomes. They carry transcription factor motifs, nucleosome-positioning signals, splice and polyadenylation signals, noncoding RNA promoters, and sequence features that can be co-opted into enhancers, promoters, insulators, and repressive chromatin domains. Yet the regulatory potential of TEs is highly conditional. Most copies of a repeat family remain inactive in most cell states, while a subset becomes accessible, bound by transcription factors, marked by enhancer-associated histone modifications, transcribed as enhancer RNAs, or connected to promoters through chromatin looping. This discrepancy creates a fundamental problem in molecular and cellular biology: how do widely dispersed molecular sequence features become integrated into cell-type-specific regulatory systems with emergent properties that exceed the contribution of any single insertion? Current models often emphasize either intrinsic sequence affinity, such as the presence of a high-scoring transcription factor motif, or local chromatin permissiveness, such as accessibility or histone modification status. These explanations are necessary but incomplete. Regulatory activity frequently occurs in clusters of enhancers, super-enhancer-like domains, topologically associated regions, and lineage-specific chromatin neighborhoods where transcription factors, cofactors, nucleosomes, RNA polymerase, and 3D contacts interact over tens to hundreds of kilobases. TE families are uniquely suited to create such mesoscale organization because they amplify related sequence grammars throughout the genome, sometimes in lineage-specific bursts, and can distribute coordinated binding potential across regulatory landscapes. This proposal addresses an emergence question at the scale emphasized by NCEMS: when do repeated molecular components give rise to new regulatory properties at the mesoscale between individual DNA motifs and whole-cell phenotypes? Hematopoietic and immune differentiation provide an ideal initial system. Human and mouse blood lineages are among the best-characterized mammalian cellular systems, with extensive public data for transcription factor occupancy, chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, gene expression, enhancer transcription, nucleosome organization, and chromatin conformation across stem, progenitor, and differentiated states. These lineages also depend on combinatorial transcription factor programs involving factors such as GATA, PU.1, CTCF, RUNX, ETS, IRF, NF-kB, STAT, and AP-1, many of which interact with TE-derived motifs. Public repositories now contain sufficient data to move beyond single-dataset analyses and perform a community-scale synthesis across assays, species, repeat families, and cell states. However, the needed integration is beyond the scope of a typical individual laboratory. It requires expertise in repeat annotation, transcription factor biology, epigenome segmentation, high-resolution binding models, chromatin conformation analysis, machine learning, comparative genomics, and open scientific infrastructure. By synthesizing only existing public data, the working group will transform fragmented resources into a coherent framework for understanding how TE-derived regulatory grammar contributes to emergent cell-state-specific gene regulation. The resulting atlas and models will clarify how evolutionary genome expansion is translated into cellular regulatory innovation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will pursue three linked research questions. First, what distinguishes TE insertions that become active regulatory elements from inactive copies of the same family in matched cell states? We hypothesize that active insertions are not explained solely by the strongest individual motif matches. Instead, activity reflects an interaction among intrinsic sequence grammar, local chromatin accessibility, neighboring regulatory features, and lineage-specific transcription factor availability. Within a repeat family, we expect active copies to show enriched motif syntax, including motif combinations, spacing, orientation, and predicted affinity profiles that support cooperative binding by cell-state-relevant transcription factors. However, we also expect many inactive copies to contain apparently favorable motifs, demonstrating that sequence is necessary but not sufficient. Second, do related TE insertions form emergent regulatory neighborhoods whose collective behavior cannot be predicted from isolated insertions? We hypothesize that TE families generate mesoscale regulatory properties when multiple copies or TE-derived regulatory elements occur within chromatin-compatible genomic regions, share compatible transcription factor grammar, and participate in enhancer clustering or promoter contacts. These neighborhoods may recruit combinations of transcription factors, cofactors, nucleosomes, architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase in ways that produce nonlinear regulatory outcomes, including enhanced occupancy, stronger enhancer RNA signal, increased contact frequency with target promoters, or coordinated activation of nearby lineage genes. We will test whether models that include neighborhood-level features outperform models based only on single-insertion sequence and local chromatin measurements. A positive result would provide operational evidence for emergence: regulatory behavior arising from the organization of multiple components rather than from any component alone. Third, how conserved or convergent are TE-derived regulatory neighborhoods across human and mouse hematopoietic and immune cell states? We hypothesize that similar regulatory outcomes arise through three mechanisms: direct conservation of ancestral insertions, lineage-specific expansion of distinct repeat families that carry comparable motif grammars, and convergent recruitment of different repeat sequences into analogous chromatin contexts. Because repeat landscapes differ substantially between species, cross-species prediction requires methods that separate conserved regulatory logic from species-specific sequence distributions. We expect that domain-adaptive models will identify both shared transcription factor grammars and species-specific repeat effects that confound simpler comparative analyses. The project will also examine whether TE-derived neighborhoods are associated with particular regulatory classes. Some families may preferentially seed enhancers for inflammatory or differentiation-responsive programs; others may contribute CTCF-associated boundary or loop-anchor activity; others may be linked to repressive chromatin transitions. These hypotheses will be evaluated with explicit, falsifiable statistical criteria: predictive improvement from neighborhood features, enrichment of TE families in reproducible chromatin states, evidence of coordinated accessibility or occupancy across nearby elements, association with promoter contacts and gene expression, and cross-species transferability of regulatory predictions. Together, the questions define a synthesis agenda that connects molecular grammar, chromatin state, 3D organization, and cell identity.
methods_and_approach: The project will use only publicly available data and will proceed through coordinated synthesis tasks. Task 1 will create a harmonized catalog of TE insertions in human and mouse genomes. We will combine RepeatMasker annotations, Dfam and Repbase-derived family classifications where licensing permits, genome build conversion resources, synteny maps, age estimates based on divergence from consensus, orthology information, conservation scores, genomic context, proximity to genes, and overlap with annotated promoters, enhancers, and insulators. Each insertion will be represented by family, subfamily, length, truncation status, orientation, age proxy, sequence quality, mappability, and local genomic features. Task 2 will assemble matched public functional genomics data across hematopoietic and immune cell states from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Cistrome, GEO, SRA, 4D Nucleome, FANTOM, Human Cell Atlas-related resources, and mouse single-cell atlases. We will prioritize datasets with clear metadata, biological replicates, quality metrics, and compatible cell type definitions. Assays will include ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo where available for transcription factors and histone marks, ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, MNase-seq or related nucleosome maps, RNA-seq, CAGE and enhancer RNA resources, Hi-C, Micro-C, promoter capture Hi-C, ChIA-PET, HiChIP, and single-cell chromatin accessibility or expression datasets. Existing processed data will be used when quality is sufficient; otherwise public raw reads will be uniformly reprocessed with documented pipelines. Task 3 will define regulatory features at individual TE insertions. We will compute motif content with curated transcription factor motif collections, model motif grammar through spacing and orientation features, infer high-resolution occupancy from ChIP and footprinting data where feasible, assign chromatin states using segmentation approaches across accessibility and histone marks, and link insertions to expression or enhancer activity using proximity, promoter contacts, and activity-by-contact models. We will explicitly account for mappability and repeat-induced alignment bias. Task 4 will detect mesoscale regulatory neighborhoods. We will construct cell-state-specific graphs in which nodes represent TE insertions and non-TE regulatory elements, and edges represent genomic distance, shared chromatin state, co-accessibility, contact frequency, promoter linkage, transcription factor co-occupancy, or membership in topological domains. Community detection, graph neural features, and statistical null models preserving TE density, GC content, mappability, and gene proximity will identify neighborhoods enriched for coordinated regulatory activity. Task 5 will build predictive and explanatory models. Baseline models will use isolated sequence features; expanded models will add local chromatin; full models will add neighborhood features. Interpretable machine learning, including regularized models, gradient-boosted trees, convolutional sequence models, and domain-adaptive neural networks, will quantify feature contributions and cross-species transfer. Rigorous validation will include held-out chromosomes, held-out cell types, held-out TE families, replicate consistency, permutation tests, and comparison against matched non-TE regulatory elements. The working group will meet in focused sprints to resolve metadata, modeling, biological interpretation, and dissemination.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The primary outcome will be an open atlas of TE-associated regulatory neighborhoods across human and mouse hematopoietic and immune cell states. The atlas will provide harmonized annotations of TE insertions, repeat family enrichments, predicted transcription factor grammar, chromatin states, occupancy evidence, enhancer or insulator classifications, promoter contacts, and links to gene expression programs. It will enable researchers to query which repeat families are associated with particular cell states, transcription factor combinations, chromatin environments, and 3D regulatory contexts. The second outcome will be a set of predictive models that distinguish inactive, locally active, and neighborhood-associated TE insertions. These models will quantify how much regulatory activity is attributable to intrinsic sequence affinity, local chromatin permissiveness, and mesoscale organization. This framework will provide a practical definition of emergent regulatory behavior and a reusable strategy for studying other repetitive, modular, or clustered genomic components. The third outcome will be comparative insight into mammalian regulatory evolution. By modeling human and mouse jointly, the project will identify cases in which conserved regulatory outputs arise from shared ancestral insertions, lineage-specific repeat expansions, or convergent motif grammars embedded in different TE families. The broader impact is conceptual and methodological. The project will shift TEs from being treated primarily as technical complications to being analyzed as distributed molecular components that may organize cell-state-specific regulatory systems. It will provide community resources for repeat-aware epigenomics, promote reproducible AI-assisted synthesis, and train trainees to work across genomics, chromatin biology, data engineering, and evolutionary biology. These outcomes align directly with NCEMS goals by using public data to address emergence at the mesoscale and by requiring a multidisciplinary working group to produce insights unavailable from isolated analyses.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The project will follow open, reproducible, and team-based science practices from its outset. All public datasets will be tracked in a versioned metadata registry that records accession identifiers, genome builds, cell type labels, assay types, quality metrics, processing status, use restrictions, and provenance. Harmonized metadata tables, derived feature matrices, analysis code, workflow descriptions, model configurations, and documentation will be released through public repositories using persistent identifiers. When redistribution of derived data is constrained by repository or annotation licenses, we will provide scripts and checksums that allow users to recreate the resource from the original public sources. Computational workflows will be implemented using portable workflow managers and containerized software environments. Core analyses will be executable through documented notebooks and command-line pipelines, with automated tests for key steps such as interval overlap, mappability filtering, motif scoring, chromatin-state assignment, graph construction, and model evaluation. Results will be accompanied by data dictionaries, parameter files, audit logs, and benchmark reports. We will use held-out validation strategies and publish negative or ambiguous findings where they clarify limits of inference. The working group will establish community guidelines for naming regulatory neighborhoods, reporting repeat-aware quality controls, and comparing TE-derived with non-TE regulatory elements. Trainees will participate in open-science training modules covering reproducible workflow design, collaborative coding, metadata standards, ethical reuse of public data, interpretable machine learning, and responsible application of AI to genomics. Meetings will include code review sessions, documentation sprints, and cross-disciplinary tutorials so that computational and biological contributors can evaluate assumptions together. Preprints, conference materials, tutorials, and final manuscripts will point to stable releases of the atlas and software. This plan ensures that the synthesis is transparent, reusable, extensible, and valuable to the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is essential because the proposed work requires coordinated synthesis across many data types, species, analytical domains, and institutions rather than a narrow single-laboratory analysis. Funds will support working group meetings, trainee participation, computational infrastructure, data engineering, open-science dissemination, and cross-disciplinary training. We anticipate a two-year working group structure with three in-person synthesis meetings hosted through NCEMS and regular virtual analysis sprints between meetings. Resources will also support participation from institutions with different research capacities and from early-career scientists who bring needed technical skills. Computational costs will include cloud or high-performance computing allocations for reprocessing selected public sequencing datasets, storing harmonized intermediate files, training machine learning models, and maintaining public releases. Funds will support data management personnel or trainee effort for metadata harmonization, workflow testing, documentation, and quality control. Additional resources will be used for open-science products, including tutorial development, container registry maintenance, web-accessible atlas prototypes, and community workshops. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase laboratory reagents, or conduct new sequencing. Existing public datasets are sufficient for the central aims; the challenge is integration, quality control, interpretation, and reproducible distribution. NCEMS resources will provide the neutral collaborative environment, synthesis expertise, open-science infrastructure, and convening capacity needed to transform fragmented public datasets into a community resource. The budget is therefore directly aligned with the call: it supports multidisciplinary collaboration, public-data synthesis, training of data-savvy scientists, and development of reusable analytical strategies for understanding emergent molecular and cellular phenomena.

author: gpt-5.5
title: A Residue-Resolved Public Data Atlas of Emergent Human Protein Assemblies
abstract:
Mesoscale protein assemblies emerge when many weak, transient, or context-dependent molecular contacts combine to produce cellular functions that cannot be inferred from individual proteins alone. Yet most public interaction resources represent protein relationships as gene-level edges, losing the residue-level proximity information needed to connect molecular interfaces to cellular pathways, tissue specificity, and disease-associated perturbation. This working group will synthesize publicly available crosslinking mass spectrometry, conventional proteomics, structural, pathway, and human genetics datasets to ask: what general principles determine when local protein contacts become higher-order cellular assemblies, and how are these assemblies rewired across tissues, pathways, and disease-relevant sequence variation?

The project will integrate public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets from ProteomeXchange-associated repositories with curated interaction resources, structural models, tissue proteome maps, Reactome pathway annotations, protein sequence metadata, post-translational modification resources, and human variant datasets. Rather than treating crosslinks only as evidence for isolated protein-protein interactions, we will reanalyze them as residue-level spatial constraints embedded in cellular context. Public raw and processed crosslinking datasets will be harmonized using transparent false discovery criteria, standardized spectrum identifiers, controlled vocabularies, and reproducible workflows. Crosslinks will be mapped to UniProt proteoforms, AlphaFold and experimentally determined structures, pathway reactions, tissue abundance profiles, and known genetic or post-translational modifications. The resulting synthesis will create an open, queryable knowledge graph linking spectra, residue pairs, proteins, complexes, pathways, tissues, and phenotypes.

This atlas will enable three analyses that are difficult for any single laboratory. First, we will identify recurrent mesoscale interaction modules supported by residue-level proximity across independent studies and determine whether they correspond to stable complexes, transient pathway intermediates, or condition-specific assemblies. Second, we will test whether tissue-specific protein abundance and pathway state explain which potential contacts are observed, distinguishing physical compatibility from biological availability. Third, we will map pathogenic, common, and post-translationally modified residues onto crosslink-supported interfaces to ask whether disease-associated perturbations preferentially target emergent assembly hubs rather than individual protein functions.

The project is well suited to NCEMS because it requires coordinated expertise in crosslinking mass spectrometry, proteomics informatics, molecular biophysics, pathway knowledge representation, network biology, structural modeling, and human genetics. It will use only existing public data but will generate new biological insight by integrating datasets that are currently fragmented across repositories, formats, and scales. The working group will also address methodological needs central to synthesis science: benchmarkable crosslink reanalysis, persistent links from conclusions to original spectra, uncertainty-aware interaction scoring, and interoperable data models for residue-resolved cellular networks.

All outputs will be released openly, including reanalysis workflows, standardized metadata templates, confidence-scored crosslink interaction tables, knowledge graph exports, tutorials, and interactive notebooks. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees focused on reproducible proteomics reanalysis, network modeling, and biological interpretation. The long-term impact will be a community resource and analytical framework for understanding how molecular contacts collectively give rise to emergent cellular organization.
background_and_significance: Cellular behavior is organized by protein assemblies that operate between the molecular and organelle scales. Ribosomes, spliceosomes, cytoskeletal condensates, signaling scaffolds, metabolic channeling assemblies, membrane contact sites, and repair foci all illustrate a common principle: collective function can arise from many contacts that are individually weak, short lived, partially redundant, or dependent on abundance, localization, modification, and pathway state. These mesoscale assemblies are central examples of emergence in molecular and cellular biology because their properties cannot be inferred by cataloging isolated proteins or even by listing pairwise protein associations alone. Understanding how residue-level contacts combine into functional cellular architecture is therefore a fundamental and timely synthesis challenge. Public molecular data now make this challenge tractable. Crosslinking mass spectrometry provides residue-resolved proximity information by identifying pairs of amino acids that were close enough to be covalently linked in a biological sample. Unlike many interaction assays, crosslinking can capture endogenous complexes, transient contacts, heterogeneous conformations, and contacts within large assemblies. However, crosslinking data are dispersed across public repositories, produced by different chemistries and search pipelines, reported using heterogeneous confidence measures, and rarely integrated with tissue proteomics, pathway knowledge, structural models, or human variation. As a result, much of the biological value of these data remains latent. Crosslinks are commonly reduced to protein-level evidence, causing loss of the interface specificity needed to distinguish an allosteric surface from a catalytic site, a constitutive complex interface from a context-specific pathway contact, or a benign variant from a variant disrupting an assembly hub. Existing public interaction resources are indispensable but are often gene-centric. They typically represent proteins as nodes and interactions as edges, with limited ability to trace claims back to spectra, residue coordinates, proteoforms, crosslinker constraints, or sample context. Structural databases and prediction resources provide three-dimensional models, but they do not generally encode whether predicted contacts are observed in cells, in which tissues they are possible, or how pathway state and disease-associated sequence changes affect them. Human genetics resources identify variants associated with Mendelian disease, complex traits, or population diversity, but these variants are rarely evaluated in the context of residue-resolved assembly maps. This proposal addresses these gaps through a community-scale synthesis using only existing public data. It aligns directly with NCEMS priorities by integrating molecular, mesoscale, cellular, and phenotypic information to study emergent properties. The central significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project will test whether higher-order assemblies follow general rules related to interface recurrence, structural compatibility, abundance, pathway colocalization, and perturbation sensitivity. Methodologically, it will produce reusable infrastructure for transparent, uncertainty-aware reanalysis of public crosslinking datasets and for linking spectral evidence to biological conclusions. The work cannot be accomplished by one laboratory because it requires crosslinking mass spectrometry expertise, proteomics standards, structural interpretation, pathway curation, graph modeling, network biology, and genetics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated synthesis across these communities and create a public framework for interpreting mesoscale protein organization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: The working group will address three linked scientific questions. First, when do residue-level protein contacts observed by crosslinking mass spectrometry represent components of emergent mesoscale assemblies rather than isolated binary interactions or technical coincidences? We hypothesize that assembly-associated contacts will show recurrent support across independent studies, coherent geometry when mapped to structures, enrichment within known or predicted pathway neighborhoods, and nonrandom clustering into multi-protein modules. We further hypothesize that such modules will separate into classes: stable structural complexes with many mutually compatible restraints, transient pathway intermediates with directional or reaction-specific connectivity, and condition-dependent assemblies supported by specific tissues, cellular states, or perturbation contexts. A key outcome will be a quantitative definition of crosslink-supported mesoscale modules that incorporates residue evidence, spectral confidence, structural feasibility, protein abundance, and pathway topology. Second, how does biological availability constrain which physically possible contacts are observed? Many proteins have compatible surfaces in structural models, yet only a subset of possible contacts occur in a given cellular environment. We hypothesize that tissue-specific abundance, pathway co-membership, subcellular context, and proteoform state explain a substantial fraction of observed crosslink patterns beyond structural compatibility alone. Under this hypothesis, a residue pair may be physically plausible in a model but biologically unavailable if the proteins are not co-expressed, participate in separate pathway states, or are regulated by mutually exclusive modifications. Conversely, crosslinks that violate simple static structural expectations may reveal conformational ensembles, flexible regions, mixed proteoforms, or assembly states not captured by single reference structures. This question directly probes emergence because assembly formation depends on the coordinated presence and state of many components rather than on intrinsic binding compatibility alone. Third, do disease-associated sequence variants and post-translational modifications preferentially affect residues that participate in emergent assembly hubs? We hypothesize that pathogenic variants, high-impact common variants, and regulatory modifications will be enriched at crosslink-supported interfaces that connect multiple proteins, pathways, or tissue-specific modules. Such residues may be more informative than protein-level annotations because a single protein can participate in several assemblies through distinct surfaces. A variant on one surface may disrupt a neuronal assembly while leaving a metabolic or housekeeping role intact. Similarly, phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, or other modifications near crosslinked residues may act as switches that rewire proximity relationships. We will test whether interface-level burden explains disease relevance better than gene degree, protein abundance, or membership in a known complex alone. These questions will be approached with explicit, falsifiable predictions. Recurrent assembly modules should replicate across datasets more often than degree-matched random networks. Tissue-aware models should outperform structure-only models in predicting crosslink observability. Interface-localized variant and modification signals should show stronger associations with pathway perturbation and phenotype annotations than protein-level aggregation. Negative results will also be informative: failure to detect recurrence or tissue effects would identify limitations in current public data and guide community standards for future deposition. Together, these questions define a rigorous synthesis agenda for discovering principles by which local molecular contacts generate higher-order cellular organization.
methods_and_approach: The project will proceed through five coordinated work packages, all using existing publicly available data. Work package 1 will assemble and audit public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets from ProteomeXchange-associated repositories and other community repositories that provide raw spectra, search results, metadata, or published crosslink tables. We will prioritize human and human-relevant mammalian datasets, while retaining selected model-system datasets for conserved assemblies when orthology mapping is robust. Each dataset will be annotated for sample type, organism, crosslinker chemistry, enrichment method, instrument, search engine, database, reported false discovery approach, and availability of spectrum-level evidence. Universal spectrum identifiers or equivalent persistent spectral references will be assigned wherever possible so that every retained residue-pair claim can be traced to source evidence. Work package 2 will harmonize and reanalyze crosslink evidence. Where raw data and sufficient metadata are available, spectra will be processed through containerized open workflows using documented protein sequence databases, decoy strategies, peptide-spectrum match criteria, and crosslink-level error estimation. Where only processed data are available, reported identifications will be normalized to common controlled vocabularies and confidence fields, while preserving provenance and uncertainty. Crosslinks will be mapped to UniProt accessions, isoforms, sequence variants, and residue coordinates using reproducible sequence reconciliation. Ambiguous peptide mappings, paralog conflicts, missing residues, and proteoform uncertainty will be retained rather than silently discarded. The output will be confidence-scored residue-pair evidence with explicit error, provenance, and mapping status. Work package 3 will build the integrated knowledge graph. Nodes will include spectra, peptides, residues, proteins, proteoforms, crosslinks, protein complexes, pathway reactions, tissues, variants, modifications, structures, and phenotypes. Edges will encode evidence relationships, residue proximity, structural mapping, pathway participation, abundance support, genetic association, and modification annotation. Data sources will include public crosslinking datasets, UniProt, experimentally determined structures, AlphaFold models, curated protein interaction and complex resources, Reactome pathways, tissue proteome maps, post-translational modification repositories, ClinVar and other public variant resources, genome-wide association catalogs, and relevant phenotype ontologies. The graph schema will be developed with community input and will support exports in tabular, RDF-compatible, and property-graph formats. Work package 4 will perform synthesis analyses. Module detection will combine multilayer network clustering, residue-interface aggregation, structural-distance filtering, and pathway enrichment. We will compare crosslink-supported modules to known complexes, pathway reaction neighborhoods, and predicted structural assemblies. Tissue-aware observability models will use protein abundance, co-expression, pathway context, subcellular annotation, and structural compatibility to predict whether a residue-pair contact is observed in a given dataset. Variant and modification analyses will test enrichment at interface residues using matched controls for protein length, domain architecture, solvent accessibility, abundance, study intensity, and network degree. Sensitivity analyses will evaluate alternative false discovery thresholds and mapping assumptions. Work package 5 will organize collaborative data jamborees and interpretation sprints. Crosslinking specialists, proteomics informaticians, structural biologists, pathway curators, network scientists, geneticists, and trainees will jointly review benchmark cases and biological findings. No new experimental data will be generated; all outputs will arise from synthesis, reanalysis, integration, and interpretation of public data.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The primary deliverable will be an open residue-resolved atlas of human protein assembly evidence that connects spectra to residue pairs, proteins, structures, pathways, tissues, variants, modifications, and phenotypes. The atlas will provide confidence-scored crosslink tables, provenance-rich metadata, structural mappings, tissue-aware context fields, and graph exports that can be queried by the community. It will transform public crosslinking data from a dispersed collection of study-specific identifications into a reusable synthesis resource for mesoscale biology. Scientifically, the project will produce a ranked set of recurrent assembly modules supported by residue-level evidence across independent studies. These modules will be classified as likely stable complexes, transient pathway intermediates, condition-specific assemblies, or uncertain cases requiring future investigation. The analyses will reveal whether recurring interface patterns align with pathway organization, whether tissue abundance explains assembly observability, and whether disease-associated variants and post-translational modifications concentrate at assembly hubs. The results will generate testable principles for how many local contacts combine to form emergent cellular functions. Methodologically, the project will establish practical standards for public crosslinking reanalysis, persistent spectral traceability, uncertainty-aware interaction scoring, proteoform-resolved residue mapping, and interoperable graph representation. These methods will be broadly applicable to proteomics and systems biology beyond this specific atlas. The impact for NCEMS will be a high-value synthesis project that addresses a fundamental emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale using only public data and multidisciplinary collaboration. The resource will help researchers interpret disease variants, prioritize interfaces for mechanistic studies, compare assemblies across tissues, and evaluate structural predictions in cellular context. It will also create training opportunities for data-savvy trainees who can move between mass spectrometry, structural biology, network analysis, and biological interpretation.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from inception. All code, workflow definitions, graph schemas, metadata templates, documentation, issue tracking, and analysis notebooks will be developed in public version-controlled repositories unless temporary privacy is needed for manuscript coordination. Releases will be assigned persistent identifiers through open archival services, and final datasets will be deposited in appropriate community repositories with permissive reuse licenses. The working group will publish a data management and sharing plan at project launch and update it as community feedback is incorporated. Reproducibility will be enforced through containerized workflows, pinned software versions, recorded reference databases, documented parameter files, and continuous integration tests on representative public datasets. Each crosslink assertion in the atlas will include provenance fields linking it to the original dataset, search or reanalysis workflow, confidence score, residue-mapping status, and, where possible, a persistent spectrum identifier. We will distinguish primary observations from derived inferences so users can evaluate uncertainty at the spectrum, peptide, crosslink, protein, module, and pathway levels. Open science will also shape governance. The group will adopt a contributor policy, authorship and credit guidelines, meeting notes where appropriate, and a lightweight decision process for schema changes. Trainees will receive structured instruction in FAIR data principles, proteomics standards, workflow engineering, graph analysis, and responsible biological interpretation. Tutorials, example notebooks, and recorded training materials will enable reuse by researchers who are not crosslinking specialists. Community review will be sought through public workshops, repository issues, and targeted consultation with standards and pathway-resource experts. The goal is not only to release results but to provide auditable evidence chains and reusable practices that raise the reliability of synthesis research in molecular and cellular sciences.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained coordination, shared computational infrastructure, cross-disciplinary meetings, trainee participation, and community curation beyond the scope of a single laboratory. Funds will be used only for synthesis activities and will not support generation of new experimental data. The largest budget category will be personnel effort for a project coordinator or data scientist, trainee participants, and partial support for workflow development, metadata harmonization, and knowledge-graph engineering. This support will ensure continuity across laboratories, repositories, and analytical domains. A second category will support collaborative working group activities, including in-person synthesis meetings at NCEMS, virtual work sessions, data jamborees, and focused interpretation sprints. Travel support will prioritize participation by early-career researchers, trainees, investigators from institutions with different research capacities, and experts whose perspectives are needed for crosslinking mass spectrometry, proteomics standards, structural modeling, pathway representation, network biology, and human genetics. Meeting time will be used for schema design, benchmark decisions, biological interpretation, training, and community feedback, not for experimental planning. A third category will cover computational resources for reanalysis of public raw files, storage of intermediate outputs, graph construction, interactive notebooks, and public web-accessible demonstrations. Where possible, workflows will use open-source tools and cloud or institutional resources compatible with NCEMS reproducibility expectations. Modest funds will support software maintenance, documentation, archival deposition, and accessibility of training materials. Existing public repositories, knowledgebases, and standards will provide the core data resources, including proteomics repositories, protein sequence resources, structural databases, pathway knowledgebases, tissue proteome maps, modification resources, and public genetic-variant catalogs. NCEMS will add value by convening the necessary expertise, providing synthesis infrastructure, promoting open science practices, and enabling trainees to learn reproducible, integrative data science in a real community-scale project.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Emergent Microbial Chemical Phenotypes from Public Metagenomic, Proteomic, and Untargeted Mass Spectrometry Data
abstract: Microbial cells and communities routinely produce chemical phenotypes that cannot be inferred from any single gene, genome, or organism in isolation. These phenotypes emerge from mesoscale organization: co-regulated gene neighborhoods, multi-enzyme pathway fragments, protein complexes, metabolite transformations, and ecological sharing of intermediates. Yet the public record contains the ingredients needed to study this emergence at scale: billions of tandem mass spectra from microbiome-associated metabolomics experiments, thousands of public metagenomes and isolate genomes, and growing proteomics repositories. This working group will synthesize these data to ask a central question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will not generate new experimental data. Instead, we will integrate public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, and public isolate genome resources, prioritizing studies with shared samples, related environments, or compatible metadata. The project will develop an open computational framework that links three layers: (1) spectral evidence for metabolite families and diagnostic chemical substructures from untargeted MS/MS, including reusable query patterns for known and unknown molecular motifs; (2) microbial functional potential from metagenomes and isolate genomes, including gene-neighborhood, operon-like, and pathway-fragment organization rather than only single-gene annotations; and (3) protein-level evidence from public metaproteomics and proteomics datasets where available. The synthesis will combine mass spectrometry pattern querying, molecular networking, alignment-free sequence embeddings, gene-block evolutionary reconstruction, and multilevel statistical models that explicitly test for emergence: metabolite features whose occurrence is better predicted by combinations of genes, taxa, or gene neighborhoods than by any component alone. A key innovation is to treat unknown genes and unknown metabolites as first-class signals. Instead of discarding unannotated spectra or hypothetical proteins, we will create cross-modal embeddings that identify recurring associations between spectral motifs and microbial sequence modules across independent studies. We will then evaluate whether these associations are conserved across environments, enriched in particular microbial lineages, or repeatedly assembled through different taxonomic routes. This will distinguish lineage-specific chemistry from convergent community-level biochemical capacity. The expected outcomes are: a public atlas of microbial gene-module-to-metabolite associations; a ranked set of candidate emergent chemical phenotypes, including metabolite families associated with multi-organism or multi-module genetic configurations; reusable MassQL-style spectral queries and gene-neighborhood search workflows; and benchmark datasets for testing future AI methods in metabolomics-metagenomics integration. The working group requires NCEMS support because the problem spans multiple communities that rarely share standards: mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, evolutionary bioinformatics, statistics, and data stewardship. NCEMS will enable coordinated metadata harmonization, community curation of reusable feature definitions, collaborative software development, and trainee-led cross-training workshops. All workflows, derived feature tables, models, documentation, and negative results will be released openly. By synthesizing existing public data across molecular and cellular scales, this project will reveal how distributed microbial molecular components assemble into reproducible chemical properties of cells and communities.
background_and_significance: Microbial chemistry is a central driver of cellular physiology, host-microbe interaction, nutrient cycling, and environmental adaptation. However, many microbial chemical phenotypes are not attributable to a single enzyme, genome, or taxon. They arise when genetic modules, expressed proteins, metabolite intermediates, spatially associated cells, and ecological exchanges combine to produce higher-order biochemical outcomes. This is a classic problem of emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences: mesoscale organization between individual biomolecules and whole-cell or community phenotypes generates properties that are difficult to predict from isolated parts. Examples include multi-step biotransformations distributed across community members, chemically related metabolite families produced by variable pathway fragments, and molecular signatures that appear only when taxa with complementary functions co-occur. Public data now make it possible to study these phenomena at a scale not achievable by individual laboratories. Untargeted tandem mass spectrometry repositories contain enormous numbers of spectra from host-associated and environmental microbiomes. Public metagenomic and isolate genome resources provide information on microbial functional potential, gene neighborhoods, operon-like architectures, and evolutionary conservation. Public proteomics and metaproteomics repositories provide partial but crucial evidence about which proteins are expressed in relevant samples. Yet these resources remain under-integrated. Metabolomics data are often analyzed without genomic context; metagenomes are frequently reduced to single-gene annotations; proteomics is rarely linked to untargeted metabolite families; and unknown spectra and hypothetical proteins are commonly discarded even though they may contain the strongest signals of uncharacterized microbial chemistry. This proposal addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do similar microbiome chemical phenotypes recur across studies and environments even when the exact species composition differs? We hypothesize that recurrent chemical phenotypes are often generated by combinations of conserved gene modules, pathway fragments, and protein expression patterns that can be assembled through multiple taxonomic routes. Detecting such combinations requires synthesis across repositories, data types, and scientific communities. The project aligns directly with NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, focusing on mesoscale emergence, integrating molecular and cellular scales, advancing analytical strategies, and requiring collaboration among mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, evolutionary bioinformatics, statistics, and data stewardship. NCEMS support is essential because the central barrier is not a lack of data but a lack of coordinated synthesis: harmonized metadata, reusable feature definitions, interoperable workflows, and community standards for connecting unknown chemical and genetic signals. The resulting framework will enable discovery of reproducible microbial chemical phenotypes, provide benchmark datasets for artificial intelligence methods, and train a new cohort of researchers to work across metabolomics, genomics, proteomics, and open computational science.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: The working group will address one overarching question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will decompose this question into four testable research questions. First, which metabolite families and diagnostic spectral motifs recur across public microbiome-associated untargeted MS/MS datasets after accounting for instrument type, acquisition mode, sample preparation, and metadata heterogeneity? We hypothesize that many recurring motifs represent conserved chemical substructures or transformation series rather than isolated annotated compounds, and that pattern-based spectral querying will recover these signals more robustly than library matching alone. Second, which microbial genomic features best predict these metabolite motifs: individual genes, gene families, gene neighborhoods, operon-like blocks, pathway fragments, taxa, or combinations of these features? We hypothesize that multi-feature representations will outperform single genes or taxonomic profiles, particularly for metabolite families produced by modular biosynthesis, microbial transformation, or distributed metabolism. Third, does protein-level evidence improve the inference of emergent chemical phenotypes? We hypothesize that public metaproteomic and proteomic datasets, although sparser than metagenomic data, will identify a high-confidence subset of associations in which genetic potential is supported by expressed enzymes, transporters, or protein complexes. Fourth, are similar chemical phenotypes generated by shared ancestry, convergent gene-block assembly, or community-level complementation among different organisms? We hypothesize that both lineage-specific and convergent routes exist, and that evolutionary reconstruction of gene neighborhoods combined with cross-study statistical modeling can distinguish these mechanisms. Emergence will be operationally defined and tested quantitatively. A metabolite feature, spectral motif, or metabolite family will be considered a candidate emergent chemical phenotype when its occurrence, abundance, or transformation pattern is predicted significantly better by combinations of genes, taxa, gene neighborhoods, or expressed proteins than by any single component alone. This definition permits explicit comparisons among additive, interactive, and hierarchical models. We will also test whether emergent predictions replicate across independent datasets, environments, and repository sources. A key hypothesis is that unknowns carry essential information. Unannotated spectra may correspond to microbial metabolites absent from reference libraries, while hypothetical proteins may represent uncharacterized enzymes or pathway components. Rather than treating these as missing data, we will represent unknown spectra through spectral motifs, neutral-loss patterns, molecular-network neighborhoods, and learned embeddings, and represent unknown genes through sequence embeddings, genomic context, co-occurrence, and evolutionary conservation. We expect recurring cross-modal associations between unknown chemical and genetic features to reveal candidate biochemical systems that would be invisible to annotation-dependent analysis. These questions are intentionally structured to produce both biological discoveries and reusable methodological advances for community-scale synthesis.
methods_and_approach: The project will proceed through coordinated synthesis work packages and will generate no new experimental data. Work package 1 will identify and harmonize public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, public isolate genome collections, and related repositories. We will prioritize studies with shared samples, matched or related environments, microbiome relevance, accessible raw data, and sufficient metadata. A metadata team will map sample descriptors to common vocabularies for environment, host, body site, extraction method, instrument, acquisition parameters, sequencing strategy, and proteomics workflow. Dataset inclusion, exclusion, and quality criteria will be public and versioned. Work package 2 will derive metabolomics features. Public MS/MS data will be standardized, quality controlled, and processed into spectral features, molecular networks, and motif tables. We will use reusable query patterns for diagnostic ions, neutral losses, mass differences, and fragmentation relationships, while allowing discovery of unknown molecular motifs. Feature definitions will include confidence levels distinguishing library matches, analog matches, motif-level evidence, and unannotated recurrent spectra. Work package 3 will derive genomic and metagenomic features. Public metagenomes and isolate genomes will be annotated using reproducible pipelines, but analysis will not depend solely on reference functions. We will extract gene families, pathway fragments, predicted operon-like neighborhoods, co-localized gene blocks, mobile-context indicators, taxonomic profiles, and alignment-free sequence embeddings. Gene-block conservation and rearrangement will be evaluated across isolate genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes when public assemblies are available. Work package 4 will incorporate protein-level evidence from PRIDE and other public proteomics resources. Where matched samples exist, peptide and protein evidence will be linked directly; where only related environments exist, expression evidence will be incorporated as an orthogonal support layer with appropriate uncertainty. Work package 5 will integrate modalities and test emergence. We will construct sample-by-feature matrices and cross-modal embeddings linking spectral motifs, metabolite families, gene modules, taxa, and proteins. Statistical models will include regularized regression, hierarchical Bayesian models, mixed effects models controlling for study and technology, interaction models, and cross-validation across studies. Emergence tests will compare predictive performance of single-component models against combinatorial models and will require replication in held-out datasets. We will evaluate confounding from batch effects, compositionality, uneven sampling, and metadata sparsity through sensitivity analyses, negative controls, permutation tests, and environment-stratified validation. Work package 6 will convene expert curation sprints to review high-ranking associations, refine feature definitions, and identify candidate mechanisms. Trainees will lead focused analyses under mentorship from specialists in mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, statistics, and software engineering.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will produce four major outcomes. First, we will release a public atlas of microbial gene-module-to-metabolite associations spanning host-associated and environmental microbiomes. The atlas will rank associations by reproducibility, effect size, evidence type, support from protein data, and strength of emergence relative to single-component explanations. Second, we will identify candidate emergent chemical phenotypes: metabolite families or spectral motifs whose recurrence is best explained by combinations of microbial genes, gene neighborhoods, taxa, or expressed proteins. These candidates will include both interpretable known chemistry and unknown chemical-genetic associations suitable for future experimental follow-up by the broader community. Third, we will provide reusable analytical assets, including MassQL-style spectral query collections, gene-neighborhood search workflows, cross-modal feature tables, curated metadata mappings, and benchmark datasets for testing artificial intelligence methods in multi-omics integration. Fourth, the working group will generate community guidance for analyzing unknown spectra and hypothetical proteins as informative biological signals rather than disposable artifacts. The broader impact is to shift microbiome molecular analysis from cataloging isolated genes or metabolites toward explaining how distributed molecular components assemble into reproducible cellular and community properties. This will directly advance NCEMS goals by revealing mesoscale emergence across genetic organization, protein expression, and chemical phenotype. The project will also lower barriers for researchers who wish to reuse public metabolomics, metagenomics, and proteomics data but lack expertise across all three domains. Through trainee-led cross-training, open workflows, and collaborative synthesis meetings, the project will help develop a data-savvy workforce capable of working across molecular data types, computational methods, and biological scales.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All activities will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices. The project will use only publicly available data and will maintain a versioned registry of every dataset considered, including accession identifiers, inclusion decisions, metadata completeness, quality-control outcomes, and known limitations. Workflows will be implemented with portable workflow systems and containerized software environments so that analyses can be rerun on institutional, cloud, or NCEMS-supported computing resources. Code will be developed in public repositories with issue tracking, continuous integration tests where feasible, documented releases, and archived versions with persistent identifiers. Derived feature tables, metadata mappings, spectral queries, gene-neighborhood definitions, model outputs, and benchmark splits will be released under permissive licenses consistent with source repository requirements. We will distinguish raw public data, processed intermediate data, and curated analysis products so users can trace each result back to original accessions. Reproducibility will be supported through predefined analysis plans, provenance tracking, parameter files, executable notebooks for figures and tables, and independent reruns of key analyses by trainees from different disciplinary backgrounds. Negative results will be reported, including metabolite classes or environments where no reproducible association is detected, because these outcomes are essential for benchmarking and preventing publication bias. Community engagement will include open virtual tutorials, documentation sprints, and curation workshops to refine feature definitions and metadata mappings. Authorship, contribution tracking, and data-use expectations will be established at project launch. The working group will also create training materials that introduce mass spectrometry pattern querying, microbial gene-neighborhood analysis, metaproteomics integration, and statistical tests for emergence. These materials will remain public after the award and will be designed for reuse in graduate courses, short workshops, and independent study.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS resources are requested to support coordination, computation, trainee participation, and community synthesis that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory. The budget will prioritize working group meetings, trainee exchanges, collaborative software development, cloud or high-performance computing time, data stewardship, and open dissemination. Funds will support two in-person synthesis meetings at NCEMS or a comparable host site, supplemented by regular virtual meetings.
