author: gpt-5.5
title: A Public-Data Atlas of Collective Allosteric State Variables Linking Nuclear Receptor Ligands to Transcriptional Phenotypes
abstract:
Nuclear receptors provide a powerful system for understanding emergence in molecular and cellular biology: binding of chemically diverse ligands to a buried pocket produces collective conformational shifts, altered coregulator recruitment, chromatin engagement, and cell-type-specific transcriptional outcomes. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do ligands with similar affinity for the same receptor often produce distinct efficacy, selectivity, and disease-relevant phenotypes? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to identify the collective allosteric state variables that connect residue-level perturbations in nuclear receptor ligand-binding domains to mesoscale receptor-coregulator-DNA assemblies and downstream transcriptional responses.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate structural data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, NMR and cryo-EM-derived conformational information, public molecular dynamics trajectories where available, ligand chemistry and activity data from ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR, protein sequence and evolutionary data from UniProt, OrthoDB, and public phylogenomic resources, coregulator interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, and cell-level functional data from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas. The resulting resource, NR-AlloState, will harmonize ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, mutations, post-translational modifications, coregulator motifs, DNA response elements, chromatin context, and transcriptomic outcomes into a reproducible graph-based knowledge base.

The central hypothesis is that ligand-specific transcriptional phenotypes emerge from low-dimensional, evolutionarily constrained patterns of dynamic coupling rather than from individual contacts alone. We will test this by deriving structure-based flexibility and coupling descriptors from public structures and models, comparing apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, and coregulator-bound states across the nuclear receptor superfamily. These descriptors will be integrated with ligand chemical features, mutational effects, disease variants, and transcriptional signatures using uncertainty-aware machine learning and interpretable latent-variable models. The models will be evaluated by their ability to predict held-out ligand efficacy classes, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment profiles, and transcriptomic responses across cell types.

The synthesis will address three fundamental questions. First, are there conserved dynamic architectures that explain how nuclear receptors convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence? Second, which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, partial agonism, or antagonism? Third, when do molecular allosteric changes scale up into predictable cellular transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin or coregulator context? By combining evolutionary analysis, protein dynamics, chemical informatics, and functional genomics, the working group will reveal when mesoscale regulatory behavior is encoded in the receptor itself and when it emerges from receptor partnerships in the nucleus.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis spans structural biology, molecular simulation, nuclear receptor pharmacology, evolutionary biophysics, machine learning, and genomics, and depends on harmonizing fragmented datasets that no single laboratory could curate or analyze comprehensively. All curated datasets, code, model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and tutorials will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees and reproducible workflow development, producing both a scientific atlas of nuclear receptor allostery and a generalizable framework for linking molecular conformational ensembles to emergent cellular regulation.
background_and_significance: Nuclear receptors are ligand-regulated transcription factors that convert molecular recognition events into genome-scale regulatory programs. Their ligand-binding domains accommodate endogenous metabolites, drugs, environmental chemicals, and synthetic modulators, yet the same receptor can produce agonism, partial agonism, inverse agonism, antagonism, or selective tissue responses depending on ligand identity and cellular context. This makes nuclear receptors an ideal mesoscale system for studying emergence: residue-level interactions in a buried binding pocket reshape conformational ensembles, alter helix positioning and surface dynamics, modulate coregulator recruitment, influence receptor dimerization and DNA engagement, and ultimately affect transcriptional phenotypes in a cell-type-specific chromatin environment. The central unresolved problem is that ligand affinity alone is a poor predictor of biological output. Compounds with similar binding constants can produce sharply different efficacy, receptor subtype selectivity, therapeutic windows, and disease-associated transcriptional signatures. Static structures have revealed many ligand contacts and canonical conformational changes, particularly around activation surfaces, but they do not fully explain how chemically diverse ligands bias dynamic receptor ensembles or why the same ligand can generate different outcomes across tissues. Molecular dynamics, evolutionary analysis, mutational studies, and functional genomics each provide partial views, but these data streams are fragmented across repositories, receptor subfamilies, species, assays, and cell types. A synthesis approach is now timely because public data have reached sufficient scale to connect molecular structure to cellular function. The Protein Data Bank contains numerous nuclear receptor structures in apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, dimeric, and coregulator-bound forms. AlphaFold and related public models extend structural coverage to poorly characterized isoforms and orthologs. Public molecular dynamics trajectories, NMR restraints, cryo-EM models, and ensemble descriptions provide additional evidence about conformational heterogeneity. Ligand databases such as ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR contain chemical structures, affinities, activity annotations, and pharmacological classifications. UniProt, OrthoDB, and phylogenomic resources enable comparison of conserved and variable positions across receptor evolution. Interaction databases capture receptor-coregulator and protein-protein associations, while GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas provide transcriptomic, chromatin occupancy, and regulatory context across cell types and perturbations. Integrating these resources can reveal whether nuclear receptor outputs are governed by low-dimensional collective variables: dynamic coupling patterns, flexible hinges, allosteric communication pathways, and evolutionarily tunable residue networks. Such variables would represent emergent order parameters linking atomistic ligand recognition to mesoscale receptor assemblies and cellular phenotypes. This proposal directly addresses NCEMS priorities by using only public data, requiring collaboration across protein dynamics, nuclear receptor biology, evolutionary biophysics, cheminformatics, machine learning, and functional genomics, and producing reusable community resources. The project is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires harmonizing heterogeneous molecular and cellular data, establishing shared ontologies, building reproducible workflows, and interpreting results across multiple biological scales. The resulting NR-AlloState atlas will advance fundamental understanding of allostery as an emergent phenomenon and provide a generalizable framework for linking conformational ensembles to regulatory outcomes.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will address three integrated research questions. Question 1: Are there conserved dynamic architectures that allow nuclear receptors to convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence and ligand chemical diversity? We hypothesize that receptor ligand-binding domains share a limited set of dynamic coupling architectures that connect the ligand pocket, activation function surfaces, dimer interfaces, DNA-binding domain contacts, and coregulator interaction motifs. These architectures will not be captured by individual ligand contacts alone. Instead, they will appear as recurring patterns in flexibility, residue-residue coupling, coevolution, and conformational state shifts across apo, ligand-bound, coregulator-bound, and DNA-bound structures. Question 2: Which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, selectivity, partial agonism, and antagonism? We hypothesize that functionally important tuning positions are enriched at dynamically coupled hinges, allosteric pathway bottlenecks, and subfamily-specific sequence divergence sites rather than only at directly contacting ligand-pocket residues. These positions may explain how orthologs and paralogs preserve a shared fold while evolving different endogenous ligands, pharmacological profiles, and regulatory programs. We further hypothesize that known disease variants and experimentally reported activity-altering mutations will concentrate in networks that control conformational redistribution rather than simply destabilizing the global structure. Question 3: When do molecular allosteric state variables scale up into predictable transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin, coregulator abundance, or cell identity? We hypothesize that ligand-biased receptor states will predict coregulator recruitment and transcriptional signatures most strongly in cellular contexts where the relevant receptor, partner factors, response elements, and chromatin accessibility are present. Conversely, the same molecular state may yield divergent phenotypes when cell-specific cofactors, competing receptors, post-translational modifications, or chromatin states impose alternative regulatory constraints. These questions define a testable model of emergence. At the molecular scale, ligand chemistry perturbs local contacts and pocket hydration, sterics, electrostatics, and shape complementarity. At the protein mesoscale, these perturbations are amplified or buffered by collective conformational networks. At the assembly scale, receptor states determine the probability of coregulator binding, dimer formation, DNA response element engagement, and interaction with chromatin-associated factors. At the cellular scale, these assemblies produce transcriptional changes conditioned by cell type and regulatory context. The central hypothesis is that interpretable, low-dimensional allosteric state variables can bridge these scales. We will test this hypothesis through prediction and explanation. Predictive tests will evaluate whether state variables inferred from public structural, sequence, and ligand data improve prediction of held-out ligand efficacy, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment, and transcriptomic response compared with models based only on affinity, ligand fingerprints, or receptor identity. Explanatory tests will assess whether inferred variables recover known mechanisms, identify conserved and subfamily-specific allosteric networks, and distinguish receptor-encoded effects from context-dependent cellular modulation. The project will explicitly represent uncertainty arising from assay heterogeneity, incomplete structures, inconsistent ligand annotations, and cell-type differences, so that conclusions are robust rather than artifacts of uneven public data coverage.
methods_and_approach: Aim 1 will construct NR-AlloState, a harmonized public-data knowledge base linking receptors, ligands, structures, dynamics, interactions, genomic context, and functional outcomes. We will include human nuclear receptors and selected orthologs with sufficient public sequence, structural, pharmacological, or functional data. Structures will be obtained from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, and public ensemble resources, with metadata describing receptor isoform, domain boundaries, ligand identity, oligomeric state, DNA or coregulator binding, mutations, post-translational modifications, resolution, and experimental method. Ligands will be standardized across ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR using chemical identifiers, protonation-aware structure normalization, activity units, assay type, target mapping, and efficacy labels. Functional genomics data will be curated from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas, emphasizing studies with defined receptor perturbation, ligand exposure, cell type, time point, and readout. Interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct will be mapped to coregulator motifs, receptor domains, and evidence codes. Aim 2 will derive collective allosteric descriptors from public structures and models. We will compute residue-level flexibility, elastic-network and contact-network coupling, solvent exposure, pocket geometry, ligand interaction fingerprints, coevolutionary constraints, conservation scores, and dynamic communication metrics. Where public molecular dynamics trajectories exist, we will extract ensemble-based features such as conformational populations, correlated motions, pocket breathing, and activation-surface variability. For systems without public trajectories, we will use structure-based statistical mechanics and normal-mode methods that require no new simulation data generation beyond reproducible analysis of public coordinates and models. Descriptors will be aligned across the receptor superfamily using domain-aware structural alignment and sequence homology mapping, enabling comparison of equivalent positions and networks. Aim 3 will integrate molecular descriptors with ligand and cellular phenotypes using uncertainty-aware, interpretable models. We will build a graph knowledge base in which nodes represent receptors, isoforms, orthologs, residues, ligands, structures, assays, coregulators, DNA elements, cell types, and transcriptomic signatures; edges encode binding, homology, physical contacts, dynamic coupling, regulatory association, and evidence provenance. Machine learning will include hierarchical Bayesian models, graph neural networks with attribution constraints, matrix factorization, multi-view latent-variable models, and calibrated classifiers. Model evaluation will use receptor-family-aware, ligand-scaffold-aware, and cell-type-aware splits to prevent information leakage. Primary outcomes will include prediction of ligand efficacy class, subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment, disease-variant impact, and differential expression signatures. Baseline models will use affinity, ligand fingerprints, or receptor identity alone; improvement over these baselines will test the value of collective allosteric variables. Aim 4 will conduct community working sessions for ontology refinement, benchmark creation, trainee training, and interpretation. No new experimental datasets will be generated. All work will synthesize existing public data through transparent curation, reproducible computation, and cross-disciplinary analysis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will deliver three major scientific products. First, NR-AlloState will provide a curated, queryable, graph-based atlas connecting nuclear receptor ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, structures, dynamic descriptors, coregulators, chromatin annotations, and transcriptional outcomes. This resource will transform scattered public information into an integrated framework for testing mechanisms of nuclear receptor allostery. Second, the working group will identify conserved and receptor-specific collective allosteric state variables that explain ligand efficacy, selectivity, and context-dependent transcriptional regulation better than affinity or static contact maps alone. These state variables will clarify how local chemical perturbations propagate through receptor conformational networks to alter mesoscale assemblies. Third, the project will produce benchmark datasets and interpretable predictive models for ligand efficacy, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment, and transcriptomic response. Scientifically, the results will address a long-standing puzzle in pharmacology and molecular regulation: why similar binding does not imply similar biological effect. The synthesis will reveal when regulatory information is encoded in receptor dynamics and when it emerges from interactions with coregulators, DNA elements, chromatin landscapes, and cell-specific factors. This distinction is central to understanding emergence across molecular and cellular scales. Practically, the atlas will support hypothesis generation for selective receptor modulation, interpretation of disease-associated variants, and prioritization of public data gaps. The broader impact is a reusable, open framework for linking structural ensembles to cellular phenotypes in other allosteric signaling systems. Trainees will gain experience in public-data synthesis, reproducible workflow engineering, uncertainty-aware machine learning, and team science. By bringing together expertise in protein dynamics, nuclear receptor biology, evolutionary analysis, cheminformatics, and functional genomics, the project will create discoveries and training outcomes that are not achievable by isolated laboratories.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The project will follow open, team-oriented, and reproducible science practices from inception. All input datasets will be public, and each record in NR-AlloState will retain source identifiers, accession numbers, version dates, license information where available, and evidence provenance. Curated metadata, harmonized tables, graph schemas, model-ready benchmark splits, trained model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and documentation will be released through public repositories such as GitHub and Zenodo under permissive licenses consistent with source database terms. Analysis workflows will be implemented as modular pipelines using open-source languages and workflow managers. Computational environments will be captured with containers and lock files so that analyses can be rerun on NCEMS resources, institutional clusters, or cloud platforms. Continuous integration tests will check data validation rules, identifier mapping, unit conversions, ligand standardization, structural alignment consistency, and model reproducibility. Major analyses will be accompanied by executable notebooks and narrative tutorials for users with different backgrounds, including structural biology, genomics, and machine learning. Reproducibility will be strengthened through preregistered benchmark definitions before final model comparison. We will define training, validation, and test splits that account for receptor homology, ligand scaffold similarity, assay source, and cell type to reduce data leakage. Model reports will include calibration, confidence intervals, sensitivity to missing data, and performance stratified by receptor family, ligand class, and functional assay type. Negative or inconclusive results, such as receptor families for which public data are insufficient to infer reliable state variables, will be reported with the same transparency as positive findings. The working group will develop community guidelines for nuclear receptor allostery data integration, including recommended metadata fields for structures, ligand assays, coregulator measurements, and transcriptomic perturbation studies. Trainees will help maintain documentation, lead reproducibility checks, and participate in data jamborees. Publications will be preprinted when appropriate, and final manuscripts will be open access whenever possible.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is requested to enable a community-scale synthesis effort that exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing bilateral collaboration. Funds and center resources will be used for working group meetings, trainee participation, data curation sprints, computational workflow development, benchmark evaluation, and dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new wet-lab experimental data. The major resource need is coordinated personnel time and shared infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous public datasets across structural biology, ligand pharmacology, protein evolution, interaction networks, and functional genomics. We anticipate two in-person NCEMS working group meetings per year, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings and focused data jamborees. Travel support will prioritize participation by graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career investigators, researchers from institutions with varied research intensity, and domain experts needed for specific synthesis challenges. Meeting time will be structured around data-modeling milestones: ontology finalization, receptor and ligand mapping, structural descriptor validation, genomics integration, benchmark design, model interpretation, and release preparation. Computational resources will support storage of curated public datasets, graph database development, containerized workflow execution, model training, uncertainty quantification, and public hosting of derived nonrestricted data products. We will use NCEMS cyberinfrastructure and open-source tools whenever possible, reserving cloud or high-performance computing allocations for tasks that require scalable graph analytics, structural feature extraction, or repeated model validation. Personnel effort will include working group leadership, a project data scientist or research software engineer, trainee contributors, and domain-specific curation teams. The project also requires modest support for documentation, tutorial development, accessibility review, and long-term archiving of releases. NCEMS is essential because it provides the neutral convening environment, synthesis expertise, data science support, and collaborative structure needed to align communities that rarely share a common data model. The investment will produce durable resources: NR-AlloState, reusable workflows, benchmark datasets, open tutorials, trained personnel, and a transferable strategy for studying emergent allostery in other molecular regulatory systems.

author: gpt-5.5
title: From Entangled Proteins to Entangled Genomes: A Synthesis Framework Linking Molecular Topology of Chromatin Regulators to Emergent 3D Genome Organization
abstract:
A central unresolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how molecular-scale constraints imposed by chromatin-associated proteins give rise to mesoscale nuclear properties such as chromatin loops, domains, compartments, and chromosome mechanics. Many proteins that act on DNA and chromatin are not simple globular binders: they form rings, clamps, bridged circuits, coiled-coil assemblies, topological traps, or deep entanglements that can constrain polymer motion. Yet current models of 3D genome organization typically represent these proteins as generic binders or loop extruders, without incorporating their structural topology. This Working Group will synthesize public structural, genomic, and biophysical data to ask: do the topological features of chromatin-regulating proteins predict where, when, and how stable mesoscale genome structures emerge?

We will build an open, cross-scale atlas connecting protein topology to chromatin architecture. First, we will annotate the molecular topology of chromatin regulators across eukaryotes and bacteria using existing structures from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, model organism proteomes, UniProt, ComplexPortal, and curated chromatin-factor databases. The atlas will classify knots, slipknots, lassos, theta-like circuits, ring-forming assemblies, disulfide- or metal-stabilized closures, coiled-coil bridges, and confidence-scored predicted entanglements. Second, we will integrate these annotations with public Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, SPRITE, DamID, ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA-tracing, and perturbation datasets for cohesin, condensin, CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodeling complexes, and bacterial SMC systems. Third, we will use polymer-physics and maximum-entropy modeling to test whether incorporating molecular-topology-informed constraints improves prediction of emergent chromatin features, including loop lifetime proxies, domain boundary strength, compartmental segregation, mitotic compaction, and inferred mechanical response.

The project’s central synthesis product will be a reusable computational framework that treats chromatin regulators not only by sequence identity or binding location, but by the topological constraints their structures can impose on DNA and chromatin polymers. Comparative analyses across cell types, cell-cycle states, species, and perturbations will identify whether particular protein topologies are associated with recurrent mesoscale outcomes. For example, ring-like and bridged architectures may correlate with persistent loop anchors, topological-clamp-like complexes with boundary insulation, and topologically complex remodeling or chaperone systems with regions requiring high chromatin reorganization. We will also evaluate alternative explanations, including expression level, binding affinity, domain composition, evolutionary conservation, and local chromatin state, to determine when topology adds explanatory power beyond existing molecular annotations.

This effort requires NCEMS-scale support because it combines mathematical topology, structural bioinformatics, chromatin genomics, polymer physics, machine learning, and open-science infrastructure in a way that exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. The Working Group will convene protein topologists, genome modelers, structural biologists, chromatin experimentalists, data scientists, and trainees to define shared standards for representing molecular topology across scales. All annotations, workflows, benchmark datasets, visualization tools, and model outputs will be released openly. By training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to work across protein structure, genome organization, and mesoscale modeling, the project will create a data-savvy community positioned to explain how molecular entanglement contributes to emergent cellular organization.
background_and_significance: Chromosomes are not passive polymers. Their mesoscale organization emerges from interactions among DNA sequence, epigenetic state, transcriptional activity, molecular motors, architectural proteins, and physical constraints. Public Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, SPRITE, DamID, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA-tracing, microscopy-derived distance, and perturbation datasets have revealed loops, topologically associating domains, compartments, mitotic compaction, bacterial chromosome domains, and cell-type-specific structural heterogeneity. Yet a persistent gap remains between the molecular structures of chromatin regulators and the emergent physical behavior of chromosomes. Most genome-organization models encode chromatin-associated proteins as occupancy tracks, binders, barriers, or generic loop-extruding agents. This representation has been productive, but it discards structural features that may be central to function: rings, clamps, coiled-coil arms, bridged circuits, knots, slipknots, lassos, pseudo-closed loops, disulfide-stabilized closures, metal-mediated constraints, and topological traps. These structural motifs can alter polymer threading, residence time, release probability, cooperative assembly, mechanical response, and the ability of a protein complex to constrain DNA segments over time. Molecular topology is therefore a plausible but underused explanatory layer for mesoscale genome organization. Cohesin and condensin illustrate the opportunity. These SMC complexes form extended coiled-coil assemblies with ring-like architectures and dynamic gates that are often modeled as loop extruders. However, different SMC complexes operate in interphase, mitosis, meiosis, and bacteria, producing distinct loop sizes, compaction states, boundary interactions, and mechanical properties. CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodeling complexes, transcription-associated factors, and bacterial nucleoid proteins impose additional constraints whose structural topologies differ widely. Some act as bridges, some modulate DNA supercoiling or strand passage, some remodel nucleosomes, and some organize higher-order assemblies. The field lacks a systematic public synthesis linking these molecular topologies to genomic locations, perturbation outcomes, evolutionary conservation, and polymer-physics models. The timing is ideal for an NCEMS Working Group because the required data already exist but are dispersed across communities. Structural data are available in the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, model organism proteomes, UniProt, ComplexPortal, domain databases, and curated chromatin-factor resources. Genome-organization data exist across species, cell types, developmental states, cell-cycle stages, mutants, degron perturbations, drug treatments, and imaging platforms. Topological algorithms can classify open-chain entanglement and closed or pseudo-closed circuits, while polymer models can test whether topology-informed constraints improve predictions beyond occupancy and epigenetic covariates. This project addresses NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, assembling expertise that exceeds any single laboratory, and focusing on emergence across molecular and mesoscale levels. It asks whether the shape and topology of chromatin regulators help explain how local molecular constraints generate stable, dynamic, and mechanically responsive genome architecture.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: The Working Group will address one overarching question: do topological features of chromatin-regulating proteins provide predictive information about emergent three-dimensional genome organization that is not captured by binding location, expression level, domain composition, sequence conservation, or chromatin state alone? We will decompose this question into four linked research questions. First, what topological classes are present among proteins and protein complexes that regulate chromatin and DNA organization across eukaryotes and bacteria? We hypothesize that chromatin regulators are enriched for specific constraint-generating architectures, including ring-like assemblies, coiled-coil bridged circuits, clamp-like domains, strand-passage enzymes, lasso-like motifs, metal-stabilized closures, and deep entanglements, relative to matched nuclear or cytosolic protein sets. Second, are these topological classes associated with distinct mesoscale chromatin features? We hypothesize that ring-forming and gated architectures are preferentially associated with persistent loop structures and mitotic compaction; bridged or theta-like architectures are associated with boundary insulation and long-range contact hubs; topoisomerase and strand-passage topologies correlate with regions exhibiting high reorganization or supercoiling-linked changes; and remodeling or chaperone complexes with complex flexible topologies are enriched at loci showing rapid structural transitions across cell states. Third, does topology improve predictive models of chromatin architecture? We hypothesize that models incorporating topology-informed constraints will better predict loop strength, loop persistence proxies, boundary insulation, compartment segregation, contact decay, and inferred mechanical response than models using only genomic annotations, ChIP-seq intensity, epigenetic marks, gene expression, and protein identity. Improvement will be evaluated through held-out chromosomes, held-out cell types, perturbation prediction, and cross-species transfer. Fourth, when does topology fail to explain genome organization? This question is essential for rigor. We hypothesize that topology contributes most strongly where a protein physically constrains polymer motion for timescales comparable to chromatin relaxation, and contributes weakly where observed patterns are dominated by transcriptional state, phase separation, local chromatin accessibility, copy number, technical platform effects, or transient low-affinity binding. We will explicitly test alternative explanations, including protein abundance, binding affinity proxies, motif density, post-translational regulation, complex stoichiometry, evolutionary conservation, compartment state, replication timing, transcription, and local mappability. These hypotheses frame molecular topology as neither a universal cause nor a decorative structural feature, but as a testable mechanistic variable. The project will also produce methodological hypotheses: that a shared ontology of protein topology can be made interoperable with genome browser tracks and polymer simulation parameters; that confidence-scored AlphaFold and experimentally resolved structures can be integrated without conflating reliable and uncertain entanglements; and that mesoscale emergence can be studied by comparing recurrent outcomes across independent public datasets rather than by relying on a single assay. Success will be measured by reproducible associations, improved predictive performance, interpretable polymer-model parameters, and community adoption of the atlas and workflows.
methods_and_approach: This project will be organized as a synthesis-only Working Group with three integrated workstreams. Workstream 1 will construct a public topology atlas of chromatin regulators. We will assemble candidate proteins and complexes from UniProt, Gene Ontology, ComplexPortal, model organism databases, curated chromatin-factor resources, bacterial nucleoid protein catalogs, and literature-derived lists for cohesin, condensin, CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodelers, SMC-associated factors, transcriptional architectural proteins, and bacterial chromosome organizers. Structural inputs will include Protein Data Bank coordinates, AlphaFold Database models, available multimeric complex models, domain annotations, disulfide and metal-binding annotations, and confidence metrics. Topological classification will use established computational approaches for open-chain knot detection, slipknot analysis, lasso and pierced-loop identification, genus and circuit descriptors, theta-like graph representations, coiled-coil bridge detection, and ring or clamp architecture annotation. Each annotation will include provenance, algorithmic parameters, confidence level, structure source, biological assembly state, and uncertainty flags. Workstream 2 will integrate topology annotations with public genome-organization datasets. We will curate interoperable datasets from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, 4DN, modENCODE, organism-specific repositories, and published supplementary resources, prioritizing matched Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, HiChIP, SPRITE, DamID, ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag, degron or knockout perturbations, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA tracing, and microscopy-based distance measurements. Harmonization will use existing genome builds, lifted coordinates where appropriate, standardized quality metrics, replicate-aware normalization, and metadata describing cell type, species, cell-cycle state, perturbation, assay, resolution, and batch. Derived mesoscale phenotypes will include loop strength, boundary insulation, compartment eigenvectors, contact probability scaling, chromatin domain persistence, inter-locus distance distributions, mitotic compaction measures, bacterial macrodomains, and perturbation effect sizes. Workstream 3 will test predictive and mechanistic models. Statistical models will evaluate whether topology classes explain variance in mesoscale phenotypes after controlling for occupancy, expression, conservation, domain architecture, chromatin state, transcription, GC content, mappability, and assay platform. Machine-learning models will use nested cross-validation, held-out cell types, held-out species, and perturbation-based tests to estimate generalization. Polymer-physics and maximum-entropy models will translate topology classes into explicit constraints, such as loop-capture probability, residence-time priors, bridge valency, gated passage, compaction strength, and release kinetics. We will compare topology-aware and topology-agnostic models using contact-map likelihoods, distance-distribution accuracy, insulation prediction, and recovery of perturbation phenotypes. NCEMS convenings will support ontology design, benchmark selection, code review, trainee exchanges, and synthesis workshops. No new experimental data will be generated. All work will reuse public data, and any manual curation will be documented as a reproducible scholarly product.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will deliver an open cross-scale atlas linking chromatin-regulator molecular topology to emergent genome organization. The atlas will include confidence-scored annotations of knots, slipknots, lassos, theta-like circuits, rings, clamps, coiled-coil bridges, stabilized closures, and complex assemblies for chromatin-associated proteins across selected eukaryotic and bacterial systems. It will be interoperable with genome browsers, structural viewers, and modeling workflows, allowing researchers to ask whether a bound protein is merely present at a locus or is structurally capable of imposing a particular polymer constraint. A second outcome will be benchmark datasets connecting topology annotations with public chromatin conformation, protein occupancy, perturbation, imaging, and cell-state metadata. These benchmarks will support transparent comparison of models for loops, domains, compartments, compaction, and mechanical response. A third outcome will be a reusable computational framework for topology-aware genome modeling. If topology-informed features improve prediction, the project will establish a new mechanistic layer connecting molecular structure to mesoscale nuclear emergence. If improvements are context-dependent or limited, the project will still clarify when occupancy, chromatin state, or other variables dominate, thereby sharpening mechanistic models. The broader impact is conceptual and practical. Conceptually, the project will bridge protein topology, structural biology, chromatin genomics, and polymer physics, showing how constraints embedded in molecular architecture can propagate to mesoscale cellular organization. Practically, the atlas and workflows will help researchers prioritize chromatin regulators for reanalysis, perturbation interpretation, comparative genomics, and protein engineering. The Working Group will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in open data synthesis, topological analysis, statistical modeling, and collaborative software development. By producing reusable standards rather than a one-off analysis, the project will build community capacity for studying emergence from molecular constraints to cellular-scale organization.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from inception. All source code, workflow definitions, documentation, issue tracking, and analysis notebooks will be developed in public version-controlled repositories under permissive open-source licenses. Data products will use persistent identifiers, semantic versioning, machine-readable metadata, and clear provenance records linking each annotation or derived phenotype to its original public source. Because the project uses only existing public data, no embargoed experimental datasets or restricted human subject data will be incorporated unless they are already approved for open use under the relevant repository terms. Reproducibility will be supported through containerized software environments, workflow managers, automated tests, continuous integration, and archived releases on public repositories such as Zenodo. We will define benchmark datasets with frozen versions so that topology-aware and topology-agnostic models can be compared consistently over time. Each major result will include executable scripts for data download, preprocessing, model fitting, visualization, and statistical evaluation. Uncertainty will be reported explicitly, especially for predicted protein structures, multimeric assemblies, low-confidence AlphaFold regions, ambiguous knot closure choices, incomplete complexes, and chromatin datasets with variable resolution or replicate quality. The Working Group will establish community guidelines for topology annotation of chromatin regulators, including nomenclature, confidence categories, minimum metadata, and recommended visualizations. Trainees will participate in code review, data-curation sprints, reproducibility audits, and short training modules on structural bioinformatics, chromatin data formats, polymer modeling, and responsible use of AI-assisted analysis. Publications will be submitted as preprints and to peer-reviewed venues, with all figures traceable to public workflows. We will also provide tutorials, example notebooks, and lightweight web-based visualization tools to make the atlas useful to experimentalists, theorists, and data scientists. These practices will ensure that NCEMS support yields durable community infrastructure, not merely static conclusions.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination among communities that rarely share data standards or modeling languages. Requested resources will support four categories. First, Working Group convenings will include two in-person synthesis meetings per year and regular virtual meetings for topology ontology development, dataset prioritization, model benchmarking, and manuscript or software sprints. Travel funds will prioritize participation by trainees, early-career researchers, members from diverse institution types, and collaborators with complementary expertise in protein topology, chromatin biology, polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, statistics, and open-source infrastructure. Second, personnel and trainee support will fund graduate student and postdoctoral effort for data harmonization, software engineering, documentation, benchmark construction, and cross-training. Short trainee exchanges will pair structural-topology trainees with chromatin-modeling groups and genome-data trainees with protein-structure groups. Third, computational resources will support public-data processing, contact-map normalization, structural annotation at proteome scale, model comparison, container builds, and web-accessible visualization. These needs include cloud storage, high-performance computing time, continuous integration services, and archival deposition fees where applicable. Fourth, community dissemination funds will support online tutorials, hackathons, documentation, accessibility improvements, and maintenance of the atlas and benchmark releases. Existing public resources provide the raw material, but NCEMS infrastructure provides the collaborative environment needed to transform scattered structural, genomic, and biophysical datasets into an interoperable framework. By investing in coordination, reproducible workflows, and trainee development, the project will create reusable capacity for future synthesis efforts on molecular and cellular emergence.

title: Emergent Translational Reserve as a Multiscale Determinant of Skeletal Muscle Growth, Repair, and Inflammatory Failure
abstract:
Skeletal muscle exhibits striking emergent behavior: molecular changes in signaling, chromatin state, ribosome production, autophagy, immune activity, and mechanical response collectively produce higher-order outcomes such as hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, or functional decline. Yet a central unresolved question remains: why do similar anabolic or mechanical cues produce robust growth in some contexts but maladaptive inflammation, impaired repair, or wasting in others? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define and model an emergent property we call “translational reserve”: the coordinated capacity of muscle cells and their local niche to expand ribosome biogenesis, maintain protein synthesis, buffer proteostatic stress, and support tissue remodeling under mechanical or inflammatory challenge.

This project will use only publicly available datasets to integrate molecular, cellular, and tissue-scale information across human and animal skeletal muscle studies. Data sources will include bulk and single-nucleus RNA-seq from exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, muscular disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, and injury models; public proteomics and phosphoproteomics datasets related to mTOR signaling, ribosome assembly, autophagy, and inflammatory pathways; DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility datasets where available; ribosome profiling and translation-associated datasets from muscle and related cell types; and histological or imaging-derived public metadata on fiber size, fiber type, fibrosis, immune infiltration, and functional outcomes. The project will harmonize these heterogeneous resources into a shared cross-species atlas of muscle adaptation states.

The central hypothesis is that tissue-level muscle outcomes emerge from nonlinear interactions among three mesoscale modules: nucleolar/ribosome biogenesis capacity, proteostasis-autophagy buffering, and immune-fibrotic niche signaling. We will test this by developing an AI-driven multiscale integration framework combining graph neural networks, interpretable latent variable models, and mathematical dynamical modeling. The graph representation will connect genes, proteins, pathways, cell states, perturbations, species, disease contexts, and phenotypic outcomes. GPU-accelerated workflows will enable large-scale reanalysis of sequencing and methylation datasets, standardized feature extraction, and scalable model training across many public studies. Mathematical models will then translate learned network structure into dynamic hypotheses about threshold behavior, feedback loops, and tipping points that separate adaptive hypertrophy from maladaptive remodeling.

The expected product is not merely a catalog of exercise-responsive genes, but a predictive synthesis of how molecular and cellular modules combine to generate emergent muscle phenotypes. We will identify conserved and context-specific signatures of translational reserve, determine whether inflammatory disease shifts muscle toward a low-reserve state, and evaluate whether ribosome biogenesis, autophagy, and immune-cell composition jointly predict fiber growth or fibrosis better than any single pathway. Cross-species analyses will distinguish mechanisms conserved between rodent overload models and human training or disease cohorts, while cell-type-resolved analyses will reveal how myonuclei, satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, endothelial cells, and immune cells contribute to the emergent tissue response.

NCEMS support is essential because this effort requires coordinated expertise in muscle biology, translational control, inflammation, high-performance computing, graph-based AI, and mechanistic mathematical modeling, as well as community agreement on data standards and reproducible workflows. The working group will release an open atlas, curated metadata schema, analysis pipelines, trained models, and interactive visualization tools. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will receive cross-training in muscle physiology, public-data reuse, GPU-enabled bioinformatics, network modeling, and open collaborative science. By synthesizing dispersed public data into a mechanistic, predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence: how molecular-scale control of protein production and stress buffering gives rise to cell- and tissue-scale muscle adaptation or failure.
background_and_significance: Skeletal muscle is a highly plastic tissue in which molecular, cellular, and niche-level processes combine to produce system-level outcomes that cannot be inferred from any single pathway alone. Mechanical loading, resistance exercise, injury, disuse, aging, inflammatory disease, and metabolic stress can all activate overlapping signaling programs, including mTOR-associated anabolic signaling, ribosome biogenesis, autophagy, inflammatory cytokine networks, extracellular matrix remodeling, and satellite cell responses. Despite these shared components, the tissue response varies widely. One context yields fiber hypertrophy and improved function; another yields fibrosis, immune infiltration, impaired regeneration, or wasting. This divergence represents a fundamental problem in emergence: how do molecular-scale changes in protein production and stress regulation become coordinated, or fail to become coordinated, into adaptive tissue remodeling? A long-standing gap in muscle biology is the lack of an integrative framework linking translational control to tissue-level adaptation across physiological and disease contexts. Ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis are essential for sustained growth, but their effects depend on energetic state, proteostasis capacity, autophagy, inflammatory milieu, myonuclear transcriptional state, vascular support, and the behavior of fibro-adipogenic progenitors and immune cells. Conversely, inflammation and fibrosis do not simply suppress anabolism; they may reshape the mesoscale organization of muscle, altering cell-cell communication, nutrient flux, extracellular constraints, and translational capacity. Public data now make it possible to examine these relationships at a community scale. Large numbers of bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq, proteomic, phosphoproteomic, epigenomic, ribosome-associated, imaging, and phenotypic datasets have been deposited from human exercise training studies, rodent overload models, immobilization, aging, dystrophy, injury, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, cachexia, and related perturbations. However, these resources remain fragmented by species, platform, metadata conventions, analytical pipelines, and disease focus. Most analyses ask whether individual genes or pathways change within a study; few synthesize across contexts to determine whether higher-order modules jointly define adaptive capacity. We propose translational reserve as an emergent mesoscale property: the coordinated capacity of muscle fibers and their niche to expand ribosome production, sustain translation, maintain proteostatic balance, and remodel tissue under challenge. Translational reserve is not equivalent to expression of ribosomal genes, mTOR activity, or autophagy markers alone. It is a systems-level state arising from nonlinear interactions among nucleolar activity, translation machinery, protein quality control, immune-fibrotic signaling, chromatin state, and cell composition. Defining this property requires integration of diverse public datasets and expertise spanning muscle physiology, translational control, inflammatory disease, high-performance computing, graph-based artificial intelligence, and mathematical modeling. This proposal is well aligned with NCEMS because it uses only existing public data to address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence at the mesoscale. The work is beyond the scope of any single laboratory: it requires cross-species data harmonization, scalable reanalysis, community metadata standards, interpretable AI, and mechanistic modeling. The resulting atlas and models will transform dispersed studies into a predictive framework for understanding why muscle adapts, repairs, or fails.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will address four linked scientific questions. Question 1: Can translational reserve be operationally defined from public multi-omic and phenotypic data as a reproducible, cross-context state of skeletal muscle? We hypothesize that adaptive hypertrophy and effective regeneration share a conserved multivariate signature characterized by coordinated ribosome biogenesis, translation initiation and elongation capacity, balanced autophagy and proteasome activity, restrained inflammatory signaling, and permissive niche remodeling. This signature will be detectable across human and animal datasets despite differences in species, platform, and perturbation. Question 2: Do inflammatory and degenerative conditions shift muscle into a low-reserve or misallocated-reserve state? We hypothesize that rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, aging, immobilization, cachexia, and dystrophic contexts will not simply show reduced anabolic signaling. Instead, they will display disrupted coupling among ribosome biogenesis, proteostasis, and tissue remodeling. In some cases, translation-associated programs may be activated without adequate autophagic buffering or extracellular support, producing stress, maladaptive immune activation, and impaired growth. In other cases, inflammatory and fibrotic signaling may suppress nucleolar and translational capacity, lowering the threshold for wasting after mechanical or metabolic challenge. Question 3: Which cell types and niche interactions contribute most strongly to translational reserve? We hypothesize that myonuclei encode much of the core ribosome and translation program, but the emergent reserve state depends on coordinated signals from satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, macrophages, endothelial cells, and other stromal or immune populations. Single-nucleus and single-cell datasets will reveal whether high-reserve states require specific ligand-receptor networks, extracellular matrix states, vascular-associated signals, or immune phenotypes. We further hypothesize that fibro-inflammatory niche states can predict whether ribosome biogenesis is coupled to productive growth or diverted toward repair failure and fibrosis. Question 4: Can integrated AI and dynamical models identify tipping points that distinguish adaptive hypertrophy from maladaptive remodeling? We hypothesize that muscle adaptation is governed by nonlinear thresholds rather than linear pathway activity. A moderate inflammatory response may support repair, whereas excessive or persistent immune-fibrotic signaling may decouple translational capacity from tissue growth. Similarly, increased ribosome biogenesis may promote hypertrophy only when proteostasis and autophagy remain sufficient to buffer the increased protein production load. The project will test whether graph neural networks and interpretable latent variable models can predict fiber size, fibrosis, immune infiltration, functional status, or disease state better than single-pathway scores. Mathematical dynamical models will then translate these learned relationships into candidate feedback structures, including mTOR-ribosome-autophagy loops, cytokine-mediated suppression of translational capacity, and niche-driven extracellular constraints. Collectively, these hypotheses frame translational reserve as a measurable and predictive emergent property. The goal is not to identify a universal marker, but to determine how molecular and cellular modules combine differently across contexts to produce growth, repair, decline, or inflammatory failure.
methods_and_approach: The project will proceed through four integrated workstreams using only publicly available data. Workstream 1 will create a curated cross-species skeletal muscle adaptation atlas. We will identify datasets from repositories including Gene Expression Omnibus, Sequence Read Archive, ArrayExpress, PRIDE, MassIVE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, HuBMAP where applicable, and domain-specific resources linked to human exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, injury, muscular disease, inflammatory rheumatic disease, myositis, and cachexia. Eligible datasets will include bulk RNA-seq, microarray data where valuable, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq, proteomics, phosphoproteomics, DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility, ribosome profiling or translation-associated assays, and public histological or functional metadata. No new specimens, experiments, or unpublished restricted datasets will be used. Workstream 2 will harmonize data and metadata. We will define a shared schema for species, muscle group, age, sex, perturbation, time point, disease status, training or overload protocol, injury model, assay type, cell type, fiber type, histology, function, and outcome class. Raw sequencing datasets will be reprocessed where feasible through containerized workflows; processed datasets will be incorporated when raw data are unavailable but quality criteria are met. Ortholog mapping will support mouse-rat-human comparisons. Batch effects will be addressed using study-aware normalization, negative-control evaluations, and sensitivity analyses that preserve biological contrasts. Single-cell and single-nucleus studies will be integrated with standardized quality control, cell annotation, and label transfer, while proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets will be mapped to pathway and protein-complex features. Workstream 3 will build multiscale models of translational reserve. We will compute interpretable module scores for nucleolar and ribosome biogenesis activity, translation initiation and elongation, mTOR and nutrient signaling, autophagy, proteasome activity, unfolded protein response, inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, vascular programs, and immune-cell composition. These features will seed a heterogeneous graph connecting genes, proteins, complexes, pathways, cell states, perturbations, species, studies, and phenotypic outcomes. Graph neural networks will learn cross-context relationships and predict adaptive versus maladaptive outcomes. Interpretable latent variable models will define reserve axes and quantify uncertainty. GPU-accelerated workflows will support scalable alignment, methylation calling where public nanopore data exist, feature extraction, and model training. Workstream 4 will convert statistical associations into dynamic hypotheses. Using learned network structures, we will formulate reduced ordinary differential equation and, where appropriate, partial differential or compartmental models representing interactions among ribosome biogenesis, proteostasis-autophagy buffering, immune-fibrotic signaling, and tissue remodeling. These models will be fit to public time-course data from overload, injury, immobilization, and training studies. Bifurcation and sensitivity analyses will identify candidate thresholds and feedback loops separating hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, and wasting. The working group will meet through NCEMS-supported in-person synthesis sessions and virtual hackathons. Subteams will focus on data curation, muscle biology interpretation, computational infrastructure, graph AI, mathematical modeling, and trainee-led reproducibility audits.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will deliver a public, cross-species atlas of skeletal muscle adaptation states spanning growth, repair, disuse, aging, inflammatory disease, and degenerative failure. The atlas will include harmonized metadata, standardized molecular features, cell-type annotations, phenotype mappings, and quality metrics. Its primary scientific output will be a testable definition of translational reserve as an emergent mesoscale property linking ribosome biogenesis, translation, proteostasis, autophagy, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. We expect to identify conserved high-reserve signatures associated with adaptive hypertrophy and regeneration, as well as low-reserve or uncoupled-reserve states associated with fibrosis, immune infiltration, impaired repair, and functional decline. A major impact will be predictive rather than descriptive. The integrated models will determine whether combinations of ribosome biogenesis, autophagy buffering, and immune-fibrotic niche state predict tissue outcomes better than any single pathway. Cross-species comparisons will clarify which mechanisms from rodent overload and injury models translate to human training and disease cohorts. Cell-resolved analyses will indicate how myonuclei, satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, endothelial cells, and immune populations jointly shape emergent outcomes. The project will also produce reusable computational tools: graph-based models, interpretable reserve scores, visualization dashboards, and dynamical model templates. These resources will support future synthesis projects in other tissues where translational capacity and proteostatic stress interact with inflammation, such as heart, tendon, and immune-rich epithelial barriers. For NCEMS, the work directly advances the center mission by using existing public data, AI, and mathematical modeling to explain emergence at the molecular-to-cellular-to-tissue interface. For the broader community, it will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding why similar anabolic cues produce growth in some settings and maladaptive remodeling in others.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The working group will operate under open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from project initiation. All data used will be publicly available, and each dataset will be documented with accession numbers, licensing status, provenance, assay type, inclusion criteria, quality metrics, and processing decisions. We will release a living data catalog and metadata schema early in the project to invite community feedback before final modeling decisions are locked. Analysis workflows will be implemented with version-controlled repositories, containerized software environments, workflow managers, and continuous integration tests for key pipeline components. Code will be deposited on public platforms under permissive open-source licenses, with stable archival releases assigned digital object identifiers. Reprocessed feature matrices, harmonized metadata, model inputs, trained model weights, and non-restricted derived outputs will be shared through appropriate public repositories. When redistribution of processed data is constrained by repository terms, we will provide scripts that regenerate the features from the original accessions. Reproducibility will be strengthened through prespecified analysis plans, blinded outcome prediction tasks where feasible, independent replication across held-out studies, and negative-control analyses. Model performance will be reported with uncertainty estimates, study-level cross-validation, and explicit tests for species, sex, age, disease, and platform bias. Interpretability methods will be used to identify which features drive predictions, but mechanistic claims will be restricted to patterns supported across independent datasets or dynamic model analyses. Trainees will participate in reproducibility rotations in which they attempt to rerun workflows, inspect metadata consistency, and document failure modes. The group will also create user-facing tutorials for muscle biologists, computational scientists, and mathematical modelers. Publications will be submitted as open access whenever possible, and preprints will be posted. Interactive dashboards will allow users to explore reserve signatures, cell states, perturbations, and model predictions without requiring advanced programming skills.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is requested for the coordination, computational infrastructure, trainee development, and community engagement required for a synthesis project of this scale. Personnel effort will support a project coordinator or data steward to manage dataset inventories, metadata standards, meeting logistics, documentation, and public releases. Funds will also support graduate student and postdoctoral participation from the collaborating groups, with dedicated time for data curation, GPU-enabled workflow development, graph modeling, mathematical analysis, and reproducibility testing. Travel support is essential for two NCEMS-hosted in-person working group meetings per year, supplemented by virtual analysis sprints. In-person sessions will focus on ontology decisions, biological interpretation of model outputs, trainee training, and integration across muscle physiology, inflammatory disease, AI, and dynamical modeling. Computational resources will include cloud or institutional high-performance computing time, GPU access for large-scale reprocessing and model training, secure project storage for public raw and derived data, and web hosting for dashboards and documentation. The project will not budget for new experimental data generation, animal studies, clinical recruitment, sample acquisition, sequencing, imaging, or wet-lab validation. All analyses will reuse public datasets. Additional resources will support software engineering, container maintenance, data archival fees, open-access publication costs, and accessibility of training materials. NCEMS resources are uniquely necessary because the project requires neutral convening, shared infrastructure, community standards, and cross-disciplinary collaboration beyond existing bilateral collaborations. The working group will include expertise in skeletal muscle adaptation, translational control, inflammation and rheumatic disease, public multi-omic data reuse, high-performance computing, graph neural networks, and mathematical modeling. Trainees will receive structured cross-training through workshops on muscle biology, public repository mining, reproducible bioinformatics, GPU-accelerated analysis, network learning, and dynamical systems. Deliverables tied to budget milestones will include the public dataset catalog, harmonized atlas release, baseline reserve scoring pipeline, graph model release, dynamic model notebooks, visualization portal, and final synthesis manuscripts.
