author: gpt-5.5
title: A Public Data Atlas Linking Disordered-Region Sequence Grammar to Emergent Condensate Material States
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates emerge from many weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, structured domains, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level answer to a central question: which molecular features determine whether a condensate remains a dynamic cellular compartment, becomes a gel-like regulatory hub, or crosses into aberrant aggregation? We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate public sequence, biophysical, imaging, proteomic, and disease-variant data to build a predictive atlas connecting disordered-region molecular grammar to mesoscale condensate material properties.

The working group will assemble and harmonize existing public data from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, and published supplementary datasets reporting phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, viscosity proxies, SAXS/NMR-derived ensemble parameters, turbidity, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. The project will focus on three biologically important condensate classes that are rarely analyzed together: RNA-binding protein granules linked to neurodegeneration, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates involving polyamines, phosphorylation, oxidation, or other cellular-state variables.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate material state is not encoded by single features such as net charge or aromatic content alone, but by higher-order patterns: sticker valence and spacing, charge blockiness, transient structure propensity, partner valence, nucleic acid context, post-translational modification state, and cellular concentration regimes. These features jointly produce emergent mesoscale properties that can be inferred only by integrating heterogeneous datasets across proteins, organisms, experimental modalities, and disease contexts.

The synthesis will proceed in four coordinated activities. First, we will create an open condensate-material ontology that standardizes experimental descriptors such as liquid-like exchange, viscoelasticity, aging, demixing, gelation, and irreversible aggregation. Second, we will extract quantitative and semi-quantitative material-state labels from public tables, figures, repositories, and curated literature using reproducible text-mining and human-in-the-loop annotation. Third, we will compute interpretable polymer-physics and sequence-patterning features for disordered regions and combine them with PTM, mutation, abundance, localization, RNA-binding, and interaction-network features. Fourth, we will train benchmarked machine-learning and statistical models to predict condensate state transitions and identify conserved physical rules shared across neurodegenerative proteins, transcription factors, histone tails, and synthetic condensate scaffolds.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, normalize, and interpret the dispersed data spanning biophysics, cell biology, neurodegeneration, genomics, image analysis, and polymer theory. The working group will bring together experts in intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate physics, chromatin organization, neurodegenerative disease, proteomics, bioimage informatics, evolutionary analysis, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly licensed database, FAIR workflows, benchmark datasets, interactive visualization tools, and training modules for graduate students and postdocs in reproducible data synthesis. By transforming scattered public observations into an integrated mesoscale atlas, the project will provide a general framework for predicting how molecular disorder gives rise to emergent cellular organization and when that organization becomes pathological.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates provide a prominent example of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. They are not defined by a single molecular bond or a fixed stoichiometric structure, but by collective interactions among proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, post-translational modifications, and cellular environments. Intrinsically disordered regions are especially important because their sequence patterns encode weak, multivalent contacts that can produce liquid droplets, viscoelastic assemblies, gels, demixed subphases, or aggregates. These material states influence RNA metabolism, transcription, chromatin organization, stress responses, signaling, and proteostasis. However, the field still lacks a general synthesis-level framework that connects molecular grammar to condensate material state across biological contexts.

This gap is scientifically important because condensates can be functional, adaptive, or pathological depending on their emergent physical properties. RNA-binding proteins such as TDP-43, FUS, hnRNPA1, Tau, and alpha-synuclein illustrate how dynamic assemblies can support cellular regulation yet become associated with neurodegenerative disease when aging, mutation, oxidation, altered concentration, or partner composition shifts the material state toward gelation or aggregation. Transcription factors, chromatin regulators, histone tails, and enhancer-associated proteins form condensates that may concentrate regulatory machinery and reorganize nuclear space. Stress-responsive condensates, including assemblies modulated by phosphorylation, oxidation, metabolites, and polyamines, reveal that cellular state can tune phase behavior without changing the underlying primary sequence. These classes are usually studied in separate communities, limiting discovery of conserved principles.

Public data now make synthesis possible. Databases such as LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, ClinVar, gnomAD, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, and AlphaFold confidence profiles contain complementary information on phase separation, intrinsic disorder, protein domains, post-translational modifications, variants, abundance, localization, structure prediction confidence, imaging, and disease relevance. Published supplementary datasets further report phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet coalescence, turbidity, viscosity proxies, SAXS and NMR ensemble measurements, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. Yet these observations remain dispersed, inconsistently annotated, and difficult to compare quantitatively.

NCEMS support is essential because the required integration exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. The project demands expertise in polymer physics, protein disorder, condensate biology, neurodegeneration, chromatin, proteomics, bioimage analysis, evolutionary genomics, ontology development, and interpretable AI. It also requires community standards for defining material-state labels and uncertainty. By synthesizing only publicly available data, this working group will directly address NCEMS priorities: discovering emergent principles at the mesoscale, building open analytical strategies, training data-savvy trainees, and creating reusable community infrastructure. The proposed atlas will transform isolated observations into a coherent resource for understanding when molecular disorder generates dynamic cellular organization and when the same principles promote pathological transitions.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The overarching research question is: which combinations of disordered-region sequence features, molecular partners, modifications, and cellular context determine the emergent material state of biomolecular condensates? We will address this question through five linked subquestions designed for synthesis across publicly available data.

Question 1 asks whether condensate material states can be represented by a shared ontology across experimental systems. Current studies use overlapping but inconsistent descriptors, including liquid-like, dynamic, gel-like, aged, solid-like, immobile, demixed, fibrillar, and aggregated. We hypothesize that these descriptors can be mapped onto a multidimensional material-state framework defined by exchange kinetics, coalescence behavior, viscoelasticity, reversibility, internal organization, and aggregation propensity. This framework will allow both quantitative labels, such as FRAP half-time and mobile fraction, and semi-quantitative labels, such as rapid fusion or irreversible puncta, to be used with explicit uncertainty.

Question 2 asks whether higher-order sequence grammar predicts material state more effectively than simple composition. We hypothesize that sticker valence, aromatic and cationic residue spacing, charge patterning, glycine and proline distribution, hydrophobic clustering, transient helical or beta propensity, low-complexity architecture, and domain-disorder boundaries jointly encode the interaction landscape that drives phase behavior. Single variables such as net charge per residue or fraction of aromatic residues will be informative but insufficient.

Question 3 asks how molecular partners reshape the sequence-to-material relationship. Many condensates arise through interactions among disordered regions, structured RNA-binding domains, RNA or DNA, chromatin, folded enzymes, scaffolds, clients, metabolites, and polyamines. We hypothesize that partner valence and chemical type act as context-dependent modifiers: RNA and chromatin can either solubilize or crosslink condensates, polyamines can strengthen electrostatic bridges, and structured domains can nucleate demixing or aggregation when local unfolding exposes additional stickers.

Question 4 asks how post-translational modifications and disease variants alter emergent states. We hypothesize that phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, oxidation, and disease-associated substitutions shift material state by perturbing charge blocks, sticker accessibility, transient structure, and interaction specificity. Some modifications will dissolve condensates, whereas others will create new crosslinks or alter aging kinetics. Disease variants will be most interpretable when analyzed as perturbations to sequence grammar and partner networks rather than as isolated annotations.

Question 5 asks whether physical rules are conserved across condensate classes. We hypothesize that RNA-binding granules, transcriptional and chromatin condensates, and stress-responsive condensates share general principles but occupy different regions of a common feature space. The working group will test whether models trained on one condensate class transfer to another, whether conserved sequence patterns correlate with similar material states across species, and whether synthetic condensate systems reveal design rules that also explain natural assemblies. Together, these hypotheses frame condensate material state as an emergent mesoscale phenotype arising from molecular grammar plus context.
methods_and_approach:
This project will use only existing publicly available data and will be organized as a coordinated NCEMS working group with four integrated workstreams. No new experimental measurements will be generated.

Workstream 1 will define the data model and condensate-material ontology. Domain experts will establish controlled vocabularies for molecular components, experimental modality, perturbation type, environmental condition, concentration regime, phase behavior, material-state descriptor, and evidence strength. The ontology will represent liquid-like exchange, coarsening, fusion, aging, viscoelasticity, gelation, demixing, fibrillization, and irreversible aggregation as related but separable observables. Each label will include provenance, uncertainty, and links to the original public source.

Workstream 2 will assemble and harmonize public datasets. We will integrate entries from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold predicted confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, STRING, BioGRID, and relevant supplementary tables from published studies. The working group will focus on RNA-binding and neurodegeneration-linked proteins; transcription factors, histone tails, and chromatin regulators; and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates. Automated pipelines will retrieve sequences, isoforms, domains, disorder annotations, PTMs, abundance estimates, localization, interaction partners, variants, and available image or biophysical metadata. Literature tables and figures reporting phase diagrams, FRAP, droplet fusion, turbidity, SAXS, NMR, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes will be extracted through text mining, table parsing, figure digitization, and human-in-the-loop curation.

Workstream 3 will compute interpretable features. Sequence-level features will include net charge, charge patterning, kappa-like metrics, sticker valence, aromatic spacing, arginine and lysine distribution, hydrophobic clustering, glycine and proline content, predicted disorder, low-complexity segmentation, transient structure propensity, prion-like composition, and domain adjacency. Context features will include RNA-binding annotation, nucleic acid type, partner valence, PTM state, disease or population variants, concentration, salt, temperature, crowding, oxidative condition, polyamine or metabolite presence, cellular compartment, species, and experimental modality. Where possible, ensemble descriptors from public SAXS or NMR studies will be linked to sequence features.

Workstream 4 will build benchmark models and visualization tools. We will train baseline statistical models, regularized regression, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, graph-based models, and uncertainty-aware classifiers to predict material-state labels and transitions. Evaluation will use nested cross-validation, protein-family holdouts, condensate-class holdouts, and modality-specific holdouts to test generalization rather than memorization. Model interpretation will emphasize feature effects, interaction terms, counterfactual sequence perturbations, and transferability across condensate classes. Trainees will participate in annotation sprints, reproducible workflow development, model benchmarking, and community tutorials. NCEMS meetings will enable iterative standard setting, conflict resolution, and cross-disciplinary synthesis that cannot be achieved by isolated groups.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The project will produce a publicly accessible condensate-material atlas that links molecular grammar, biological context, and emergent mesoscale material state. The primary deliverables will be an openly licensed harmonized database, an ontology for condensate material descriptors, benchmark datasets for prediction tasks, reproducible feature-generation pipelines, interpretable modeling workflows, and an interactive web interface for exploring proteins, variants, modifications, partners, and predicted state transitions.

Scientifically, the atlas will address a fundamental unresolved problem: why similar classes of disordered proteins can form dynamic compartments in one context, gel-like regulatory assemblies in another, and pathological aggregates under stress or mutation. By comparing RNA-binding granules, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress-responsive condensates in a common framework, the project will reveal whether shared polymer-physics principles govern diverse cellular assemblies. It will also identify where biological specificity enters through RNA, chromatin, structured domains, PTMs, abundance, localization, or disease variants.

The impact will extend beyond cataloging known condensates. The project will generate testable predictions for future experimental studies, including sequence motifs likely to promote aging, PTMs predicted to dissolve or harden condensates, and variants that may shift functional assemblies toward pathological states. The benchmark datasets will support more rigorous development of machine-learning models for intrinsically disordered proteins and condensates. The ontology will improve communication across communities that currently use inconsistent terminology. For NCEMS, the project directly advances synthesis research on mesoscale emergence by converting heterogeneous public observations into reusable, quantitative knowledge. It will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in data integration, reproducible computation, public-resource curation, and cross-disciplinary collaboration.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The working group will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from project launch. All data products derived from public sources will be released under permissive licenses whenever source licenses allow, with clear attribution and provenance. The atlas will use persistent identifiers for proteins, isoforms, variants, publications, datasets, images, and curated observations. Each record will include source information, extraction method, curator identity or automated pipeline version, evidence type, and uncertainty level.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, and documented release tags. Computational workflows will be implemented in reproducible workflow systems such as Snakemake or Nextflow, with containerized environments using Docker or Apptainer. Processed data, benchmark splits, model artifacts, and documentation will be deposited in stable repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, OSF, or institutional archives with DOIs. Interactive notebooks will demonstrate data retrieval, feature calculation, model training, and visualization.

To ensure reliability, the project will implement independent double annotation for a subset of curated material-state labels, adjudication of disagreements, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and versioned updates. Models will be evaluated on pre-specified benchmark tasks with transparent reporting of missingness, class imbalance, uncertainty, and domain limitations. Negative and ambiguous cases will be retained rather than discarded, because they are essential for robust synthesis.

Training will be embedded in open-science practice. Graduate students and postdocs will receive instruction in FAIR data principles, ontology design, reproducible workflows, responsible machine learning, and public documentation. Community tutorials, annotation guides, and recorded workshops will allow external researchers to reuse and extend the resource. The project will not generate new experimental data, but it will generate openly available synthesis products that enable the broader community to ask sharper mechanistic questions.

No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase laboratory reagents, or conduct new wet-lab assays. The budget is therefore tightly aligned with NCEMS goals: synthesizing existing public molecular and cellular data, supporting collaboration beyond any single laboratory, creating reusable open infrastructure, and training a data-savvy workforce capable of studying emergent mesoscale biological phenomena.

title: A Comparative Multi-Omics Atlas of Reversible Metabolic Suppression Across Mammalian Hibernators
abstract: Mammalian hibernation is an extreme example of biological emergence: coordinated molecular changes across cells and tissues generate organism-level phenotypes that include profound metabolic suppression, altered insulin sensitivity, muscle maintenance, immune modulation, and reversible shifts in body temperature. Although public transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets now exist for bears, ground squirrels, bats, hamsters, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and laboratory mouse models of torpor, these datasets remain fragmented across species, tissues, seasons, and analytical frameworks. This working group will synthesize existing public data to ask a central question: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs allow diverse mammals to reversibly reorganize cellular energy use during hibernation without pathological damage? We will build an open, comparative atlas integrating publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq where available, proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating mammals. The project will focus on emergent mesoscale processes that link molecules to cellular and tissue phenotypes, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-cell state shifts. By mapping orthologous genes and pathways across species and tissues, we will identify modules that repeatedly change during torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and experimentally induced metabolic shifts. We will then test whether these modules show signatures of convergent regulatory architecture across independent hibernating lineages, using comparative genomics, gene regulatory network inference, ancestral-state-aware enrichment analyses, and machine learning approaches that explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness. A major innovation will be to move beyond lists of differentially expressed genes toward cross-scale synthesis: we will infer how regulatory changes in individual pathways combine into tissue-level and organism-level hibernation states. For example, we will evaluate whether mitochondrial genes, lipid-handling genes, circadian regulators, and inflammatory mediators form conserved cross-tissue network motifs that predict hibernation state better than any single tissue or pathway. We will also compare natural hibernation datasets with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, and aging models to distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic stress responses. The resulting resource will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic depression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular changes across tissues. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires a transdisciplinary working group spanning evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, comparative transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, network biology, data harmonization, and phylogenetic statistics. No single laboratory currently has the breadth of expertise or the capacity to curate, standardize, and jointly analyze these diverse public datasets at community scale. Deliverables will include a FAIR hibernation multi-omics atlas, reproducible analysis workflows, orthology-aware gene module annotations, interactive network visualizations, and training materials for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. By synthesizing existing public data across mammals, this project will reveal how molecular programs combine into emergent cellular and physiological states, while creating a reusable open-science platform for future studies of metabolic resilience.
background_and_significance: Hibernation is among the most striking mammalian examples of reversible physiological reorganization. During torpor and seasonal dormancy, animals can suppress metabolic rate, alter fuel use, tolerate prolonged fasting, preserve skeletal muscle and bone, modulate immune activity, and repeatedly transition between low-temperature and euthermic states without the damage typically associated with hypothermia, starvation, insulin resistance, disuse, or ischemia-reperfusion. These organismal phenotypes emerge from coordinated changes across molecular pathways, cell states, tissues, and endocrine axes. Yet the field lacks a unified comparative framework for identifying which molecular programs are conserved across hibernating mammals, which are lineage-specific, and how these programs combine across biological scales to generate resilient metabolic suppression. Public data now make such a synthesis timely and feasible. Transcriptomic resources are available for hibernating and active-season bears, ground squirrels, hamsters, bats, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and mouse models of torpor-like states. Several studies include multiple tissues such as liver, skeletal muscle, adipose, heart, brain, and immune-related tissues; some include time-series or experimentally perturbed conditions, including feeding, cold exposure, and in vitro temperature manipulations. Public proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets add complementary information on protein abundance, energy metabolites, lipid species, gene family evolution, and cis-regulatory landscapes. However, these datasets are dispersed across repositories, generated using distinct library preparation methods and annotation versions, and analyzed with species-specific pipelines. As a result, current knowledge remains fragmented into organism- or tissue-specific findings, limiting the ability to detect shared emergent principles. This project directly addresses NCEMS priorities by synthesizing existing public molecular and cellular data to investigate an emergent mesoscale phenomenon: the transition from molecular regulatory changes to tissue-level and whole-organism metabolic states. The proposed atlas will focus on cellular processes that sit between individual biomolecules and organelles or tissues, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress buffering, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune-cell state changes, and proteostasis. These mesoscale processes are plausible points at which coordinated gene, protein, and metabolite changes generate higher-order hibernation phenotypes. A comparative evolutionary perspective is essential because hibernation and torpor have arisen in multiple mammalian lineages with different body sizes, thermal strategies, diets, and life histories. Convergent molecular patterns across independent lineages would indicate deeply reusable regulatory solutions, whereas lineage-specific patterns may reveal alternative routes to metabolic resilience. Integrating phylogenetic methods with multi-omics network analysis will allow us to separate shared ancestry from repeated evolutionary recruitment of pathways. The proposed working group is beyond the capacity of a single laboratory. It requires expertise in hibernation biology, evolutionary genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, data harmonization, network inference, comparative methods, and open computational infrastructure. NCEMS support will enable a community-scale synthesis that transforms scattered public datasets into a reusable resource and a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic suppression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular processes.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: The central research question is: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs enable diverse mammals to reversibly suppress metabolism while avoiding pathological consequences? We will address this question through four integrated aims. Aim 1 asks which genes, proteins, metabolites, pathways, and cellular modules consistently change across torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and active-season states. We hypothesize that conserved hibernation modules will be enriched for mitochondrial substrate switching, fatty acid transport and beta-oxidation, lipid droplet regulation, redox control, circadian timing, unfolded protein response modulation, and anti-inflammatory signaling. We further hypothesize that these modules will be more reproducible at the pathway and network level than at the individual gene level because orthologous genes may be regulated differently while preserving higher-order cellular functions. Aim 2 asks whether hibernation-associated modules are shared across tissues or specialized by tissue context. We hypothesize that liver, adipose, skeletal muscle, heart, brain, and immune-enriched tissues will show distinct implementations of a common seasonal metabolic program. For example, adipose may emphasize lipid mobilization and endocrine signaling, muscle may emphasize proteostasis and contractile maintenance, liver may emphasize ketogenesis and detoxification, and brain may emphasize circadian and neuroendocrine regulation. We predict that cross-tissue network motifs, rather than any single tissue signature, will best classify hibernation state. Aim 3 asks whether repeated hibernation phenotypes across mammals are associated with convergent regulatory architecture. We hypothesize that independent hibernating lineages will show enrichment of regulatory changes near orthologs involved in energy sensing, nuclear receptor signaling, circadian regulation, and stress-response buffering. We will test whether these signals exceed expectations under phylogenetic null models that account for shared ancestry, genome quality, tissue sampling, and study design. This aim distinguishes true convergence from conservation of ancient mammalian stress responses or lineage-specific adaptation. Aim 4 asks which components of hibernation resemble generic responses to fasting, cold, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, inflammation, or aging, and which appear specific to protective reversible metabolic suppression. We hypothesize that hibernators share some molecular responses with non-hibernating stress models, such as increased lipid utilization during fasting and altered inflammatory tone during cold exposure. However, we expect hibernation-specific protective programs to include coordinated suppression of damage-associated inflammation, maintenance of insulin signaling flexibility, preservation of muscle structural networks, and reversible remodeling of mitochondrial function without chronic oxidative injury. Across these aims, our overarching hypothesis is that hibernation is not produced by a single master pathway but by a distributed, modular regulatory architecture. Emergent resilience arises when cellular energy handling, circadian timing, stress buffering, immune modulation, and tissue remodeling are synchronized across organs. This proposal will test that hypothesis using only existing public datasets, with explicit attention to uncertainty, batch effects, phylogenetic non-independence, and differences in sampling design among species.
methods_and_approach: The working group will build a curated, orthology-aware multi-omics atlas from public datasets. We will identify datasets through NCBI SRA, GEO, ArrayExpress, ENA, PRIDE, MetaboLights, MassIVE, Dryad, Figshare, Zenodo, Ensembl, NCBI RefSeq, UCSC, and published supplementary materials. Eligible datasets will include publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell or single-nucleus RNA-seq, proteomics, metabolomics, genome annotations, regulatory annotations, and relevant metadata from hibernating mammals and non-hibernating comparator models. No new experimental data will be generated. Inclusion criteria will document species, tissue or cell type, season or physiological state, sex and age when available, sampling temperature, fasting status, library or assay type, repository accession, license, and genome annotation version. Aim 1 will harmonize molecular features across species. For transcriptomes, we will process raw reads where feasible using reproducible workflows for quality control, trimming, alignment or quasi-mapping, transcript quantification, and gene-level summarization. When raw data are unavailable, we will incorporate author-provided count matrices with provenance annotations. Orthology will be established using Ensembl Compara, OrthoDB, NCBI orthologs, and reciprocal sequence searches for species with incomplete annotations. Analyses will be conducted at multiple feature resolutions: one-to-one orthologs, gene families, pathways, and data-driven co-expression modules. Proteomic and metabolomic datasets will be mapped to standardized identifiers, including UniProt, KEGG, Reactome, HMDB, LipidMaps, and MetaboLights vocabularies. Aim 2 will identify conserved and tissue-specific hibernation modules. Within each dataset, we will model state-associated changes using appropriate generalized linear or mixed models, controlling for tissue, sex, batch, season, and study-specific covariates when available. Cross-study synthesis will use random-effects meta-analysis, rank-based aggregation, and pathway-level enrichment to reduce dependence on platform-specific effects. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis, multi-omics factor analysis, and graph-based community detection will identify modules associated with torpor, arousal, interbout euthermia, winter fasting, active season, and experimental perturbations. Single-cell data will be reannotated using reference mapping and marker-based approaches, then integrated to test whether hibernation shifts cell-type abundance, within-cell transcriptional states, or both. Aim 3 will incorporate evolutionary models. We will construct or use published mammalian phylogenies and apply phylogenetic generalized least squares, phylogenetic mixed models, ancestral-state-aware enrichment, and permutation tests that preserve clade structure. We will test whether hibernating lineages independently recruit similar pathways or regulatory features while accounting for genome assembly quality and uneven sampling. Regulatory analyses will integrate public ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, promoter annotations, conserved noncoding elements, transcription factor motif databases, and inferred regulatory networks. Aim 4 will compare natural hibernation with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, diabetes, obesity, aging, inflammation, hypoxia, and muscle disuse. Machine learning classifiers, including regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, and graph neural network approaches where appropriate, will evaluate whether multi-tissue modules predict hibernation state better than single-pathway models. All models will use nested cross-validation, leave-one-species-out testing, and sensitivity analyses to quantify robustness.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will produce five major outcomes. First, we will deliver a FAIR comparative hibernation multi-omics atlas that links species, tissues, physiological states, molecular features, orthology relationships, and analysis-ready data matrices. Second, we will identify conserved and lineage-specific modules associated with reversible metabolic suppression, including modules related to mitochondrial remodeling, lipid handling, circadian regulation, immune modulation, extracellular matrix dynamics, and stress-response buffering. Third, we will generate cross-tissue network models that explain how molecular changes combine into higher-order hibernation states. Fourth, we will distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic responses to fasting, cold exposure, metabolic disease, disuse, and aging. Fifth, we will provide reusable workflows, visualizations, and training materials for the broader molecular and cellular biology community. The scientific impact will be substantial. By moving beyond single-species differential expression studies, the project will reveal whether hibernation relies on deeply conserved mammalian pathways, convergent regulatory solutions, or diverse lineage-specific mechanisms. This will advance fundamental understanding of emergence by showing how coordinated molecular processes produce resilient cellular and organismal phenotypes. The atlas will also create a foundation for hypothesis generation in areas relevant to metabolic disease, muscle preservation, inflammation, hypothermia tolerance, and aging biology, while remaining focused on synthesis of existing data rather than translational claims. The broader impact aligns closely with NCEMS goals. The project requires collaboration across evolutionary biology, physiology, molecular biology, computational biology, and data science. It will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in public data reuse, reproducible workflows, comparative methods, and team science. By making all outputs open and reusable, the working group will lower barriers for future researchers, including those at institutions without extensive experimental infrastructure, to participate in discovery-oriented synthesis biology.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science principles from initiation. All public dataset accessions, inclusion decisions, metadata fields, processing steps, and quality-control outcomes will be documented in a version-controlled repository. We will use community standards wherever possible, including MIAME and MINSEQE-inspired metadata for transcriptomics, ProteomeXchange conventions for proteomics, metabolomics identifier standards, NCBI Taxonomy, Uberon tissue terms, Cell Ontology cell-type terms, Gene Ontology, KEGG, Reactome, and standardized orthology resources. Derived data products will be released under permissive licenses compatible with source repositories and journal requirements. Computational workflows will be implemented in workflow managers such as Nextflow or Snakemake and distributed with containerized software environments using Docker, Apptainer, Conda, or Bioconda. Analyses will be documented in executable notebooks and scripted reports. Major results will include provenance records linking every figure, table, and model output to input datasets, software versions, parameters, and commit identifiers. We will deposit code on GitHub or GitLab, archive stable releases on Zenodo, and host analysis-ready matrices, metadata, orthology tables, and network objects on repositories suitable for long-term access. Interactive visualizations will be built using open frameworks and will allow users to query species, tissues, states, pathways, and modules. Reproducibility will be strengthened through internal code review, benchmark datasets, unit tests for data transformations, continuous integration where feasible, and independent reruns by trainees from different participating laboratories. The working group will establish authorship, contribution, data-use, and conflict-resolution policies at the outset, following transparent team-science practices. Training activities will include hands-on workshops in public data retrieval, orthology mapping, phylogenetic comparative analysis, multi-omics integration, workflow management, and responsible use of machine learning. These materials will be released publicly so that the atlas functions not only as a research product but also as an educational platform for data-savvy molecular and cellular science.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated, community-scale synthesis rather than routine single-laboratory analysis. We request support for working group meetings, trainee participation, computational infrastructure, data curation, and open dissemination. Funds for in-person and virtual meetings will enable investigators from evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, comparative transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, network biology, and phylogenetic statistics to develop shared standards, resolve curation challenges, interpret results, and train early-career scientists. Meeting support will prioritize geographic and institutional diversity, including participation from researchers at institutions with different levels of computational and research infrastructure. Trainee support will provide graduate students and postdoctoral researchers with protected time for dataset curation, workflow development, cross-lab analysis sprints, and workshop participation. These trainees will gain practical experience in open-source software, public repository mining, comparative methods, and collaborative project management. We will also request modest support for professional data management assistance to ensure metadata consistency, identifier harmonization, documentation, and repository deposition. Computational resources will be used for storage of raw and processed public datasets, containerized workflow execution, versioned analysis environments, and interactive visualization hosting. Where possible, we will leverage institutional high-performance computing, cloud credits, open-source software, and public repositories to minimize cost and maximize sustainability. NCEMS resources will add value by providing synthesis-center coordination, collaborative workspace, facilitation of interdisciplinary meetings, open-science guidance, and connections to broader data-science expertise. The budget will not support any new experimental sample collection, sequencing, proteomic assays, metabolomic assays, animal work, or wet-laboratory activities. All funds will be directed toward synthesis of existing public data, computational integration, training, and dissemination. By concentrating resources on coordination and reusable infrastructure, the project will produce durable community assets: a curated atlas, reproducible workflows, orthology-aware annotations, network visualizations, and training modules that remain useful after the working group ends.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Predicting Condensate-Scale Emergence from Evolutionary and Structural Coupling Networks in Multivalent Proteins
abstract:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how weak, distributed molecular interactions give rise to sharply different mesoscale outcomes, such as liquid-like compartments, gels, aggregates, or dispersed cellular states. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent biomolecular condensate behavior can be predicted from evolutionarily conserved networks of residue, domain, and motif couplings within multivalent proteins and their interaction partners. The guiding hypothesis is that many condensate-forming systems are regulated by hidden coupling architectures: perturbations at folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, RNA-binding surfaces, post-translational modification sites, or ion-binding regions propagate through molecular ensembles to alter mesoscale assembly thresholds and material states.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate protein family alignments from UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, and model-organism databases; structural models and experimental structures from AlphaFold DB, PDB, SASBDB, and integrative structure repositories; condensate annotations and phase behavior measurements from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and curated literature-derived datasets; public mutational scans and variant-effect datasets from MaveDB, ClinVar, cBioPortal, and organismal resources; proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets from PRIDE, MassIVE, and ProteomeXchange; RNA-binding and chromatin-associated interaction datasets from ENCODE and related repositories; and reusable molecular simulation trajectories from public simulation archives where available. These heterogeneous resources will be harmonized into a FAIR, versioned knowledge graph linking sequence features, coevolutionary constraints, structural contacts, dynamic ensembles, modification sites, disease or engineered variants, and observed condensate phenotypes.

Analytically, the working group will combine statistical sequence models, direct coupling and sector-like analyses, information-theoretic measures, graph-based structural communication models, and machine learning on experimentally annotated phase behavior. For each protein family, we will infer conserved coupling networks and map them onto folded domains, disordered regions, short linear motifs, RNA-binding interfaces, and multivalent interaction modules. We will then ask whether particular coupling architectures distinguish proteins that form regulated condensates from homologs that do not, and whether these architectures predict sensitivity to temperature, salt, RNA, phosphorylation, disease mutation, or engineered sequence changes. A major methodological outcome will be an open cross-scale framework that converts evolutionary and structural coupling information into testable predictions of mesoscale assembly propensity and state transitions.

The emergent property addressed here is not any single molecular contact, but the appearance of cellular-scale organization from ensembles of many weakly coupled molecular features. The synthesis is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in molecular evolution, protein allostery, statistical physics, biomolecular simulation, phase separation, structural bioinformatics, proteomics, RNA biology, and open data engineering. NCEMS support would enable the coordinated curation standards, shared computational infrastructure, trainee-led cross-training, and community benchmarking necessary to make the results reusable.

The project will deliver an open atlas of coupling networks in condensate-associated protein families, reproducible workflows for integrating evolutionary, structural, simulation, and cellular phenotype data, and prioritized predictions for variants or modification sites likely to shift mesoscale organization. By linking molecular information flow to condensate-level behavior, this synthesis will provide a general strategy for understanding how cellular material states emerge from protein sequence, structure, dynamics, and evolution.
background_and_significance: Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences: many individually weak and transient molecular interactions collectively produce distinct mesoscale states with cellular consequences. Proteins and nucleic acids that remain dispersed under one condition can form liquid-like droplets, viscoelastic gels, solid-like assemblies, or pathological aggregates under another. These transitions influence transcription, RNA processing, stress responses, signaling, chromatin organization, and proteostasis. Yet the field lacks a general framework for predicting when sequence-encoded molecular features will generate a particular condensate-scale outcome. This gap limits our ability to explain why closely related proteins differ in assembly behavior, why specific mutations or post-translational modifications alter material state, and how evolution tunes cellular organization without relying on stable stoichiometric complexes alone. Current condensate research has produced rich public resources, but they remain fragmented across scales. Sequence databases capture homologous families and evolutionary variation. Structural repositories contain experimental structures, predicted folded domains, and low-resolution ensemble descriptions. Phase separation databases collect reports of condensate localization, in vitro phase diagrams, disease-associated aggregation, and curated functional annotations. Public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, RNA-binding, chromatin-associated, variant-effect, and simulation datasets provide additional information on regulatory context and molecular dynamics. However, these resources are not yet integrated in a way that supports cross-family inference about how molecular coupling networks generate emergent mesoscale states. The proposed working group addresses this opportunity through synthesis research only, using existing public data to build a multiscale picture of condensate-forming proteins and their interaction partners. The central scientific premise is that condensate behavior is shaped not just by aggregate properties such as net charge, aromaticity, or valence, but by conserved networks of coupled residues, motifs, domains, disorder regions, binding surfaces, and regulatory sites. These networks may act analogously to distributed allosteric systems: perturbations at one site can shift conformational ensembles, interaction preferences, multivalent binding patterns, and ultimately phase boundaries or material states. Such coupling architectures may be visible through evolutionary covariation, structural contact maps, dynamic contact fluctuations, conserved short linear motifs, and recurrent modification or disease-variant patterns. This proposal aligns closely with NCEMS priorities because it focuses on emergence at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles, uses only publicly available data, and requires a transdisciplinary team. No single laboratory can assemble, standardize, analyze, and benchmark sequence evolution, structural bioinformatics, molecular simulation, condensate phenotyping, proteomics, RNA biology, and knowledge-graph infrastructure at the necessary community scale. NCEMS support will enable shared curation standards, collaborative analysis sprints, trainee cross-training, and open dissemination. The project will convert heterogeneous public resources into a reusable atlas and computational framework that links molecular information flow to cellular material organization. Its significance is both conceptual and practical: it will test whether principles of allosteric coupling and evolutionary constraint can predict emergent condensate states, and it will provide prioritized variants, sites, and protein families for future experimental study by the broader community.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will pursue four integrated research questions. First, do condensate-associated multivalent proteins contain conserved coupling architectures that distinguish them from homologs or paralogs with similar composition but different mesoscale behavior? Many predictors of phase separation rely on local sequence features, including charge patterning, low-complexity content, aromatic residues, sticker-spacer grammar, disorder propensity, and prion-like domains. These features are informative, but they do not fully explain condition-specific assembly, regulated reversibility, or differences among homologous proteins. We hypothesize that condensate-forming proteins are enriched for statistically detectable networks of coevolving residues, domains, motifs, and regulatory sites that coordinate weak interactions across folded and disordered regions. Second, can these coupling networks predict sensitivity to environmental and biochemical regulators? Condensates often respond sharply to temperature, salt, pH, RNA concentration, nucleotide state, phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, or ion binding. We hypothesize that regulator sensitivity is encoded in the topology and physical placement of coupling networks: sites that connect interaction modules, disorder regions, folded domains, and nucleic acid binding surfaces will be more likely to shift assembly thresholds than isolated sites with similar local chemistry. This hypothesis will be tested by mapping coupling features to public phase behavior annotations, phosphoproteomic datasets, RNA-binding datasets, known ion-binding sites, and available simulation-derived contact ensembles. Third, do disease-associated and engineered variants that alter condensate phenotypes preferentially occur at network control points? Variants in RNA-binding proteins, transcriptional regulators, signaling scaffolds, and chromatin-associated proteins can convert functional condensates into persistent aggregates or disrupt assembly entirely. We hypothesize that variants with strong condensate effects are enriched at evolutionarily constrained positions, interdomain communication paths, motif interfaces, or modification-linked nodes, even when those positions are not obvious from composition-based analysis. This question will integrate public mutational scans, ClinVar, cBioPortal, MaveDB, model-organism variant resources, and curated literature reports. Fourth, can a cross-scale predictive model generalize across protein families and condensate classes? Condensates differ widely in molecular composition and cellular role. Some are dominated by RNA-protein interactions, others by multivalent signaling domains, chromatin contacts, stress granule scaffolds, or amyloid-like transitions. We hypothesize that distinct coupling architectures correspond to recurrent mesoscale outcomes, such as reversible liquid-like assembly, gelation, temperature-triggered condensation, RNA-dependent buffering, phosphorylation-controlled dissolution, or aggregation-prone hardening. The proposed synthesis will therefore evaluate both family-specific models and transferable representations. Success will be measured by retrospective prediction of held-out condensate annotations, variant effects, and condition sensitivities, as well as by the generation of transparent, ranked hypotheses for future community testing. These questions are designed to advance a general theory of emergence: how distributed molecular constraints, acquired through evolution and expressed through structure and dynamics, combine to produce new cellular-scale material properties.
methods_and_approach: The project will proceed through coordinated synthesis modules, all using existing public data. Module 1 will define protein families and phenotype sets. We will compile condensate-associated proteins and controls from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, UniProt annotations, model-organism databases, and curated literature-derived datasets. Each entry will be assigned evidence codes for in vivo localization, in vitro phase separation, material state, reversibility, stimulus dependence, RNA involvement, disease association, and perturbation evidence. Control sets will include homologs without condensate annotations, proteins with similar composition but different localization, and paralogs with divergent assembly behavior. Module 2 will construct evolutionary and sequence-feature resources. For each family, we will retrieve homologs from UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, and organismal databases, remove redundancy, assess alignment depth, and build multiple sequence alignments suitable for statistical modeling. We will annotate folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity segments, short linear motifs, prion-like regions, charge patterning, aromatic clusters, RNA-binding motifs, and known post-translational modification sites. Module 3 will infer coupling networks. We will apply direct coupling analysis, Potts-type statistical models, sector-like decomposition, mutual information with phylogenetic correction, and conservation-weighted motif covariance. Couplings will be represented at residue, motif, domain, and protein-interaction levels. Network metrics will include centrality, modularity, path structure, community overlap, evolutionary conservation, and enrichment for regulatory or variant sites. Module 4 will map couplings onto structure and dynamics. Experimental structures from PDB, predicted structures from AlphaFold DB, small-angle scattering data from SASBDB, integrative models, and available public simulation trajectories will be used to determine whether inferred couplings correspond to physical contacts, alternative contact modes, domain interfaces, disordered-region docking sites, or dynamic communication paths. Graph-based structural communication models will estimate how perturbations at specific positions could propagate through folded and disordered interaction modules. Where reusable simulations exist, contact probability networks and ensemble heterogeneity will be extracted; where they do not, the project will not generate new simulations but will mark gaps for future work. Module 5 will integrate data in a FAIR knowledge graph. Nodes will include proteins, isoforms, residues, domains, motifs, modifications, structures, variants, interactions, conditions, and condensate phenotypes. Edges will encode evidence provenance, confidence, database source, and version. This graph will support machine learning and transparent querying. Module 6 will build and benchmark predictive models. We will train interpretable classifiers and regression models to predict condensate association, material class, regulator sensitivity, and variant impact from coupling-network, structural, compositional, proteomic, and interaction features. Evaluation will use nested cross-validation, family-level holdouts, negative-control sampling, literature-time splits where possible, and robustness tests for annotation bias. Trainees will participate in cross-lab analysis teams focused on curation, evolutionary inference, structural mapping, and model evaluation. NCEMS working-group meetings will be used for ontology harmonization, code review, benchmark design, and community feedback.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will deliver three primary scientific products. First, we will create an open atlas of evolutionary and structural coupling networks for condensate-associated multivalent protein families. The atlas will connect sequence variation, domains, disordered regions, motifs, modification sites, structures, interaction partners, variants, and condensate phenotypes in a form that can be searched, downloaded, and extended. Second, we will produce validated computational workflows that convert public sequence, structure, proteomic, interaction, variant, and phase-behavior data into predictions of mesoscale assembly propensity, material state, regulator sensitivity, and variant impact. Third, we will generate prioritized hypotheses for residues, motifs, domains, and post-translational modification sites that are likely to control condensate transitions. These predictions will be immediately useful to experimental groups studying stress granules, transcriptional condensates, chromatin compartments, RNA-processing bodies, signaling assemblies, and aggregation-linked disease proteins. The broader impact is a shift from cataloging condensate components to explaining emergent material behavior through conserved molecular information flow. By testing whether principles from allostery, molecular evolution, statistical physics, structural bioinformatics, and phase separation can be unified, the project will address a central NCEMS theme: how new biological properties appear across scales of composition, space, time, motion, and information. The synthesis will also establish community standards for representing condensate evidence, condition dependence, and uncertainty. The resulting knowledge graph and benchmarks will provide durable infrastructure for future method development. Training outcomes will include a cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who gain practical experience in open data integration, reproducible computational biology, molecular evolution, structural analysis, and collaborative team science. Because the project uses only public data and produces reusable outputs, its impact will extend well beyond the working group.

Reproducibility will be strengthened through benchmark datasets with frozen training and test splits, negative controls, uncertainty estimates, and documented exclusion criteria. Model performance will be reported with family-level holdouts and sensitivity analyses to identify annotation bias, phylogenetic leakage, and overfitting. The project will follow open team-science practices, including shared authorship expectations, transparent decision logs, regular code review, and trainee-accessible onboarding materials. NCEMS meetings will include reproducibility checkpoints where independent subgroup members rerun selected workflows and compare outputs. Educational materials, including tutorials on coupling inference, condensate data curation, structural mapping, and knowledge-graph queries, will be made publicly available. Publications will be submitted as preprints and, where possible, to open-access venues. The final products will include a public web portal, downloadable graph files, documented APIs, and archived software releases.

This allocation directly matches NCEMS goals of catalyzing collaborative synthesis research on mesoscale emergence.
