title: Evolutionary Discovery of Metabolic Network Modules that Generate Mesoscale Membrane and Organelle Organization
abstract:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how evolutionary changes in genes and metabolic reactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular properties such as membrane composition, lipid droplet abundance, mitochondrial remodeling, peroxisome activity, and stress-dependent organelle organization. These properties are not encoded by single genes; they emerge from coordinated flux through lipid, amino acid, redox, and energy metabolism. Yet the public data needed to connect evolutionary pressures, metabolic network architecture, and mesoscale cellular organization now exist across human populations, model organisms, microbes, plants, and immune cell systems. This working group will synthesize these resources to ask: which metabolic network modules are repeatedly targeted by evolution and environmental response because they control emergent mesoscale organization?

The project will integrate only publicly available data: population genomic datasets from humans and other species; comparative genomes and orthology resources; transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets from environmental perturbations including temperature, diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, and immune activation; genome-scale metabolic reconstructions from BiGG, ModelSEED, Human-GEM, plant metabolic databases, and organism-specific reconstructions; and public microscopy-derived organelle and cellular morphology datasets from resources such as the Image Data Resource and Cell Painting repositories. We will construct a cross-species reaction-centered knowledge graph linking genes, orthologs, variants, selection statistics, reactions, metabolites, lipid classes, predicted flux states, and mesoscale phenotypes. This graph will allow evolutionary signals and cellular systems measurements to be analyzed in a shared metabolic coordinate system rather than as disconnected gene lists.

Methodologically, the group will combine interpretable population-genetic machine learning with constraint-based metabolic modeling. Deep learning models trained on simulated neutral and selected haplotypes will identify genomic regions whose evolutionary histories are inconsistent with neutrality, while interpretable feature attribution will distinguish selection acting on individual loci from selection on coordinated metabolic modules. In parallel, context-specific genome-scale metabolic models will be reconstructed from public multi-omic datasets to infer flux reorganization under environmental and cellular states. A synthesis layer will then test whether selected genes are enriched not merely in pathways, but in flux-controlling modules predicted to alter mesoscale properties such as phospholipid saturation, sterol balance, acyl-chain remodeling, mitochondrial redox coupling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, and lipid storage capacity.

The expected outcome is a generalizable atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules that generate mesoscale cellular organization across species and conditions. The project will address whether convergent environmental pressures produce convergent metabolic network solutions, whether human adaptive loci disproportionately affect emergent membrane and organelle states, and whether stress-responsive flux modules in cells correspond to modules recurrently shaped by natural selection across populations and taxa. This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it spans population genetics, genome-scale metabolic modeling, lipid metabolism, comparative genomics, machine learning interpretability, and image-based cell phenotyping—expertise and data integration beyond the scope of a single laboratory.

All workflows, harmonized datasets, metabolic model annotations, trained models, and interactive visualizations will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary hackathons and reproducible analysis teams, gaining experience in evolutionary genomics, metabolic network modeling, public data integration, and interpretable AI for molecular and cellular emergence.
background_and_significance:
Cells convert molecular variation into organized mesoscale states: membranes with characteristic lipid composition, organelles with regulated abundance and morphology, and spatially coordinated metabolic compartments that respond to stress. These properties are emergent because they arise from many coupled reactions, transport processes, redox constraints, and regulatory feedbacks rather than from single genes acting independently. Despite extensive knowledge of individual lipid enzymes, mitochondrial proteins, peroxisomal functions, and stress-response pathways, the field lacks a general synthesis explaining why particular metabolic subnetworks repeatedly shape mesoscale organization across species, environments, and evolutionary histories.

This gap is timely and tractable because public data now span the relevant biological scales. Population genomic resources contain signals of recent and ancient adaptation in humans and other organisms. Comparative genomics and orthology databases support mapping of genes and reactions across taxa. Public transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets describe cellular responses to temperature, diet, oxygen availability, infection, nutrient limitation, immune activation, and other perturbations. Genome-scale metabolic reconstructions provide mechanistic representations of reaction stoichiometry, compartmentalization, biomass requirements, thermodynamic constraints, and feasible flux states. Public imaging resources, including high-content microscopy and Cell Painting datasets, increasingly quantify mitochondrial structure, lipid droplets, cell shape, organelle texture, and other phenotypes that reflect mesoscale organization.

The central significance of this working group is that these data have rarely been integrated in a shared coordinate system. Evolutionary studies often produce lists of candidate genes or genomic intervals under selection. Metabolic modeling studies often infer reaction-level consequences of environmental or cellular states. Imaging studies often quantify phenotypes without explicit links to evolutionary pressures or biochemical flux. By organizing public data around reactions, metabolites, orthologs, flux modules, and mesoscale phenotypes, this project will make it possible to ask whether evolution recurrently targets the metabolic architecture that generates membrane and organelle states.

The proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by focusing on emergent properties at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles. It is also inherently synthetic: no new experimental data will be collected. The work requires a collaborative team because the scientific question sits at the intersection of population genetics, interpretable machine learning, genome-scale metabolic modeling, comparative genomics, lipid and redox metabolism, and image-based cell phenotyping. A single laboratory could analyze one data type or one organism, but not construct a cross-species synthesis linking adaptive history, reaction network structure, predicted flux states, and cellular organization.

The project will also address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences: why similar environmental pressures often produce similar cellular phenotypes through partly different genes. We hypothesize that convergence may occur at the level of flux-controlling modules rather than at the level of individual orthologous genes. Identifying these modules would provide a mechanistic bridge between genotype, metabolism, and mesoscale phenotype, revealing principles by which evolution and environmental response exploit the same biochemical design space.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address one overarching question: which metabolic network modules are repeatedly shaped by evolution and environmental response because they control emergent mesoscale membrane and organelle organization? We define a module as a connected set of reactions, metabolites, transport steps, and associated genes whose coordinated activity changes a predicted or observed cellular property, such as phospholipid saturation, sterol balance, acyl-chain remodeling, lipid storage, mitochondrial redox coupling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, or organelle morphology.

Question 1: Do adaptive evolutionary signals concentrate in metabolic modules that control mesoscale organization? Hypothesis 1 is that genomic regions showing evidence of natural selection in humans and other taxa will be enriched for genes mapped to reaction modules controlling lipid remodeling, redox balance, mitochondrial energy coupling, peroxisomal fatty acid processing, and membrane precursor allocation. We further hypothesize that enrichment will be stronger at the reaction-module level than at conventional pathway or gene ontology levels, because mesoscale phenotypes emerge from distributed biochemical functions rather than single annotated pathways.

Question 2: Do similar environmental pressures produce convergent metabolic network solutions across species? Hypothesis 2 is that cold exposure, lipid-rich diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, and immune activation will induce recurrent flux reorganizations in homologous or functionally analogous metabolic modules. These changes may involve different genes across bacteria, plants, animals, and immune cell systems, but they will converge on shared reaction-level functions such as fatty acid desaturation, cardiolipin remodeling, NADPH allocation, amino acid catabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, reactive oxygen management, and lipid droplet storage capacity.

Question 3: Are stress-responsive flux modules in cellular datasets the same modules recurrently shaped by evolutionary history? Hypothesis 3 is that modules inferred to change flux under public perturbation datasets will overlap with modules enriched for population-genetic signatures of selection. Such overlap would indicate that short-term physiological plasticity and long-term adaptation act on common metabolic control points. Conversely, modules that respond strongly to perturbation but lack evolutionary signals may represent constrained or essential functions where genetic change is deleterious.

Question 4: Can interpretable machine learning distinguish selection on isolated loci from selection on coordinated metabolic systems? Hypothesis 4 is that deep learning models trained on neutral and selected haplotype simulations, combined with feature attribution and reaction-level aggregation, will reveal whether apparent selection signals are distributed across genes in the same module. This approach will help identify cases where modest signals across multiple genes collectively indicate selection on a mesoscale-generating process.

Question 5: Can public image-derived phenotypes validate predicted metabolic modules? Hypothesis 5 is that modules predicted to affect membrane lipid composition, mitochondrial redox state, peroxisomal activity, or neutral lipid storage will be statistically associated with public microscopy phenotypes such as lipid droplet abundance, mitochondrial branching, organelle texture, cell size, and stress-dependent morphology. This test will connect biochemical network inference to observable cellular organization.

Together, these questions will evaluate whether evolution repeatedly discovers a limited set of metabolic strategies for producing robust mesoscale cellular states.
methods_and_approach:
The project will be organized as a synthesis working group using only existing publicly available data. Work will proceed in five integrated activities conducted through NCEMS-supported meetings, virtual analysis sprints, and trainee-led reproducible workflows.

Activity 1: Data inventory and harmonization. We will curate public population genomic datasets from humans and selected nonhuman taxa; comparative genome and orthology resources; public transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets from environmental and cellular perturbations; genome-scale metabolic reconstructions from BiGG, ModelSEED, Human-GEM, plant databases, and organism-specific models; and public image-derived organelle and cell morphology datasets. Candidate perturbations will include temperature, diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, immune activation, oxidative stress, and developmental or metabolic state transitions. All datasets will be selected using predefined criteria: public accessibility, metadata quality, organism annotation, relevance to metabolism or mesoscale organization, and compatibility with reproducible reanalysis.

Activity 2: Reaction-centered knowledge graph construction. We will build a graph linking variants, genes, orthologs, enzymes, reactions, metabolites, lipid classes, compartments, predicted fluxes, omic measurements, selection statistics, and image phenotypes. Gene identifiers will be mapped through Ensembl, UniProt, KEGG, MetaNetX, and orthology resources. Reactions will be standardized across metabolic reconstructions using shared metabolite and reaction identifiers where possible. The graph will allow all evidence to be queried at gene, reaction, module, organism, environment, and phenotype levels.

Activity 3: Evolutionary inference. For population genomic datasets, we will compile established selection statistics and train interpretable machine learning models on simulated neutral and selected haplotypes matched to relevant demographic scenarios. Models will include convolutional and generative approaches that classify deviations from neutrality while enabling interpretation through feature attribution, summary-statistic comparison, and module-level aggregation. The objective is not only to nominate loci, but to detect whether selection signals cluster within reaction modules more strongly than expected under matched genomic and network null models.

Activity 4: Context-specific metabolic modeling. We will reconstruct or adapt genome-scale metabolic models for selected species and cell types using public omic datasets. Context-specific models will be generated with transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic constraints when available. Flux balance analysis, flux variability analysis, parsimonious flux inference, thermodynamic constraints where feasible, and sampling-based methods will estimate condition-dependent flux changes. Particular attention will be given to modules controlling fatty acid synthesis and desaturation, phospholipid and sterol metabolism, cardiolipin remodeling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, mitochondrial redox coupling, amino acid catabolism, and NADPH regeneration.

Activity 5: Cross-scale synthesis and validation. We will test whether selected genes are enriched in flux-controlling modules; whether environmental perturbations induce convergent flux responses across taxa; and whether predicted modules associate with image-derived phenotypes. Statistical analyses will use permutation tests preserving gene length, recombination rate, expression level, pathway size, and network degree; hierarchical models for species and condition effects; and robustness analyses across orthology definitions and model assumptions. Deliverables will include an atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules, an interactive knowledge graph, reusable modeling pipelines, and prioritized mechanistic hypotheses for future experimental studies by the broader community.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The primary outcome will be an open atlas of metabolic network modules that link evolutionary history, environmental response, predicted flux organization, and mesoscale cellular phenotypes. Rather than producing disconnected lists of adaptive genes or stress-regulated pathways, the project will identify reaction-centered modules that plausibly generate emergent cellular properties such as membrane saturation state, lipid droplet formation, mitochondrial remodeling, peroxisomal activity, and redox-dependent organelle behavior.

A second outcome will be a generalizable synthesis framework for connecting population genetics with genome-scale metabolic modeling and image-based cell phenotyping. This framework will enable researchers to analyze evolutionary and cellular systems data in a common metabolic coordinate system. It will be reusable for questions beyond the initial focus, including host-pathogen adaptation, plant stress tolerance, immune cell polarization, microbial niche specialization, and metabolic disease susceptibility.

A third outcome will be a set of testable principles about mesoscale emergence. The project will determine whether convergent environmental pressures act on shared flux modules, whether human adaptive loci disproportionately affect membrane and organelle states, and whether physiological plasticity and evolutionary adaptation use common metabolic control points. These findings will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular changes scale up to cellular organization.

The impact for NCEMS will be substantial. The proposal addresses a fundamental question in emergence at the molecular-to-organelle interface, relies entirely on public data synthesis, requires expertise beyond any single lab, and produces open resources for the community. It will also train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in cross-disciplinary synthesis science, interpretable AI, metabolic modeling, evolutionary inference, and reproducible team-based research. The resulting products will support future experimental prioritization without generating new data under this award.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
All project activities will follow open, team-oriented, and reproducible science practices. The working group will create a public project repository at the start of the award containing governance documents, contribution guidelines, data dictionaries, issue tracking, workflow documentation, and meeting summaries. Code will be released under a permissive open-source license. Harmonized metadata, derived feature tables, model annotations, trained machine learning models, and knowledge graph exports will be deposited in stable public repositories with persistent identifiers.

Because the project uses only public data, reproducibility will focus on transparent provenance and executable workflows. Each dataset will be accompanied by source accession numbers, download dates, license information, inclusion criteria, preprocessing scripts, quality-control metrics, and known limitations. Analyses will be implemented with version-controlled pipelines using containerized software environments. Where computational cost is substantial, we will release lightweight test datasets, cached intermediate products, and documented instructions for reproducing full analyses on institutional or cloud infrastructure.

The knowledge graph will be distributed in interoperable formats suitable for reuse by both computational and experimental researchers. Metabolic models will include clear records of identifier mappings, reaction additions or removals, objective functions, constraints, and assumptions used for context-specific reconstruction. Machine learning models will include architecture descriptions, training simulations, demographic assumptions, evaluation metrics, and interpretability outputs.

The working group will implement internal reproducibility checks before public release. At least one analyst not involved in developing a workflow will rerun key steps from raw public inputs to final figures or tables. Statistical analyses will include predefined null models, sensitivity analyses, and negative controls. Trainees will be integrated into reproducibility teams so that training is embedded in deliverable production. Publications and preprints will link directly to data, code, workflows, and interactive visualizations, enabling community evaluation and extension.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires sustained coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and cross-disciplinary training that exceed the scope of an ordinary bilateral collaboration. The requested resources will support working group meetings, trainee participation, collaborative analysis sprints, data-management assistance, computational resources for large-scale synthesis, and dissemination of open products.

Major resource categories include personnel effort for coordination and synthesis, trainee support, travel and meeting costs, computation, and open-science dissemination. Personnel effort will focus on harmonizing public datasets, maintaining the reaction-centered knowledge graph, developing reproducible workflows, and coordinating analyses across evolutionary genomics, metabolic modeling, and image phenotyping subteams. Trainee funds will support graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who will participate in hackathons, lead reproducibility checks, and develop cross-training modules.

Travel and convening funds will enable two in-person working group meetings and regular virtual workshops. The first meeting will finalize data inclusion criteria, graph schema, analysis standards, and team roles. The second will focus on synthesis of results, validation, manuscript planning, and release of community resources. Short virtual analysis sprints will maintain momentum between meetings and allow participation by researchers from diverse institutions and career stages.

Computational resources will be used for population-genetic simulations, deep learning training and interpretation, graph construction, metabolic flux analyses, and large-scale statistical resampling. Cloud or center-supported compute will be used only for reanalysis of public data and generation of derived public resources. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

NCEMS resources will also support open dissemination, including repository maintenance, documentation, tutorials, interactive visualization hosting, and community webinars. These investments will ensure that the project produces durable, reusable products: harmonized datasets, metabolic annotations, trained models, executable workflows, and an accessible atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules underlying mesoscale cellular organization.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Proteome Flux Codes for Emergent Mesoscale Remodeling During Cellular Stress and Disease
abstract:
Cells often respond to stress not by changing the abundance of individual molecules alone, but by reorganizing mesoscale protein systems: ribonucleoprotein assemblies, cytoskeletal and nuclear scaffolds, extracellular matrices, metabolic enzyme clusters, and organelle-associated protein communities. A central unsolved question is how molecular flux through the proteome—translation, degradation, post-translational modification, disorder-mediated interaction, and localization—combines to produce these emergent cellular structures and phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define generalizable “proteome flux codes” that predict when changes in protein synthesis and turnover produce mesoscale remodeling across stress, aging, and cardiometabolic disease contexts.

This working group will integrate only publicly available datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Core inputs will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-labeling and protein turnover datasets, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, protein disorder and structural annotations, subcellular localization resources, protein interaction networks, phase-separation and condensate-associated protein catalogs, and public single-cell or bulk transcriptomic and proteomic datasets from stress models, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells, cardiovascular tissues, cancer stress states, and aging-related systems. Rather than treating mRNA, translation, protein abundance, and degradation as separate regulatory layers, we will build harmonized models of protein residence time, production rate, degradation rate, modification state, and mesoscale membership.

The central hypothesis is that emergent mesoscale remodeling is governed by coordinated shifts in proteome flux, especially among proteins with long residence times, intrinsically disordered regions, modification-rich segments, scaffold-like interaction properties, or compartment-specific localization. These features may explain why some cellular responses are rapid and reversible, whereas others become persistent, pathological, or tissue-specific. We will test this through three synthesis aims. First, we will create an interoperable atlas of proteome flux across public datasets, with uncertainty-aware normalization of turnover, translation, and abundance measurements across organisms, cell types, perturbations, and technologies. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with mesoscale assemblies, including stress granule-like systems, nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated networks, mitochondrial and metabolic complexes, extracellular matrix remodeling modules, and cytoskeletal or contractile structures. Third, we will develop predictive machine-learning and mechanistic network models that link molecular flux signatures to higher-order cellular outcomes such as stress adaptation, proteostasis collapse, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, and age-associated remodeling.

This project requires NCEMS-scale synthesis because no single laboratory can curate, reconcile, and model the diverse public datasets needed to connect translation dynamics, proteome turnover, structural disorder, post-translational regulation, and disease-relevant cell phenotypes. The working group would bring together experts in proteomics, ribosome profiling, cardiovascular and stem-cell models, structural bioinformatics, stress biology, network science, and open computational infrastructure. Deliverables will include a FAIR public proteome-flux atlas, reproducible workflows, benchmark datasets for turnover inference, interactive visualization tools, and trainee-led tutorials on integrative molecular data synthesis. By focusing on how molecular rates and regulatory layers combine to generate mesoscale biological organization, this project directly addresses NCEMS priorities and offers a new framework for understanding emergent cellular behavior from existing public data.
background_and_significance: Cellular stress responses are frequently interpreted through changes in transcript or protein abundance, yet many decisive biological outcomes arise from reorganization at the mesoscale. Stress granules, ribonucleoprotein assemblies, nuclear lamina networks, mitochondrial contact sites, extracellular matrices, contractile cytoskeletal systems, and metabolic enzyme clusters are not single-gene phenomena. They emerge from coordinated molecular rates, molecular interactions, localization constraints, structural disorder, post-translational modification, and protein residence time. Existing public datasets now make it possible to ask whether these mesoscale transitions follow general rules that are conserved across cell types and disease contexts, but the relevant measurements remain fragmented across repositories, technologies, organisms, and analytical conventions. Proteome flux provides a unifying concept for this synthesis. At steady state, protein abundance reflects production and removal, but during stress or disease, the timing of synthesis, degradation, modification, sequestration, and relocalization can diverge. A rapidly translated protein may have little mesoscale effect if it is unstable or excluded from the relevant compartment. Conversely, a long-lived scaffold with intrinsically disordered regions or dense modification sites may stabilize a cellular structure after only modest abundance change. Such rate-dependent behavior is central to emergence: new system properties can arise when molecular turnover and interaction kinetics exceed thresholds that are not obvious from abundance measurements alone. The proposed working group will focus on public data relevant to stress adaptation, aging, cardiometabolic dysfunction, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte remodeling, cancer stress states, proteostasis impairment, and structural organization of the nucleus and cytoplasm. These domains are scientifically connected by recurring questions about translation control, protein degradation, post-transcriptional regulation, proteome stability, scaffold proteins, and disease-associated cellular phenotypes. They also provide diverse perturbations and biological scales for rigorous comparative synthesis, including acute stress responses, chronic remodeling, developmental or differentiation-associated transitions, and tissue-specific disease states. NCEMS support is essential because the project depends on integration that exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. Ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, mass-spectrometry proteomics, pulse-labeling turnover studies, phosphoproteomics, protein interaction networks, localization resources, disorder annotations, condensate catalogs, and single-cell atlases each use distinct identifiers, normalization schemes, noise structures, and biological assumptions. A community-scale working group can establish shared standards, benchmark inference methods, quantify uncertainty, and produce generalizable models rather than dataset-specific observations. The significance is both biological and methodological. Biologically, the project will identify molecular flux patterns that distinguish reversible adaptive remodeling from persistent pathological restructuring. Methodologically, it will transform static omics comparisons into dynamic, interpretable models of protein system behavior. The work directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, addressing emergence at the mesoscale, building transdisciplinary synthesis capacity, training data-savvy trainees, and delivering open resources for the molecular and cellular sciences community.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This proposal is organized around one overarching question: how do molecular rates and regulatory states combine to produce emergent mesoscale protein organization during stress and disease? We define proteome flux as the integrated behavior of protein production, residence time, degradation, modification, localization, structural interaction potential, and assignment to mesoscale systems. We will use publicly available data to test whether combinations of these features form reproducible codes that predict cellular remodeling more effectively than any single omics layer. Research Question 1 asks whether protein turnover, translation, and abundance can be harmonized across public datasets to reveal conserved flux regimes. We hypothesize that proteins partition into reproducible classes, including fast-response transient regulators, long-residence structural scaffolds, high-production metabolic proteins, stress-inducible short-lived effectors, and stable compartmental anchors. These classes will be detectable across organisms and cell types after accounting for technology, growth state, and annotation uncertainty. Research Question 2 asks whether specific flux regimes are enriched in mesoscale assemblies. We hypothesize that stress granule and ribonucleoprotein systems will show rapid translational and localization shifts in proteins enriched for RNA-binding domains and disordered regions; nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated systems will show long residence times, modification-sensitive remodeling, and disease-linked persistence; mitochondrial and metabolic assemblies will show coordinated production and turnover changes coupled to energy-state perturbations; extracellular matrix and cytoskeletal modules will show slow remodeling and tissue-specific stabilization. These predictions reflect the idea that mesoscale structures are governed by distinct kinetic constraints. Research Question 3 asks which molecular features explain the transition from adaptive remodeling to pathological remodeling. We hypothesize that persistent disease phenotypes arise when long-lived scaffold proteins, proteins with disordered or low-complexity segments, and modification-rich regulators undergo coordinated flux changes that resist reversal after stress removal. This mechanism may help explain chronic endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte contractile dysfunction, age-associated extracellular matrix remodeling, proteostasis collapse, and malignant stress adaptation. Research Question 4 asks whether proteome flux models improve prediction of higher-order phenotypes compared with transcriptomic or proteomic abundance models alone. We hypothesize that incorporating translation efficiency, turnover rate, degradation uncertainty, localization, modification state, disorder, and network position will increase predictive accuracy and improve interpretability. We further hypothesize that cross-context models will reveal both universal flux principles and tissue-specific exceptions. Research Question 5 asks which public datasets are most informative for synthesis and where current measurement gaps limit inference. We hypothesize that uncertainty-aware integration will identify robust findings despite heterogeneous data quality, while also defining community benchmark needs for future public datasets. The project will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will use comparative synthesis to formulate testable principles, open computational models, and prioritizable predictions for future investigators. Together, these questions directly address emergence by linking molecular-scale rate processes to mesoscale structures and cellular phenotypes.
methods_and_approach: The working group will implement three integrated synthesis aims using only existing publicly available data. Aim 1 will build a FAIR proteome-flux atlas. We will curate datasets from public repositories including GEO, SRA, PRIDE, MassIVE, ProteomeXchange, CPTAC resources, Human Protein Atlas, UniProt, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, PhosphoSitePlus where licensing permits, DepMap, public single-cell portals, and specialized resources for condensate-associated proteins, protein disorder, localization, domains, and structural predictions. Eligible datasets will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-SILAC and related turnover measurements, dynamic labeling studies, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, bulk and single-cell stress datasets, iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte and endothelial cell studies, cardiovascular tissue omics, cancer stress datasets, aging systems, and perturbation studies relevant to proteostasis or metabolism. We will record provenance, organism, cell type, perturbation, time scale, technology, identifiers, normalization status, and uncertainty. Orthology and isoform mapping will be performed conservatively, with analyses repeated at protein group, gene, and orthogroup levels as appropriate. Aim 2 will infer standardized flux features and mesoscale membership. For each protein, we will estimate or annotate transcript abundance, translation efficiency, protein abundance, synthesis rate proxies, degradation or residence time, modification burden, dynamic modification change, subcellular localization, interaction degree, complex membership, disorder content, low-complexity regions, RNA-binding status, scaffold potential, and association with condensates, cytoskeleton, extracellular matrix, nuclear lamina, chromatin, mitochondria, metabolic complexes, or other compartments. Turnover and translation measurements will be harmonized using hierarchical Bayesian or mixed-effect models that account for dataset, organism, technology, labeling strategy, time point, and measurement error. Missing features will be treated explicitly rather than imputed indiscriminately; when imputation is used, downstream sensitivity analyses will quantify its influence. Aim 3 will model relationships between flux codes and cellular outcomes. We will use complementary strategies: unsupervised clustering to define recurrent flux states; network propagation to identify coordinated mesoscale modules; supervised machine learning to predict stress adaptation, inflammatory activation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, proteostasis impairment, disease class, or age-associated remodeling; and mechanistic ordinary differential equation or probabilistic graphical models for selected modules where time-series data support dynamic inference. Predictive models will be evaluated by nested cross-validation, leave-dataset-out validation, leave-cell-type-out validation, and orthogonal validation using datasets not used for model training. Feature importance will be assessed with interpretable methods such as permutation analysis, SHAP-style summaries, stability selection, and network-level enrichment. The working group structure will include domain subteams for data curation, turnover and translation modeling, structural and localization annotation, disease-context interpretation, software engineering, and trainee-led benchmarking. NCEMS meetings will be used for standards development, code sprints, cross-disciplinary interpretation sessions, and community feedback. Feasibility is high because the project synthesizes mature public data types and produces modular deliverables at each stage.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will produce five major outcomes. First, we will deliver a public proteome-flux atlas that harmonizes translation, abundance, turnover, modification, localization, structural, and mesoscale membership information across stress and disease-relevant systems. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with ribonucleoprotein assemblies, nuclear and chromatin scaffolds, mitochondrial and metabolic modules, extracellular matrix networks, cytoskeletal systems, and contractile structures. Third, we will generate predictive models that test whether integrated flux features outperform transcript or protein abundance alone in explaining emergent cellular phenotypes. Fourth, we will create benchmark datasets and evaluation criteria for protein turnover and translation inference across heterogeneous public resources. Fifth, we will provide open tutorials and visualization tools that enable trainees and external researchers to reuse the resource. The scientific impact will be a shift from static molecular lists toward rate-aware explanations of cellular organization. The project will clarify why some stress responses are transient and reversible, whereas others become persistent, tissue-specific, or pathological. It will also provide a framework for connecting molecular regulation to cardiovascular remodeling, endothelial inflammation, proteostasis failure, cancer stress adaptation, and aging-associated structural change without generating new data. The broader impact is the establishment of a community model for synthesis research in molecular and cellular biology. By bringing together proteomics, translation biology, disease modeling, structural bioinformatics, network science, and computational infrastructure, the working group will create resources that individual laboratories could not assemble alone. The results will support hypothesis generation for future experimental studies, but all funded activities will remain centered on public data synthesis, open analysis, workforce training, and reproducible computational discovery aligned with NCEMS priorities.
open_science_and_reproducibility: All project outputs will follow open, reproducible, and team-science practices from the start. We will release a living data-management plan describing dataset inclusion criteria, provenance tracking, identifier mapping, licensing, metadata standards, versioning, quality-control metrics, and procedures for community correction. Only publicly available datasets will be used, and each dataset will retain links to its original repository and accession. Processed harmonized tables will include clear documentation of transformations, normalization, uncertainty estimates, and known limitations. Analysis workflows will be developed in public version-controlled repositories. Code will use containerized environments, workflow managers such as Snakemake, Nextflow, or comparable reproducible systems, and continuous integration tests for core functions. Major analyses will be accompanied by executable notebooks, scripted figures, software release tags, and archived computational environments. Data products will be deposited in appropriate open repositories with persistent identifiers, permissive licenses when compatible with source data, and machine-readable metadata. We will distinguish primary curated data, derived features, model-ready matrices, and summary visualizations to support reuse at different expertise levels. Reproducibility will be assessed through internal rerun challenges in which trainees or collaborating laboratories independently regenerate key figures and model outputs from documented workflows. Model evaluation will include preregistered benchmark splits, leave-dataset-out validation, sensitivity analyses for missingness and orthology mapping, and transparent reporting of negative or non-generalizable findings. The working group will also create community-facing tutorials, short courses, and example analyses focused on turnover inference, ribosome profiling integration, proteomics normalization, network modeling, and responsible machine learning for molecular data. Authorship and contribution policies will be established early using transparent contributor roles. Regular open office hours and public milestone reports will invite feedback from the broader NCEMS community. These practices will ensure that the project is not only scientifically rigorous but also reusable, extensible, and educational for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.
budget_and_resources: We request NCEMS support to enable the coordination, computing, training, and open-resource development required for a community-scale synthesis project. The largest resource need is personnel time for data curation, software engineering, trainee participation, and cross-disciplinary integration. Funds will support graduate students or postdoctoral trainees who will curate public datasets, implement reproducible workflows, benchmark turnover and translation models, build visualization tools, and lead tutorials. Partial support for a data scientist or research software engineer is essential to maintain interoperable infrastructure, containerized workflows, documentation, testing, and public releases. NCEMS meeting support is central to feasibility. We propose recurring virtual working sessions and in-person synthesis meetings for data standardization, model review, hackathons, trainee mentoring, and community feedback. Travel funds will prioritize participation across institutions, career stages, and geographic regions, including early-career investigators and trainees from institutions with varied research resources. Funds will also support accessibility needs, hybrid participation, and dissemination through workshops or conference-adjacent training events. Computational resources will be used for storage of harmonized public datasets, model training, workflow execution, web-based visualization, and archival releases. The project will leverage institutional clusters and free public repositories whenever possible, but NCEMS support is needed for shared cloud computing, managed storage, collaborative platforms, and persistent hosting of lightweight interactive tools. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, recruit human subjects, or conduct animal studies. The requested budget directly supports NCEMS goals: synthesis of existing data, multidisciplinary collaboration, open infrastructure, and workforce training. Without NCEMS, the necessary coordination across proteomics, ribosome profiling, structural annotation, disease biology, network modeling, and software development would remain fragmented. With NCEMS support, the working group can deliver a durable public atlas, reproducible analytical standards, predictive models, and training materials that benefit the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.

title: Inferring Conserved Mesoscale Kinetic Programs from Public Spatial Omics and Fluorescence Microscopy Atlases
abstract:
Cell states are usually defined by transcriptional profiles, yet many consequential state transitions emerge from mesoscale organization: RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane localization, molecular mobility, and organelle-associated trafficking. A macrophage-exposed tumor cell, a differentiating neural progenitor, or a stressed neuron may share little transcriptomic identity, but may converge on similar mesoscale kinetic solutions such as altered nuclear export, enhanced membrane-proximal signaling, or increased residence time of regulatory proteins in subcellular compartments. This working group will test the hypothesis that diverse cellular transitions are governed by a small set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred by synthesizing existing public spatial omics, proteomics, and fluorescence microscopy data.

We will build an open synthesis framework that links three public data classes that are rarely analyzed together. First, we will harmonize single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets from public repositories, including brain development and adult brain atlases, tumor microenvironment datasets, MERFISH/seqFISH-style measurements with subcellular RNA localization, and spatial cancer atlases. Second, we will integrate proteomic and immunofluorescence resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, public CODEX/IMC datasets, and subcellular protein localization maps. Third, we will mine public microscopy repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive for live-cell, single-particle, FRAP/FCS, super-resolution, and organelle-tracking datasets that report protein mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, or trafficking dynamics. No new experimental data will be generated.

The central methodological innovation will be a Bayesian multimodal model that translates heterogeneous public measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Rather than treating images as qualitative annotations, the framework will extract probabilistic features including nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning, local transcript density, protein puncta size and number, apparent oligomeric state, organelle adjacency, membrane enrichment, and effective mobility or residence-time estimates where time-resolved data exist. These features will be linked to matched or harmonized transcriptomic cell states using batch-aware integration and uncertainty propagation. The model will explicitly account for differences in optical resolution, fluorophore sampling, segmentation quality, and assay modality, enabling principled comparison across datasets and laboratories.

We will apply the framework to three biological transitions with abundant public data and strong mesoscale relevance: neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling of tumor cells and immune neighborhoods, and cellular stress states involving mitochondrial and membrane-trafficking pathways. Across these systems, we will ask whether transcriptionally distinct cell types reuse common mesoscale programs; whether spatially localized RNAs predict protein compartmentalization or mobility; and whether emergent cellular phenotypes are better explained by inferred kinetic features than by gene expression alone. Expected products include an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs, reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public microscopy data, benchmark datasets for spatial omics–image integration, and candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in single-cell and spatial data integration, statistical optics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule biophysics, image analysis, cell-state biology, and open data engineering. The working group will include trainees as core contributors through hackathon-style data integration sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-training modules on spatial omics, microscopy uncertainty, and probabilistic modeling. All curated data links, derived features, code, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly to support community reuse and future synthesis studies of emergent cellular organization.
background_and_significance:
Molecular and cellular biology has entered an era in which public datasets describe the same biological processes from complementary viewpoints: single-cell gene expression, spatial transcript localization, multiplexed protein abundance, subcellular imaging, and time-resolved molecular motion. Yet these data classes remain largely siloed. Cell states are often operationally defined by transcript abundance because single-cell RNA sequencing is broad, scalable, and analytically mature. However, many emergent cellular behaviors arise between molecular interactions and organelle-scale outcomes, where the relevant variables are mesoscale: molecular crowding, local concentration, phase-like clustering, nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, protein residence time, membrane recruitment, organelle proximity, and trafficking flux. These properties can create functional states that are not obvious from transcript counts alone.

This gap is particularly important for cellular transitions. During neural differentiation, RNA localization and nuclear export help coordinate maturation programs before stable cell identities are fully established. In tumors, inflammatory and immune cues can reorganize signaling proteins, membrane receptors, and RNA localization in ways that alter plasticity, invasion, and therapy response. Under metabolic or proteotoxic stress, mitochondrial organization, copper and metal handling, vesicular trafficking, and protein mobility can shift rapidly, generating phenotypes that precede or exceed transcriptional remodeling. These examples suggest that apparently unrelated transitions may reuse conserved mesoscale kinetic strategies, even when their gene-expression signatures differ.

Public data now make it possible to test this idea without generating new experimental data. Spatial transcriptomic atlases provide tissue context and, in image-based platforms, direct measurements of subcellular RNA distributions. Single-cell atlases offer harmonized cell-state maps across development, adult tissues, cancer, and perturbation conditions. Protein resources such as immunofluorescence localization maps, multiplexed tissue imaging, and proteomic atlases provide information on abundance, compartment, and cell-neighborhood structure. Public microscopy archives contain live-cell movies, fluorescence recovery measurements, fluctuation spectroscopy, super-resolution images, single-particle tracking datasets, and organelle-tracking experiments that report mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, and trafficking. Individually, these datasets are valuable; synthesized together, they can reveal whether cell states are governed by recurring mesoscale kinetic programs.

The proposed working group addresses a fundamental NCEMS question: how do new system properties emerge at the mesoscale from molecular components? Our premise is that mesoscale organization is not merely a downstream readout of transcription. Instead, it is a partially independent layer of regulation that can integrate gene expression, physical constraints, biochemical interactions, and spatial context into coherent cellular phenotypes. A synthesis approach is essential because no single dataset contains all relevant modalities, and no single laboratory typically combines expertise in spatial omics, statistical optics, single-molecule biophysics, probabilistic modeling, cell-state biology, and open data engineering.

By integrating existing public datasets, this project will transform scattered observations into a reusable framework for asking whether distinct biological systems share common kinetic solutions. The work directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by addressing emergence in molecular and cellular sciences, developing analytical strategies for heterogeneous public data, building a multidisciplinary working group, training data-savvy trainees, and producing open community resources.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The overarching question is whether diverse cellular transitions are organized by a limited set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred from public spatial omics, proteomic, and microscopy datasets. We define a mesoscale kinetic program as a coordinated pattern of subcellular organization and dynamics, including RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane recruitment, molecular mobility, organelle association, and trafficking-related redistribution, that recurs across biological systems and is associated with a reproducible cellular outcome.

Question 1: Do transcriptionally distinct cell states reuse common mesoscale kinetic programs? We will compare neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling in tumor-immune microenvironments, and stress-associated mitochondrial or membrane-trafficking states. These systems differ in tissue, lineage, and stimulus, but all involve transitions in which molecular localization and motion are expected to influence phenotype. Hypothesis 1 is that cross-system integration will identify a small number of reusable mesoscale programs, such as nuclear-retained RNA and delayed export, membrane-proximal signaling enrichment, increased protein residence time in regulatory compartments, puncta-associated concentration of signaling or RNA-binding factors, and enhanced organelle adjacency linked to metabolic adaptation. These programs will be more conserved than the identities of individual marker genes.

Question 2: Can spatial RNA features predict protein localization and dynamic behavior? Image-based transcriptomic data can report nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, local transcript density, and proximity of RNAs to organelles or membranes. Protein atlases and microscopy datasets can report compartment enrichment, puncta formation, oligomeric state proxies, and mobility. Hypothesis 2 is that spatial RNA organization will improve prediction of protein localization and kinetic behavior beyond total transcript abundance. For example, nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning may predict delayed protein accumulation or altered regulatory timing, while locally enriched transcripts may predict compartment-specific protein abundance or clustering.

Question 3: Do inferred mesoscale kinetic features explain emergent phenotypes better than gene expression alone? Many outcomes, including cell-cycle progression, differentiation potential, immune activation, mesenchymal-like tumor remodeling, and stress tolerance, arise from the combined effects of molecular abundance, spatial organization, and kinetic constraints. Hypothesis 3 is that multimodal latent variables incorporating mesoscale features will improve prediction of transition stage, neighborhood response, and stress-associated state compared with transcriptomic embeddings alone. This will be evaluated using held-out datasets and phenotypic annotations available in public resources.

Question 4: Which molecular modules link transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization? Hypothesis 4 is that regulators of RNA processing and export, cytoskeletal transport, membrane trafficking, metal and mitochondrial homeostasis, chromatin-associated residence, and receptor-proximal signaling will repeatedly associate with inferred kinetic programs across systems. The goal is not to claim direct causality from synthesis alone, but to generate ranked, cross-validated candidate modules that explain how molecular components give rise to mesoscale organization.

Question 5: What methodological principles are required to compare heterogeneous public imaging and omics data? Hypothesis 5 is that uncertainty-aware Bayesian integration, explicit optical and sampling metadata, and batch-aware cell-state harmonization will outperform approaches that treat images as categorical annotations. This methodological question is central to feasibility and community reuse, because public data vary in resolution, labeling strategy, segmentation quality, field of view, and experimental design.
methods_and_approach:
This working group will conduct a synthesis-only project using existing public datasets. No new experimental measurements will be generated. The work will proceed through coordinated data inventory, harmonization, feature extraction, probabilistic modeling, biological analysis, benchmarking, and community release.

Aim 1: Curate and harmonize public datasets. We will assemble three linked data collections. The transcriptomic collection will include public single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets, spatial transcriptomic atlases, and image-based MERFISH or seqFISH-style datasets from developing and adult brain, tumor microenvironments, and stress-relevant cell systems. The protein and tissue-imaging collection will include Human Protein Atlas immunofluorescence, public CODEX and imaging mass cytometry data, and subcellular protein localization resources. The microscopy collection will include datasets from repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive containing live-cell imaging, single-particle tracking, FRAP, FCS, super-resolution localization, organelle tracking, and related measurements. Each dataset will be annotated with modality, species, tissue, cell type, perturbation, imaging resolution, labeling method, temporal sampling, segmentation availability, and licensing.

Aim 2: Extract uncertainty-aware mesoscale features. For spatial RNA data, we will quantify nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, transcript dispersion, local density, cell-edge enrichment, neighborhood gradients, and, when possible, organelle-proximal localization. For protein imaging, we will estimate compartment enrichment, puncta number and size, spatial anisotropy, membrane enrichment, cell-to-cell variability, and colocalization or adjacency to organelle markers. For live and time-resolved microscopy, we will extract or re-estimate apparent diffusion, residence time, recovery kinetics, track confinement, cluster lifetime, and trafficking directionality using published raw data where available and published summary statistics where raw data are unavailable. All features will include uncertainty estimates reflecting photon noise, optical resolution, sampling density, segmentation error, batch, and missing metadata.

Aim 3: Build a Bayesian multimodal latent-state model. We will develop a hierarchical model that maps heterogeneous measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Dataset-specific likelihoods will represent count-based transcriptomics, spatial point patterns, fluorescence intensity images, localization data, and time-series measurements. Batch and platform effects will be modeled explicitly rather than removed blindly. Transcriptomic cell states will be harmonized using established batch-aware integration strategies, then linked to imaging-derived features through probabilistic alignment based on cell type, tissue, perturbation, marker genes, and spatial context. The model will propagate uncertainty from feature extraction to latent program assignment and will permit partial observations, allowing datasets with only one or two modalities to contribute.

Aim 4: Identify conserved programs and test predictive value. We will infer recurring mesoscale programs across three transition classes: neural maturation, tumor-immune inflammatory remodeling, and mitochondrial or membrane-trafficking stress states. We will evaluate conservation by cross-dataset replication, leave-one-dataset-out prediction, permutation controls, and comparison to transcript-only baselines. Predictive tasks will include transition-stage classification, inflammatory or stress-state annotation, spatial neighborhood response, and protein localization or mobility prediction from RNA features. Candidate molecular modules will be identified by associating latent programs with gene sets, protein families, regulatory factors, and pathway annotations.

Aim 5: Organize NCEMS-enabled working group activities. Participants will include experts in spatial and single-cell omics, microscopy physics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule dynamics, image analysis, cell biology, and data infrastructure. Trainees will lead reproducible workflow modules during data-integration sprints and receive cross-training in spatial omics, statistical optics, and probabilistic modeling. Milestones include a curated data registry by month 3, feature-extraction workflows by month 6, first integrated model by month 9, biological program atlas by month 12, benchmark release by month 15, and manuscripts and community tutorials by month 18.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will deliver four primary products. First, we will create an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs across neural maturation, tumor-immune remodeling, and cellular stress states. The atlas will include program scores, uncertainty estimates, associated cell states, dataset provenance, and interpretable features such as RNA partitioning, protein clustering, membrane enrichment, organelle adjacency, and mobility proxies. Second, we will release reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public spatial omics and microscopy data. These workflows will support community analysis of images as quantitative measurements rather than qualitative illustrations. Third, we will produce benchmark datasets and evaluation tasks for multimodal integration across transcriptomics, proteomics, and microscopy. Fourth, we will nominate candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

The scientific impact will be to test whether emergent cell states can be understood as combinations of conserved mesoscale kinetic strategies. If successful, the project will shift interpretation of cell states from transcript abundance alone toward a more physical and spatially grounded view of cellular regulation. This will help explain why different biological systems can produce similar phenotypes through different marker genes, and why some transitions are poorly predicted by expression profiles alone.

The methodological impact will be a generalizable framework for uncertainty-aware synthesis of heterogeneous public data. The project will also provide a model for NCEMS-style community synthesis: no new experiments, broad collaboration, transparent workflows, and trainee-centered data science training. The resulting resources will enable future studies of organelle dynamics, RNA localization, protein mobility, signaling compartmentalization, and emergent cellular organization across many public datasets beyond the initial biological domains.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
All project activities will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices. We will use only publicly available datasets with documented access conditions and will maintain a public data registry containing dataset identifiers, repository links, licenses, file formats, metadata completeness, modality descriptions, and processing status. Because raw imaging files can be large and may have repository-specific access requirements, we will not duplicate restricted data unnecessarily. Instead, we will provide persistent links, checksums when available, standardized metadata tables, and derived features that are permissible to redistribute.

Code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories under a permissive open-source license. Workflows will be implemented with reproducible workflow managers and containerized computational environments so that analyses can be rerun on local clusters or cloud systems. Each major analysis will include executable notebooks, parameter files, software versions, and automated tests for core functions such as segmentation import, feature extraction, uncertainty calculation, batch-aware alignment, and model fitting. Model outputs will include uncertainty intervals and diagnostics rather than only point estimates.

We will preregister major benchmark tasks and evaluation metrics before final model comparison, including transcript-only baselines, leave-one-dataset-out tests, and negative controls based on permuted labels or spatial coordinates. Data and code releases will be versioned, assigned persistent identifiers when stable, and accompanied by tutorials for researchers with different computational backgrounds.

Collaborative practices will include written contribution guidelines, authorship and credit policies, issue tracking, regular open documentation sprints, and trainee-led code reviews. Training materials from working group meetings will be released publicly, including modules on spatial omics harmonization, microscopy uncertainty, Bayesian multimodal modeling, and responsible reuse of public biological data. These practices will ensure that the project produces not only publications, but durable community infrastructure for synthesis research.
budget_and_resources:
The requested NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis across multiple disciplines, institutions, data repositories, and computational environments. Funds will support working group meetings, trainee participation, data engineering, computing, and open dissemination. No funds will be used for new experimental data generation, sample acquisition, wet-lab reagents, or instrument time.

Meeting support will enable two in-person NCEMS working group meetings and regular virtual coordination. The first meeting will finalize dataset inclusion criteria, metadata standards, benchmark questions, and model architecture. The second will focus on cross-dataset interpretation, community release, manuscript planning, and sustainability. Shorter virtual hackathon-style sprints will support data curation, image feature extraction, workflow testing, and benchmark evaluation.

Trainee support will be a central budget priority. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will receive travel support, short-term effort for workflow development, and structured mentoring across computational biology, microscopy, and Bayesian inference. Trainees will lead defined modules such as public dataset registry construction, uncertainty-aware feature extraction, baseline model comparison, documentation, and tutorial development.

Computational resources will be used for cloud or high-performance computing storage, containerized workflow execution, image processing, model fitting, and public release preparation. Budgeted data engineering effort will support metadata harmonization, conversion of heterogeneous image and omics formats into analysis-ready structures, quality control dashboards, and long-term documentation. Dissemination resources will cover persistent archiving, web documentation, and community tutorials.

NCEMS provides the convening structure and synthesis environment needed for this effort. The project exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory because it requires integration of public spatial omics, proteomics, live-cell imaging, statistical optics, probabilistic modeling, and biological interpretation. NCEMS support will transform dispersed public datasets into a coherent, reusable resource for understanding mesoscale emergence.
