author: gpt-5.5
title: Emergent Chromatin and Immune Cell States from tRNA Modification–Controlled Translation Dynamics
abstract:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how chemical changes on a small number of RNAs produce system-level cell states that are not predictable from transcript abundance alone. This working group will test the hypothesis that tRNA modifications act as mesoscale control points by reshaping ribosome traffic, protein complex stoichiometry, and chromatin-regulatory assemblies, thereby generating emergent epigenomic and immune phenotypes across microbes and human cells. The project will use only publicly available data and will synthesize information across RNA modification biology, ribosome profiling, proteomics, structural modeling, single-cell genomics, and microbial metabolism.

We will build an open, cross-kingdom atlas linking tRNA modification capacity to translation and cellular phenotype. Public resources will include MODOMICS and curated bacterial and eukaryotic tRNA modification enzyme annotations; published tRNA modification mapping datasets; ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, and proteomics from bacteria, yeast, mammalian cells, cancer models, immune perturbation studies, neurodegeneration cohorts, and metabolic stress datasets; public single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq atlases from tumor, brain, and cardiovascular tissues; microbial genome and metagenome datasets with annotated micronutrient and RNA-modification pathways; and public protein structures from PDB and AlphaFold. No new experimental data will be generated.

The scientific question is deliberately multiscale: when a tRNA modification is lost, altered, or metabolite-limited, which codon contexts experience altered elongation, which proteins become selectively under- or over-produced, and which higher-order cellular structures or regulatory programs are most vulnerable? We will develop a codon-aware synthesis framework that integrates ribosome pausing signatures with transcript abundance, protein abundance, protein complex membership, post-translational modification data, and chromatin accessibility. Graph-based imputation and feature-propagation methods will harmonize sparse single-cell and bulk datasets, while interpretable machine-learning models will identify conserved translation-sensitive modules. Structural and coarse-grained molecular modeling will be used not to create new simulations as primary data, but to contextualize public structures of affected chromatin regulators, RNA-binding proteins, metabolic enzymes, and immune signaling proteins in terms of complex formation, DNA engagement, and mesoscale assembly potential.

The expected outcome is a quantitative map of how nucleotide-scale chemical information propagates to emergent mesoscale organization. We will focus on three synthesis products: first, a conserved catalog of codon- and modification-sensitive translation bottlenecks across organisms; second, a ranked set of chromatin, immune, and metabolic protein complexes whose stoichiometry is predicted to be unusually sensitive to tRNA modification state; and third, a set of cell-state transition models connecting microbial micronutrient availability, host tRNA modification capacity, ribosome pausing, chromatin accessibility, and immune phenotypes. This framework could help explain why similar transcriptional programs diverge into distinct proteomic or epigenomic outcomes, and why microbial metabolites or transporter variation can have unexpectedly broad cellular effects.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in microbial genomics, RNA modification biology, single-cell data integration, proteomics, chromatin biophysics, structural modeling, and AI. The working group will release harmonized datasets, reproducible workflows, interactive network browsers, and training modules for trainees in open, data-intensive molecular synthesis research.
background_and_significance: Emergent properties in molecular and cellular systems often arise when many individually modest molecular effects combine to reorganize cellular behavior. tRNA modifications provide an underexplored example of this principle. More than one hundred chemical modifications decorate tRNAs across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes, with many concentrated near the anticodon loop where they influence decoding accuracy, codon recognition, frameshifting, and elongation kinetics. Although individual enzymes and modifications have been characterized, the field lacks a synthesis-level understanding of how variation in tRNA modification capacity propagates from codon-specific translation dynamics to proteome remodeling, protein complex stoichiometry, chromatin regulation, and immune or disease-associated cell states. This gap is increasingly tractable because extensive public data now span tRNA modification annotations, ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, proteomics, single-cell transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility, microbial genomes and metagenomes, metabolomics, and predicted protein structures. Transcript abundance alone does not reliably predict protein abundance or cellular phenotype. Codon usage, tRNA availability, modification state, local mRNA context, ribosome traffic, protein stability, and complex assembly all contribute to the final functional proteome. tRNA modifications are especially compelling mesoscale control points because their effects are neither purely molecular nor fully cellular. A modification defect may slow translation at specific codon contexts, alter co-translational folding, bias production of proteins enriched for sensitive codons, and destabilize multi-protein assemblies. If those assemblies include chromatin remodelers, histone modifiers, RNA-binding proteins, metabolic enzymes, or immune signaling complexes, small RNA chemical changes could create large system-level shifts in epigenomic accessibility, inflammatory responses, differentiation, or stress adaptation. Cross-kingdom synthesis is essential. In microbes, tRNA modification pathways are shaped by genome content, temperature, nutrient availability, and metabolic cofactors, and can affect motility, stress responses, translation pausing, and virulence-related phenotypes. In host cells, micronutrients and microbiome-derived metabolites can influence RNA modification substrates and transport, while cancer, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular stress, and immune activation are associated with altered metabolism, chromatin accessibility, and proteome composition. These observations suggest that microbial metabolic capacity and host tRNA modification state may jointly influence translation-sensitive cell-state transitions. However, existing studies are fragmented by organism, assay type, disease context, and analytical framework. NCEMS is uniquely aligned with this challenge because the proposed work focuses on emergence at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles: ribosome traffic, protein complex formation, chromatin-regulatory assemblies, and immune-state networks. The project will not generate new data. Instead, it will integrate public datasets using codon-aware statistics, graph-based harmonization, interpretable machine learning, and structural context from public models. The result will be a community resource and conceptual framework for predicting when nucleotide-scale chemical variation becomes a higher-order cellular phenotype.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This working group will address one overarching question: how do tRNA modification states reshape translation dynamics in ways that generate emergent chromatin, immune, metabolic, and stress-response phenotypes across biological systems? We will decompose this question into four linked synthesis questions. First, which tRNA modifications and modifying enzymes are associated with reproducible codon-specific ribosome pausing signatures across bacteria, yeast, and mammalian cells? We hypothesize that loss, depletion, or metabolic limitation of anticodon-adjacent modifications will produce conserved pausing signatures at defined codons and codon neighborhoods, but that the phenotypic impact will depend on organism-specific codon usage, transcript expression, and protein network architecture. Second, which proteins and protein complexes are most vulnerable to tRNA modification-dependent translation changes? We hypothesize that sensitivity will be enriched in proteins whose coding sequences contain clusters of modification-dependent codons, whose abundance must be tightly balanced within complexes, or whose domains require coordinated translation for folding, binding, or assembly. Candidate vulnerable systems include chromatin regulators, histone-modifying enzymes, RNA-binding proteins, mitochondrial and metabolic enzymes, immune receptors, cytokine signaling components, and stress-response regulators. Third, how do translation-sensitive protein modules relate to single-cell chromatin and immune cell states? We hypothesize that tRNA modification-dependent translation bottlenecks create proteomic shifts that are not visible from mRNA abundance alone but become detectable as altered chromatin accessibility, regulatory motif activity, ligand-receptor signaling, immune activation, exhaustion, tissue-resident memory programs, glial states, or metabolic inflammatory states in public single-cell atlases. Fourth, can microbial genome and metagenome features help explain host variation in tRNA modification-linked phenotypes? We hypothesize that microbial pathways affecting queuine, queuosine, sulfur metabolism, folate-related chemistry, flavin-dependent reactions, and other RNA modification cofactors will correlate with host translation-sensitive modules and immune or chromatin states in datasets where microbiome, metabolomic, transcriptomic, or clinical metadata are publicly available. These questions share a central emergence hypothesis: tRNA modifications act as information filters that convert chemical and metabolic conditions into selective translation-rate changes; these changes alter protein stoichiometry and assembly; altered assemblies remodel chromatin and signaling networks; and the resulting cell states can differ sharply even when transcriptomes are similar. The proposal is intentionally falsifiable. We will test whether observed pausing signatures exceed matched codon-usage and expression controls; whether predicted sensitive proteins show discordant RNA-protein behavior in independent datasets; whether sensitive complexes are enriched for known stoichiometric constraints; and whether cell-state associations replicate across tissues, diseases, and species. Alternative outcomes are informative. If sensitivity is highly organism-specific, the atlas will identify the rules governing context dependence. If chromatin and immune modules are not enriched, the project will delimit where tRNA modification control is strongest. The synthesis will therefore produce both mechanistic hypotheses and rigorous negative evidence.
methods_and_approach: The project will proceed through four integrated workstreams using only existing public data. Workstream 1 will construct a cross-kingdom tRNA modification knowledge graph. We will curate modification identities, enzyme families, target tRNAs, anticodon positions, cofactor requirements, organismal distributions, and genetic perturbations from MODOMICS, UniProt, KEGG, BioCyc, NCBI genomes, microbial pangenome resources, published tRNA modification maps, and literature-curated datasets. Orthology relationships will be mapped across bacteria, yeast, mouse, and human, with confidence scores for experimentally supported versus inferred annotations. Workstream 2 will quantify codon-aware translation effects. Public ribosome profiling, matched RNA-seq, and proteomics datasets will be reprocessed through standardized workflows for quality control, read periodicity, codon-site assignment, differential ribosome occupancy, translational efficiency, and protein-RNA discordance. We will prioritize datasets with perturbations in tRNA modification enzymes, nutrient or cofactor limitation, stress responses, immune activation, cancer models, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disease. Models will include codon identity, codon pairs, local sequence context, transcript abundance, initiation effects, mRNA structure proxies, and batch covariates. Pausing signatures will be compared with matched null models based on amino acid composition, codon usage, expression, and gene length. Workstream 3 will connect translation sensitivity to proteins, complexes, and mesoscale assemblies. We will integrate protein abundance, phosphoproteomics and other post-translational modification datasets, CORUM and Complex Portal annotations, STRING and BioGRID interaction networks, Reactome pathways, chromatin regulator catalogs, immune signaling databases, and metabolic enzyme networks. Coding sequences will be scored for modification-sensitive codon burden, ribosome pausing evidence, RNA-protein discordance, complex stoichiometry risk, and network centrality. Public PDB and AlphaFold structures will be used to annotate affected domains, interfaces, DNA- or RNA-binding regions, oligomerization sites, and intrinsically disordered segments. Structural and coarse-grained reasoning will contextualize assembly vulnerability but will not generate new experimental data or rely on new simulations as primary evidence. Workstream 4 will infer cell-state consequences. Public single-cell RNA-seq, single-nucleus RNA-seq, single-cell ATAC-seq, and multiome atlases from tumors, immune perturbations, brain disease, cardiovascular and metabolic tissues will be harmonized using graph-based feature propagation, batch-aware integration, label transfer, and probabilistic mapping from bulk proteomic signatures to cell states. We will estimate activity of translation-sensitive modules, chromatin accessibility programs, transcription-factor motifs, cell-cell communication pathways, and immune states. Microbial genome and metagenome datasets will be annotated for RNA modification and micronutrient pathways and linked to host signatures where public paired data exist. The working group will meet through structured NCEMS workshops, hackathons, trainee-led analysis sprints, and cross-disciplinary interpretation sessions. Milestones include a curated atlas in year one, integrated models in year two, and public synthesis products and manuscripts in year three.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The project will deliver three major synthesis products. First, we will release a conserved catalog of tRNA modification-linked translation bottlenecks, including codons, codon contexts, organisms, perturbation types, confidence levels, and supporting ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, and proteomic evidence. This catalog will allow the community to distinguish broadly conserved decoding sensitivities from context-specific effects. Second, we will generate a ranked atlas of protein complexes and pathways predicted to be unusually vulnerable to tRNA modification state. The atlas will highlight chromatin regulators, immune signaling systems, metabolic pathways, RNA-binding proteins, and stress-response assemblies where small translation shifts may alter stoichiometry, assembly, or downstream cell behavior. Third, we will produce cell-state transition models connecting microbial micronutrient capacity, host tRNA modification pathways, ribosome pausing, protein module activity, chromatin accessibility, and immune phenotypes. These models will generate testable predictions for future experimental groups without requiring this working group to produce new data. The impact is conceptual, methodological, and practical. Conceptually, the work will clarify how nucleotide-scale RNA chemistry can become a mesoscale emergent phenotype through ribosome traffic and protein assembly. Methodologically, it will provide reusable codon-aware and graph-based data synthesis workflows for integrating ribosome profiling, proteomics, single-cell genomics, microbial genomics, and structural annotations. Practically, it may help explain why similar transcriptomes produce divergent proteomes, why metabolic or microbial changes can have unexpectedly broad immunological consequences, and why chromatin or immune states may be sensitive to translation dynamics. The project directly advances NCEMS goals by addressing emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences through multidisciplinary synthesis of public data, producing open resources, engaging trainees, and creating analytical strategies that exceed the scope of any single laboratory.
open_science_and_reproducibility: The working group will follow open, reproducible, and team-based science practices from project initiation through dissemination. All public datasets will be documented in a living data inventory containing accession numbers, source databases, licenses, organism, tissue, assay type, perturbation, processing status, quality metrics, and reuse constraints. No restricted or newly generated experimental data will be used. Derived harmonized datasets, metadata tables, code, model outputs, and visualization files will be deposited in appropriate public repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, OSF, and domain repositories when required by data type. Analysis workflows will be implemented with containerized environments using Docker or Apptainer and reproducible workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or WDL. Versioned releases will include software dependencies, parameter files, quality-control reports, and example datasets. Statistical models will include pre-specified evaluation criteria, negative controls, matched null models, and sensitivity analyses. Machine-learning components will emphasize interpretability, uncertainty estimates, transparent feature definitions, and independent validation across organisms or datasets. We will maintain clear separation between training, tuning, and replication datasets wherever possible. Interactive resources will include a web-accessible atlas or network browser enabling users to explore tRNA modification enzymes, codon pausing signatures, sensitive proteins, complexes, pathways, cell types, and microbial metabolic annotations. Documentation will include tutorials for trainees and external users. Authorship, contribution tracking, code review, and decision-making will follow community standards for collaborative science, with contributor roles recorded using CRediT taxonomy. Trainee training will be embedded in the work through workshops on ribosome profiling analysis, single-cell integration, microbial genome annotation, structural interpretation, machine-learning reproducibility, and responsible use of AI. We will invite feedback from external domain experts and potential users before final release. Publications will be submitted as open access when feasible, and preprints will be posted to accelerate community review. These practices will ensure that the project is auditable, reusable, extensible, and aligned with NCEMS expectations for open synthesis research.
budget_and_resources: NCEMS support is required because this project depends on sustained coordination among experts in RNA modification biology, microbial genomics, ribosome profiling, proteomics, chromatin biophysics, structural biology, single-cell genomics, immunology, and AI-enabled data integration. The budget will be organized around activities that enable community-scale synthesis rather than new data generation. Major cost categories will include working group meetings, trainee participation, computational resources, open-science infrastructure, and dissemination. We request support for two in-person NCEMS working group meetings per year, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings and focused analysis sprints. Travel funds will prioritize balanced participation across institutions, career stages, and geographic regions, including graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career investigators, and investigators from institutions with varying research capacities. Trainee support will cover short-term analytical fellowships, workshop participation, and protected time for reproducible workflow development and documentation. Computational costs will support cloud or high-performance computing for reprocessing public ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, proteomics, microbial genome, metagenome, and single-cell datasets; storage of harmonized intermediate files; container builds; and hosting of the interactive atlas. Funds for software engineering and data curation will support metadata standardization, workflow hardening, code review, user documentation, and public release. Dissemination funds will support open-access publication fees when needed, public webinars, training materials, and community feedback sessions. No funds will be used for wet-lab experiments, sequencing, animal studies, clinical recruitment, or generation of new primary experimental data. NCEMS resources are essential because the scientific scope exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: the project requires harmonized standards across data modalities, shared computational infrastructure, cross-disciplinary interpretation, and neutral convening to produce resources useful to the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community. The investment will yield durable public assets, trained data-savvy researchers, and a reusable model for studying emergent mesoscale biology through synthesis of existing data.

title: A Public-Data Atlas of Emergent Metal-Redox Compartmentalization Across Bacteria and Archaea
abstract:
Bacteria and archaea build diverse mesoscale compartments that concentrate metals, redox cofactors, enzymes, membranes, and shell proteins into structures with properties not predictable from any single component. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level framework for determining when a gene cluster encodes a true organelle-like system, what physiological pressures favor compartment formation, and how different compartment types converge on common solutions for metal storage, oxidative stress control, and metabolic electron flow. This working group will integrate publicly available genomic, metagenomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and imaging data to define the molecular rules by which metal-redox organelles emerge in prokaryotic cells.

The central question is: what combinations of genes, regulatory programs, protein architectures, ecological contexts, and cellular stress signatures predict the emergence of prokaryotic compartments that manage iron, heme, reactive oxygen chemistry, and cofactor balance? We will synthesize data across known and candidate compartment systems, including magnetosome-like loci, iron-storage organelle loci, encapsulin-associated metalloprotein systems, carboxysome and non-carboxysome bacterial microcompartments, and atypical shell-protein clusters with incomplete or repurposed modules. Rather than treating each organelle class separately, we will ask whether recurrent mesoscale design principles can be detected across independently evolved systems.

The project will use only existing public data. Genome and metagenome assemblies from NCBI, GTDB, IMG/M, MGnify, and public MAG/SAG collections will be mined for shell proteins, membrane remodeling factors, metalloproteins, redox enzymes, transporters, cytoskeletal factors, and regulatory elements. Public RNA-seq and proteomics datasets from pathogens, environmental bacteria, cyanobacteria, anaerobes, and host-associated communities will be reanalyzed to determine when candidate compartment loci are co-regulated with iron limitation, heme exposure, oxidative stress, desiccation, carbon fixation, anaerobic metabolism, or infection-relevant conditions. AlphaFold and structural databases, EMDB/EMPIAR image repositories, and published cryo-electron tomography annotations will be used to connect gene clusters with predicted mesoscale architecture. We will adapt mutational-signature-style decomposition, network community detection, phylogenetic profiling, and interpretable machine learning to identify recurrent “compartment signatures” that distinguish bona fide organelle systems from ordinary metabolic operons.

A major deliverable will be an open, versioned atlas of prokaryotic metal-redox compartmentalization, including standardized locus annotations, confidence scores, ecological metadata, predicted compartment architecture, and links to public omics evidence. We will also develop a reproducible workflow that assigns each candidate locus a quantitative “emergent compartment potential” score based on genomic modularity, co-expression, structural compatibility, taxonomic distribution, and environmental association. This score will allow the community to prioritize unstudied systems for future experimental work while remaining fully grounded in synthesis of public data.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordination among microbial cell biologists, bioinformaticians, structural modelers, metallobiochemists, evolutionary biologists, imaging specialists, and data scientists. The working group will create open tutorials and trainee-led analysis sprints focused on genome mining, public omics reanalysis, structural annotation, and reproducible workflow development. By unifying scattered datasets across organelle biology, metal homeostasis, redox metabolism, and microbial ecology, the project will reveal general principles by which molecular components self-organize into mesoscale cellular structures with new physiological capabilities.
background_and_significance:
Prokaryotic cells are not compositionally simple reaction vessels. Many bacteria and archaea assemble mesoscale compartments that spatially organize chemistry, create local microenvironments, and generate functions that cannot be inferred from isolated enzymes or membranes. Magnetosomes align magnetic minerals within lipid-bounded vesicles, bacterial microcompartments package metabolic pathways inside protein shells, encapsulins sequester metalloproteins, and recently described iron-storage compartments reveal additional strategies for controlling metal availability. These systems occupy the scale emphasized by NCEMS: between individual biomolecules and whole organelles or cells, where collective assembly produces emergent properties in space, energy flow, information processing, and chemical regulation.

Metal-redox physiology is a particularly powerful setting for synthesis research because metals and electron carriers are both essential and hazardous. Iron, heme, flavins, quinones, iron-sulfur clusters, and nicotinamide cofactors support respiration, carbon fixation, stress responses, virulence, and environmental adaptation. The same chemistry can catalyze oxidative damage, disrupt membranes, or poison enzymes when poorly controlled. Compartmentalization offers a route to concentrate substrates, protect the cytoplasm, tune diffusion, and route electrons across selective barriers. However, the field remains organized around named compartment classes rather than general principles. Magnetosomes, microcompartments, carboxysomes, encapsulins, and iron-storage structures are usually annotated through separate vocabularies, databases, and experimental traditions. As a result, potential convergence among these systems is difficult to detect.

A central unsolved problem is how to decide from public data when a gene cluster encodes a true compartment-forming system rather than an ordinary operon. Many loci contain partial shells, accessory metalloproteins, transporters, regulatory genes, or membrane-associated factors, but lack complete canonical markers. These atypical or hybrid loci are often dismissed, inconsistently annotated, or treated as isolated curiosities. Conversely, remote homologs and environmentally restricted systems may be missed by marker-based searches. The absence of a cross-system synthesis framework limits discovery, comparative evolutionary analysis, and the ability to prioritize future experiments.

The proposed working group will address this gap using only existing public data. The timing is favorable because genome and metagenome repositories now include broad bacterial and archaeal diversity, public transcriptomes and proteomes capture many stress and metabolic conditions, structural prediction resources cover vast protein families, and cryo-electron tomography and electron microscopy archives increasingly document intracellular architecture. No individual laboratory is positioned to integrate these data types across microbial cell biology, metal homeostasis, redox biochemistry, comparative genomics, structural modeling, imaging, ecology, and data science. NCEMS support is therefore essential for convening a community-scale effort.

The significance extends beyond cataloging compartments. By developing a public atlas and quantitative framework for emergent compartment potential, this project will reveal how combinations of genes, physical structures, regulatory programs, and environmental pressures generate new cellular capabilities. The work will transform scattered observations into testable design rules for prokaryotic organelle emergence, clarify evolutionary relationships among independently evolved systems, and provide a durable resource for microbiology, cell biology, bioengineering, pathogenesis, and environmental science.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The overarching research question is: what publicly observable combinations of genomic organization, protein architecture, regulation, ecological distribution, and stress-associated expression predict the emergence of prokaryotic mesoscale compartments that manage metal and redox chemistry? We will address this question through four linked aims that convert heterogeneous public data into mechanistic hypotheses and community resources.

Question 1 asks which gene-cluster features distinguish compartment-forming loci from ordinary metabolic operons. We hypothesize that bona fide metal-redox compartments are marked by recurrent modular architectures: a boundary-forming module such as a membrane biogenesis system, protein shell, encapsulin shell, or microcompartment shell; a cargo or catalytic module enriched in metalloproteins, redox enzymes, mineralizing proteins, or cofactor-handling enzymes; a transport or permeability module; and a regulation or positioning module. We further hypothesize that incomplete or atypical loci can still represent functional compartments when they preserve key combinations of these modules or recruit missing functions from elsewhere in the genome.

Question 2 asks whether independently evolved compartments converge on shared solutions for metal toxicity, oxidative stress, heme exposure, anaerobic redox balance, and carbon or energy metabolism. We hypothesize that diverse compartment types will share detectable signatures, including enrichment for iron-sulfur proteins, ferritin-like proteins, heme-handling systems, oxidoreductases, redox-active shell pores, membrane remodeling factors, reactive oxygen stress regulators, and environmental associations with fluctuating metal or oxygen availability. These signatures may reveal common mesoscale design principles even when the structural scaffolds differ.

Question 3 asks how physiological and ecological contexts shape compartment emergence. We hypothesize that candidate loci will show nonrandom distributions across habitats and lifestyles, including host-associated pathogens exposed to nutritional immunity and heme stress, anaerobes managing low-potential electron transfer, cyanobacteria and chemoautotrophs requiring concentrated carbon fixation chemistry, desiccation-tolerant organisms requiring protection of sensitive proteins, and sediment or aquatic microorganisms experiencing steep redox and metal gradients. We also hypothesize that public transcriptomic and proteomic datasets will show coordinated induction of compartment loci with iron limitation, iron excess, peroxide or superoxide stress, heme exposure, oxygen shifts, carbon limitation, infection-relevant conditions, or stationary-phase survival.

Question 4 asks whether public structural and imaging data can connect gene clusters to mesoscale architecture. We hypothesize that candidate loci with high emergent compartment potential will encode proteins with compatible oligomerization, curvature, permeability, targeting, cargo-loading, or membrane-remodeling features. Structural predictions and deposited microscopy data will allow us to infer whether a locus is more likely to form a protein shell, lipid-bounded body, mineral-associated structure, or hybrid assembly.

These hypotheses are intentionally integrative and falsifiable. They predict measurable enrichment patterns, co-expression relationships, phylogenetic distributions, and structural compatibilities that can be tested across public datasets. Negative results will also be informative: loci lacking coordinated regulation, modular structure, or ecological association will help define boundaries between compartmentalized and non-compartmentalized metal-redox metabolism. The outcome will be a quantitative, evidence-weighted model rather than a binary annotation scheme, enabling the community to evaluate known systems, ambiguous loci, and newly discovered candidates within a common framework.
methods_and_approach:
The working group will execute a synthesis-only project using existing public datasets. No new experimental data will be generated. The project will be organized into four coordinated analysis streams with shared standards, quarterly integration meetings, trainee-led coding sprints, and external community feedback.

First, we will construct a reference corpus of known and candidate metal-redox compartment systems. Sources will include NCBI RefSeq and GenBank, GTDB representative genomes, IMG/M, MGnify, public metagenome-assembled and single-cell amplified genome collections, and published supplementary tables for magnetosome, microcompartment, encapsulin, carboxysome, iron-storage, and atypical shell-protein loci. We will build profile hidden Markov models, orthology groups, and rule-based locus definitions for shell proteins, encapsulins, magnetosome-associated proteins, membrane remodeling factors, ferritin-like and other metalloproteins, heme and iron transporters, oxidoreductases, redox cofactor enzymes, cytoskeletal or positioning factors, and regulators. Loci will be annotated in a standardized format that records gene order, strand, intergenic distance, module composition, genomic neighborhood, taxonomy, assembly quality, and habitat metadata.

Second, we will reanalyze public transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to determine regulatory coherence. We will search NCBI SRA, GEO, ENA, PRIDE, MassIVE, and related repositories for bacterial and archaeal datasets involving iron limitation or excess, heme exposure, oxidative stress, desiccation, oxygen transitions, anaerobic metabolism, carbon fixation, host interaction, infection, and stationary-phase or biofilm states. RNA-seq datasets will be processed with documented pipelines for quality control, read mapping or pseudoalignment, normalization, and differential expression. Public proteomics will be reanalyzed where raw files and metadata permit, or harmonized from published protein abundance tables when raw reprocessing is not feasible. Candidate compartment loci will be scored for co-expression, condition responsiveness, regulator association, and alignment with known stress-response signatures.

Third, we will integrate structural and imaging evidence. Protein sequences will be linked to AlphaFold Database models, experimentally determined structures in PDB, domain databases, and predicted oligomeric assemblies when public models are available. We will annotate shell-pore residues, metal-binding motifs, cofactor-binding domains, targeting peptides, curvature-associated surfaces, transmembrane segments, low-complexity regions, and likely cargo-loading interfaces. Public EMDB, EMPIAR, and published cryo-electron tomography annotations will be surveyed for organisms or compartments represented in the genomic atlas. Imaging evidence will not be treated as required for inclusion, but will provide high-confidence anchors and benchmarking examples.

Fourth, we will develop the emergent compartment potential score. Features from genome architecture, phylogenetic profiling, ecological metadata, expression coherence, proteomic support, structural compatibility, and literature-curated evidence will be combined using interpretable machine learning, network community detection, and nonnegative matrix factorization adapted from signature-decomposition approaches. Known experimentally characterized compartments will form positive reference sets, while matched metabolic operons lacking compartment features will form comparison sets. We will use cross-validation across taxonomic groups to reduce overfitting, uncertainty estimates to flag ambiguous cases, and feature-attribution methods to explain each score. The final outputs will include confidence tiers rather than unsupported absolute classifications. All analyses will be reproducible, versioned, and executable through containerized workflows.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The project will deliver three major products. First, we will release an open atlas of prokaryotic metal-redox compartmentalization spanning bacteria and archaea. The atlas will include standardized locus annotations, organism and habitat metadata, candidate compartment class, module composition, taxonomic distribution, evidence links, and confidence tiers. It will unify information that is currently fragmented across genome papers, metagenomic surveys, structural studies, microscopy reports, and stress-response datasets.

Second, we will produce an interpretable emergent compartment potential score for candidate loci. This score will help distinguish well-supported organelle-like systems from ordinary metabolic operons, partial loci, assembly remnants, and ambiguous clusters. Because the score will report the evidence underlying each prediction, users will be able to identify whether a candidate is supported primarily by genomic modularity, co-expression, structural compatibility, ecological association, or public imaging evidence. This will enable rational prioritization of future experimental work without requiring this project to generate new data.

Third, the working group will identify general design principles for metal-redox compartment emergence. Expected insights include recurrent combinations of boundary-forming proteins and metalloprotein cargo, convergence between lipid-bounded and protein-bounded systems, ecological pressures associated with compartment formation, and regulatory programs linking compartment loci to metal limitation, heme stress, oxidative damage, anaerobic electron flow, or carbon fixation. These results will advance NCEMS priorities by explaining how molecular components self-organize into mesoscale structures with emergent cellular functions.

The impact will be broad. Microbial cell biologists will gain candidates for organelle discovery. Evolutionary biologists will gain a framework for comparing independently evolved compartments. Biochemists and structural biologists will gain predicted protein assemblies and redox modules. Synthetic biologists will gain design rules for engineering compartmentalized metabolism. Trainees will gain experience in collaborative synthesis science, public-data stewardship, and reproducible computation.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from the start. All nonrestricted outputs will be public, including code, workflow documentation, data dictionaries, intermediate annotation tables, final atlas releases, model parameters, benchmark sets, tutorials, and meeting-derived methodological decisions. Because the project uses only existing public data, we will maintain full provenance for every record, including accession numbers, repository links, download dates, software versions, filtering criteria, and citation metadata.

Analyses will be implemented in version-controlled repositories using transparent issue tracking and pull-request review. Genome-mining, omics-reanalysis, structural-annotation, and scoring workflows will be packaged using portable workflow managers and containers so they can be rerun by external users. Where computational costs are high, we will provide both full workflows and smaller demonstration datasets for teaching and verification. Major atlas releases will be assigned persistent identifiers through an appropriate public archive, and code releases will be archived with versioned digital object identifiers.

Data standards will be developed collaboratively. The working group will define controlled vocabularies for compartment modules, evidence types, confidence tiers, environmental metadata, and structural features. These standards will be documented in a public schema so that community members can submit corrections or additions. We will distinguish primary public data from derived annotations and will clearly flag predictions, literature-supported annotations, and experimentally confirmed examples.

Training will be embedded in the open-science plan. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will lead reproducible analysis sprints, co-develop tutorials, and present workflow modules during working group meetings. Tutorials will cover public genome mining, metadata harmonization, transcriptomic reanalysis, structural annotation, interpretable modeling, and responsible reuse of public data. Authorship and contribution policies will be established at project launch, using transparent contribution tracking to recognize data curation, software, analysis, visualization, writing, and mentoring. These practices will make the project reusable, auditable, and inclusive.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is requested because the project requires sustained coordination across disciplines and institutions rather than isolated analysis by a single laboratory. The primary budget categories are working group convening, trainee participation, computational infrastructure, open-science dissemination, and project coordination.

Convening funds will support two in-person working group meetings at NCEMS and regular virtual meetings among subteams focused on comparative genomics, omics reanalysis, structural modeling, imaging synthesis, metal-redox physiology, microbial ecology, and data science. In-person meetings are essential for harmonizing definitions across compartment fields, resolving annotation disagreements, designing benchmark datasets, and integrating results into a coherent atlas. Funds will also support participation by scientists at different career stages and institution types, including researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and trainees who would otherwise lack travel support.

Computational resources will support cloud or center-hosted storage, workflow execution, and collaborative development. The project will process large public genome and metagenome collections, public RNA-seq and proteomics datasets, structural models, and metadata tables. Although all primary data are public, integration at this scale requires shared compute, persistent storage, container registries, workflow testing, and web-accessible distribution of derived products. We will avoid duplicating large repositories when stable links are sufficient, but will archive derived annotations and reproducible manifests.

Open-science funds will support website or portal development, digital object identifier deposition, documentation, tutorial preparation, and community webinars. Modest support for a part-time data coordinator or scientific programmer will ensure consistent schemas, accession tracking, release management, and code review. Trainee support will enable graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to participate in analysis sprints and receive mentoring in synthesis research.

No funds will be used for new experiments, sample collection, sequencing, microscopy, proteomics generation, or animal studies. The requested resources directly match NCEMS goals: enabling a transdisciplinary team to synthesize public molecular and cellular data, produce reusable community resources, train data-savvy scientists, and reveal emergent mesoscale principles in microbial cell biology.
